monogr.title: Nihon koten bungaku taikei 32-33: Heike monogatari
日本古典文学大系 32-33: 平家物語

biblStruct.note: Based on the Kakuichi-bon (覚一本) textual lineage.

projectDesc.p: This text was converted to TEI P5 XML so that it could be digitally cited and aligned to additional resources (such as translations). I have added identifiers to each section, paragraph and (more tentatively) sentence.

editorialDecl.p: Text follows the division of scrolls (Book) and chapters found in the UVA edition.

div.p: [1.1.1] The sound of the bells of Gion Shoja echoes the impermanence of all things. The color of the flowers of the sal trees reveals the truth that the prosperous must decline. The proud do not endure, they are but a dream of a spring night. Even the mighty perish in the end; they are just like dust before the wind. Looking far abroad to foreign lands, there were Zhao Gao of Qin, Wang Mang of Han, Zhou Yi of Liang, and Lu Shan of Tang. All of them, not following the governance of their former lords and previous emperors, indulged in pleasure, paid no heed to remonstrance, failed to perceive that the realm would fall into disorder, and did not know the sorrows of the people. Thus, before long, they perished. When I look closely at our own land, Masakado of the Shohei era, Sumitomo of the Tengyo era, Yoshichika of the Kowa era, Nobuyori of the Heiji era—these men, in their pride and their boldness, were each extraordinary in their own way; but more recently, the lay monk of Rokuhara, the former Grand Minister of State, Lord Taira no Kiyomori—the manner of this man, as it has been passed down and received, is beyond the reach of both words and understanding.

[1.1.2] Tracing his ancestry, he was the ninth-generation descendant of Prince Kazurahara, the fifth son of Emperor Kanmu and holder of the first rank and office of Shikibu-kyō, and the legitimate son of Taira no Tadamori, the Governor of Sanuki and Minister of Justice. The son of that prince, Prince Takashinno, died without rank or office. From the time of his son Prince Takamochi, when he first received the surname Taira and became the governor of Kazusa, he suddenly left the imperial family and joined the ranks of subjects. 其子鎭守府將軍義茂後には國香とあらたむ。 國香より正盛に至る迄、六代は諸國の受領たりしかども、殿上の仙籍をばいまだゆるされず。

[1.2.1] しかるを忠盛備前守たりし時、鳥羽院の御願得長壽院を造進して三十三間の御堂をたて、一千一體の御佛をすゑ奉る。 供養は天承元年三月十三日なり。 勸賞には闕國を給ふべき由仰下されける。 境節但馬國のあきたりけるを給にけり。 上皇御感のあまりに内の昇殿をゆるさる。 忠盛三十六にて始て昇殿す。 雲の上人是を嫉み、同き年の十一月廿三日、五節豐明の節會の夜、忠盛を闇討にせむとぞ擬せられける。 忠盛是を傳へ聞て、「われ右筆の身にあらず、武勇の家に生れて、今不慮の恥にあはむ事、家の爲、身の爲、こゝろうかるべし。 せむずるところ、身を全して君に仕といふ本文あり。 」とて、兼て用意をいたす。 參内のはじめより大なる鞘卷を用意して束帶のしたにしどけなげにさし、火のほのくらき方にむかて、やはら、此刀をぬき出し、鬢にひきあてられけるが、氷などの樣にぞみえける。 諸人目をすましけり。 其上忠盛の郎等もとは一門たりし木工助平貞光が孫しんの三郎太夫家房が子、左兵衞尉家貞といふ者ありけり。 薄青の狩衣の下に萠黄威の腹卷をき、弦袋つけたる太刀脇はさんで、殿上の小庭に畏てぞ候ける。 貫首以下あやしみをなし、「うつぼ柱よりうち、鈴の綱のへんに布衣の者の候ふはなにものぞ。 狼藉なり。 罷出よ。 」と、六位をもていはせければ、家貞申けるは「相傳の主、備前守殿今夜闇討にせられ給べき由承候あひだ、其ならむ樣を見むとて、かくて候。 えこそ罷出まじけれ。 」とて畏て候ければ、是等をよしなしとやおもはれけん、其夜の闇討なかりけり。

[1.2.2] 忠盛御前のめしにまはれければ、人々拍子をかへて「伊勢平氏はすがめなりけり。 」とぞはやされける。 此人々はかけまくもかたじけなく柏原天皇の御末とは申ながら、中比は都の住居もうと／＼しく、地下にのみ振舞なて伊勢國に住國ふかかりしかば、其國の器に事よせて、伊勢平氏とぞ申ける。 其うへ忠盛目のすがまれたりければ、加樣にはやされけり。 いかにすべき樣もなくして、御遊もいまだをはらざるに、竊に罷出らるとて、よこたへさされたりける刀をば紫宸殿の御後にして、かたへの殿上人のみられける所にて、主殿司をめしてあづけ置てぞ出られける。 家貞待うけたてまつて、「さていかゞ候つる。 」と申ければ、かくともいはまほしう思はれけれども、いひつるものならば、殿上までもやがてきりのぼらんずる者にてある間、「別の事もなし。 」とぞ答られける。

[1.2.3] 五節には、「白薄樣、こぜむじの紙、卷上の筆、鞆繪ゑがいたる筆の軸」なんどさま％＼面白き事をのみこそうたひまはるるに、中比太宰權帥季仲卿といふ人ありけり。 あまりに色のくろかりければ、見る人黒帥とぞ申ける。 其人いまだ藏人頭なりし時、五節にまはれければ、それも拍子をかへて、「あなくろ／＼、くろき頭かな。 いかなる人のうるしぬりけむ。 」とぞはやされける。 又花山院前太政大臣忠雅公、いまだ十歳と申し時、父中納言忠宗卿におくれたてまつて孤にておはしけるを、故中御門藤中納言家成卿いまだ播磨守たりし時、聟に執て、聲花にもてなされければ、それも五節に「播磨米はとくさか、むくの葉か、人のきらをみがくは。 And so it was sung. In ancient times it was like this, but no such thing occurred. How will it be in the latter age? People said it was uncertain.

[1.2.4] As expected, when the Gosechi festival ended, the courtiers all said: "Wearing a sword at a public banquet, receiving weapons, and entering and leaving the palace are all ancient precedents that follow the rules of etiquette and the imperial commands." Nevertheless, Tadamori, calling his hereditary retainers 'commoner soldiers', had them wait in the small garden of the palace, and with his sword thrust sideways at his hip, he took his place among the seats for the festival. This is an unprecedented outrage, the like of which has never been heard. The matter has already accumulated. The crime is especially hard to escape. They appealed, saying, 'Quickly strip him of his rank and dismiss him from office.' The Retired Emperor was greatly alarmed, summoned Tadamori, and questioned him. He explained, 'First, regarding my retainers waiting in the small garden, I had no knowledge at all.' However, since there is a matter that people have recently been secretly plotting, in order to save that shame, a retainer of many years, without letting Tadamori know, has secretly come to court; this is a situation beyond my power. If there should still be any fault, should we summon that person? Next, regarding the matter of the sword, it has not been left with the Chamberlain's Office. Should we summon it and, based on the truth or falsity of the sword, determine guilt? he said. Saying it was appropriate, he had the sword brought out and inspected it. The outside was a scabbard lacquered black, but inside was a wooden sword with silver foil pressed on it. Although he revealed the reason for wearing a sword was to escape the shame of the moment, knowing of future lawsuits, the prudence of wearing a wooden sword was truly admirable. The plans of those who engage in archery should indeed be like this. Moreover, the fact that retainers attend in the small garden is also the custom of samurai retainers. It is not Tadamori's fault. And so, far from being punished, he was even rewarded by the Emperor's favor.
[1.3.1] His children became captains of the various guards, and when they were granted access to the imperial palace, no one could avoid associating with them in the courtiers' hall.
[1.3.2] At that time, when Tadamori was going up to the capital from Bizen Province, Emperor Toba asked, "How is Akashi Bay?" he asked.

lg.l: あり明の月もあかしのうら風に、浪ばかりこそよると見えしか。

div.p: [1.3.3] he replied, and the Emperor was impressed. This poem was included in the Kin'yōshū.

[1.3.4] Tadamori also used to visit a beloved lady-in-waiting at the Sentō Palace, but once, when he left her room forgetting a fan on which the moon had appeared, the other ladies-in-waiting said, "Where is this moonlight from?" Its origin is uncertain. They laughed and made fun of her, so that lady-in-waiting,

lg.l: 雲井よりたゞもりきたる月なれば、おぼろげにてはいはじとぞ思ふ。

div.p: [1.3.5] When she composed a poem, he came to feel even more deeply for her. This is the mother of Satsuma no Kami Tadanori. Because Tadamori also had a taste for the elegance of 'boiling (something) as a companion,' that lady too was refined. Thus Tadamori became Gyōbu-kyō, and on the fifteenth day of the first month of Ninpei 3, at the age of fifty-eight, he passed away. Because Kiyomori was the eldest son, he succeeded to that position.

[1.3.6] In the seventh month of Hōgen 1, when the Uji Sadaijin raised a rebellion, as Aki no Kami he rendered distinguished service on the imperial side, so he was transferred to Harima no Kami, and in the third year of the same era he became Dazai no Daini. Next, in the first year of Heiji, in the twelfth month, at the time of Lord Nobuyori's rebellion, he fought on the side of the emperor and subdued the rebels; his meritorious deeds were not few, and it was thought that his rewards should be great, so in the following year he was promoted to Senior Third Rank, and successively rose through the offices of Counselor, Captain of the Palace Guards, Chief of the Imperial Police, Middle Counselor, and Major Counselor, and moreover attained the position of Chancellor, and without passing through the offices of Minister of the Left or Right, he rose from Minister of the Interior to Grand Minister of State, Junior First Rank. Though he was not a general, he was granted weapons and allowed to have attendants. He received imperial permission to use ox-drawn carriages and hand-drawn carriages, and rode in them in and out of the palace. He was just like a regent. "The Grand Minister of State is the teacher of the emperor and the model for the whole country." He governed the country, discoursed on the Way, and harmonized yin and yang. If he is not that person, then he should immediately resign. So it is said. Therefore it was also named the Office of the Missing (Ketsukan). Although it is an office that should not be defiled except by that person, once he had grasped the whole realm in his palm, there was no room for argument.

[1.3.7] It was said that the Heike prospered in this way due to the divine favor of Kumano Gongen. The reason is that long ago, when Lord Kiyomori was still the governor of Aki, he went by ship from the sea of Ise to Kumano, and a large sea bass jumped into the ship. The guide said, "This is the divine favor of the Gongen. You should hurry and go. When he said that, Kiyomori said, "Long ago, a white fish jumped into the boat of King Wu of Zhou. This is an auspicious sign. Saying this, although he kept the ten precepts and followed the path of purity and abstinence, he seasoned the food and gave it to his retainers and samurai to eat. Perhaps because of this, only auspicious events continued, and he rose to the rank of Grand Minister. The official careers of his descendants were even swifter than a dragon ascending to the clouds. It is splendid that he surpassed the precedents of nine generations.

[1.4.1] Then Lord Kiyomori, in the eleventh month of the third year of Nin'an, at the age of fifty-one, was struck by illness, and for the sake of his life he suddenly became a monk. His Buddhist name was indeed Jōkai. Perhaps as a sign of this, his chronic illness was cured immediately, and he fulfilled his natural lifespan. The way people follow and submit is like the wind that blows and bends the grasses and trees. It is like the rain that falls from heaven, moistening the whole land.

[1.4.2] When they were called the young lords of the Rokuhara household, there was no one among the flower clans or heroes who could face them or stand shoulder to shoulder with them. Therefore, the lay monk prime minister's brother-in-law, Taira no Dainagon Tokitada, said, "Anyone who is not of this clan must be a non-human." And so it was said. Since it was like that, people of every kind strove to attach themselves to that connection. Beginning with the way of folding robes and the style of wearing eboshi, in everything they said 'the Rokuhara style,' and people throughout the realm all imitated it.

[1.4.3] 又いかなる賢王聖主の御政も攝政關白の御成敗も世にあまされたるいたづら者な どの、人のきかぬ處にてなにとなうそしり傾け申事は常の習なれども、此禪門世ざか りの程は聊いるかせにも申者なし。其故は入道相國のはかりごとに十四五六の童部を 三百人そろへて、髮をかぶろにきりまはし、あかき直垂をきせて、めしつかはれける が、京中にみち／＼て、往反しけり。自ら平家の事あしざまに申者あれば、一人きゝ 出さぬほどこそありけれ、餘黨に觸廻して、其家に亂入し資材雜具を追捕し、其奴を 搦とて、六波羅へゐてまゐる。されば目に見、心に知るといへども、詞にあらはれて 申者なし。六波羅殿の禿と云ひてしかば、道をすぐる馬車もよぎてぞ、通りける。禁 門を出入すといへども姓名を尋らるゝに及ばず、京師の長吏これが為に目を側むとみ えたり。
[1.5.1] 吾身の榮花を極るのみならず、一門共に繁昌して、嫡子重盛、内大臣の左大將、次男宗盛、中納言の右大將、三男知盛、三位中將、嫡孫維盛、四位少將、すべて一門 の公卿十六人、殿上人三十餘人、諸國の受領、衞府、諸司、都合六十餘人なり。 世にはまた人なくぞ見えられける。

[1.5.2] 昔奈良の御門の御時、神龜五年、朝家に中衞の大將をはじめおかれ、大同四年に 中衞を近衞と改られしよりこのかた、兄弟左右に相並事僅に三四箇度なり。文徳天皇 の御時は左に良房右大臣左大將、右に良相、大納言の右大將、是は閑院の左大臣冬嗣 の御子なり。朱雀院の御宇には左に實頼、小野宮殿、右に師輔、九條殿、貞信公の御 子なり。御冷泉院の御時は、左に教通、大二條殿、右に頼宗、堀河殿、御堂の關白の 御子なり。二條院の御宇には左に基房、松殿、右に兼實、月輪殿、法性寺殿の御子な り。是皆攝祿の臣の御子息、凡人にとりては其例なし。殿上 の交をだにきらはれし人の子孫にて禁色雜袍をゆり、綾羅錦繍を身にまとひ、大臣大 將になて、兄弟、左右に相並事、末代とはいひながら不思議なりし事どもなり。

[1.5.3] 其外御娘八人おはしき。 All of them went off to their respective places. One of them was the wife of the Middle Counselor Shigemasa of Sakura-machi, but at the age of eight, after only a betrothal, she was taken away after the Heiji Rebellion, and became the lady-in-waiting of the Minister of the Left of Kazan-in, and had many children.

[1.5.4] Now, the reason this Lord Shigeyori was called the Middle Counselor of Cherry Blossom Town was that he was a man of exceptionally refined taste: he always longed for Mount Yoshino, and in the town he planted cherry trees in rows, built a house among them, and lived there; so every spring, people who saw it called it Cherry Blossom Town. Cherry blossoms bloom and scatter within seven days, but he regretted their passing and prayed to the Sun Goddess Amaterasu, so they remained for twenty-one days. Because the lord was a wise ruler, the god displayed divine virtue, and because the flowers had a heart, they kept their life for twenty days.

[1.5.5] One became the Empress. When the prince was born and became Crown Prince, and ascended the throne, she received the title of Empress Dowager, and was called Kenreimon-in. Being the daughter of the Lay Monk Chancellor, and moreover the mother of the nation, there was no need to say anything. One became the legal wife of the Rokujo Regent. During the reign of Emperor Takakura, she received the title of Jun-Sango as the emperor's mother, and was called Shirakawa-dono, a person of great importance. One became the wife of the Lord of Fugenji-dono. One was the wife of Reizei Dainagon Takafusa. One was married to Shichijo Shuri no Daibu Nobutaka. Also, one child born to the Naishi of Itsukushima in Aki Province was sent to the Cloistered Emperor Goshirakawa and was treated like a court lady. Besides, one child was born to Tokiwa, a servant at Kujo-in. This was a high-ranking lady-in-waiting at Kazan-in Palace, and she was called Rō no Onkata.

[1.5.6] Japan, the Land of Abundant Autumns, is barely sixty-six provinces, but the provinces under the Heike's control number more than thirty, already exceeding half the country. Besides these, the number of manors, fields, and rice paddies is beyond counting. Their splendor was so abundant that the palace seemed like a garden of flowers. Their carriages and horsemen gathered in throngs, making the gate front as busy as a marketplace. Gold from Yangzhou, pearls from Jingzhou, damask from Wu Commandery, brocade from the Shu River—of the seven treasures and myriad jewels, not one was lacking. The foundations of the singing halls and dancing pavilions, the curiosities of fish-dragons and bird-horses—surely even the imperial palace and the retired emperor's residence could not surpass this, it seemed.

div.head: 1.6. 祇王

div.p: [1.6.1] While the Lay Monk Chancellor held the whole realm in the palm of his hand, he did not shrink from the world's censure, nor did he look back at people's ridicule, but only did extraordinary things. For example, at that time there were two sisters, Gio and Ginyo, who were famous shirabyoshi dancers in the capital; they were the daughters of a shirabyoshi named Toji. Because the Lay Monk Chancellor loved the elder sister Gio most dearly, because of this, the world's treatment of the younger sister Ginyo was not ordinary. He had a fine house built for his mother, and every month he sent her a hundred koku of rice and a hundred kan of coins, so the household prospered and their happiness was beyond compare.

[1.6.2] Now, the origin of shirabyōshi dancing in our country was when, in the reign of Emperor Toba, two women named Shima no Chitose and Waka no Mae first performed it. At first, wearing a suikan robe and a tall eboshi cap, and carrying a white-sheathed sword, he danced, and so it was called a male dance. However, from around the middle period, the eboshi cap and sword were removed, and only the suikan robe was used; thus it came to be called shirabyoshi.

[1.6.3] Among the shirabyoshi of the capital, there were those who envied Gio's good fortune upon hearing of it, and those who were jealous. The envious ones said, "Ah, how wonderful is Lady Gio's good fortune!" If one is to be a courtesan, everyone would want to be like her. Why is it that she, having the character 'Gi' in her name, is so fortunate? Come, let us also take that name! So saying, some took the name Giichi, some Gini, and there were also those called Gifuku or Gitoku. The envious ones said, "What lineage? You should rely on the written word." Fortune is just something you are born with from your previous life. Saying so, there were many who did not attach themselves to her.

[1.6.4] Thus, after three years, another famous shirabyōshi dancer appeared in the capital. She was from Kaga Province. Her name was called Buddha. She was said to be sixteen years old. "Although there have been many shirabyōshi since ancient times, I have never seen such a dance. " So saying, the high and low of the capital praised her beyond measure. Buddha Gozen said, "Although I am renowned throughout the realm, it is my deepest regret that I have not been summoned by the Lay Monk of Heike, the Grand Minister, who is now so flourishing." It is the way of entertainers; what is there to be ashamed of? I will go uninvited and see. Saying so, at one time he went to Nishi-Hachijo. A person came and said, "The dancer Hotoke-gozen, who is now famous in the capital, has come." When he said this, the novice replied, "Why should such an entertainer come unless summoned by someone?" How can you come in without being summoned? Where Gio is, even if you are a god or a buddha, you cannot go. Quickly, leave! Thus he said. Hotoke-gozen, having been told such cruel words, was about to leave, but Gio said to the Nyudo, "For entertainers to come uninvited is a common thing." Moreover, since he is still young, and has come to think of you with all his heart, it would be pitiful if you were to refuse him coldly and send him back. How ashamed and embarrassed he must be! Since it is the path I have chosen, I do not feel it is someone else's affair. Even if you do not watch the dance or listen to the song, if you would just grant him an audience and then send him back, it would be a rare kindness. Just bend the rules, summon him back, and grant him an audience. When he said this, the novice replied, "Well, well, since my lady has spoken so much, I shall go and see her and send her back." So saying, he sent a messenger. Lady Hotoke, having been dismissed so coldly, had gotten into her carriage and was about to leave, but was summoned back and returned. The novice came out to meet her and said, "I had not intended to see you today, but Gio, for some reason, urged me so strongly that I have summoned you like this. Since I have summoned you, how could I not hear your voice?" Sing one imayo song. When he said this, Hotoke-gozen replied, "I shall receive your command." Saying this, she sang one imayo song.

lg.l: 君をはじめて見るをりは、千代も歴ぬべし姫小松、
御前の池なる龜岡に、鶴こそ群れ居て遊ぶめれ。

div.p: [1.6.5] When she had sung it through three times, all the people who saw and heard were astonished. The priest also thought it was delightful and said, "You are skilled at imayo, aren't you!" With this arrangement, the dance will surely be good. I want to see one dance. Summon the drum player. So saying, he summoned him. He had him play and danced one dance.

[1.6.6] Hotoke-gozen, from her hair and appearance, was beautiful, had a good voice, and was skilled in melody, so how could she not excel in dance? She danced with all her heart, and the priest-prime minister was charmed by her dance and fell in love with Hotoke. Buddha's attendant said, "What is this? What is the matter?" From the beginning, I was sent out as an uninvited person, but because of Gio's petition I was called back, and if I am treated like this, I will be ashamed of Gio's feelings. Quickly, give me leave to go out. When she said this, the novice replied, "That is absolutely out of the question. But are you holding back because Gio is here? If that is the case, I should send Gio away. So he said. Lady Buddha said, "How could such a thing possibly be? Even if we were both summoned together, it would be distressing; how much more so if I alone were summoned and Lady Giō were made to leave—I would feel ashamed before Lady Giō. If it is a matter you will not forget even later, then even if I am summoned and come again, today please grant me leave. Thus she said. The novice monk said, "Why should that be so?" Giō, leave at once! And the messenger was sent again, up to three times. Although Gio had anticipated this from the beginning, she had not expected it to be today or tomorrow. While he repeatedly urged her to leave quickly, she swept, wiped, had the dust picked up, tidied the unsightly things, and it was decided that she should leave. Even lodging together under the shade of one tree, or drawing water from the same stream, parting is a sorrowful custom. Moreover, since it was the place where she had lived for these three years, the regret was painful and sad, and useless tears fell. Since it was not something that should be so, Giō, thinking that now it must be so, went out, but perhaps thinking to leave a memento for after she was gone, she wrote a poem on the sliding door, weeping all the while.

lg.l: 萠出るも枯るゝも同じ野邊の草、何れか秋にあはではつべき。

div.p: [1.6.7] Then she got into the carriage, returned to her lodging, collapsed inside the sliding doors, and did nothing but weep. Her mother and younger sister saw this and asked, "What is it? What is it?" They asked, but she could not even answer one way or another. They asked the woman who had accompanied her, and only then learned that such a thing had happened. Meanwhile, the hundred koku of rice and hundred strings of cash that had been sent every month were now stopped, and it was the relatives of Hotoke-gozen who, for the first time, prospered and flourished. People of all classes in the capital said, "Gio has indeed been dismissed by the lay priest and has left. Let's go and see her and have some fun. So saying, some sent letters, and some dispatched messengers. But Gio, thinking that she could not now meet people and amuse herself, did not even take in the letters, much less respond to the messengers. Even at this, she was sad, and she sank ever deeper into tears.

[1.6.8] Thus the year came to an end. In the spring of the following year, the Lay Monk Prime Minister sent a messenger to Giō's place, saying, "How have you been since then? Is there anything new?" Since Hotoke-gozen seems so very bored, come and sing imayō songs and dance, and comfort her." Thus he said. Gio could not even reply to this message. The priest said, "Why doesn't Gio reply?" Will she not come? If she will not come, tell me so. Jokai also has a plan. Thus he declared. When the mother heard this, she was saddened, and without knowing what to do, she admonished her, weeping: "Lady Gio, please give some reply, rather than being treated so harshly." When he said that, Giō replied, "If it were a path I intended to take, I would say I would come at once; but since I have no intention of coming, I do not know what answer to give." Since I have no intention of coming, I do not know what answer to give. If I do not come this time, and you say that there is some plan, will you send me out of the capital, or will you take my life? It will surely be one of these two. Even if you leave the capital, it is not something to lament. Even if my life is taken, is it a body that should be regretted? Once I have been thought of as a hateful person, it is not a matter of meeting face to face a second time. Saying this, she still did not send a reply, but the mother repeatedly admonished her: "As long as you live under heaven, you must not disobey the orders of the Nyudo-dono in any way. The bond between man and woman is not something that begins only now, by karma from past lives. Even if they vow to be together for a thousand or ten thousand years, there are couples who eventually part. Even if they think it is a fleeting bond, there are couples who live long together. In this world, the unfixed nature of things is the way of men and women. And yet, my lord, because you have loved me for these three years, it is a rare kindness indeed. Even if I do not go to see you, it is unlikely that I would lose my life over it. They will surely be sent out of the capital. Even if we are made to leave the capital, since you, my attendants, are young, you will surely be able to pass your lives in any crevice among the rocks and trees. My aged and weakened mother will surely be sent out of the capital. The unfamiliar dwelling of a journey is indeed sad to think of beforehand. Just let me live out my life within the capital. That, I thought, would be filial piety for this life and the next. When she said this, Gio, though she felt it was a painful path, resolved not to disobey her mother's command, and weeping bitterly, set out again; the state of her heart was truly pitiful. Thinking it would be too lonely to go alone, she took her younger sister Gijo with her. Besides them, two other shirabyoshi dancers, four in all, got into one carriage and went to Nishi-Hachijo. They were not allowed into the place where they had been summoned before, but were made to sit in a room far removed. Gio said, "What is this? What can it be?" Though I have done nothing wrong, even being abandoned is hard enough, but to have my seat lowered as well—how bitter! What shall I do? As she thought this, tears overflowed from between the sleeves she pressed to hide her feelings. Hotoke-gozen saw this and, thinking it too pitiful, said, "What is that? If it were a place where you are not usually summoned, then..." Please come here. Otherwise, give me leave to go. I will go out and see him. When he said this, the priest replied, "That is absolutely out of the question." While he was saying this, the boy, unable to resist, went out. After that, the priest, not knowing Gio's inner feelings, said, "Well, has anything happened since then?" Well then, since Hotoke-gozen seems so very bored, sing me a song. When he said this, Gio, as she came forward, thought that in any case she must not disobey the Novice's command, so she held back her falling tears and sang just one imayo song.

lg.l: 佛も昔は凡夫なり、我等も遂には佛なり、
何も佛性具せる身を、隔つるのみこそ悲しけれ。

div.p: [1.6.9] When she had sung it twice, weeping, all the Heike nobles, courtiers, and samurai seated in a row there, down to the last man, shed tears of emotion. The Novice, too, was pleased and said, "You have spoken admirably, as befits the occasion." Well then, I have seen the dance, but today something has come up that distracts me. From now on, even if I do not summon you, always come and sing imayo songs and dance dances to console the Buddha. Thus he said. Giō, unable to reply in any way, held back her tears and left.

[1.6.10] "I went down a painful path, determined not to disobey my parent's command, and twice saw sorrowful sights—how bitter it is!" If I remain in this world, I will surely see more sorrows. Now I think only of throwing myself into the water. When she said this, her younger sister Gijo said, "If you, elder sister, throw yourself in, I will throw myself in with you." she said. When their mother heard this, she was so sad that she did not know what to do. Weeping, he admonished again: "Truly, it is natural that you, my lord, bear resentment. How regrettable it is that I admonished you without knowing such a thing would happen! But if I throw myself into the water before Your Majesty, my younger sister will also throw herself in together with me. After both daughters have died, what would the aged mother do by living on? So I think I will also throw myself in together with them. Would making a parent whose time to die has not yet come throw herself into the water be the sin of the five grave offenses? This world is a temporary lodging. No matter how ashamed I am, it is of no avail. Only the darkness of the long night is distressing. It is in this life that it should be. How sad it is that even in the afterlife one must go to the evil paths! When she said this, weeping bitterly, Giō held back her tears and said, "Indeed, if it is as you say, there is no doubt that I have committed the five grave sins." Then I will give up the idea of killing myself. If I remain in the capital like this, I will surely see more sorrow. Now I will leave the capital. Saying this, Giō became a nun at the age of twenty-one, and in a mountain village deep in Sagano, she built a brushwood hut and lived there, chanting the nembutsu. Her younger sister Gijo also said, "If my elder sister throws herself into the water, I too will throw myself in with her—so we had promised. How much less should I be inferior when it comes to renouncing the world?" So saying, at nineteen she changed her appearance, and living in seclusion together with her elder sister, she prayed for the afterlife—how touching! The mother saw this and thought, "Even young girls change their appearance in this world; what would it avail an old, feeble mother to put on white hair?" So at forty-five she shaved her head, and together with her two daughters devoted herself single-mindedly to the nembutsu, praying solely for the afterlife.

[1.6.11] Thus spring passed and summer ended; when the first autumn wind blew, gazing at the sky where the stars meet, she thought of the kaji leaves crossing the River of Heaven—was her longing as deep as this? Even seeing the evening sun's light hidden behind the western mountain ridge, she thought, "The place where the sun sets is the Western Pure Land." When will we too be born there and pass away without sorrow? Even at such thoughts, the sad memories of the past come one after another, and the only thing that never runs dry is tears. When dusk had passed, they closed the bamboo lattice door, stirred up the dim lamp, and the three, parent and children, were chanting the nembutsu when someone came and knocked loudly on the bamboo lattice door. At that moment the nuns were terrified. "Alas, this must be a demonic temptation coming to hinder our chanting of the nembutsu, which is of no avail." Even in the daytime no one comes to ask after us; in this brushwood hut deep in the mountains, who would visit at this late hour of the night? Since it is only a bamboo lattice door, even if we do not open it, it would be easy to break it down. Rather, I think we should just open it and let them in. If, without showing compassion, we were to lose our lives, then we should firmly believe in the original vow of Amida Buddha, whom we have long relied upon, and ceaselessly chant his name. If it is the coming of the holy assembly that seeks out the voice and comes to welcome us, why should there be no reception? Be sure not to neglect the nembutsu. So saying, they admonished each other, and when they opened the bamboo lattice door, it was not a demonic temptation; it was Lady Buddha who had appeared. Giō said, "What is that?" Is what I see as Hotoke-gozen a dream, or reality? When she said this, Hotoke-gozen, holding back her tears, said: "If I tell you such a thing, it will be a fresh matter, but if I do not tell you, I will become one who does not understand, so I will tell you from the beginning." Originally I was a person who had intruded uninvited, and when I was sent away, it was due to the petition of Gio Gozen that I was called back; but the helplessness of a woman, not having my own body at my disposal, being detained against my will—that was truly mortifying. Yet at some point I was summoned again and you had me sing an imayo, and I felt that you had remembered me. When I think that it will never be my own fate, I do not feel happy at all. On the sliding door, again, was written: "Which one will not meet autumn?" The traces of the brush with which he wrote that, I thought, were indeed so. After that, I did not know where he was, but when I heard that he had changed his appearance in this way and was staying in one place, I was so envious that I always asked for leave, but the lay priest would not grant it at all. When I think about things, the glory of this world is a dream within a dream; even if one prospers in pleasure, what is the use? It is difficult to receive a human body, and it is difficult to encounter the Buddha's teachings. Once you sink into the hell of Avici, even if you pass many lifetimes and countless kalpas, it will be difficult to rise up again. One should not rely on youth. In this world where death comes to young and old alike, one cannot wait even for the next breath to be drawn. Even more fleeting than a heat shimmer or a flash of lightning. Having boasted of momentary pleasures and not knowing the afterlife, I slipped out this morning and have come to be like this. Saying this, when he looked at the robe he had thrown off, she had come out having become a nun. "Since I have come having changed my appearance in this way, please forgive my past offenses." If you permit it, we will recite the nembutsu together and become one in the same lotus. If even then my heart is not satisfied, I will wander away from here to wherever, and on some mossy seat or at the root of a pine tree I will lie down, and as long as life lasts I will recite the nembutsu, and I intend to fulfill my long-cherished desire for rebirth in the Pure Land. So she spoke through her tears, and Giō, holding back her own tears, said, "Truly, that you have thought of me so deeply..." Even in dreams I did not know it, but since it is the way of this sorrowful world, I should have thought it was my own misfortune; yet, whenever I did, I felt only resentment toward you, and it did not seem possible that I could fulfill my long-cherished wish for rebirth in the Pure Land. In both this life and the next, I had the feeling of having half-failed, but now that you have come in this changed form, the faults of past days have not left even a speck of dust, and now there is no doubt about my rebirth. To fulfill my long-cherished wish this time would be more joyful than anything else. People said, and I myself also thought, that my becoming a nun was an unprecedented thing in the world. That was because I resented the world and resented myself, so it was natural that I changed my appearance. Now, compared with Wakoze's becoming a nun, it was not even worth mentioning. You have no resentment and no grief. This year, a person who has just turned seventeen, deeply resolving to loathe this defiled world and aspire to the Pure Land—this indeed appears to be a true aspiration for enlightenment. What a joyful spiritual friend! Come, let us pray together. So saying, the four of them secluded themselves together in one place, and morning and evening offered flowers and incense before the Buddha, and prayed with single-minded devotion; and though there was difference in time, it is said that all four nuns fulfilled their long-cherished desire for rebirth in the Pure Land. Therefore, in the past-life register of Chōkōdō of the Cloistered Emperor Goshirakawa, the honored spirits of Giō, Ginyo, Hotoke, and Togi were enshrined together in one place as four persons. These were all moving events.

div.note: [_] [1] Nihon Koten Bungaku Taikei (Tokyo: Iwanami Shoten, 1957, vol. 32; hereafter cited as NKBT) reads いかなるべしともおぼえず。.
[_] [2] NKBT reads なげば.
[_] [3] NKBT reads わごぜ.

div.p: [1.7.1] From ancient times down to the present, the Minamoto and Taira clans were both summoned to serve the imperial court; and when any of them failed to follow the royal will or made light of the court's authority, they would each in turn inflict punishment upon them, so that there was no disturbance of the age. But after Tameyoshi was executed in the Hōgen era and Yoshitomo was put to death in the Heiji era, the remaining Minamoto of the younger generations were either exiled or killed, and now only the Taira clan flourishes, with no one to raise a head against them. Even in the final age, however it may be, what events will occur? — so it appeared. However, after Emperor Toba's death, wars continued, and death penalties, exiles, dismissals from office, and suspensions of appointments were constantly carried out, so the realm was not at peace. The world, too, was not settled. In particular, from around the Eiryaku and Ōhō eras, the retired emperor's close attendants were admonished by the emperor, and the emperor's close attendants were admonished by the retired emperor, so that high and low alike trembled in fear and had no peace of mind. It was just like treading on thin ice over a deep abyss; between the Emperor and the Retired Emperor, father and son, what distance could there possibly be? Yet there were unexpected events. This too is because the world has reached a degenerate age, and people put wickedness first. Even amid the Retired Emperor's constant messages to the Emperor, there were things that startled people's eyes and ears and greatly shook the world.

[1.7.2] The late Emperor Konoe's empress, called Grand Empress Dowager, was the daughter of the Minister of the Right, Lord Kin'yoshi of Oimikado. After she was left behind by the late emperor, she moved to live at the Konoe-gawara palace outside the nine-fold palace walls. She had been living in quiet seclusion in the palace of the former empress, but around the Eiryaku era, she must have been about twenty-two or twenty-three, and her beauty was just beginning to fade. However, because she had the reputation of being the most beautiful woman in the realm, the emperor, with a heart dyed only in passion, secretly ordered Gao Lishi to search for her outside the palace, and sent a love letter to this grand lady. The grand lady did not deign to listen to it at all. Therefore, it was decided that she should appear openly as the Empress, and an imperial edict was issued to the Udaijin's household that the Empress should enter the palace. As this was an extraordinary auspicious event in the realm, a council of nobles was held, and each expressed their opinions. First, when we inquire into precedents of foreign lands, Empress Wu Zetian of China was the consort of Emperor Taizong of Tang and the stepmother of Emperor Gaozong. After Emperor Taizong's death, she became the consort of Emperor Gaozong. That is a precedent of a foreign land, and moreover an exceptional case. However, in our realm, from Emperor Jimmu onward, through more than seventy generations of human sovereigns, we have never heard of an example of a second empress being installed. Thus all the court nobles together made their remonstrance. When the Retired Emperor also remonstrated that it was not proper, the Emperor said: "The Son of Heaven has no parents. It is by virtue of my ten good precepts that I maintain the imperial throne. Why should I not follow my own will in such a matter as this?" And so, on the very day of her entry into the palace, the imperial decree was issued, and there was no way to oppose it.

[1.7.3] When the Empress Dowager heard this, she sank into tears. If, at the beginning of autumn in the Kyūju era, when I had caused the late emperor to abdicate, I had vanished like dew on the same field, left my home, and renounced the world, I would not have had to hear such grievous tidings—so she lamented. The father, the Minister, said in consolation: "It seems that because he does not follow the world, he is considered a madman. An imperial edict has already been issued. There is no room to explain the details. You should just come quickly. If an imperial prince is born, you will be called the mother of the nation, and I, an old fool, will be revered as the maternal grandfather—could this be an auspicious sign? This is entirely the ultimate filial piety of your helping me. He said this, but there was no reply. At that time, the Great Lady, in the course of her idle calligraphy practice,

lg.l: うきふしにしづみもやらで河竹の、世にためしなき名をやながさん。

div.p: [1.7.4] How in the world did it leak out? People were telling each other that it was a touching and gentle example.

[1.7.5] When the day of her entering the palace had already arrived, her father, the Minister, and the attending court nobles, the ceremony of the carriage procession, and so on, were all carried out with special care. The Empress Dowager was reluctant to depart, so she did not send her off immediately. When the night had grown very late and the small hours had passed, she secretly slipped into the carriage. After entering the palace, she resided in the Reikeiden. She was entirely devoted to urging on the government of the realm. In the imperial palace of the Shishinden, there stood the screen of the wise sages. There were also screens depicting Koretada, Teigorin, Yu Shinan, Taikōbō, Rikuri Sensei, Li Ji, Sima, long-armed and long-legged figures, horse-shaped screens, the demon room, and a screen faithfully portraying General Li. The calligraphy by Ono no Michikaze, the governor of Owari, on the sliding doors of the Seven Sages, also seemed to be in accordance with reason. On the painted sliding doors of that Seiryōden, there was also, they say, the moon at dawn over distant mountains that Kanaoka had painted long ago. When the late emperor was still a young child, in the course of some idle play with his hands, he had drawn something; and seeing that it remained unchanged, not differing in the least, he must have felt a longing for the former emperor of old.

lg.l: 思ひきや憂き身ながらにめぐり來て、おなじ雲井の月を見むとは。

div.p: [1.7.6] The relationship between them during that time was indescribably touching and tender.

[1.7.7] Meanwhile, from around the spring of the first year of Eiman, it was heard that the Emperor was unwell, and when it became early summer, his illness grew serious. Because of this, when it was heard that the two-year-old first prince of the reigning emperor, born to the daughter of Ōkura no Taifu Iki no Kanemori, should be made crown prince, on the twenty-fifth day of the sixth month of the same year, an imperial decree was suddenly issued making him prince, and that very night he received the abdication, so the whole realm was in a state of confusion. The knowledgeable people of that time said, "If we look for examples of child emperors in our country, Emperor Seiwa received the abdication of Emperor Montoku at the age of nine." That was likened to the case of Zhou Gongdan, who, acting as regent for King Cheng, faced south and governed all the affairs of state, and so the maternal grandfather, Lord Tadahira, supported the young sovereign. This was the beginning of the regency. Emperor Toba was five years old, and Emperor Konoe was three years old when they ascended the throne. When people said that he was too young, he was only two years old. There was no precedent. It was not just a disturbance; it was foolish.

[1.8.1] In due course, on the twenty-seventh day of the same seventh month, the Retired Emperor finally passed away. His age was twenty-three. It was like a flower that had budded and then scattered. Within the jeweled blinds and brocade curtains, everyone was choked with tears. Immediately, that night, they enshrined him to the northeast of Kōryūji, in the depths of Rendaino, on Mount Funaoka. At the time of the imperial funeral, the monks of Enryakuji and Kōfukuji brought up a dispute called the 'gaku-uchi' (striking of the plaques), and each side resorted to violence. After the emperor passes away, the custom at the time of conveying him to the imperial mausoleum is that the monks of both the Southern and Northern Capitals all attend in procession, and around the mausoleum they strike the plaques of their respective temples. First, since there is no temple that can rival the vow of Emperor Shōmu, they strike the plaque of Tōdaiji. Next, saying it is the vow of Lord Tankai, they strike the plaque of Kōfukuji. In the Northern Capital, facing Kōfukuji, they strike the plaque of Enryakuji. Next, as the imperial vow of Emperor Tenmu, and as the founding by Master Kyōtai and Chishō Daishi, they inscribed the plaque of Onjō-ji. However, the monks of Enryaku-ji, for some reason, went against precedent and, after Tōdai-ji, above Kōfuku-ji, inscribed the plaque of Enryaku-ji. While the monks of Nanto were deliberating whether to do this or that, there were two notorious evil monks of the Western Golden Hall of Kōfuku-ji, known as Kannon-bō and Seishi-bō. Kannon-bō, wearing a black-laced belly armor and gripping a white-hilted long sword short, and Seishi-bō, wearing a yellowish-green-laced belly armor and carrying a black-lacquered great sword, the two of them dashed out together, struck down the plaque of Enryaku-ji, smashed it to pieces, and sang, "How delightful! Water, the water of the waterfall—though the sun may shine, it never ceases to flow." Thus cheering, they entered into the midst of the monks of the Southern Capital.

[1.9.1] If the monks of the mountain gate were to commit violence, there might have been someone who was deeply plotting to oppose them. He did not utter a single word. When the Emperor passed away, even the heartless trees and plants should have taken on a sorrowful color, but in the horror of this disturbance, both high and low lost their wits and fled in all directions. On the same twenty-ninth day, around the hour of the horse, when it was heard that the monks of the mountain gate were descending upon the capital in great numbers, warriors and police officers rushed to Nishi-Sakamoto to stop them, but the monks, paying no heed, broke through and forced their way in. Who could have proposed it? The retired emperor commanded the monks of the mountain gate, and it was heard that the Heike were to be attacked. Meanwhile, soldiers gathered at the palace and guarded the four gates. All the members of the Heike clan rushed to Rokuhara. The Retired Emperor also hurriedly made an imperial visit to Rokuhara. Lord Kiyomori at that time was still a Dainagon, and he was greatly frightened and alarmed. Lord Komatsu said, "Why should such a thing happen just now?" He tried to calm them down, but the uproar among high and low was tremendous. The monks of the mountain gate did not approach Rokuhara, but rushed to the unrelated Kiyomizu Temple and burned down every hall and monk's quarters, leaving not a single building. This was, they say, to wipe away the shame of the night of the funeral procession at Kuaiji. Kiyomizu-dera was because it was a branch temple of Kōfuku-ji. On the morning when Kiyomizu-dera burned, someone—who could it have been?—wrote on a placard, "How about the Kannon's vow to turn the fiery pit into a cool pond?" and stood it in front of the great gate. The next day, someone else posted a reply placard: "The power of countless kalpas of unfathomable vows cannot reach it."

[1.9.2] When the monks returned, the Retired Emperor returned to his palace from Rokuhara. Only Lord Shigemori accompanied him. His father, the lord, did not come. It was said that it was still for the sake of caution. When Shigemori returned from seeing the Emperor off, his father, the Grand Minister, said, "The Emperor's visit is a matter of great awe. Since there is a reason for His Majesty's command, as he has long intended, you must not let your guard down. When he said this, Shigemori replied, "You must not let this matter show in your expression or words; it would be a bad thing if people were to notice." If, even so, you do not go against the imperial will and bestow your compassion upon people, the gods and the Three Treasures will surely protect you. If you do not do so, there is no need for you to fear for your own safety. Saying this, he stood up, and his father said, "Lord Shigemori is indeed a formidable and great man." Thus spoke his father, the lord.

[1.9.3] After the Retired Emperor returned to his palace, there were many close attendants before him, and he said, "What a strange thing he has brought up!" I had not the slightest thought of it. When he said this, among the guards of the palace there was a man called Saikō Hōshi. He was near the throne at that time, and said, "Heaven has no mouth, so it makes people speak. The Heike have exceeded their proper station, so this must be Heaven's judgment. So he said. People said, "This matter is of no importance. Walls have ears; beware, beware. Thus they said.

[1.10.1] Meanwhile, because that year was a year of imperial mourning, the Great Thanksgiving Festival and the Great Purification were not performed. On the twenty-fourth day of the twelfth month of the same year, a prince was born to Kenshunmon-in, who was then still called the Lady of the East, and he was given the title of Imperial Prince.

[1.10.2] When it dawned, there was a change of era name, and it was called Nin'an. On the eighth day of the tenth month of the same year, the prince who had received the imperial decree last year was installed as Crown Prince at Higashi-Sanjō. The Crown Prince was his uncle, six years old; the Emperor was his nephew, three years old; neither was in accordance with the proper order of succession. However, in Kanna 2, Emperor Ichijō ascended the throne at the age of seven. Emperor Sanjō was made Crown Prince at the age of eleven. It is not without precedent. The Emperor received the abdication at the age of two, and on the nineteenth day of the second month, when he was just five years old, the Crown Prince ascended the throne, so he yielded the throne and was called the Retired Emperor. He had not yet undergone his coming-of-age ceremony, but he had the title of Retired Emperor. Was this the first time in China or Japan?

[1.10.3] On the twentieth day of the third month of Nin'an 3, the new Emperor had his enthronement ceremony at the Daigokuden. That he has ascended to the throne of this lord is seen as the very flourishing of the Heike. The one called the Empress Mother, Kenshunmon-in, is of the Heike clan, and moreover she is the younger sister of the Lady of the Second Rank, the wife of the Lay Monk Chancellor. Also, the one called Taira no Dainagon Tokitada is the Empress's elder brother, so he is a maternal relative of the Emperor. He was seen as a minister who held power both within and without the court. Even the conferring of ranks and appointments to office was entirely at the will of this Lord Tokitada. It was like when Yang Guifei was favored, and Yang Guozhong flourished. His worldly reputation and the brilliance of the times were splendid. Because the Lay Monk Chancellor governed all affairs of the realm, the people of the time called him the Heike Chancellor.

[1.11.1] In the meantime, on the sixteenth day of the seventh month of the first year of Kao, the Retired Emperor took Buddhist vows. Even after his ordination, as he continued to administer the affairs of state, there was no limit to his influence within the court. The court nobles and senior officials who were summoned to serve close to the imperial palace, down to the northern guardsmen of both upper and lower ranks, all received official ranks and stipends beyond what they deserved. However, as is the way of the human heart, they were still not satisfied, and thought, "Ah, if only that person were to fall, that province would become vacant; if that person were to die, I could attain that office." Thus, those who were not distant whispered to one another, gathering together. The Retired Emperor also privately said, "Although there have been many who have subdued the enemies of the court from generation to generation since ancient times, there has never been such a thing as this." When Sadamori and Hidesato defeated Masakado, when Yoriyoshi destroyed Sadato and Muneto, and when Yoshiie attacked Takehira and Iehira, the rewards that were given did not exceed the rank of provincial governor. That Kiyomori behaves just as he pleases is truly improper. This too is because the world has reached its end and the imperial law has perished. Though he said so, since it was not the proper order, there was no imperial command. The Heike, too, had no particular reason to bear a grudge against the imperial court, but the root of the world's disorder began on the sixteenth day of the tenth month of the second year of Kaō, when the second son of Lord Komatsu, the newly appointed Third Rank Middle Captain Sukemori, who was then still thirteen and known as the Governor of Echizen, was out in the falling snow. The scenery of the withered fields was truly delightful, so he took along about thirty young samurai and rode out to Rendaino, Murasakino, and Ukon-no-baba, had many hawks set loose, flushed quail and larks again and again, spent the whole day hunting, and as dusk fell he returned to Rokuhara. The regent at that time was Lord Matsudono, and he was on his way to the palace from his residence at Nakamikado Higashinotoin. He was to enter through the Ikuhomon Gate, so he went south along Higashinotoin and west along Oimikado. Sukemori, the Assistant Captain, met the regent's procession head-on at Oimikado Inokuma. The attendants said, "Who is it? This is outrageous!" Since His Excellency is passing, get down from your carriage!" Although he said so, they were excessively proud and bold, and besides, the samurai he had brought along were all young men under twenty, and there was not a single one who understood etiquette or proper conduct. Without even saying that it was the regent's departure, they did not even bother to dismount as etiquette required, and as they tried to force their way through, it was dark, and they did not realize at all that he was the grandson of the monk. Although they knew a little, they were not aware, and starting with Lord Sukemori, all the samurai were pulled off their horses and thrown down, and they suffered great humiliation. Lord Sukemori hurriedly went to Rokuhara and reported this matter to his grandfather, the lay priest Chancellor. The lay priest became very angry and said, "Even if it were the Regent himself, he should have shown respect to Jōkai's vicinity. To have so unceremoniously humiliated a young man is truly a cause for regret." It is from such things that one is deceived by people. If I do not make you realize this, it would be inexcusable. Shall I bear a grudge against the Lord? When he said this, Lord Shigemori replied, "This is not at all troublesome. If we are deceived by the Minamoto clan such as Yorimasa and Mitsumoto, it would truly be a disgrace to our family. It would be rude if my children, being called Shigemori's children, were to meet the Lord's procession and not dismount from their carriages. Saying this, he summoned the samurai who were present at that time and said, "From now on, you must be very careful. If you mistakenly report any disrespect to His Highness, I will have you punished." Saying this, he returned.

[1.11.2] After that, the Lay Monk Chancellor, without even informing Lord Komatsu, summoned about sixty men in all, beginning with Namba and Senoo, rough fellows from remote provinces who thought that, apart from the Lay Monk Chancellor's orders, there was nothing else to fear, and said, "On the coming twenty-first, His Majesty's coming-of-age ceremony is to be held, and the Regent is to go out." Wherever it may be, lie in wait for him, seize the outriders and attendants, and cut off their topknots, and so wipe away Sukemori's disgrace. Thus he spoke. The Chancellor had not dreamed of this; the Emperor, for the ceremony of his coming-of-age, capping, and appointment to office next year, was to stay temporarily in the imperial residence, and so he had been made to dress more splendidly than usual, and this time he was to enter through the Taiken Gate, and he went out westward through the Middle Gate. At the edge of Inokuma Horikawa, more than three hundred mounted warriors of the Rokuhara forces in full armor awaited him, surrounded the Chancellor, and from front and rear at once raised a battle cry. The imperial guards and attendants, making today their day of triumph, chased them here and cornered them there, pulled them from their horses, and beat them mercilessly, cutting off each one's topknot. Among the ten attendants, the topknot of the Right Division official Takeki was also cut off. Among them, when cutting the topknot of the Chamberlain Takayori, he said, "Do not think this is your own topknot; think it is your lord's topknot." So saying, he admonished them and returned. After that, they thrust the nock of a bow into the carriage, tore off the blinds, cut the crupper and breast-strap of the ox, scattered everything about, raised a shout of joy, and went to Rokuhara. The novice monk said, "Admirable!" So he said. As for the carriage attendant, a man named Inaba no Saitsukai, Toba no Kunihisamaru, though of low rank, was a man of sensibility, and weeping, he attended the carriage and escorted the emperor back to the Nakamikado palace. With the sleeves of his court robe he wiped away his tears; the spectacle of the imperial return was so dreadful that even to speak of it would be utterly inadequate. As for the matters of Taishokukan and Lord Tankai, it is beyond words to mention them; from Lord Chūjin and Lord Shōsen onward, I have never heard of a regent or chancellor meeting with such an ordeal. This indeed was the beginning of the Heike's evil deeds.

[1.11.3] Lord Komatsu was greatly agitated. All the samurai who had gone to meet him were disowned. "Even if the Novice commands some miracle, why did he not show the dream to Shigemori?" In general, Sukemori is strange; sandalwood is fragrant from its first leaves, as they say. A boy who is already about to turn twelve or thirteen should now behave with propriety, but to commit such a disgrace and bring shame upon the Novice—this is the height of unfilial conduct, and it lies with you alone. So saying, he banished him to Ise Province for a time. Thus, both lord and vassal were deeply moved by this commander, it was said.

[1.12.1] Because of this, the decision for the Emperor's coming-of-age ceremony was postponed. On the twenty-fifth of the same month, the decision for the coming-of-age ceremony was made in the palace hall. Since the Regent could not attend, on the ninth day of the twelfth month he received a joint imperial edict, and on the fourteenth he was promoted to Grand Minister. Soon after, on the seventeenth of the same month, a congratulatory address was made, but the world seemed bitter and unpleasant.

[1.12.2] Meanwhile, this year too came to an end. When it dawned, on the fifth day of the first month of Kaō 3, the emperor had his coming-of-age ceremony. On the thirteenth of the same month, there was an imperial visit for the morning audience. The Retired Emperor and the Empress Dowager received him, and how lovely they must have thought his first cap was! The daughter of the Lay Monk Chancellor was presented as a court lady. She was fifteen years old. It was a ceremony of the Cloistered Emperor's adopted son.

[1.12.3] At that time, the Grand Minister of Myōon-in, who was then still the Inner Minister and Major General of the Left, resigned from the position of Major General. At that time, it was heard that the Major Counselor Sanesada of Tokudaiji was appointed to that position. Also, the Middle Counselor Kanemasa of Kazanin had a desire for it. Besides, the third son of the late Middle Counselor Ienari of Nakamikado, the new Major Counselor Narichika, also earnestly requested it. Because the Retired Emperor's mood was good, they began various prayers. First, they confined one hundred monks in Hachiman Shrine and had them read the True Reading of the Great Perfection of Wisdom Sutra for seven days. In the midst of that, three mountain doves flew from the direction of Otokoyama to the tachibana tree in front of the Great Deity of Kora, and they fought and died. The dove is the first messenger of Hachiman Daibosatsu. Saying that such a wonder had never occurred in the shrine-temple, the then Kengyo Kyoshin Hoin reported it to the throne. There was a divination at the Bureau of Divinities. They divined that it was an omen of turmoil in the realm. "But it is not a matter for Your Majesty to be concerned about; it is a matter for your subjects to be cautious about. So they reported. The new Dainagon was not at all frightened by this; since there were many eyes during the day, he went on foot night after night from his residence at Nakamikado Karasumaru to the Upper Kamo Shrine for seven consecutive nights. On the night that completed the seven nights, he returned to his residence, and in his exhaustion he lay down and dozed off; in a dream, he felt as if he had gone to the Upper Kamo Shrine, and pushing open the doors of the sacred hall, a voice, awe-inspiring and noble, said:

lg.l: 櫻花賀茂の川かぜうらむなよ、散るをばえこそとゞめざりけれ。

div.p: [1.12.4] The new Dainagon, still not showing any fear, confined a holy man in the upper shrine of Kamo, set up an altar in a hollow of the great cedar behind the sacred hall, and had him perform the rite of Dakini for a hundred days. During that time, lightning struck that great cedar, and the fire blazed up so fiercely that the shrine seemed already in danger, but many shrine attendants rushed to the spot and extinguished it. When they tried to drive out that holy man who was practicing the heterodox rite, he said, "I have a great vow to remain in this shrine for a hundred days; today is the seventy-fifth day." I will absolutely not come out. Saying so, he did not work. When this matter was reported from the shrine family to the imperial palace, [the emperor] said, "Just follow the law and expel him." And he issued an imperial decree to that effect. At that time, the shrine servants, using white staffs, struck the holy man on the back of the neck and drove him out southward from First Avenue. It is said that the gods do not accept improper prayers, but because this Grand Counselor prayed for an unreasonable generalship, such a wonder came to pass.

[1.12.5] The appointments to court ranks and offices at that time were not at the discretion of the retired emperor, nor did they come under the authority of the regent or chancellor; they were entirely as the Heike pleased. Thus, even Tokudaiji and Kazan'in were not appointed, and the eldest son of the Lay Monk Chancellor, Lord Komatsu, who was a Major General of the Right, moved to the Left, while the second son, Munemori, who was a Middle Counselor, surpassed many senior nobles and was added to the Right—this was beyond words. Above all, Lord Tokudaiji, who was a Senior First Rank Counselor, a noble of distinguished lineage, a hero, a man of outstanding talent, and the heir to his family, was surpassed—this was a cause for resentment. People privately said to one another, "Surely he will become a monk or something," but for a while, thinking to see how the world would turn out, he resigned the office of Dainagon and was heard to have secluded himself.

[1.12.6] The new Dainagon Narichika said, "If I am surpassed by Tokudaiji or Kazanin, what shall I do? To be surpassed by the second son of the Heike is unbearable. This too is the doing of one who has everything as he wishes. By some means or other I will destroy the Heike and fulfill my long-cherished desire. How frightening it was that he said such a thing! His father, the lord, had risen only as far as Middle Counselor. As the youngest son, he rose to the rank of Senior Second Rank and the office of Major Counselor, was granted many large provinces, and his sons and retainers prided themselves on imperial favor. What dissatisfaction could have caused such a state of mind? This appeared to be entirely the work of a demon. Even in the Heiji era, as the Echigo Middle Captain, he had been in league with Lord Nobuyori, and when he was about to be executed, Lord Komatsu interceded repeatedly and saved his life. Yet, forgetting that favor, in a place where no outsiders were present, he prepared weapons and gathered soldiers; apart from that endeavor, he had no other concerns.

[1.12.7] The place called Shika-no-tani at the foot of the Eastern Hills was, behind, connected to Mii-dera, and was a formidable fortress. There was the mountain villa of the monk Shunkan. There they constantly gathered and plotted the destruction of the Heike. At one time, the Cloistered Emperor also went on an imperial visit. The late Minor Counselor, the monk Shinzei's son, Jōken Hōin, served as attendant. At that night's banquet, when he was told this matter by Jōken Hōin, he said, "Oh, how shameful! Many people have heard it. Right now it will leak out and become a great matter for the realm. " he said with great agitation, and the new Major Counselor's expression changed, and he abruptly stood up, but the wine bottle that was before him, he caught on the sleeve of his hunting robe and knocked it over, and the Cloistered Emperor said, "What is that?" When he said this, the Major Counselor turned back and said, "The Heike have fallen." He said. The Cloistered Emperor entered the garden and said, "Let people come and perform sarugaku." When he said this, Taira no Hangan Yasuyori came forward and said, "Ah, I have drunk too much and am drunk." He said. Shunkan Sozu said, "Well, how shall we do that?" When he said that, Saiko Hoshi said, "Nothing is better than taking the head." Saying that, he took the head of the vase and entered. Jogen Hoin, in his extreme astonishment, could not say a word. These were truly dreadful events. Who are the followers? Starting with the lay monk Renjō, whose secular name was Masanari, the administrator of Hōshō-ji, the monk Shunkan, Yamashiro no kami Motokane, Shikibu no taifu Masatsuna, Taira no hōgan Yasuyori, Sō no hōgan Nobufusa, Shinpei hōgan Sukeyuki, and Tada no Kurōdo Yukitsuna of the Genji of Settsu Province, many of the Northern Guard became followers.

[1.13.1] The one called the shugyō of this Hōshō-ji was the grandson of the Lord Kyōgoku no Minamoto Dainagon Masatoshi, and the son of the Hōin Kangyō of Kidera. Although he was not of a house that took up bows and arrows as his grandfather the Dainagon did, he was a man of exceedingly violent temper, and he would not let people pass easily before his residence at Sanjo Bomon Kyogoku; he would always stand at the middle gate, gnashing his teeth, and rage. Perhaps because he was the grandson of such a man, this Shunkan too, though a monk, was a person of fierce and proud heart, and so he joined in a reckless rebellion. The new Dainagon Narichika called Tada no Kurando Yukitsuna and said, "I am relying on you as the commander of one side." If you accomplish this matter, you may have any province or estate you desire. First, for the bow case. Saying this, he sent fifty bolts of white cloth.

[1.13.2] On the fifth day of the third month of Angen 3, when Myōon-in-dono was promoted to Grand Minister, Komatsu-dono became Inner Minister, passing over Dainagon Sadafusa. The Minister of the Left, who was also a great general, was splendid. Immediately a grand banquet was held. As for the guest of honor, it was said to be the Minister of the Left from Ōimikado, Lord Tsunemune. The first place was indeed the most honorable, but there was hesitation because of the precedent of his father, the evil Left Minister of Uji.

[1.13.3] The northern guard did not exist in ancient times. From the time of Emperor Shirakawa, when they were first established, there were many guards of the imperial guard offices. Tameyoshi, Morishige, from childhood Chizurumaru, and now Imainumaru—these were peerless swordsmen. Even in the time of Emperor Toba, Suenori and Sueyori, father and son, both served the court and had occasions to act as transmitters of petitions, but they all conducted themselves within their proper station. The Northern Guard of this time, however, were excessively beyond their rank, treating even court nobles and senior courtiers as nothing, with no regard for etiquette or decorum. There were also those who rose from the Lower Northern Guard to the Upper Northern Guard, and from the Upper Northern Guard were granted permission to enter the Courtiers' Hall. While such things were being done, arrogant hearts also emerged, and they became involved in a groundless rebellion. Among them there was a man called Moromitsu and Narikage, who served the late Minor Counselor and lay priest Shinzei. Moromitsu was a local official of Awa Province, and Narikage was a man of the capital; both were of lowly and humble birth. They were summoned to serve as pageboys or as diligent attendants, and because they were clever, Moromitsu became the Lieutenant of the Left Gate Guards, and Narikage the Lieutenant of the Right Gate Guards; the two of them at once became officers of the Gate Guards. When they met with the affair of Shinzei, the two of them together became monks, and were called the Lay Monk of the Left Gate Guards Saikō and the Lay Monk of the Right Gate Guards Saikei; these men, even after becoming monks, were the custodians of the retired emperor's storehouse.

[1.13.4] That Saikō had a son named Morotaka. He too was a man of the sword, and rose to the office of Kebiishi no Goi no Jō, and on the twenty-ninth day of the twelfth month of the first year of Angen, at the Tsuina appointment ceremony, he was made Governor of Kaga. While carrying out the duties of his province, he forcibly carried out illegal and unjust acts, confiscated the estates of shrines and temples and of powerful families, and committed all manner of outrages. Even if one says that the traces of the late lord are distant, he should have carried out moderate government; but because he behaved just as he pleased, in the summer of the second year of the same era, the younger brother of the provincial governor Morotaka, the judicial officer Morotsune of Kondo, was appointed as the deputy governor of Kaga. When the deputy governor first went down, there was a mountain temple called Ukawa near the provincial office. When the temple monks were boiling water at the boundary hot spring and bathing, he burst in, drove them up, bathed himself, made his servants get in, and had his horse washed, and so on. The temple monks became angry and said, "Since olden times, no one from the province has entered this place." Quickly, following precedent, stop the obstruction of the entry. Thus they said. "The previous mokudai were despised because of their negligence. The current mokudai will not do such a thing." Just follow the Law. Just as he said this, the temple monks were about to drive out the provincial forces. The provincial forces, using the next [moment], were about to force their way in. While they were fighting each other, they broke the leg of the horse that the deputy governor Moritsune had treasured. After that, they faced each other with bows and arrows and weapons, shooting and cutting at each other for hours. Perhaps thinking he could not win, the mokudai withdrew as night fell. After that, the local officials of the province gathered together, and with a force of over a thousand horsemen they pressed on to Ukawa and burned down every single temple building, leaving not one standing. Ukawa is a branch temple of Hakusan. Who were the old monks who came forward to appeal this matter? It was Chishaku, Gakumyō, Hōdaibō, Shōchi, Gakuon, and Tosa Ajari who came forward. The three shrines of Hakusan and the great assembly of the eight temples all rose up together; their total force was more than two thousand men, and on the evening of the ninth day of the seventh month they pressed close upon the mansion of the deputy governor Moritsune. Today the day has ended. Deciding that the battle would be tomorrow, they withdrew that day and rested. The autumn wind that blows the dew flutters the sleeves of the archers, and the lightning that illuminates the sky makes the stars on their helmets glitter. The deputy governor, thinking he could not prevail, fled by night and went up to the capital. At dawn, at the hour of the rabbit, they pressed forward and raised a battle cry. Inside the castle, not a sound was made. When they sent someone in to look, they reported that everyone had fled. The monks, unable to resist, retreated. Then, intending to appeal to the mountain gate, they adorned the sacred palanquin of Shirayama Chūgū and carried it up to Mount Hiei. On the twelfth day of the same eighth month, around noon, the sacred palanquin of Hakusan had already arrived at Higashi-Sakamoto on Mount Hiei, they said. From the direction of the northern provinces, thunder roared terribly and, aiming at the capital, rolled upward. White snow fell and buried the earth; on the mountain and in the capital alike, even the tips of the evergreen trees all became pure white.

[1.14.1] The sacred palanquin was brought into the Guest Shrine. The one called the Guest is the manifestation of Hakusan Myori Gongen. If one speaks of it, it is a matter between father and son. Whether the previous matter succeeds or fails is unknown; the joy of this life lies solely in this. It surpasses even Urashima's child meeting the seventh-generation descendant, and exceeds even the unborn child seeing the father on Vulture Peak. The three thousand monks follow one after another, the shrine attendants of the seven shrines line up in rows, and the offerings and prayers at every moment are beyond description.

[1.14.2] The monks of the mountain gate petitioned the throne to sentence the provincial governor, Kaga no kami Moritaka, to exile, and to imprison the deputy governor, Kondo no hogan Moritsune. Because the judgment was delayed, the court nobles and senior officials who were present said, "Alas, the imperial decision should be given quickly. Since ancient times, the lawsuits of the mountain gate have been different from others. Ōkura-kyō Tamefusa and Dazai no Gon no So Suenaka, although they were such important retainers of the imperial court, were exiled because of the mountain gate's lawsuit." How much more should Morotaka be counted among the number? Should we go into the details? Though they said this, the great ministers, valuing their stipends, did not remonstrate, and the lesser officials, fearing punishment, did not speak. Because it was such a situation, everyone kept their mouths shut. "The waters of the Kamo River, the dice of sugoroku, and the mountain monks—these are the things that do not go as I wish. And so, it is said, even the Retired Emperor Shirakawa spoke. In the reign of Emperor Toba, when Heisenji in Echizen was attached to the Enryakuji temple, because his devotion to this mountain was not shallow, he made the wrong into the right. Thus was the imperial decree proclaimed, and the edict was issued. As the Governor of the River, Lord Masafusa, had said, "If we carry the sacred palanquin to the camp and appeal, how will you decide?" When he said this, the emperor replied, "Indeed, the appeal of the mountain monks cannot be ignored." Thus he said.

[1.14.3] On the second day of the third month of Kahō 2, Minamoto no Yoshitsuna, the governor of Mino, destroyed the newly established estate of Tōgoku, and killed Ennō, a long-time resident of the mountain. Because of this, the shrine officials of Hiyoshi and the temple officials of Enryakuji, totaling more than thirty people, presented a petition and went to the camp, but the Chancellor of the Second Rank, Lord Nijō, ordered Yamato Genji Chūnagon no Shōshō Yoriharu to stop them. Yoriharu's retainers shot arrows. Eight people were shot dead on the spot, more than ten were wounded, and the shrine and temple officials scattered in all directions. When it was heard that the monks of the mountain gate were coming down to the capital to report the matter to the throne, warriors and police officers rushed to West Sakamoto and turned them all back.

[1.14.4] At the mountain gate, while the imperial judgment was delayed, they raised the sacred palanquins of the seven shrines to the Konpon Chudo and, before them, recited the Great Perfection of Wisdom Sutra for seven days, cursing the Chancellor. As the officiant for the concluding ceremony, Nakatsukasa Hōin—who at that time was still called Nakatsukasa Kubu—ascended the high seat, struck the gong, and in the words of the declaration said: "O gods who have raised us from the seedling leaves of our lineage, shoot a single whistling arrow and strike the former Chancellor Nijō, O Great Hachiman Bodhisattva." Thus he prayed in a loud voice. Immediately that night a strange thing happened. From the palace of the Eight Princes, the sound of a whistling arrow went forth, and it was seen in a person's dream that it flew toward the imperial capital. That morning, when they raised the lattice shutters of the Regent's palace, there was a single branch of star anise, wet with dew, as if it had just come from the mountains, and it was terrifying. Then, saying it was the punishment of Sannō, the Kampaku of the Second Rank, Lord Fujiwara no Moronaga, fell gravely ill. His mother, the Kita no Mandokoro of the Great Palace, grieved deeply, and disguising herself, imitating a lowly servant, she confined herself in the shrine of Hiyoshi and prayed for seven days and seven nights. For the prayers that were revealed, there were one hundred performances of shiba-sarugaku, one hundred performances of hitotsumono, horse racing, yabusame, sumo wrestling, one hundred each; one hundred sessions of the Niō lecture, one hundred sessions of the Yakushi lecture, one hundred statues of Yakushi of one and a half shaku, one life-size statue of Yakushi, and statues of Shaka and Amida, all of which were made and dedicated. Also, in her heart, there were three vows. Since it is a matter of your heart, how could anyone know and serve you? What was strange about that was that on the night completing the seventh day, among the many shrine visitors at the Hachioji Shrine, a young shrine maiden who had come all the way from Mutsu suddenly fell into a trance around midnight. When they fanned her from a distance and prayed, she soon revived and immediately stood up and danced, clapping her hands. People thought it was a miracle and watched her. After she danced for about half an hour, the deity of Sanno descended, and the oracle was awe-inspiring. "All you beings, listen carefully. The Great Lord's wife of the north mansion has been confined in my presence for seven days now. There were three vows. First, save the life of His Excellency the Regent; if it may be so, I will mingle with the cripples who serve in the lower palace, and for a thousand days, morning and evening, I will serve at the palace. In the north mansion of the Great Lord, she did not think of the world as the world, and in her heart that was passing the days in sorrow, because she had lost her way in the path of love for her child, she forgot even her gloom, and mingled with the pitiful cripples, and said that for a thousand days, morning and evening, she would serve at the palace—this was truly pitiful to think of. Second, from the Omiya wave-stop at Doton to the shrine of Hachioji, I will build a corridor. When the three thousand monks go to the shrine, whether in rain or shine, it is painful; if a corridor were built, how wonderful it would be. Third, if you will save the life of the present regent, at the shrine of Hachioji, a daily Lotus Sutra question-and-answer lecture should be held without interruption. None of them is insignificant, but the first two could be omitted. The daily Lotus Sutra question-and-answer lecture is truly what I desire. But this lawsuit should have been settled easily; yet without a judgment, the shrine servant was shot dead, wounded, and came weeping to appeal. The matter is so distressing that I cannot think I will ever forget it, no matter what age may come. Moreover, the arrows that struck them are exactly those that pierced the sacred flesh of the manifested deity. Whether true or false, look at this! Saying this, he bared his shoulder, and when they looked, there was a large gaping wound under his left armpit, as big as the mouth of a large earthenware cup.
