"Because this is so distressing, no matter what I say, the matter will not be settled." If there is to be a Hokke question-and-answer lecture, I will extend my life by three years and offer it. If you consider that insufficient, it cannot be helped. Saying this, he had the deity of Sannō ascend. As for the mother, since she had not spoken of her vow to anyone, she had not the slightest suspicion as to who might have leaked it. When the oracle revealed the innermost thoughts of her heart exactly as they were, she felt it was especially precious, piercing her heart and liver, and weeping, she said, "Even if it were only for a single day or a moment, it would be something to be grateful for; how much more so if you extend my life by three years—that would be most fitting." Saying this, he departed in tears. He hurried back to the capital, and donated in perpetuity to the shrine of Hachiman a place called Tanaka-no-shō in Kii Province, the domain of the Chancellor. From then on, the Hokke debate lectures have been held daily without interruption down to the present day, so it is said.

[1.14.5] In the midst of this, the Chancellor of the Latter Nijō recovered from his illness and became as he was before. While high and low rejoiced and were moved, three years passed like a dream, and it became the second year of Eijō. On the twenty-first day of the sixth month, the former Kampaku of the Second Rank developed a malignant boil at the hairline and took to his bed; on the twenty-seventh of the same month, at the age of thirty-eight, he passed away. Though he was a man of fierce spirit and strong will, when the matter became urgent, he regretted his life. Truly, it must be regrettable. Not even reaching forty, you have passed away before the Great Minister—how sad it is! It is not necessarily the rule that one must die before one's father, but according to the law of life and death, even the World-Honored One of perfect virtue and the great bodhisattvas who have attained the tenth stage could not prevent it. Since the Sanno deity, full of compassion, employs skillful means for the benefit of sentient beings, I do not think there will be any blame.

[1.15.1] Meanwhile, the monks of Enryakuji repeatedly petitioned the court to sentence the provincial governor Kaga no kami Morotaka to exile and to imprison his deputy Kondo no hogan Morotsune, but since no imperial sanction was given, they halted the festival of Hiyoshi and on the thirteenth day of the fourth month of Angen 3, at the hour of the dragon (around 8 a.m.), they decorated the sacred palanquins of the three shrines—Jūzenji, Kyakujin, and Hachioji—and carried them to the imperial palace. At Shimomatsu, Kiretsutsumi, the Kamo riverbed, Tadasu, Umetada, Yanagihara, and around Tōhokuin, white-robed monks, shrine servants, palace servants, and temple administrators thronged in countless numbers, and the palanquins proceeded westward along Ichijō. The sacred treasures shone in the sky, and it was astonishing as if the sun and moon had fallen to the earth. Because of this, the great generals of the Minamoto and Taira clans fortified the encampments on all sides and issued orders that the monks should be repelled. On the Taira side, the Minister of the Interior Komatsu, the Major Captain of the Left Shigemori, with a force of more than three thousand horsemen, guarded the three gates of Yōmei, Taiken, and Ikuō on the Ōmiya front. His younger brothers Munemori, Tomomori, and Shigehira, and his uncles Yorimori, Norimori, and Tsunemori, among others, fortified the southwestern encampment. On the Genji side, with the Imperial Palace Guard Minamoto no Yorimasa and Watanabe no Shōji as commanders, their force was only about three hundred horsemen, and they fortified the northern gate, the Nuidono encampment. The place was wide, the forces were few, and they appeared sparse indeed.

[1.15.2] Because the monks were few in number, they tried to bring the sacred palanquin in through the north gate, from the Nuido no Jin. Lord Yorimasa, being such a person, dismounted from his horse, removed his helmet, and worshipped the sacred palanquin. All the warriors were like this. They sent a messenger to the monks and had a message to convey. That messenger was a man called Watanabe no Chōshichi Ton. On that day, Ton wore a hitatare of yellow-ground with small cherry blossoms, donned armor, girded on a sword of red copper, shouldered white-feathered arrows, tucked a bow of black-vine wrapped rattan under his arm, removed his helmet and hung it on the high cord, and prostrated himself before the sacred palanquin, saying: "Minamoto no Sanmi has sent me to the assembly of monks." This time, the mountain temple's lawsuit is undoubtedly reasonable. The delay in your judgment would surely be resented even from afar. Then, bringing in the sacred palanquin would not be a matter of any difficulty. However, Yorimasa has few troops. Moreover, if you enter through the gate where the palanquin is brought in after dawn, the monks of the mountain gate would be pleased, and the talk of the capital boys would become a future difficulty. If you bring in the sacred palanquin, it would be like disobeying the imperial decree. Moreover, if I were to prevent it, I, who have for years bowed my head to the Medicine King and the Mountain King, would from today onward part ways with the path of the bow and arrow. Whether one speaks of that or this, both seem difficult to cure. The eastern camp is firmly held by Lord Komatsu with a large force. Would it be possible for him to enter from that camp? When he sent this message, the shrine servant, blocked by Sho's words, wavered for a while in his service.

[1.15.3] The young monks said, "Why should there be any falsehood? Just bring the sacred palanquin in from this camp." Although there were many who said such things, among the old monks, the one renowned as the foremost debater of the three pagodas, the steadfast scholar Gōun of Settsu, stepped forward and said, "You are quite right." If we carry the sacred palanquin before us and make our appeal, we must break through the great crowd, and only then will our fame be known to posterity. Above all, this Lord Yorimasa, from the time of Rokusonno onward, is the legitimate heir of the Genji line, and in taking up the bow and arrow, he has never yet been known to fail. He excels not only in martial arts but also in the art of poetry. During the reign of Emperor Konoe, at an impromptu poetry gathering, when the topic 'Flowers in the Deep Mountains' was given, everyone was struggling to compose, when this Lord Yorimasa,

lg.l: 深山木のその梢とも見えざりし、櫻ははなにあらはれにけり。

div.p: [1.15.4] —a man of such refined sensibility that he composed a famous poem and received imperial praise—how could you, at such a moment, so heartlessly subject him to humiliation? Let us overturn this sacred palanquin! When they consulted thus, the multitude of several thousand monks, from the vanguard to the rearguard, all agreed, saying, "Indeed, indeed." Then, having the sacred palanquin carried in front, when they tried to have it brought in through the eastern gate, Taikenmon, a violent disturbance suddenly broke out, and the warriors shot at them mercilessly. Many arrows were also shot into the sacred palanquin of the Jūzenji. Shrine servants and palace attendants were shot to death, and many monks were wounded. The clamor and shouting reached even Brahma's heaven, and it seemed that even the firm earth deity was startled. The monks threw down the sacred palanquin at the camp gate and, weeping, returned to the main temple.

[1.16.1] The Emperor commanded the Chamberlain and Left Minor Controller Kanemitsu, and a sudden council of nobles was held in the palace. In the seventh month of Hōan 4, when the sacred palanquin entered the capital, he ordered the head priest and had it enshrined at the Akayama shrine. Again, in the fourth month of Hōen 4, when the sacred palanquin entered the capital, he ordered the head priest of Gion and had it enshrined at the Gion shrine. Saying that this time should follow the precedent of the Hōen era, he ordered the bettō of Gion, Gon-no-Daisōzu Chōken, and, lighting torches, they entered the Gion shrine. The arrows stuck in the portable shrine were pulled out by the shrine servants. The occasions on which the monks of Enryakuji brought the portable shrine of Hiyoshi to the imperial palace were six times from the Eikyū era onward until the Jishō era. Each time they summoned warriors to defend against it, but the shooting of the sacred palanquin—this, they say, was the beginning. "When the divine spirits are angered, disasters fill the land," it is said. How frightening, how frightening! So everyone said to one another.

[1.16.2] On the night of the fourteenth of the same month, when it was heard that the monks of Mount Hiei were again descending upon the capital, in the middle of the night the emperor was placed in a palanquin and proceeded to the retired emperor's residence at Hōjūji. The Empress was placed in a palanquin and departed. The Komatsu Minister, wearing informal court dress and carrying arrows on his back, attended the procession. His eldest son, the Lesser Captain Koremori, wearing formal court dress and carrying a quiver, came along. Beginning with the Chancellor, the Grand Minister and all the nobles and courtiers below him came rushing, each vying to be first. The clamor of all the people of the capital, high and low, and of the palace, upper and lower, was tremendous. At the mountain gate, arrows were shot at the sacred palanquin, shrine servants and priests were shot dead, and many monks were wounded, so the three thousand monks all agreed that they should burn down every hall—the Great Shrine, the Second Shrine, the Lecture Hall, the Central Hall, and all other buildings—leaving not one standing, and that they should scatter into the mountains and fields. When it was heard that, because of this, the monks' request should be granted, the mountain gate's senior monks went up the mountain to inform the monks of the details, but the monks became angry and drove them all back from West Sakamoto.

[1.16.3] The Grand Counselor Taira no Tokitada, who at that time was still the Captain of the Left Gate Guards, stood as the senior noble. The three monastic orders assembled in the courtyard of the Great Lecture Hall and tried to seize the senior noble and drag him away. "Knock off his cap, seize him, and throw him into the lake!" Thus they deliberated. When it seemed that it had already come to this, Lord Tokitada said, "Please be quiet for a while. There is something I must say to the assembled monks. Saying this, he took out a small inkstone and folded paper from his bosom, wrote a single line, and sent it into the midst of the great assembly. When they opened and read it, it said, "The monks' committing violence is the work of demonic temptation. The restraint imposed by the Wisdom King is the protection of the Buddha. Thus it was written. Seeing this, without delay, all agreed, and went down to the valleys and entered the temples. Tokitada, who with a single sheet and a single phrase calmed the anger of the three pagodas and three thousand monks and escaped public and private shame, was truly admirable. The people too, thinking that the monks of the mountain gate were only noisy in their departure, were impressed that they also understood reason.

[1.16.4] On the same twentieth day, with the Provisional Middle Counselor Lord Tadafusa of Kazan-in as the senior noble, the provincial governor, Kaga no kami Morotaka, was finally dismissed from office and exiled to Ido-ta in Owari. The deputy governor, Kondo no Hangan Morotsune, was imprisoned. Also, on the thirteenth of the previous month, the six warriors who had shot arrows at the sacred palanquin were sentenced to imprisonment. The Left Guards Officer Fujiwara no Masazumi, the Right Guards Officer Masasue, the Left Guards Officer Oe no Iekane, the Right Guards Officer Iekuni of the same family, the Left Military Guards Officer Kiyowara no Yasuie, and the Right Military Guards Officer Yasutomo of the same family—all of these were retainers of Lord Komatsu.

[1.16.5] On the twenty-eighth day of the same fourth month, around the hour of the boar, a fire broke out from Higuchi-Tominokoji, and because a strong southeast wind was blowing, much of the capital burned down. 大なる車輪の如くなるほむらが、三町五町を隔てゝ、戌亥の方へすぢかへに、飛び越え／＼燒け行けば、怖しなどもおろかなり。 或は具平親王の千種殿、或は北野の天神の紅梅殿、橘逸勢のはひ松殿、鬼殿、高松殿、鴨居殿、東三條、冬嗣の大臣の閑院殿、昭宣公の堀川殿、これを始めて、昔今の名所三十餘箇所、公卿の家だにも、十六箇所まで燒にけり。 その外殿上人、諸大夫の家々は注すに及ばず。 はては大内に吹きつけて、朱雀門より始めて、應天門、會昌門、大極殿、豐樂院、諸司、八省、朝所、一時がうちに灰燼の地とぞなりにける。 家々の日記、代々の文書、 七珍萬寶さながら塵灰となりぬ。その間の費如何ばかりぞ。人の燒け死ぬること數百人、牛馬の類は數を知らず。これ徒事にあらず、山王の御咎とて、比叡山より大なる 猿共が、二三千おりくだり、手に手に松火をともいて、京中を燒くとぞ、人の夢には見えたりける。大極殿は清和天皇の御宇、貞觀十八年に始めて燒けたりければ、同十九年正月三日、陽成院の御即位は、豐樂院にてぞありける。元慶元年四月九日事始ありて同二年十月八日にぞ造り出されたりける。後冷泉院の御宇、天喜五年二月二十六日、又やけにけり。治歴四年八月十四日事始ありしかども、造りいだされずして、後冷泉院崩御なりぬ。後三條院の御宇、延久四年四月十五日造り出して、文人詩を作り奉り、伶人樂を奏して遷幸なし奉る。今は世末になて、國の力も皆衰たれば、その後 はつひに造られず。

[2.1.1] On the fifth day of the fifth month of the first year of Jishō, the Tendai abbot Myōun Daisōjō had his public invitation stopped, and, sending a chamberlain as an imperial messenger, had the sacred image of Nyoirin recalled and his personal chaplain dismissed. Already, attaching an official of the office of the messenger, they summoned the ringleaders of the monks who were about to carry the sacred palanquin into the imperial palace. In Kaga Province there was an estate of the abbot. The provincial governor Morotaka, while abolishing this, because of that grudge, incited the monks and brought a lawsuit. When it finally came to a grave matter of the imperial court, because of the slander of the priest Saikō and his son, the cloistered emperor was greatly enraged. It was heard that he would especially be subjected to severe punishment. Because the Cloistered Emperor's mood was bad, Myōun returned the seal and key and resigned from the position of head priest. On the eleventh of the same month, Prince Kakukai, the seventh son of Emperor Toba, became the head priest of the Tendai sect. He was a disciple of the Great Archbishop Gyōgen of Shōren-in. On the twelfth of the same month, the former head priest was removed from his position, and two kebiishi were attached to him; they covered the well, poured water on the fire, and subjected him to the torture of water and fire. Because of this, when it was heard that the monks would still come up to the capital, the whole city was again in an uproar.

[2.1.2] On the same eighteenth day, the Grand Minister and thirteen other court nobles entered the palace, took their seats in the council hall, and held a deliberation on the punishment of the former abbot. The Middle Counselor Nagakata of the Eighth Ward, who was then still the Consultant of the Left Gate Guards, was seated at the lowest seat and said: "According to the judgment of the legal experts, it appears that the death penalty should be reduced by one degree and he should be exiled to a distant land. However, the former head priest Myoun Daisojo, who was learned in both exoteric and esoteric Buddhism, and who, in addition to observing the precepts purely, had bestowed the Mahayana scriptures upon the Emperor and had administered the bodhisattva precepts to the Retired Emperor— For the teacher of the scriptures and the teacher of the precepts to be subjected to a heavy punishment—the judgment of the unseen world is unfathomable. Should he be pardoned from laicization and distant exile? When he said this without any hesitation, all the court nobles present agreed with Nagakata's opinion, but because the Cloistered Emperor's anger was deep, he was still sentenced to exile. The Prime Minister also intended to speak about this matter and went to the palace, but because the Cloistered Emperor had a cold and did not summon him to his presence, he left feeling disappointed. As a punishment for the monk, they took back his ordination certificate, made him return to lay life, and gave him the lay name Dainagon Daisuke, Fujii Matsue. This Myoun was the sixth-generation descendant of Prince Tomohira, the seventh son of Emperor Murakami, and the son of Kuga Dainagon Akimichi. Truly he was a peerless great virtue, the foremost high priest in the realm, so both lord and vassals revered him, and he was also appointed abbot of Tennoji and Rokushoji. However, when the Yin-Yang master Abe no Yasuchika said, "I cannot understand why such a wise man as Myoun would call himself that." Above, the light of the sun and moon shines side by side; below, there are clouds. Thus he criticized. In the first year of Nin'an, on the twentieth day of the second month, he became the head priest of the Tendai sect. On the fifteenth day of the third month of the same year, there was an imperial audience. When he opened the treasure house of the central hall, among various precious treasures there was a box one foot square. It was wrapped in white cloth. The abbot, who had kept his vows of celibacy all his life, opened that box and looked inside; there was a scroll of writing on yellow paper. The Great Teacher Dengyo had written down in advance the names of future abbots. It was the custom to look only as far as one's own name appeared, not to look beyond that, and to roll it back up as before. Therefore, this bishop too must have been like that. Though he is a noble person, he cannot escape the karma of his previous life. These were sorrowful events.

[2.1.3] On the same twenty-first day, the place of exile was decided to be Izu Province. Although various people made appeals, due to the slanderous report of the priest Saiko and his son, it was carried out in this way. Immediately, saying that he should be driven out of the capital today, the official in charge of expulsion went to the Shirakawa residence to drive him out. The archbishop, unable to bear it, left the temple and entered the detached hall of the complete scriptures at Awataguchi. At the mountain gate, they said, "In the end, our enemies are none other than Saikō and his son," and wrote down the names of those father and son, and had them trampled under the left foot of the great general Kompira, among the twelve divine generals seated in the Konpon Chūdō, saying, "Twelve divine generals, seven thousand yakshas, without delay, take the lives of Saikō and his son!" As he cried out and cursed, even hearing it was frightening.

[2.1.4] On the same twenty-third day, he departed from the separate hall of the complete scriptures to the place of exile. For a person of such rank as a Dharma-master and Great Archbishop, to be driven out by the escorting envoy, leaving the capital today as the last day, and heading east beyond the barrier—one can imagine the feelings in his heart, and it is sorrowful. When they came to the beach of Uchiide in Ōtsu, the white gleam of the eaves of Monju Tower was visible, but he did not look at it a second time; pressing his sleeve to his face, he choked with tears. Though there were many venerable elders at the monastery, the Dharma Seal Chōken, who was then still a Sōzu, so deeply regretted the departure that he accompanied him as far as Awazu; and when he could not remain longer, he took his leave and returned. The Archbishop, moved by his earnest devotion, bestowed upon him the secret transmission of the One Mind, Three Contemplations, which he had kept hidden in his heart for years. This teaching was transmitted in succession from the Buddha's entrustment, through the venerable Ashvaghosha of the country of Varanasi and the bodhisattva Nagarjuna of southern India, and has now been bestowed upon the feelings of the present day. Indeed, although our country is called a remote borderland of scattered millet and an age of defilement and the latter days, Chōken, having been entrusted with this teaching, wrung the sleeves of his priestly robe and returned to the capital—how noble was the heart within him! At the mountain gate, the assembly rose and deliberated. From the time of the Venerable Gishin onward, since the beginning of the Tendai abbots, down to the fifty-fifth generation, we have never heard of an example of banishment. When I reflect on the meaning of this matter, since the time when, in the Enryaku era, the Emperor established the imperial capital and the Great Master climbed this mountain and propagated the teachings of the Fourfold Wisdom here, women of the five obstacles have ceased to come, and three thousand pure monks have occupied this place. On the peak, the Lotus Sutra has been recited for years; at the foot, the seven shrines' miracles are renewed daily. That Moon Clan's sacred mountain is a great holy cave northeast of the royal capital. This land of Japan's sacred peak also stands at the demon gate of the imperial capital, a holy ground protecting the nation. Wise kings and sagacious ministers of successive generations have chosen this place for their altars. Since it is the latter age, how could one bring disgrace upon this mountain? How regrettable! Saying this, they cried out and shouted, and then the entire assembly of monks descended to Higashi-Sakamoto.

div.head: 2.2. 一行阿闍梨之沙汰

div.p: [2.2.1] First, let us go to Awazu and seize the abbot and detain him. But since there are the pursuers' escorts and the sending officials, it is difficult to seize and present him without incident. There is no one to rely on except the divine power of Sanno Daishi. "Truly, if there is no particular reason and you can seize and present him, then show us an auspicious sign here first." So said the old monks, and they prayed with all their hearts.

[2.2.2] Then the boy Tsurumaru, a page of the priest Jōen of Mudōji Temple, who was eighteen years old, tormented his mind and body, broke out in sweat all over, and suddenly went mad. "Our master, the tenth abbot, is residing here." Even if it is the Latter Age, how could our mountain's head be moved to another province? It is heartbreaking for all lives to come. If that is to be, even if I remain at the foot of this mountain, what good would it do? Saying this, he pressed his sleeves to his face and shed tears in streams. The monks thought this strange and said, "If this is truly the divine message of Jūzenji Gongen, we will test it; return it to its original owner without any mistake." Saying this, four or five hundred old monks threw the rosaries they held in their hands up onto the great dais of Jūzenji. This madman ran around, picked up and gathered them, and without the slightest mistake, returned each and every one to its original owner. At the wonder of the divine efficacy of the great assembly and the gods being so newly manifest, all pressed their palms together and shed tears of rejoicing. "If that is the case, go and seize it and bring it back!" Just as he said this, they set out like clouds and mist. Some monks walked along the shore road of Shiga and Karasaki. Some monks pushed out boats onto the lake at Yamada and Yabase. Seeing this, the pursuers and escorts who had been so stern all fled in every direction.

[2.2.3] The monks went to Kokubunji. The former head priest was greatly startled and said, "They say that a person under imperial censure must not even be touched by the light of the sun or moon." How much more so, then, when an imperial decree has been issued that you must be expelled from the capital at once, you must not delay even for a moment. Monks, return to the mountain at once. Saying this, he came out to the edge of the veranda and said, "Since I left the house of the Three Terraces and the Gate of the Paulownia and entered the window of the Four Brightnesses and the secluded valley, I have studied the teachings of the Perfect School widely and learned both the exoteric and esoteric doctrines. I have thought only of the prosperity of our mountain. Moreover, his prayers for the nation were not negligent. His intention to nurture the monks was also deep. The deities of both shrines will surely see and know. There is no fault in myself. Because of a false accusation, I suffer the heavy punishment of exile, but I bear no resentment against the world, people, gods, or Buddhas. The kindness of the monks who have come to visit me up to now is truly hard to repay fully. Saying this, he did not even wring the sleeves of his incense-dyed robe, and all the monks shed tears. They brought the palanquin close and said, "Please get in, quickly." When they said this, he replied, "In the past I was the head of three thousand monks, but now I have become a mere exile. How could I be carried up on the shoulders of noble scholars and wise priests?" Even if I were to go up, I should put on shoes and walk up on foot like everyone else. Saying this, he did not board.

[2.2.4] Here there was an evil monk, the abbot Yukei of Kaijo-bo, a resident monk of the Western Pagoda. He was about seven feet tall, wearing a suit of armor laced with black leather, with large gold studs on the rough surface, the skirt hanging long, his helmet removed and carried by a servant, leaning on a long-handled halberd with a white shaft, and said, "Open up!" Saying this, he pushed his way through the crowd of monks and rushed to where the former chief abbot was. He glared with wide eyes, stared at him for a while, and said, "It is because of that heart of yours that you have met with such a fate." I will summon you soon. When he said that, in fear he quickly boarded. In their joy at having taken the abbot, the lowly monks—not just any common monks, but distinguished scholars—carried him aloft, shouting and crying out as they went up. The others changed, but Yūkei did not; he carried the front of the palanquin, and with the handle of his long sword and the shaft of the palanquin, he struck as if to shatter them, making the steep eastern slope seem like level ground. They set the palanquin down in the courtyard of the Great Lecture Hall and held a council: "Well now, we went to Awazu and seized the abbot. Now that he has incurred imperial censure and is to be exiled, how could it be right for us to seize him and make him our abbot?" " they deliberated. The Ajari Kaijōbō, again stepping forward as before, deliberated: "Now, this mountain is a sacred place unparalleled in Japan, a training ground for the protection of the nation; the divine power of Sannō is flourishing, and the Buddhist Law and the Imperial Law are like the two horns of a bull. Therefore, even down to the intentions of the monks, there is nothing to be despised; even the lowly priests are not looked down upon by the world. How much more so is he wise and noble, and the head of the three thousand monks. Now he is virtuous in conduct and the abbot of the whole mountain. Without having committed any crime, he incurs punishment. Is this not the indignation of the mountain monks and the people of the capital, and the mockery of Kofukuji and Onjoji? At this time, having lost the head of both exoteric and esoteric Buddhism, the many scholar-monks will surely find it painful to neglect their diligent study by the light of fireflies and snow. In the end, Yukei will be named as the ringleader, will be imprisoned and exiled, and will be beheaded; this will be his honor in this life and his memory in the afterlife. Saying this, he shed tears streaming from both eyes, and the whole assembly agreed, saying, 'Indeed, indeed.' From that time on, they called Yūkei 'Ikame-bō' (the fierce monk). His disciple, the Vinaya master Ekei, was called by the people of the time 'Ko-ikame-bō' (the little fierce monk).

[2.2.5] The monks first escorted the former head priest into Myōkō-bō in the South Valley of the East Pagoda. Was it that even an incarnation of the Buddha could not escape the calamity of the times? Long ago in Great Tang, the Acharya Ichigyō was the personal monk of Emperor Xuanzong, but he was defamed by the emperor's consort Yang Guifei. In ancient times and now, in great countries and small, the maliciousness of people's mouths is a thing that leaves no trace, but because of that suspicion, he was exiled to the Land of Kara. To that country there are three roads. One is called the Rinchi Road, the imperial procession road; one is called the Yūchi Road, the road common people travel; and one is called the Anketsu Road, the road on which serious criminals are sent. Therefore, because that Ichigyō Ajari was a person of grave offense, he was sent along the Anketsu Road. For seven days and seven nights, without seeing the light of the sun or moon, he performed religious practices. It was dark and deserted, with no one about; as they walked, they lost their way ahead, and the mountains were deep and densely forested. Only the cry of a bird in the valley could be heard; unable to dry their clothes wet with moss, they suffered the heavy punishment of exile for a crime they did not commit. Heaven took pity on them, and the Nine Luminaries appeared to protect the priest Ichigyō. At that time, Ichigyō bit off the finger of his right hand and drew the form of the Nine Luminaries on his left sleeve. This is the Mandala of the Nine Luminaries, which is the principal object of worship of the Shingon sect in both Japan and China.

div.note: [_] [1] The kanji in our copy-text is New Nelson 3330.

div.p: [2.3.1] When the Retired Emperor heard that the monks had seized the former head priest, he became even more uneasy. The monk Saikō said, "Although it is said that the monks of the mountain gate have not just now begun to make violent appeals, this time it is beyond all reason." We have never heard of such an outrage. Please admonish them thoroughly. Thus he spoke. Without regard for his own imminent destruction, and without heeding the divine will of Sannō and Daishi, he spoke in this way and troubled the imperial heart. It is said that slanderous ministers bring disorder to the country. Truly, "Though the clustered orchids would flourish, the autumn wind defeats them; though the king would be enlightened, slanderous ministers darken him." Should one say such things? When this matter was reported to the new Grand Minister Narichika and his close attendants, and it was heard that the mountain would be attacked, the monks of Enryakuji, harboring resentment against the imperial court, said that they should not disobey the imperial command, and some monks secretly obeyed the retired emperor's decree. The former head priest Myoun Daisojo was staying at Myokobo, and when he heard that the monks were divided in their intentions, he said, "What kind of fate will I meet in the end?" He said with a feeling of helplessness. However, there was no sentence of exile.

[2.3.2] The new Grand Counselor Narichika, because of the disturbance at the mountain gate, had for a while suppressed his private resentment. Although the secret plans were various, since with only Yoshikata's forces this rebellion did not seem likely to succeed, Tada no Kurando Yukitsuna, who had been so deeply trusted, came to think it was futile. The cloth that had been sent for bow-bags they sewed into hitatare and hakama, and dressed their retainers in them, and sat there blinking their eyes; but when they observed the flourishing state of the Heike, it seemed that they could not be easily overthrown at that time. He had joined a futile cause. If this matter should leak out, Yukitsuna would be the first to be destroyed. Before it leaks from another's mouth, I will turn loyal and save my life—that is the thought that came to me.

[2.3.3] On the twenty-ninth day of the same fifth month, late at night, Tada no Kurando Yukitsuna came to the Lay Monk Chancellor's mansion in Nishihachijo and said, "I, Yukitsuna, have come because there is a matter I must report." When he had them say this, the Lay Monk said, "What is it that a man who does not usually come has come for?" Listen to that. Saying this, he sent out Shume-no-hangan Morikuni. "This is a matter that should not be spoken of through people." While saying this, "Well then," and the priest came out to the corridor from the middle gate. "The night has grown far advanced; what is the matter now?" When he said this, "Because in the daytime people's eyes are many, I have come mingling with the night." Meanwhile, how did you hear that the people of the palace are preparing weapons and summoning soldiers? "I heard that they will surely attack from the mountain." "He said it as if it were nothing." Yukitsuna came close and said in a low voice, "It is not so; I have heard that it is entirely about the imperial family." "Then, does the Cloistered Emperor also know about that?" "Do you really know the details?" The mustering of Lord Narichika's troops, too, was surely summoned by imperial decree. Shunkan behaved thus, Yasukata said this, Saikō said that. He blurted out all these things from the beginning without holding back, and then took his leave and went out. The Novice was greatly startled and, in a loud voice, called out for his retainers; the sound of it was tremendous. Yukitsuna, fearing that he might be called as a witness for having rashly spoken out, felt as if he had set fire to Ono, and without anyone chasing him, he tucked up his hakama and fled out the gate in haste. The Novice first summoned Sadayoshi and said, "The rebels who are plotting to overthrow our family are filling the capital." Notify the members of our clan and summon the warriors." When he said this, they ran around and summoned them. The Right Grand General Lord Munemori, the Third Rank Middle Captain Tomomori, the Head Middle Captain Shigehira, the Left Horse Bureau Director Yukimori, and others below them, donned armor, girded on bows and arrows, and gathered in haste. Besides these, soldiers gathered like clouds and mist. That night, in Nishi-Hachijo, it appeared that there were as many as six or seven thousand mounted warriors. When it dawned, it was the first day of the sixth month. While it was still dark, the Novice summoned the kebiishi Abe no Sanenari and said, "Go quickly to the imperial palace." The plan I intend to tell Nobunari is this: the close attendants are plotting to destroy this clan and throw the realm into chaos. Summon them one by one and conduct an inquiry. Say that even His Majesty surely does not know about that. Thus he said. Sukenari hurriedly came running, summoned Daizen no Daibu Nobunari, and when he told him this, Nobunari turned pale. When he went before the Retired Emperor and reported this matter, the Retired Emperor said, "Ah, so their secret plotting has leaked out!" He thought this was outrageous. Even so, "What is this?" He only said that, and gave no clear answer. Sukenari hurried back and reported this to the Lay Monk Chancellor, who said, "That's exactly it." Yukitsuna told the truth. If Yukitsuna had not informed him of this matter, would Jōkai have been safe? Saying this, Hida no kami Kageie and Chikugo no kami Sadanari gave orders to arrest the rebels. So two hundred and some tens of horsemen, three hundred and some tens of horsemen, pressed in here and there and arrested them.

[2.3.4] The Taira no Nyūdō first sent a servant to the residence of the new Dainagon Narichika at Nakamikado Karasumaru, saying, "There is something we need to discuss." Please come quickly. When he was told this, the Dainagon, not realizing in the least that it concerned himself, said, "Ah, this must be about the Retired Emperor's plan to attack the mountain; there is an imperial edict, and I should go and dissuade him." His anger seemed deep. It is something that cannot possibly be helped. Saying this, he put on a soft, plain robe, got into a splendid carriage, and taking along three or four attendants, even down to the servants and ox-drivers, they were all dressed up more than usual. Indeed, it was only later that he realized this was his last moment. When he approached Nishi-Hachijo and looked, soldiers filled the area for four or five blocks. How numerous! What is this? His heart pounding, he got down from the carriage, entered the gate, and looked; inside too, soldiers filled every space without a gap. At the middle gate, many fierce-looking warriors were waiting; they took the Dainagon by both hands and pulled him, saying, "We should bind him." They said this, and the Nyudo Sagami no Kuni no Kami looked out from behind the blinds and said, "It is impossible." When he said this, the warriors surrounded him on all sides, pulled him up onto the veranda, and forced him into a small room. The Major Counselor felt as if in a dream, and could not remember anything at all. The samurai who had been his attendants were pushed away and scattered in all directions. The miscellaneous servants and ox-drivers lost their composure, abandoned the ox-carriage, and fled.

[2.3.5] In the meantime, the Middle Captain of Omi, the lay priest Renjo, the temple administrator of Hosshoji, the high priest Shunkan, the governor of Yamashiro, Motokane, the assistant director of the Bureau of Ceremonies, Masatsuna, the police lieutenant Taira no Yasuyori, the police lieutenant So no Nobufusa, and the new police lieutenant Taira no Sukeyuki were also captured and brought in.

[2.3.6] When the monk Saikō heard this, he must have thought it concerned himself, and he whipped his horse and galloped to the Hōjūji Palace, the residence of the Cloistered Emperor. The Heike samurai came galloping toward him on the road and said, "You are summoned to Nishi-Hachijō. Come quickly." When they said this, he replied, "I have something to report to the sovereign, so I am going to the Hōjūji Palace. I will come presently." When he said this, [the other] said, "What a wicked lay priest!" What could he possibly report to the throne? Don't do that! Saying this, they pulled him off his horse, bound him, and took him down to Nishi-Hachijo. Because he had been a close retainer since the beginning, they bound him especially tightly and dragged him into the courtyard. The Lay Monk Prime Minister stood on the dais and said, "What a sight you've become, you wretch who tried to topple the Lay Monk!" Drag that fellow over here! Saying this, he had him dragged to the edge of the veranda, and while he was still wearing his sandals, he was trampled on the face with a crunching sound. "From the beginning, you, a lowly fellow like yourself, were taken into the lord's service, and he gave you an office you did not deserve; father and son both behaved beyond their station. And as if that were not enough, you falsely accused the innocent head of the Tendai sect and had him exiled, brought about a great national crisis, and moreover joined in a rebellion to destroy this clan. Confess everything as it is!" Confess everything as it is! Thus he spoke. Saikō was by nature a man of great courage, so he did not change color at all, nor did he show any sign of fear. He straightened himself up, laughed scornfully, and said, "That is exactly so. It is you, Lord Nyūdō, who have spoken beyond what is proper. I do not know about before others, but in a place where Saikō can hear, you cannot say such things. Since I am a person who serves in the imperial palace, I cannot say that I did not participate in the matter that was instigated by the imperial decree of the steward, the bettō Narichika. That was granted. But what things you say that linger in the ear! Although he was the son of the late Lord Tadamori of the Justice Ministry, until the age of fourteen or fifteen he did not even serve at court, and when he entered the household of the late Middle Counselor Fujinari of the Nakamikado Fujiwara, the Kyoto street boys called him 'Takahira-da'. In the Hoen era, as a reward for receiving the title of General and capturing more than thirty pirate ringleaders, he was promoted to the Fourth Rank, and even when he was called the Lieutenant of the Palace Guards of the Fourth Rank, people of that time said it was excessive. Being a descendant of a man who was even shunned from the palace floor, is it not excessive that he has risen to the rank of Grand Minister? It is not without precedent or parallel for a person of samurai status to become a zuryō or kebiishi. How could it be excessive? When he said this without any hesitation, the novice monk became extremely angry and could not speak. He had him beheaded, saying, "Cut off that fellow's head without hesitation!" Warn them thoroughly! Thus he declared. Matsuura Tarō Shigetoshi received the order, and tortured him in various ways, binding his hands and feet. Since he had not disputed from the beginning, the interrogation was severe. He confessed without omission. The confession was written down on four or five sheets, and immediately, saying 'Open his mouth,' they slit his mouth, and he was beheaded at Gojō-Suzaku. His eldest son, the former governor of Kaga, Morotaka, was exiled to Idota in Owari, but the local resident, the district magistrate Korekiyo of Kogoma, was ordered to kill him. His second son, the magistrate Kondo Moronori, was imprisoned, then taken out of prison and executed at Rokujo Kawara. His younger brother, the Left Gate Guard Morohira, and three retainers were beheaded together. These were the foremost of worthless fellows, who, in things they should not have done, incurred the wrath of the gods; the unerring Tendai Abbot was sentenced to exile, and perhaps his good fortune had run out; he incurred the divine punishment of Sannō and the Great Teacher on the spot, and met with such a fate.

[2.4.1] The new Grand Counselor was confined in a small room, drenched in sweat, and lamented, "Alas, this is because my long-standing secret affair has been leaked!" Who could have leaked it? Surely it must be among the northern guards, he thought, and as he sat there worrying endlessly, when from behind came the sound of footsteps, he thought, 'Ah, now they have come to take my life, the warriors are here,' and waited, but the priest himself came tramping loudly on the wooden floor, and abruptly slid open the sliding door behind which the Major Counselor was sitting. Wearing a short white silk robe, with a white hakama tucked up, and a sword with a hollyhock-crest scabbard thrust loosely at his side, he glared at the Major Counselor for a while with an extremely angry look and said, "Well now, you were already supposed to have been executed even in the Heiji Disturbance, but the Inner Minister exchanged his own life to plead for you and saved your neck—how is it that you now plot to destroy this clan?" For what grudge do you plot to destroy this clan? One who knows gratitude is called a human; one who does not know gratitude is called a beast. However, because the fortunes of our house had not yet run out, I was able to welcome him. I would like to hear directly the details of the construction you have been carrying out these past days. Thus he spoke. The Great Counselor said, "There is absolutely no such thing. It must be due to someone's slander." Please inquire thoroughly. When he said this, the novice monk could not finish speaking. "Is anyone there? Is anyone there?" When he called out, Sadanari came forward. "Make Saikō confess." When he said this, they brought it to him. Taking it, he read it over two or three times, pressing it back and forth, and said, "How hateful! What can I say now?" Saying this, he threw it at the Dainagon's face, slammed the sliding door shut, and went out. The priest, still unable to contain his anger, called out, "Tsunetoo! Kaneyasu!" and Seo no Taro and Naniwa no Jiro came forward. "Seize that man and throw him down into the garden!" When he said this, they could not refuse, and said, "What will Lord Komatsu's mood be?" When they said this, the Lay Monk Prime Minister became very angry and said, "Fine, fine! You fellows value the Inner Minister's orders and make light of the Lay Monk's commands, it seems. After that, it cannot be helped. When he said this, thinking that this matter would be bad, the two men stood up and pulled the Major Counselor down into the garden. At that time, the Lay Monk, looking pleased, said, "Seize him, throw him down, and make him cry out!" Thus he proclaimed. The two men put their mouths to the Great Counselor's left and right ears and whispered, "Somehow your voice should come out." When they whispered this and prostrated themselves, he cried out two or three times. That appearance, in the netherworld, when sinners of this world are put on the scales of karma or made to face the pure crystal mirror, and the torment inflicted by the demon Aborasetsu according to the gravity of their sins, seemed not to exceed this. Xiao and Fan were imprisoned, and Han and Peng were made into mincemeat. Chōsaku was executed, and Shūgi was punished. For example, Shōka, Han Shin, Hōetsu—these were all loyal retainers of Kōso, but because of the slander of petty men, even though they suffered the shame of failure, would they have said such things?

[2.4.2] As for the new Dainagon, even as his own situation had come to this, he could not help but worry about his son, the Junior Captain of Tamba, Naritsune, and the other young people, wondering what fate might befall them. In such intense heat of the sixth month, unable even to loosen their robes, the heat was unbearable; their chests felt as if they would burst, and sweat and tears flowed in competition. "Even so, Lord Komatsu would never abandon his compassionate intentions toward us." Though he said so, he did not think anyone would report it.

[2.4.3] Lord Komatsu, after a long time, placed his eldest son, the Provisional Middle Counselor, on the back of a carriage, and with four or five guards and two or three attendants, but without a single soldier, came in a very grand style. Beginning with the Novice, everyone looked at him with surprise. When he got down from the carriage, Sadayoshi came up to him and said, "Why, for such an important matter, have you not brought even one soldier?" When he said this, the reply was, "By 'important matter' I mean the great affairs of the realm; is there any way to call a private matter like this 'important'?" When he said this, even the soldiers who had been carrying weapons appeared restless. Where could the Major Counselor have been placed? As he looked, opening the sliding doors here and there, there was a place on one of the doors where a spider's web was tied. Thinking it might be here, when he opened it, the Major Counselor was sitting there. Choking with tears, he lay face down, and could not even meet his eyes. "What is the matter?" When he said this, the expression of joy on their faces as they looked up at him was like that of sinners in hell who see Jizō Bodhisattva, and it was deeply moving. "What could it be? I have met with such a fate." "But since you have come, I have relied on you, thinking that even so, you would help me." "In the Heiji Disturbance too, I was about to be executed, but by your grace my head was spared, and I rose to Senior Second Rank Grand Counselor, and my age has already exceeded forty." "Your grace is something I can never fully repay, even in all my lives to come." If it is the same this time as well, please spare my worthless life. If only my life is spared, I will become a monk, seclude myself in Kōya and Kokawa, and perform religious practices for my afterlife. When he said this, [the other] replied, "Even if that is so, I would never take your life. Even if it is so, because I, Shigemori, am here, I will take your place regarding your life. Saying this, he left. Sitting before my father, the lay monk, I said, "The matter of Lord Narichika's banishment—you must give it careful consideration." Since the time when our ancestor, the repair official Akisue, was summoned to serve Emperor Shirakawa, there has been no precedent in our family for rising to the rank of Senior Second Rank Grand Counselor, and now the Emperor's favor toward you is unparalleled. How could it be that he would soon be beheaded? If he were to be sent out of the capital, that would be sufficient. Kitano Tenjin, due to the slanderous report of Minister Tokihira, had his sorrowful name spread across the waves of the four seas; the Minister of Nishinomiya, due to the slander of Tada no Mitsunaka, entrusted his resentment to the clouds of Sanyo. Although each was without guilt, they were sentenced to exile. These are all said to be the misdeeds of the Engi era's sacred reign and Emperor Anwa's reign. Even in ancient times it was like this. How much more so in these latter days? Since you have already been summoned, even if you do not hasten to be killed, what suffering could there be? When punishment is doubtful, treat it lightly. When merit is doubtful, treat it generously. Thus it is written. Though it is a new matter, Shigemori is married to that Dainagon's younger sister. Koremori is also his son-in-law. Since I have become so close to you, you may think I am saying this out of personal feeling. It is not that. I say this for the sake of the world, for the sake of the sovereign, and for the sake of the family. It was during the time when the late Shōnagon Nyūdō Shinzei held power, and in our realm, from the time of Emperor Saga, when Uhyōe-no-kami Fujiwara no Nakanari was executed, until the Hōgen era, through twenty-five imperial reigns, the death penalty had not been carried out; but he revived it, and had the corpse of Uji no Aku-safu dug up and inspected—such acts I felt were excessive governance. Therefore, the ancients also said, 'If you carry out the death penalty, rebels in the realm will never cease.' That is what has been passed down. Following these words, after two years, in the Heiji era the world was again thrown into turmoil, and they dug up Shinzei's buried remains, cut off his head, and paraded it through the streets. The things that were carried out in the Hogen era, before long, came back upon his own person, and when he thought of that, it was truly frightening. This is not such a great enemy of the court. There must be fear on all sides. Since there is no place where the glory remains, although you may not think so, prosperity should continue even to your descendants. It seems that the good and evil of one's ancestors inevitably extends to their descendants. I have heard that a house that accumulates good deeds will surely have abundant blessings, while a house that accumulates evil deeds will surely have abundant calamities. In any case, being beheaded tonight is not something that should happen. When he said this, the Lay Monk Chancellor thought, "Indeed, that may be so," and the death sentence was stayed.

[2.4.4] After that, the Minister came out to the middle gate and said to his retainers, "Even though it is an imperial command, you must not kill the Major Counselor without good reason." If the Novice, in his anger, causes a disturbance, he will surely regret it later. Do not do anything wrong and make me resent you. When he said this, all the warriors trembled with fear, sticking out their tongues. "Even so, how strange it is that Tsuneto and Kaneyasu treated the Major Counselor so heartlessly this morning!" Why should he not fear the place where Shigemori will hear? The country folk are like that. When he said that, both Naniwa and Seo were deeply ashamed. The Minister spoke thus and returned to the Komatsu mansion. Meanwhile, the samurai who had accompanied the Dainagon ran back to the residence at Nakamikado Karasuma and reported this, and the ladies of the northern quarter and others cried out without restraint. Already the warriors are facing you. They say that beginning with the Major Captain, you lords too will be captured. Quickly, hide yourself somewhere. When he said this, [the other replied,] "Now that I have become a person of this lowly state, even if I remain behind, what could I do in peace? It is my true desire to vanish like the dew of a single night. How sad it was, not knowing that this morning would be the last! Saying this, she threw herself down and wept. When it was heard that the warriors were already approaching, thinking that it would be shameful and unpleasant to see such a sight, they put their ten-year-old daughter and eight-year-old son into a carriage and sent them off without any particular destination. Since it was not something that could be left as it was, they went up to the capital and stayed at Unrin'in in the Kitayama area. They left them at a monk's lodging nearby, and the escorts, finding it hard to part, took their leave and returned. Now only young people remained, and with no one to ask after her, the feelings of the Lady of the North must have been pitiable to imagine. As she watched the setting sun, she felt that the Dainagon's dew-like life would surely end this evening, and she herself seemed about to vanish. Although there were many court ladies and attendants, they could not even put away a single thing, nor even push open a gate. Although the horses were lined up in the stable, there was not a single person to feed them grass. When dawn broke, horses and carriages lined up at the gate, guests took their seats, they played and danced, and did not think of the world as the world; people nearby did not even speak loudly, and until yesterday they had been in fear and awe, but in the space of a night the scene changed—the principle that the prosperous must decline was manifest before their very eyes. The traces of the brush of Lord Jiang, where it is written that 'when pleasure ends, sorrow comes,' are now truly appreciated.

[2.5.1] The Lesser Captain of Tamba, Naritsune, had gone up to the Imperial Palace at Hōjūji that very night and was staying there, and had not yet come out, when the Major Counselor's retainers rushed to the palace, called out the Lesser Captain, and informed him of this matter. He said, 'Why has there been no notification from the Counselor's place until now?' He had not even finished speaking when a messenger arrived from the Counselor's residence. This Counselor was the younger brother of the Lay Monk Prime Minister, and because his residence was inside the main gate of Rokuhara, he was called the Counselor of the Gate Side. He was the father-in-law of the Lesser Captain of Tamba. "What is the matter? The Lay Monk Prime Minister says to bring you quickly to Nishi-Hachijo." When he was told this, the young captain understood the situation, summoned his close serving women, and said, "During the night, I felt somehow uneasy about the world, thinking it was just the usual mountain monks coming down, but it turned out to be about Naritsune himself." Since the Great Counselor is to be executed tonight, Naritsune too will surely share the same fate. I would like to go to the palace once more and see His Majesty, but since I have already fallen into such a state, I hesitate. Thus he spoke. When the court ladies came before him and reported this matter, the Cloistered Emperor was greatly startled and said, "So that is why the Lay Monk Prime Minister's messenger came so early this morning." "Ah, so their secret plot has leaked out!" " he thought, and was appalled. "Even so, come here." When he indicated his wish, they came before him. The Cloistered Emperor also shed tears, and had no words to command. The Lesser Captain also choked with tears and had no words to say. Since it was not right for him to remain any longer, the captain pressed his sleeve to his face and departed in tears. The Retired Emperor watched him go from afar, and said, "How sad it is that this is the last time I shall see him in this world!" and shed tears, which was most touching. All the people in the palace clung to the captain's sleeves and hems, lamenting his departure, and there was no one who did not shed tears.

[2.5.2] When he went out to the residence of his father-in-law, the Chancellor, the lady of the north was a person who was soon to give birth, but from this morning, adding this grief, she already felt as if her life was fading away. From the time the young captain left the palace, his flowing tears did not cease, and when he saw the state of the lady of the north, he appeared all the more helpless. There was a lady-in-waiting named Rokujo, the young captain's wet nurse. "When I first began to serve as your wet nurse, I took you up in my arms from within the swaddling clothes, and as months and days piled up, I did not lament the passing of my own years, but only rejoiced in your growing up, and though I knew it was presumptuous, for twenty-one years I have never been apart from you even for a moment. When you go to the palace and even your return is late, I worry anxiously; what kind of misfortune might befall you? " she said, weeping. The young captain said, "How painful!" The Chancellor, sitting there, said, "Even if my life is spared, I will surely beg for your pardon." He tried to console her, but she wept and grieved without regard for others' eyes.

[2.5.3] Because messengers came from Nishi-Hachijo-dono in rapid succession, the Chancellor said, "I will go to meet them; somehow things will work out." Saying this, he went out, and the Major Captain also got into the carriage behind the Chancellor and went out. Since the Hogen and Heiji eras, the Heike family had known only prosperity and had no sorrows, but this Chancellor alone, because of his worthless son-in-law, was made to lament thus. When they approached Nishi-Hachijo and stopped the carriage, and first sent in a message, the Prime Minister said, "The Major Captain of Tamba must not be allowed to enter here." While he was saying this, they let him down at the house of a samurai nearby, and only the Chancellor entered the gate. The soldiers quickly surrounded the Major Captain and guarded him. He departed from the Chancellor, to whom he had been attached. In the heart of the young captain, how helpless he must have felt. When the Chancellor was seated at the middle gate, the Novice did not even meet him. Through Minamoto no Daibu Hangan Kanesada he sent in a message: "Having become intimate with a worthless person, I am deeply regretful, but it is of no avail. The person I have brought with me has been ill for some time, and since this morning, adding this grief, his life is about to end." Why should there be any pain? Please entrust the young captain to Norimori for a while. Since Norimori is here, why would he let him do anything wrong? When he said this, Kiyosada came and reported the matter. Alas, that usual Minister of State, he doesn't understand things. Saying this, he did not reply at all. Then the lay priest said, "The new Dainagon Narichika has a plot to destroy this clan and throw the realm into chaos. This young captain is already the eldest son of that Dainagon. Whether distant or close, I cannot intercede for him. If this rebellion had succeeded, would even you have been safe?" he said. Thus he said. When Kanesada returned and reported this to the Chancellor, he seemed truly disappointed, and spoke again: "Since the Hōgen and Heiji eras, in battle after battle, I have thought to give my life in your place." Even after this, if we first ward off the rough wind, even if Norimori is old, since there are many young children, how could he not serve as a guard for one side? When they said that Naritsune should be entrusted to him for a while, the fact that you did not accept it means that you must think Norimori is entirely of two minds. If I am thought of with such suspicion, what is the point of remaining in this world? Now, if only I could receive leave for myself, become a monk, retire to a remote mountain village, and devote myself single-mindedly to the practice for enlightenment in the next life. It is a meaningless association in this sorrowful world. Because we are in the world, we have desires; because our desires are not fulfilled, we have resentment. Would it not be better to renounce this sorrowful world and enter the true path? Thus he spoke. Suesada came and said, "The Chancellor has already made up his mind to become a monk." Please arrange it in some suitable way." When he said this, the Lay Monk was greatly startled and said, "Even so, to go so far as to become a monk is too outrageous. If that is the case, we should say that we will entrust the young lord to your care for a while." Thus he spoke. Suesada returned and reported this to the Chancellor, who said, "Alas, one should never have children!" If I had not been bound by ties to my child, I would not have suffered so!" Saying this, he went out.

[2.5.4] The young captain awaited him and said, "Well, how did it go?" When he said this, the other replied, "The novice became extremely angry and in the end did not even grant an audience to Norimori. He repeatedly said that it was impossible, but perhaps because I even mentioned becoming a monk, he said to lodge me for a while, but I do not feel that it will go well in the end. "That is exactly why, thanks to your favor, Naritsune too may have his life prolonged for a while." Regarding that, what have you heard about the Major Counselor? "Until then, I had not even thought of it." When he said this, she shed tears and said, "Truly, by your gracious favor, it would be proper for me to live a little longer, but my regretting my life is because I wish to see my father once more." If the Dainagon is to be executed, then even for Naritsune, what use would there be in keeping this worthless life? Would it be possible for you to arrange things so that I might somehow be alone with him? When he said this, the Chancellor, looking very troubled, said, "Well, it is about you that I have been saying this and that. I had not thought that far, but as for the matter of the Major Counselor, since the Minister of the Interior has been saying various things about it since this morning, I have heard that for the time being it seems to be safe. When he said this, the captain, weeping, clasped his hands in joy. "Who, if not a child, would rejoice to this extent, setting aside his own situation right now? The true bond was indeed between parent and child. A child is something one should have, isn't it? And so he thought, and immediately his thoughts were returned. Then, as in the morning, they rode together in the same carriage and returned. At the lodging, the court ladies felt as if a dead person had come back to life, and gathering around, they all wept for joy.

div.head: 2.6. 教訓状

div.p: [2.6.1] The Grand Minister of State, even though he had bound so many people, still seemed not to be satisfied. He wore a red brocade hitatare, a belly band laced with black leather, a chest plate with white metal fittings, and at his side he carried the small halberd with silver inlay that he had received in a dream from the Great Deity of Itsukushima when he was Governor of Aki and had prayed at the shrine; he came out to the corridor of the middle gate. His appearance seemed truly dreadful. He summons Sadayoshi. Chikugo no kami Sadayoshi, wearing a hitatare of mokuranji and armor laced with scarlet leather, sits respectfully before him. After a while, the lay priest said, "Sadanori, what do you think of this matter?" In the Hogen era, starting with Taira no Umanosuke, more than half of the clan went over to the side of the Retired Emperor. As for the First Prince, since he had been the adopted son of the late Lord of the Bureau of Justice, it was hard to abandon him in every way, but following the late Retired Emperor's final admonition, I took his side and was the first to ride out. This was my first act of service. Next, in the first year of Heiji, in the twelfth month, when Nobuyori and Yoshitomo seized the Retired Emperor, barricaded themselves in the Imperial Palace, and plunged the realm into darkness, I, the Novice, threw away my life, drove off the rebels, and even went so far as to have Tsunemune and Korekata arrested; time and again I came close to losing my life for the sake of His Majesty. No matter what people may say, how could you ever abandon this clan for seven generations? Moreover, that useless fellow Narichika and the low-born, insolent Saikō—it is truly a matter of regret that you have been persuaded by their words to destroy this clan, as the Retired Emperor has planned. If there is anyone who slanders us after this, know that an imperial decree for the subjugation of our house will be issued. Once you have become an enemy of the court, no matter how much you regret it, it will be of no use. To pacify the world, should we move the Retired Emperor to the North Hall of Toba, or should we bring him here and have him make an imperial visit? What do you think? If that is the case, the northern guards will surely shoot even an arrow. Tell the samurai to prepare for that. For the most part, they have given up their service to the Retired Emperor's side. Put a saddle on the horse. Take out the long sword. Thus he declared.

[2.6.2] Morikuni, the Master of the Horse, hurried to Lord Komatsu's mansion and said, "The world has already come to this." When he said this, the Minister could not bear to listen. "Ah, has Narichika's head been cut off?" He said, "That is not so, but Lord Nyudo has put on his armor." The samurai all set out, intending to go to Hōjūji-dono. They intended to confine the Retired Emperor in Toba-dono, but secretly they planned to exile him to the western provinces. When he said this, the Minister thought, "How could such a thing be?" but, thinking that the priest's mood this morning might indeed be something frantic, he had his carriage speed along and went to Nishi-Hachijo.

[2.6.3] He got down from the carriage at the gate, and when he entered inside the gate and looked, the priest had put on a belly band, and above that, dozens of court nobles and chamberlains of the clan, each in various colored hitatare and wearing armor of their own choosing, were seated in two rows on the corridor of the middle gate. Besides them, provincial governors, officials of the guards and various offices, and others overflowed onto the veranda and stood packed together even in the garden. They were all pulling their banner poles askew, tightening their horses' girths, and fastening their helmet cords, looking as if they were about to set out at any moment, when Lord Komatsu, wearing a court cap and informal robe with trailing trousers of large pattern, tucked up the sides and came in with a rustle, and he appeared most extraordinary.

[2.6.4] The lay monk, with narrowed eyes, thought that the Inner Minister was behaving as if he would destroy the world, and he wanted to remonstrate strongly. But even though he was his son, the Inner Minister was a man who inwardly kept the five precepts and put compassion first, and outwardly did not violate the five constant virtues and performed propriety correctly. So the lay monk felt ashamed and embarrassed to face him wearing a belly armor in that appearance. He slightly opened the sliding door, and hurriedly put on a plain silk robe over the belly armor. The metal fittings of the breastplate were slightly visible, and he repeatedly pulled the front of the robe to hide them. The Minister takes his seat above his younger brother, Lord Munemori. The Lay Monk did not speak out, and the Minister also had nothing to say.

[2.6.5] After a while, the Lay Monk said, "Narichika's rebellion is not even worth counting among such matters. It was entirely the Cloistered Emperor's construction. To pacify the realm, shall we move the Cloistered Emperor to the North Hall of Toba, or if not, shall we have him come here and make an imperial visit? What do you think? When he said this, the Minister could not bear to hear it and wept profusely. The Lay Monk said, "What is it? What is it?" He said in astonishment, "What is it? What is it?" The Minister, holding back tears, said: "Hearing this command, I feel that your fortune has already come to an end. When a person's fortune is about to decline, they invariably conceive evil deeds. Moreover, your appearance does not seem at all like that of this world. Still, although our country is called a remote land of scattered millet, since the descendants of Amaterasu Omikami have ruled as sovereigns, and since the descendants of Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto have administered the government, is it not a violation of propriety for a person who has attained the office of Grand Minister to wear armor? Above all, you are now in the state of having renounced the world. To cast off the robes of the Three-World Buddhas, the garment of liberation, and suddenly don armor and gird on bow and arrows—this not only invites within the sin of breaking precepts without shame, but also goes against the external laws of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and good faith. This is a matter I mention with great trepidation, but I should not leave my true intention hidden in the depths of my heart. In previous lives there are four debts of gratitude. They are the debt to heaven and earth, the debt to the sovereign, the debt to parents, and the debt to all living beings. Among these, the most important is the debt to the sovereign. There is no saying that under heaven is not the king's land. Therefore, even the wise men who washed their ears in the waters of the Ying River and picked ferns on Mount Shouyang knew that it is hard to disobey an imperial command. How much more so, having attained the rank of Grand Minister, unheard of even among his ancestors. That is to say, Shigemori, with his untalented and ignorant person, has reached the rank of the Lotus Office and the Sophora Gate. Moreover, more than half of the provinces have become the clan's domain, and all the fields and gardens are under the family's control. Is this not an unprecedented imperial favor? Now, if you forget these great favors and recklessly attempt to overthrow the Cloistered Emperor, you will surely go against the divine will of Amaterasu Omikami and the deity of Hachiman Shrine. Japan is a divine country. The gods do not accept impropriety. Therefore, the place where the lord's thoughts have settled is not without reason. Above all, this clan, having subdued the enemies of the court for generations and calmed the rebellious waves of the four seas, is a loyalty without peer; yet to boast of its rewards is, one might say, utterly arrogant. In the Seventeen-Article Constitution of Prince Shotoku: "All people have minds, and each has his own convictions. They regard others as right and themselves as wrong, or themselves as right and others as wrong. Who can determine the truth of right and wrong? Together they are wise and foolish. Like a ring, it has no end. Therefore, even if people become angry, rather fear your own fault. That is how it appears. However, because your fortune has not yet run out, your rebellion has already been exposed. Moreover, since you have summoned and kept Lord Narichika, who was ordered to be summoned, even if the lord conceives some strange idea, what fear could there be? After the appropriate punishment is carried out, if you withdraw and state the circumstances, and for the lord's sake exert even greater loyalty and diligence, and for the people's sake show even more compassion and care, you will receive the protection of the gods and will not go against the hidden intentions of the Buddha. If the gods and Buddhas respond, how could the lord not change his mind? When comparing lord and vassal, there is no way to distinguish between close and distant. When lining up reason and wrong, how could one not side with reason?

div.note: [_] [2] Nihon Koten Bungaku Taikei (Tokyo: Iwanami Shoten, 1957, vol. 32; hereafter cited as NKBT) reads 筑後守貞能、木蘭地の直垂に.

div.p: [2.7.1] Since this is the lord's will, even if it cannot be fulfilled, I will protect the retired emperor's residence, Hōjūji Palace. The reason is that from Shigemori's first court rank to his present position as minister and general, there is nothing that is not the lord's favor. When I think of the weight of that favor, it surpasses a thousand or ten thousand jewels; when I consider the depth of that favor's color, it exceeds crimson dyed once or twice again. If so, I shall go into the palace and remain in attendance. If it comes to that, the retainers who have pledged to give their lives in place of Shigemori are few indeed. If I take these men and guard the retired emperor's palace, Hōjūji-dono, it would surely be an extraordinary and grave matter. Alas, if I try to show loyalty to my lord, I would suddenly forget the kindness of my father, which is higher than the peak of Mount Sumeru. Alas! If I try to escape the sin of filial impiety, I will surely become a disloyal traitor to my lord. I am caught between a rock and a hard place. It is truly difficult to decide either way. What I request is simply: take Shigemori's head. I cannot even protect the imperial palace. I must not even serve as an attendant on the imperial visit. That Xiao He, because his great achievements surpassed others, rose to the rank of Grand Chancellor, and although he was permitted to ascend to the palace hall wearing a sword and shoes, when he acted against the imperial will, Emperor Gaozu severely admonished him and punished him heavily. When I think of such precedents, whether it be wealth and rank, glory, imperial favor, or high office, since you have attained the utmost in all of them, it should not be difficult for your fortune to come to an end. How long should I live and see the world in chaos? It is only that I, Shigemori, who was born in these latter days and has met with such sorrow, have a wretched lot. Right now, if I were to order a single retainer to drag you out into the courtyard and have Shigemori's head cut off, it would be an easy matter indeed. Listen to this, all of you! So saying, he shed tears until the sleeves of his court robe were soaked, and as he wept and lamented, all the members of the clan, both those with feeling and those without, wet their sleeves as well.

[2.7.2] The Prime Minister, who had been so trusted, spoke thus. Feeling helpless, he said, "No, no, I never imagined it would come to this." I am only thinking that, because you have been swayed by what the villains say, some wrongdoing might occur. When he said this, the Minister replied, "Even if some wrongdoing occurs, how could I possibly fail to protect you?" Saying this, he went out to the middle gate and addressed his retainers: "Did you not hear what Shigemori just said?" Since this morning I have been here, thinking to calm such matters, but because it seemed too noisy, I returned. As for accompanying the retired emperor, watch for Shigemori's head being taken, and then serve. Then, enter. Saying thus, he returned to the Komatsu mansion. He summoned the Master of the Horse, Morikuni, and said, "Shigemori has indeed heard of a great matter of the realm. Announce that all who consider themselves my men should arm themselves and hasten here!" When he said this, this message was announced. "A person who does not make a fuss when it is vague—there must be some special reason for such an announcement." "So saying, they all armed themselves and each rushed to the scene." In the villages of Yodo, Hazukashi, Uji, Okaya, Hino, Kanjuji, Daigo, Ogurisu, Umezu, Katsura, Ohara, Shizuhara, and Seriu, the warriors who were overflowing—some wore armor but had not yet put on their helmets, and some carried arrows but did not yet hold bows. With one stirrup not yet stepped into, they rushed in confusion, making a clamor. When it was heard that there was a commotion at Komatsu-dono, the several thousand warriors who were at Nishi-Hachijo, without even informing the novice, all rushed in a clamor to Komatsu-dono. Not a single person who had any connection with bow and arrow remained. At that time, the Lay Monk was greatly startled, summoned Sadayoshi, and said, "What is the Inner Minister thinking, that he has summoned these men?" As you say, perhaps they are sending a punitive force against the Lay Monk. When he said this, Sadayoshi shed tears and said, "People do depend on people, my lord." How could such a thing happen?" All the things you have said here will surely be regretted by you. When he said this, the Novice, thinking that if he were to oppose the Inner Minister, it would be bad, perhaps thought so. The Cloistered Emperor, having given up the idea of sending a message, took off his armor, put a surplice over his plain silk robe, and sat there chanting prayers that did not even arise from his heart.

[2.7.3] At Komatsu-dono, Morikuni received the order and recorded the arrival. The forces that had rushed to join were recorded as more than ten thousand horsemen. After the roll call and inspection, the minister came out to the middle gate and announced to his retainers: "It is admirable that you have come without breaking your promise of these days." There is such an example in a foreign country. King You of Zhou had a most beloved queen named Bao Si. She was the most beautiful woman in the world. However, the one thing that did not please King You was that Bao Si never smiled, and she never laughed at all. In foreign lands, when war breaks out across the realm, they light fires in various places, beat drums, and have a plan to summon soldiers. This is called a beacon fire. Once, when war broke out across the realm and beacon fires were raised, the Empress saw them and said, 'How strange! There were that many fires!' So saying, for the first time she smiled. After this, when she smiled once, she had a hundred charms. King You, thinking it amusing, would often light the beacon fires for that purpose. The feudal lords came, but there was no enemy. Since there was no enemy, they immediately left. When this happened repeatedly, there were no longer any who came. Once, when bandits arose from a neighboring country and attacked King You's capital, although he raised the beacon fires, the soldiers, accustomed to the usual fires for the queen, did not come. At that time the capital fell, and King You finally perished. Now, this empress turned into a fox and ran away—how frightening! Since such things happen, from now on, if you are summoned, you should all come like this. Shigemori heard of this strange matter and summoned (him). However, upon hearing this matter directly, it turned out to be a mistake. Go back quickly! Saying this, they were all sent back. In truth, although he had not heard of any particular deed, following the words with which he had admonished his father, he knew whether his own power was rising or not, and though it was not that they intended to fight as father and son, it was a plan to thus soften the Nyudo Prime Minister's rebellious intentions. Even if the lord is not lordly, the retainer must not be unretainerly; even if the father is not fatherly, the son must not be unsonly. For the lord there is loyalty, and for the father there is filial piety. And so it was not contrary to what Confucius had declared. When the lord heard this, he said, "Though it is not something that has just begun, the heart of the Inner Minister is indeed shameful." He has repaid enmity with kindness. Thus he spoke. "How auspicious is his fortune! He will surely rise to become both Minister and Grand General." In bearing and attire he surpassed others, and even in wisdom and learning he must have excelled the world. Thus the people of the time felt admiration. "If there is a minister who admonishes the country, that country is at peace; if there is a son who admonishes the family, that family is surely upright." So it is said. He was a minister rare in both ancient and later ages.
