[2.8.1] On the second day of the sixth month, when they brought out the new Grand Counselor Narichika to the seats of the court nobles and served him food, his chest was so choked that he could not even lift his chopsticks. When they brought the carriage close and said, "Quickly, quickly," the Grand Counselor reluctantly boarded. Soldiers surrounded him on all sides, front, back, left, and right. There was not a single one of my own men. "If only I could see Lord Komatsu once more." Though he said so, even that was not granted. "Even those who incur grave crimes and are sent to distant provinces—is there anyone who does not have at least one person to accompany them?" As she lamented thus inside the carriage, even the warrior guards all wet their armor sleeves with tears. As they went south along West Suzaku Avenue, even the Imperial Palace now seemed a place apart. Even down to the miscellaneous servants and ox-drivers who had long served and become familiar with them, there was none who did not shed tears and wring their sleeves. The hearts of the few people of the northern quarter who remained behind in the capital, left behind as the others increased, can be imagined and are sorrowful. Even when passing Toba-dono, thinking that when he went to this palace, he had never once been left out of the imperial escort, he passed by, seeing from afar the place called his own mountain villa, Suhama-dono. They went out to the south gate and hurried the boat. "Where are we being taken? If we are to perish anyway, let it be near the capital, even here." These words were spoken in desperation.

[2.8.2] When he asked the warrior who had come close to him, "Who are you?", the man replied, "I am Nanba Jirō Tsunetō." "Is there anyone of our side around here? There is something I must tell you before you board the boat. Go and search for them. When he said this, they ran around searching that area, but there was not a single person who said, "I am of the Dainagon's side." When I was in power, I must have had a thousand or two thousand followers who attended me. Now, how sad it is that there is no one even from afar to see me off in this state! When she said this, even the fierce warriors all wet their sleeves with tears. The only thing that accompanies one's body is endless tears. On pilgrimages to Kumano and Tennoji, they used to ride in boats built with two ridges and three gables, with twenty or thirty boats rowing in succession; but now, in a strange, hastily built roofed boat with a large curtain hung, accompanied by unfamiliar soldiers, setting out from the capital for the last time, the feelings of one heading far over the waves can be imagined and are sorrowful. That day they arrived at the bay of Ōmono in Settsu Province.

[2.8.3] The fact that the new Dainagon, who was to have been executed, was pardoned and exiled was due to Lord Komatsu's repeated intercession. When this man was still a Middle Counselor, he held Mino Province as a fief. In the winter of the first year of Kaō, when a shrine servant from the Heian Shrine estate of Hiranoshō came to the deputy governor Uemon no Jō Masatomo's place to sell kudzu, the deputy got drunk on sake and smeared ink on the kudzu. When the shrine servant began to curse, the deputy said, "Don't say that!" and beat him severely. In the meantime, several hundred shrine servants broke into the deputy's place. When the deputy governor resisted according to the law, more than ten shrine servants were struck down and killed. Because of this, on the third day of the eleventh month of the same year, the monks of the mountain temple rose up in great numbers, and it was reported to the throne that the provincial governor, Lord Narichika, should be sentenced to exile, and the deputy governor, Uemon no Jō Masatomo, should be imprisoned. Narichika had already been sent into exile to Bitchū Province, and had been brought as far as Nishi-no-Shichijō, when the Emperor, perhaps thinking something, after five days summoned him back. Although it was heard that the monks of the mountain temple were cursing him violently, on the fifth day of the first month of the same year, he was appointed both Uemon-no-kami and Kebiishi-no-bettō. At that time, Sukekata was passed over by Lord Kanemasa. Lord Sukekata was an old man and was mature. Lord Kanemasa was a man of prosperity. It was regrettable that he was surpassed as the heir. This was a reward for the construction of the Sanjo Palace. In the same year, on the thirteenth day of the fourth month, he was promoted to Senior Second Rank. At that time, the Middle Counselor Muneyoshi of Nakamikado crossed over. On the twenty-seventh day of the tenth month of Angen 1, he was promoted from former Middle Counselor to Provisional Major Counselor. People mocked him, saying, "He should have been cursed by the monks of Enryakuji." they said. Nevertheless, perhaps because of that, he met with such a misfortune. In general, the punishments of the gods and the curses of people may come quickly or slowly; it is not uniform.

[2.8.4] On the same third day, there was a great commotion at the harbor of Ōmono because an imperial messenger had come from the capital. The new Dainagon said, "Is it that I am to be killed there?" When he heard this, it was not so; the imperial messenger said that he was to be exiled to Kojima in Bizen. There was a letter from Lord Komatsu. "Somehow, I wish I could have placed you in a mountain village near the capital, but though I pleaded so, it was not to be; there is nothing to be done in this world." Nevertheless, I beg only for your life. "Saying this, he sent word to Nanba as well: "Be sure to serve at court without any lapse." "Thus he sent the message, and arranged and sent off the travel attire in every detail. The new Dainagon, parting from the lord he had so gratefully cherished, and bidding farewell to the young ladies of the northern wing whom he had found so hard to leave even for a moment, wondered, "Where am I going?" It would be difficult to return to my hometown again and see my wife and children. Last year, because of the lawsuit of the temple, when I was exiled, the lord felt sorry for me and summoned me back from Nishi-no-Shichijo. This is not the lord's admonition. What is this that has happened? Saying this, he looked up to heaven and bowed down to the earth, weeping and grieving, but it was of no avail. When dawn broke, the boat was pushed out and they departed; all along the way they were choked with tears, and though they did not think they could survive, still their dew-like lives did not vanish. As the white waves of their wake separated them, the capital gradually receded, and as the days piled up, the distant provinces drew near. They rowed to Kojima in Bizen and placed him in a humble brushwood hut that looked like a commoner's dwelling. As is the way of islands, behind was a mountain, before was the sea; the wind in the pines on the shore and the sound of the waves—none failed to evoke sorrow.

[2.9.1] Not only the Dainagon—there were many who incurred punishment. Ōmi no Chūjō Nyūdō Renshō was appointed to Sado Province, Yamashiro no Kami Motokane to Hōki Province, Shikibu no Taifu Masatsuna to Harima Province, Sō no Hangan Nobufusa to Awa Province, and Shinpei Hangan Sukeyuki to Mimasaka Province—so it was heard.

[2.9.2] At that time, the Lay Monk Chancellor was at his villa in Fukuhara, and on the twentieth of the same month, he sent Settsu no Saemon Morizumi as a messenger to the Chancellor of the Gate with the message, "I have something in mind." Tamba no Shōshō, come here quickly. When the Chancellor received this message, he said, "Well then, if it had come to this while I was still alive, what would I do?" It would be sad to make me worry now, after all this time. Saying this, he announced that he would go down to Fukuhara, and the young captain set out weeping. The court ladies lamented, "Since it will not be granted, still, if only the Counselor would speak!" The Counselor said, "I have said all that I can think of. What else could I say now, other than to abandon the world? However, wherever you may be, as long as my life lasts, I will come to visit you. Thus he spoke. The young captain had a child who was three years old this year. In ordinary times, being a young person, he had not been particularly intimate with the young lords and such, but when it came to his final hour, perhaps it weighed on his mind. "If only I could see this little one once more." Thus he said. The wet nurse held him and came out. The young captain placed him on his lap, stroked his hair, and shedding tears, said, "Alas, when you turn seven, I thought I would make you a man and present you to the lord." But now it is useless to say so. If you survive and grow up, become a monk and pray for my afterlife. When he said this, though the child was still too young to understand anything, he nodded, and the young captain, the wet nurse, the mother, and all the people sitting there, both those with feeling and those without, wet their sleeves with tears. The imperial messenger from Fukuhara was to depart that very night as far as Toba, so he said, "Since it will not be delayed for long, let me at least spend this one night within the capital." Though he said this, they urged him repeatedly, and that night he departed for Toba. The Chancellor, in his extreme bitterness, did not even bring his horse this time.

[2.9.3] On the twenty-second of the same month, when he arrived at Fukuhara, the Nyudo (lay monk) of the Great Council of State ordered Seto no Taro Kaneyasu, and he was exiled to Bitchu Province. Kaneyasu, fearing the place where the Chancellor would hear of his return, comforted and consoled him in various ways along the road. Nevertheless, the young captain found no consolation at all. Day and night he only chanted the Buddha's name and lamented his father. Shin Dainagon, who was in Kojima of Bizen, was transferred to the mainland by the guard samurai Namba Jirō Tsunetō, who thought that Kojima was still too close to the port and dangerous, and was placed in a mountain temple called Ariki no Bessho in the village of Niwase, on the border of Bizen and Bitchū provinces. The distance between Bitchū's Seo and Bizen's Aruki no Bessho was barely fifty chō, so perhaps even Tanba no Shōshō felt a pang of longing for that direction; one time he summoned Kaneyasu and asked, "How far is it from here to Bizen's Aruki no Bessho, where the Dainagon is said to be crossing over?" When he asked, Kaneyasu thought that if he told him directly it would be bad, so he said, "It is twelve or thirteen leagues one way." he said. At that time, the young captain shed tears and said, "Japan was once thirty-three provinces, but later it was divided into sixty-six provinces." Even Bizen, Bitchū, and Bingo, which are called that, were originally one province. Also, the two provinces of Dewa and Mutsu, which are heard of to the east, were formerly a single province of sixty-six districts, but at that time twelve districts were divided off and it was established as the province of Dewa. Now, when the Middle Captain Sanekata was exiled to Oshu, he wanted to see the famous place in that province called the Pine of Akoya, and so he wandered about the province searching for it. When he was returning, unable to find it, an old man happened to meet him on the way, and said, "Well now, I see that you are an old person. Do you know the place called the Pine of Akoya, a famous spot in this province?" When he asked, "Is it not in this province? Perhaps it is in Dewa Province?" When he said that, "Then you did not know either." It is because, as the world has declined, people have already forgotten the names of famous places in the province. Saying so, he was about to pass by in vain, when the old man grabbed the sleeve of the Middle Counselor and said, "Alas, my lord,"

lg.l: みちのくの阿古耶の松に木隱て、出べき月の出もやらぬか。

div.p: [2.9.4] Is it by the spirit of the poem that you call it the famous pine of Akoya in this province? That is a poem composed when the two provinces were one. After dividing the twelve districts, is it in Dewa Province? When he said that, 'Then,' and Sanekata no Chūjō also went over to Dewa Province and saw the Pine of Akoya. From the Dazaifu of Tsukushi to the capital, the messenger of the haragai goes up, and it is fixed as fifteen days for the one-way journey. When it is already said to be twelve or thirteen days, from here it is almost a journey down to the western provinces. Even if you say it is far, between Bizen and Bichū, it would not take more than two or three days. To say that what is near is far is surely because they do not want Naritsune to know that the Dainagon has crossed over. And after that, though she longed for him, she did not ask.

[2.10.1] In the meantime, the administrator of Hosshō-ji, Shunkan, the Hei lieutenant Yasuyori, and this captain were exiled together to Kikaigashima in Satsuma Bay. That island is a place one reaches after leaving the capital and traveling far over the waves. Even boats do not pass by casually. On the island, people are rare. Although there are people, they do not resemble the people of this land. They are dark-skinned, like cattle. On their bodies, hair grows thickly, and they do not understand speech. The men did not even wear eboshi caps, and the women did not let their hair hang down. Without clothing, they did not even resemble human beings. Since there was nothing to eat, they made killing living beings their sole priority. Because the lowly people did not plow their mountain fields, there was no rice or grain; because they did not pick mulberry leaves from the gardens, there was no silk or cloth. Within the island there is a high mountain. Fire burns in the garrison. It is filled with a substance called sulfur. For that reason, it was also named Sulfur Island. Thunder constantly roars up and roars down, and at the foot of the mountain rain is frequent. There is no way that a person's life can endure even for a single day or a moment.

[2.10.2] Meanwhile, when the new Dainagon thought he might relax a little, he heard that his son, the Junior Captain of Tamba, Naritsune, had already been exiled to Kikaigashima. Now, thinking there was no point in remaining so indifferent, he decided to become a monk. He sent word of his intention to take the tonsure to Lord Komatsu through a convenient opportunity. When this was reported to the Cloistered Emperor, permission was granted. He immediately took the tonsure. She turned back the sleeves of her glory days and, in the ink-black sleeves of a nun, she hid herself away from the floating world.

[2.10.3] The Dainagon's wife was secretly staying near Unrin'in in the northern hills of the capital. Even without that, an unfamiliar place is depressing, and since she had to hide herself all the more, the passing months and days were spent in a state of being unable to endure the daylight and troubled by the evenings. Although there were many court ladies and attendants, some feared the world, and some were ashamed of public eyes, so there was not a single person who came to visit. However, among them, there was one samurai named Minamoto no Sadaemon no Jō Nobutoshi, whose compassion was especially deep, and he always visited and served her. One time, the lady summoned Nobutoshi and said, "Is it true that the one known as Kojima of Bizen is now staying at a detached residence in Ariki?" Somehow, I would like to once again send even a fleeting trace of my brush and hear some word from him. Thus she spoke. Nobutoshi, holding back tears, said: "Since my childhood, I have received your gracious favor, and have never left your side even for a moment." Even when you went down (from the capital), I said I would somehow accompany you, but since I was detained by Rokuhara, I was unable to do so. The voice with which you summoned me remains in my ears, and the words with which you admonished me are engraved on my heart; I have not forgotten them even for a moment. Even if this body of mine should meet with whatever fate, Quickly grant me a letter, and I will come. Thus he said. The wife was overjoyed, and immediately wrote a reply and gave it to him. The lesser attendants also each had letters. Nobutoshi received this and went down all the way to the detached residence at Ariki in Bizen Province. First, when he told the guard warrior Namba Jiro Tsuneto of his purpose, Tsuneto was moved by his sincerity and immediately admitted him to an audience. The Grand Counselor, now a monk, was still lamenting over the capital and sinking into despair, when word came that Nobutoshi had arrived from Kyoto. "Is it a dream?" Saying this, he could not wait to hear more, and rose up, calling, "Come here, come here!" When he was summoned, Nobutoshi came and looked upon him. First, the sorrow of his dwelling was one thing, but when Nobutoshi saw the ink-black sleeves, his eyes grew dim and his heart seemed to vanish. Following the orders of the lady of the north, he reported in detail, and took out the letter and presented it. When he opened and looked at it, the traces of the water-stem were blurred with tears, and though he could not tell where it was, he said, "The sight of the young people grieving so much for me—I too cannot bear this endless sorrow." When it was written thus, he grieved, saying that the longing of these days was beyond counting. Thus four or five days passed, and Nobutoshi said, "I am here, and I will see your final moments." When he said this, the guard warrior Namba Jiro Tsuneto repeatedly said that it was not possible, and so, unable to do anything, he said, "Then go up." Thus he said. I will soon be gone. If you hear that I am no longer in this world, please make sure to pray for my afterlife. Thus he said. When he received the reply, Shinshun took it and said, "I will come again." Saying this, he took his leave and departed, but the other replied, "I do not feel that I will wait for your return." Because I feel so very dear to you, wait a little. He said, and repeatedly called him back. Since it was not something that should be, Nobutoshi held back his tears and returned to the capital. When he sent a letter to the northern lady, she opened it and looked, and it seemed that he had already become a monk, and she did not look twice at the lock of hair that was inside the letter. Saying, 'A keepsake is now rather painful,' she threw herself down and wept. Even the young people wept and grieved, each in their own voice.

[2.10.4] In the meantime, on the nineteenth day of the eighth month, they finally killed the Great Counselor Nyūdō at a place called Kibi no Nakayama in the village of Niwase, on the border of the provinces of Bizen and Bitchū. The manner of his death was reported in various ways. They put poison in his sake and offered it to him, but since he would not drink it, they planted stakes about two jō high below the bank and pushed him down from above, and he was pierced by the stakes and died. These were utterly cruel deeds; I remember only a few of them. The Great Counselor's wife, hearing that he was no longer in this world, had kept her appearance unchanged until today, hoping somehow to see him once more, or to be seen by him. Now, thinking there was nothing more to be done, she went to a temple called Bodai-in, changed her appearance, performed the usual Buddhist rites, and prayed for his afterlife. This Kitakata was the daughter of Yamashiro no kami Atsufusa. She was a peerless beauty, and was the most beloved of Emperor Go-Shirakawa, but she was given to Narichika, who was a person of rare favor. The young children plucked flowers and scooped up water for the Buddhist altar, mourning their father's afterlife—how touching it was. In the meantime, as time passed and events moved on, the changing ways of the world were no different from the five signs of decay of a heavenly being.

[2.11.1] Here, the Great Counselor Sanesada of Tokudaiji, having been passed over for the position of General by Taira no Munemori, the second son of the Taira clan, secluded himself for a while. When he said he would become a monk, the courtiers and attendants all lamented together, wondering what to do. Among them was a courtier called Fujiwara no Kurando Shigekane. He was a man experienced in all matters, and one moonlit night, when Lord Sanesada was sitting alone on the south-facing veranda, whistling at the moon, Fujiwara no Kurando came, perhaps thinking to console him. "Who is it?" "It is Shigekane." "What is the matter?" When he said this, Shigekane replied, "Tonight the moon is especially bright, and as my heart is clear, I have come." Thus he said. The Dainagon said, "You have come admirably." I was feeling somehow lonely and bored. Thus he said. After that, they talked about various things and comforted him. The Dainagon said, "When I carefully observe the state of this world, the Heike's prosperity is ever increasing." The Chancellor's eldest son and second son were the generals of the left and right. And then there were also the third son Tomomori and the eldest grandson Koremori. If both he and this one were to rise in rank, it did not seem that men of other families would ever be appointed generals. And so it was the end. I will become a monk. Thus he proclaimed. Shigekane, shedding tears, said, "If Your Lordship takes the tonsure, all the people of your household, high and low, will be at a loss." Shigekane, you have thought of something wonderful. For example, the Heike have always deeply revered the Itsukushima Shrine in Aki Province, so what hardship could there be? Please go to that shrine and make a vow. If you stay in retreat for about seven days, at that shrine there are many beautiful dancing girls called naishi. They will think it strange and will entertain you. If they ask, "For what vow are you staying in retreat?", tell them the truth. Then, when you leave, they will feel regret at parting. Take the ladies-in-waiting of the inner palace and go up to the capital. If you go up to the capital, you will go to Nishihachijo. For what vow did Lord Tokudaiji go to Itsukushima? If asked, the ladies-in-waiting should answer just as it happened. The Lay Monk Prime Minister is a man who especially loves things, and he would be delighted if you went to the deity he worships and prayed. When he said this, Lord Tokudaiji said, "This is something I never thought of. What a wonderful plan!" What a wonderful plan! I will go soon. Saying this, he suddenly began abstaining from meat and went to Itsukushima.

[2.11.2] Indeed, in that palace there were many elegant women called Naishi. During the seven-day retreat, the hospitality they offered day and night was boundless. During the seven days and nights, there was even music and dance up to three times. As they played the biwa, the koto, sacred music, and danced and sang, Lord Sanesada also thought it delightful, and for the sake of the divine rites he sang imayo and roei, and there were rare pieces of court music such as fuzoku and saibara. The court ladies said, "To this shrine, it is the Heike nobles who usually come to worship; your visit is indeed rare." What vow or retreat are you making? When they said this, he replied, "It is because I was surpassed by another in the rank of general; this is a prayer for that." Thus he spoke. When, after seven days of seclusion, he took leave of the Great Deity and returned to the capital, the young court ladies, including Muneto, numbering more than ten, regretting his departure, pushed out the boat and accompanied him for a day's journey. Though he took his leave, still, because the regret was so great, he was told, "One more day's journey, two more days' journey," and so they accompanied him all the way to the capital. He entered the residence of Tokudaiji, was entertained in various ways, and was sent back with various parting gifts.

[2.11.3] The court ladies, thinking that since they had come this far, how could they not pay a visit to their lord, the Lay Monk Chancellor, went to Nishi-Hachijo. The Lay Monk Chancellor hurried out to meet them and said, "What is the reason for this visit, court ladies?" "When Lord Tokudaiji came to visit, he stayed for seven days, and when he was about to leave, I accompanied him for one day's journey. Then, saying that it was too sad to part, he asked me to go one more day, then two more days, and thus I was brought all the way here." "For what prayer did Tokudaiji go all the way to Itsukushima?" "He said it was for the General's prayer." Then the Novice nodded and said, "Ah, how pitiful! Leaving behind so many revered Buddhas and shrines in the capital, he went to pray to the deity I worship—how admirable!" If his devotion is this deep... Saying this, he had his eldest son, the Minister of the Interior Komatsudono, resign from the post of Major General of the Left, and passed over his second son, the Major Counselor Munemori, who was Major General of the Right, and made Tokudaiji the Major General of the Left. Ah, what a splendid plan it was! The new Dainagon, too, without making such a wise plan, raised a groundless rebellion, and brought ruin upon himself, and even down to his children and retainers, caused them to see such misery—how hateful it was!

[2.12.1] Meanwhile, the Cloistered Emperor, having made the monk Kōken of Mii-dera his teacher, had him transmit the secret rites of Shingon; he received the secret rites of the three scriptures—the Dainichi-kyō, the Kongōchō-kyō, and the Soshitsuji-kyō—and it was heard that on the fourth day of the ninth month, the abhisheka (initiation) was to be held at Mii-dera. The monks of Enryaku-ji were indignant and said, "Since ancient times, the imperial abhisheka and ordination have always been performed on this mountain; this is the established precedent." Above all, the divine guidance of Sannō was for the sake of receiving the precepts and the abhiṣeka. Nevertheless, if you now have it performed at Mii-dera, I will burn the temple to the ground. Thus he said. Saying it was useless, he completed the additional rites and then stopped. Nevertheless, saying it was still his original intention, he took the Sōjō Kōken of Mii-dera with him, went to Tennōji, built the Gokōin, and using the water of the Kamei well as the water of the five vases, at the sacred place where Buddhism first arose, he had the Denbō Kanjō performed.

[2.12.2] In order to quell the disturbance at the mountain gate, although the imperial consecration was not held at Miidera, on the mountain the temple servants and students caused unpleasant incidents, and battles occurred repeatedly. Each time the scholar-monks were struck down, it appeared as the destruction of the mountain gate and a great matter for the imperial court. Those called the hall attendants were boys who had been servants of the scholar-monks and had become monks, or they were of the middle-rank monk-servant class; from the time when the abbot of Kongōju-in, Kakujin Gon-no-Sōjō, governed the mountain, they were organized into shifts among the three pagodas, called the summer assembly, and were the ones who offered flowers to the Buddha. In recent years, as itinerant monks, they did not even associate with the main body of monks, but thus they won victory in battle after battle. The hall attendants, disobeying their master's orders, plotted battle; the main body of monks reported to the court that they should be swiftly punished, and appealed to the warrior houses. Accordingly, the Nyudo Chancellor received the imperial decree, and with the resident of Kii Province, Yuasa no Gon no Kami Muneshige and his followers, more than two thousand mounted warriors of the inner provinces were added to the great assembly and attacked the temple clerics. The temple clerics had been at Toyobo, but they went down to Sanga no Sho in Omi Province, led a large force, and again climbed the mountain, fortifying themselves at Hayao Slope.

[2.12.3] On the twentieth day of the same ninth month, at the hour of the Dragon, a great host of three thousand monks and over two thousand government troops, in all more than five thousand men, pressed upon Hayao Slope. This time, thinking that surely it would be so, the monks tried to make the government troops go first, and the government troops, in turn, vied to make the monks go first; thus, with each side having its own mind, they did not fight decisively. When they shot crossbows from inside the castle, the monks and government troops were all killed. The 'evil gangs' who joined the temple servants were thieves, robbers, mountain bandits, and pirates from various provinces. Because they were fellows with burning desires and no thought of life or death, they fought thinking only of themselves, and this time too they were defeated by the student monks.

[2.13.1] After that, the mountain temple became even more desolate; apart from the twelve meditation monks, even resident monks were rare, the lectures in the valleys died out, and the rituals in the halls declined. They closed the windows of study and left the seats of meditation empty. The spring flowers of the Four Teachings and Five Periods no longer gave fragrance, and the autumn moon of the Three Truths and Suchness was clouded over. There is no one to tend the lamp of the Law that has burned for over three hundred years, and the incense smoke offered without interruption through the six periods of the day has surely ceased. The halls towered high, thrusting their three-tiered structures into the blue heavens, and the ridgepoles soared far above, with the four-sided eaves suspended amid the white mists. But now, the offerings to the Buddha are left to the wind on the ridge, and the golden image is drenched by the crimson rain. The moon at night serves as a lamp, its light leaking through the gaps in the eaves; the morning dew hangs like jewels, adding to the adornment of the lotus pedestal. As for the common people of the latter age, even the Buddhism of the three countries has gradually declined. When one visits the traces of the Buddha in far-off India, the Bamboo Grove Monastery where the Buddha once preached the Law, and the Jetavana Grove, have now become the dwelling of foxes, wolves, and jackals, and only the foundation stones remain. In the White Heron Pond the water has dried up, and only the grasses grow thickly. Even the stupa of the one who retired from Brahmanism and descended from the Mahayana has become moss-covered and leaning. In China too, Mount Tiantai, Mount Wutai, White Horse Temple, and Yuquan Temple are now without resident monks and have fallen into various states of ruin; the teachings of both Mahayana and Hinayana may be rotting at the bottom of their boxes. In our country too, the seven great temples of Nara have fallen into ruin, the eight and nine sects have died out, and Atago and Takao, though in the past their halls and pagodas stood side by side, since they were ruined in a single night, have become the dwelling place of tengu. Is it because of this that even the Tendai Buddhism, which was so august, has now, in the Jishō era, come to ruin? There is no one with a heart who does not grieve and lament. On a pillar of the monk's lodging where he had left the mountain, he wrote a poem.

lg.l: 祈りこし我立杣のひきかへて、人なき嶺となりや果なん。

div.p: [2.13.2] Was this a poem composed when he recalled the prayer that the Great Teacher Dengyō had offered to the Buddhas of Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi in the old days when he founded this mountain? It sounded very elegant. The eighth day is the day of Yakushi, but there was no sound of chanting 'Namu'. Though it is the month of the god's manifestation, there is no one to offer sacred offerings. The vermilion sacred fence has grown old and divine; perhaps only the sacred rope remains.

[2.14.1] At that time, there was a report that Zenko-ji Temple had burned down. That Tathagata, it is said, long ago in India, in the kingdom of Shravasti, when five kinds of evil diseases arose and many people perished, at the earnest request of the layman Gatsu-shō, obtained gold from the palace of the Dragon King, and Shakyamuni, Maudgalyayana, and the layman, with one heart, cast and manifested a one-shaku, eight-sun Amida triad, the foremost sacred image in all of Jambudvipa. After the Buddha's passing, it remained in India for more than five hundred years. Then, in accordance with the principle of the eastward spread of Buddhism, it moved to the kingdom of Baekje. After a thousand years, during the reign of Emperor Seimei of Baekje and the reign of Emperor Kinmei of our court, it moved from that country to this country, and at the bay of Naniwa in Settsu Province, it passed the years. Because he always emitted a golden light, the era name was accordingly called Jinkō. In the first ten days of the third month of the same third year, a resident of Shinano Province, a man called Honda Zenkō of Omi, went up to the capital, and when he met that Buddha, he immediately invited him, and by day Zenkō carried the Buddha on his back, and by night the Buddha carried Zenkō on his back, and they went down to Shinano Province, and from the time he enshrined him in Minochi District, the years and months have already passed five hundred and eighty-some years, and this is said to be the first instance of destruction by fire. When the royal law comes to an end, the Buddhist law will perish first. So it is said. Perhaps for that reason, the many sacred mountains that had been so venerable have all been destroyed; this is said to be a sign that the royal law has reached its end.

[2.15.1] Meanwhile, the exiles on Kikaigashima, whose lives hung by a thread like dew on the tips of grass blades, though they had nothing to cling to, were constantly sent food and clothing from the estate of Kase no shō in Hizen Province, the domain of the Taira counselor Norimori, father-in-law of the Lesser Captain of Tanba; and so both Shunkan and Yasuyori managed to stay alive. Yasuyori, when he was exiled, became a monk at Murotsu in Suō. His religious name was indeed Shōshō. Since becoming a monk was his long-standing wish,

lg.l: つひにかくそむきはてける世の中を、とくすてざりし事ぞくやしき。

div.p: [2.15.2] The Lesser Captain of Tanba, the lay monk Yasuyori, had been a devotee of Kumano from the beginning, so he said, "Somehow, let us invite the three Kumano deities to this island and pray for our return to the capital." But the Bishop was by nature the most faithless of men and would not agree. The two of them, with one mind, wondering if there was a place resembling young Kumano, searched around the island; in some places there were exquisite ponds and groves, adorned with red brocade and embroidery in various ways, and in other places there were strange cloud-wreathed peaks, with colors of blue gauze and figured silk not of a single hue. The mountain scenery, down to the trees and groves, was even more excellent than outside. Looking south, the sea stretches endlessly, with waves of clouds and billows of mist deep; looking back north, from the towering mountains, a hundred-foot waterfall plunges and rises. The sound of the waterfall is especially eerie, and the dwelling where the wind in the pines sounds divine—it was just like the sacred mountain of Nachi where the deity Hirō Gongen resides. And so, they immediately named that place the sacred mountain of Nachi. They named the peaks one by one: this peak is the main shrine, that one is the new shrine, this is the prince of such-and-such, that is the prince of so-and-so, and with Yasuyori the lay monk as their guide, taking along the Lesser Captain of Tango, day after day they imitated a pilgrimage to Kumano and prayed for their return to the capital. "Hail, Gongen Kongō Dōji! Please have compassion and let us return to our hometown; let us see our wives and children once more." Thus he prayed. As the days accumulated, since there were no pure robes to change into, he wrapped himself in hempen garments, and when he drew water from the marsh's edge, he imagined it to be the clear stream of the Iwata River; when he climbed to a high place, he envisioned it as the Gate of Aspiration. Each time he visited, the lay monk Yasuyori offered prayers, but since there was no offering paper, he plucked flowers and held them up.In the year corresponding to the first year of Jishō, the cyclical year of the Fire Rooster, in the intercalary second month, on a day counted among the three hundred and fifty-odd days, choosing an auspicious day and hour, with deepest reverence, before the great shrine of the foremost wonder-working deity of Japan, the Three Shrines of Kumano, in accordance with the divine command of the Great Bodhisattva of the Flying Waterfall, the great patron of faith, the Captain of the Left Division of the Palace Guards, Fujiwara no Naritsune, together with the novice Shōshō, with single-hearted purity of sincerity and with devotion of body, speech, and mind in harmony, reverently make this declaration.Now, the Great Bodhisattva Shōjō is the teacher who saves beings from the sea of suffering, the fully enlightened king of the three bodies.One is the lord of the Eastern Pure Land of Lapis Lazuli, the Tathagata who removes all illnesses.One is the lord of the Southern Potalaka, the great bodhisattva who entered the gate of profound mystery; Wakaoji is the original lord of the Saha world, the great bodhisattva who bestows fearlessness.He manifested a Buddha's face on the top of his head and looked upon the wishes of all living beings.Because of this, from the highest person above down to the common people below, some for peace in this world, some for a good rebirth in the next, in the morning they scoop pure water and wash away the defilements of earthly desires, and in the evening they face the deep mountains and chant the sacred name, and their devotion never slackens.They compare the height of the towering peaks to the loftiness of divine virtue, and liken the depth of the precipitous valleys to the profundity of the great vow, parting the clouds to ascend and treading through the dew to descend.If we do not rely on this land of benefit, how can we carry our steps along the road of peril?If we do not look up to the virtue of the Gongen, how could we possibly dwell in the remote and secluded realm?Therefore, O Shōshō Daigongen and Hiro no Ōsata, with your blue lotus eyes of compassion side by side, and your ears like those of a fawn pricked up, perceive our undivided sincerity and accept each and every one of our earnest wishes.Therefore, the two deities of Yui and Hayatama, each according to their capacities, in order to guide sentient beings with whom they have a connection and to save the multitudes without connection, abandoned their dwellings adorned with the seven treasures, softened their light of eighty-four thousand rays, and became the same as the dust of the six realms and three existences.Therefore, the worship of 'fixed karma can also be changed' and 'seek long life and obtain long life' is performed with sleeves touching and offerings of sacred treasures and libations without pause.Wearing the robe of forbearance, offering the flower of enlightenment, shaking the floor of the shrine, purifying the water of faith, he filled the pond of salvation.If the gods accept this, how could my wish not be fulfilled?I pray: may the twelve shrines' deities spread the wings of salvation side by side, fly far across the sky of the sea of suffering, put an end to the sorrow of exile, and grant the fulfillment of my long-held wish to return to the capital.They bowed twice.
[2.15.3] Thus Yasuyori made his vow.

[2.16.1] The Lesser Captain of Tango and the lay priest Yasuyori often went before the shrine of the Three Deities and kept vigil there. One time the two of them kept vigil all night long, singing imayo songs. Toward dawn, Yasuyori the lay priest dozed off and dreamed: from the offing a small boat with a white sail was rowed ashore, and from within the boat came twenty or thirty ladies wearing crimson hakama, beating drums and tuning their voices.

lg.l: 萬の佛の願よりも、千手の誓ぞたのもしき、
枯れたる草木も忽に、花さき實なるとこそきけ。

div.p: [2.16.2] And singing the three verses clearly, they vanished as if wiped away. After waking from the dream, thinking it strange, Yasuyori the novice said, "This seems to be a manifestation of the dragon god. Among the three shrines, the one called Nishi no Onto has as its original form the Thousand-Armed Kannon. Since the dragon god is one of the twenty-eight attendants of the Thousand-Armed Kannon, his acceptance is indeed reassuring. Again on another night, the two kept vigil together and in a dream they both saw: a wind blowing from the offing blew two leaves onto their sleeves, and when they casually picked them up and looked, they were leaves of the sacred camphor tree of Kumano. On the leaves of that second southern tree, he had written a poem, bitten out by insects.

lg.l: ちはやぶる神にいのりの繁ければ、などか都へ歸らざるべき。

div.p: [2.16.3] Yasuyori, the lay monk, in his longing for his hometown, as a desperate plan, made a thousand stupas, and wrote on them the Sanskrit letter 'A', the year and month, his kana name, his real name, and two poems.

lg.l: 薩摩潟沖の小島に我ありと、親には告よ八重の汐風。
思ひやれしばしと思ふ旅だにも、猶ふるさとはこひしき物を。

div.p: [2.16.4] He carried it out to the shore and prayed, "Hail, homage and obeisance! Brahma, Indra, the Four Heavenly Kings, the firm earth deities, the guardian deities of the capital, especially Kumano Gongen and Itsukushima Daimyojin, please convey at least one of these to the capital." So saying, each time the white waves of the offing surged in and receded, he floated a stupa on the sea. As he made stupas and cast them into the sea, as the days accumulated, the number of stupas also accumulated. Perhaps that longing heart became a favorable wind. Perhaps the gods and Buddhas also sent them off. Among the thousand stupas, one had been washed ashore on the beach before the shrine of the Great Deity of Itsukushima in Aki Province.

[2.16.5] Now, a monk who had a connection with Yasuyori the lay monk, thinking that if there were some suitable opportunity he would somehow cross over to that island and hear of his fate, set out on a pilgrimage to the western provinces, and first of all he went to Itsukushima. There, a layman who appeared to be a courtier, dressed in a hunting costume, came out alone. When this monk was telling some story or other, he said, "Though it is said that the blessings of 'softening the light and mingling with the dust' are various, by what kind of karmic connection has this deity come to bind a connection with the scales of the sea?" he asked respectfully. The courtier answered, "This is, you see, the third princess of the dragon king Sagara, a manifestation of the Womb Realm." From the beginning when the deity manifested on this island until the present day of salvation and blessings, he told of extremely profound and wondrous matters. Perhaps because of that, the eight shrines' halls line up their roof tiles, and since the shrine is by the sea, the moon dwells in the rising and falling tides. When the tide comes in, the great torii gate is like a crimson jeweled fence, like lapis lazuli. When the tide goes out, though it is a summer night, frost falls on the white sand before the palace. Feeling increasingly reverent, he made offerings and sat there; gradually the sun set and the moon rose, and as the tide came in, among the drifting seaweed and debris, he noticed the shape of a stupa. When he casually picked it up, it was a written message saying, "I am on the offshore island." The characters had been carved and engraved, so they were not washed away by the waves, and appeared vividly. "Oh, how mysterious!" Saying this, he stuck it into the side of his backpack, went up to the capital, and showed it to Yasuyori's old wife, the nun, and his wife and children, who were secretly living in a place called Murasakino, north of Ichijō. Then she said, "If that is so, why did this stupa come all the way here without being carried off to China, and now make me grieve anew?" Thus she grieved. When the news reached the ears of the retired emperor, he looked at it and said, "How pitiful! So these people are still alive." He shed tears, which was deeply moving. When he sent it to Lord Komatsu, he showed it to his father, the Lay Monk Chancellor. Kakinomoto no Hitomaro thought of a boat disappearing behind an island, and Yamabe no Akahito gazed at cranes by the reedy shore. Sumiyoshi Myojin composed a poem about a shoulder-cut robe, and Miwa Myojin pointed at a gate where cedars stood. Since ancient times, when Susanoo-no-Mikoto first composed a thirty-one-syllable waka, all the gods and buddhas have used such verse to express their myriad thoughts and feelings. The priest, too, not being made of wood or stone, could not help but feel moved.

[2.17.1] Since the Lay Priest Chancellor took pity on them, everyone in the capital, old and young alike, would hum the songs of the exiles on Kikaigashima. Since it was a stupa that had been built up to a thousand, it must have been small indeed. That it was transmitted all the way from Satsuma Lagoon to the capital is wondrous indeed. Is it because what one thinks about so much has such efficacy?

[2.17.2] When the ancient Han king attacked the Hu kingdom, at first he sent Li Shaoqing as great general with three hundred thousand cavalry, but the Han king's army was weak and the Hu kingdom's battle was strong, and all the imperial forces were destroyed. Moreover, the great general Li Shaoqing was captured alive by the Hu king. Next, Su Wu was made a great general, and 500,000 cavalry were sent against them. Still, the Han army was weak and the barbarians' fighting was strong, and the government forces were all destroyed. More than 6,000 soldiers were taken alive. Among them, starting with the great general Su Wu, 630-odd soldiers of the clan were selected, and one by one their legs were cut off, and they were driven away. Some died immediately, and some died after a while. Even though he was in that situation, Su Wu did not die. Having become a body without one leg, he climbed the mountains and picked tree nuts, in spring he gathered wild parsley roots in the marshes, in autumn he picked up fallen ears of rice in the fields, and thus he passed his life, which was as fleeting as dew. The wild geese that were in the fields in great numbers had become accustomed to Su Wu and were not afraid, so thinking, "These are surely ones that travel to my homeland," in his longing he wrote down his thoughts in a letter and said, "Make sure to deliver this to the Han emperor." He wrote this and tied it to the wing of a wild goose and released it. How admirable! The wild geese of the rice fields always come to the capital from Koshi in autumn, but when Emperor Zhao of Han was enjoying himself in Shanglin Park, in the evening sky with thin clouds, at a moment of inexplicable sadness, a line of wild geese flew across. From among them a wild goose flew down, bit through the letter tied to its own wing, and dropped it. The official took it and presented it to the emperor. When it was opened and the emperor read it, it said: "In the past, I was confined in a rocky cave, passing the sorrowful days of spring; now I am abandoned in the fields of the northern barbarians, and have become a mere foot soldier of the Hu." Even if my body is scattered in the land of the Hu, my soul will serve you again at your side. So it was written. From this it came about that letters were called 'goose writings' and also named 'goose missives.' "Ah, how pitiful! This is the trace of Su Wu's glory." He is still in the land of the barbarians. Saying this, this time he ordered a general named Li Guang and dispatched a million cavalry. This time the Han forces fought strongly, and the barbarian army was defeated. When it was heard that our side had won the battle, Su Wu crawled out from the middle of the vast wilderness and said, "This is indeed the Su Wu of old!" He announced his name. After spending nineteen years, though one leg was cut off, he was carried in a palanquin and returned to his hometown. Su Wu, from the age of sixteen, was sent to the barbarian country; as for the banner that had been bestowed by the emperor, how did he hide it? He kept it without letting it leave his body. When he now took it out and presented it to the emperor's inspection, both lord and vassals were deeply moved. Because his great deeds for the lord were without parallel, he was granted many large provinces, and moreover was given the office called the Superintendent of Dependent States.

[2.17.3] Li Shaoqing remained in the land of the Hu and never returned. Though he only lamented, wishing somehow to return to the Han court, the Hu king would not permit it, so it could not be. The Han emperor, not knowing this, said he was a disloyal man to his lord, and had the bones of his parents, who had died in vain, dug up and beaten. Moreover, all his other relatives were punished. Li Shaoqing heard of this and became deeply resentful. Nevertheless, still longing for his homeland, he composed a letter in one scroll showing that he had not been disloyal to his lord, and presented it. Then [the emperor] said, "Well, that is a pitiful thing." And so, they dug up their parents' remains and embraced them, and were struck down; this they lamented. Su Wu of the Han dynasty attached a letter to a wild goose's wing and sent it to his old home; Yasuyori of our court sent a poem to his hometown by way of the waves. The former was a casual brushstroke, the latter two poems; the former in ancient times, the latter in the latter age; the land of the Hu and Kikaigashima are separated by borders, and though the eras differ, the poetic sentiment is the same. These were rare and precious things.

[3.1.1] On the first day of the first month of the second year of Jishō, the ceremony of obeisance was performed at the retired emperor's palace, and on the fourth day there was an imperial visit for the New Year's audience. Although nothing was different from usual, the fact that many close attendants, including the new Grand Counselor Narichika, had been lost the previous summer, and the retired emperor's anger had not yet subsided, and he felt the government was burdensome, made it an unpleasant situation. After Tada no Kurando Yukitsuna informed him, the Lay Monk Prime Minister also came to regard even the sovereign with suspicion, and though he pretended outwardly that nothing was wrong, inwardly he was on his guard, and could only smile bitterly.

[3.1.2] On the seventh day of the first month of the same year, a comet appeared in the east. It is also called the Chi You Banner. They also spoke of red emanations. On the eighteenth day, the light increased.

[3.1.3] Meanwhile, the daughter of the Lay Monk Chancellor, Kenreimon'in, who at that time was not yet called Empress, was said to be unwell, and it was a lamentation of those above the clouds and all under heaven. Sutra readings began at various temples, imperial messengers were dispatched to various shrines, physicians exhausted their medicines, yin-yang diviners plumbed their arts, and of the great rites and secret rites, not one was left unperformed. Nevertheless, her illness did not pass easily, and it was said that she was pregnant. The Emperor is eighteen this year, and the Empress has turned twenty-two. However, neither a prince nor a princess has yet been born. If it should be a prince, how auspicious that would be, and the Heike people rejoiced and celebrated as if the prince had already been born. People of other families also said, "The prosperity of the Heike has reached its peak; there is no doubt about the birth of a prince." Thus they said to one another. When it became known that she was pregnant, they summoned eminent and noble priests of proven efficacy, had them perform the great rites and secret rituals, and prayed for the birth of a prince to the stars, planets, buddhas, and bodhisattvas. On the first day of the sixth month, the Empress put on the maternity girdle. The Cloistered Prince Shukaku of Ninna-ji came to the palace and performed the rite of the Peacock Sutra as a blessing. The Tendai abbot, Prince Kakukai, likewise came and performed the rite for transformation into a male child.

[3.1.4] Meanwhile, as the months passed, the Empress suffered from her pregnancy. Even the Lady Li of Han, who when she smiled once had a hundred charms, lying ill in the bed of the Shōyōden, must have looked like this; and Yang Guifei of Tang, bearing a branch of pear blossom in the spring rain, drooping in the wind like a hibiscus, or a maidenflower heavy with dew—even more pitiful than these was her appearance. At the very time of her illness, fierce possessing spirits entered into her. Bound by the ropes of the Wisdom King, the spirit manifested itself. Especially, the spirit of Sanuki-in, the vengeful thoughts of Uji no Akusafu, the ghost of Shin Dainagon Narichika, the evil spirit of Saikō Hōshi, and the living spirits of the exiles on Kikaigashima were said to be the cause. Therefore, the Nyūdō Prime Minister, thinking that both the living and the dead spirits would be pacified, immediately gave Sanuki-in a posthumous title and called him Emperor Sutoku. 宇治惡左府、贈官贈位行はれて、太政大臣正一位を贈らる。 勅使は少内記惟基とぞ聞えし。 件の墓所は、大和國添上の郡、 河上の村、般若野の五三昧也。保元の秋掘起して捨られし後は死骸道の邊の土となて、 年々に只春の草のみ茂れり。今勅使尋來て、宣命を讀けるに、亡魂いかに嬉とおぼし けん。怨靈はかく怖ろしき事也。されば早良の廢太子をば崇道天皇と號し、井上内親 王をば、皇后の職位に復す。是皆怨靈を宥められし策也。冷泉院の御物狂う坐し、花 山の法皇十善萬乘の定位をすべらせ給しは、基方民部卿が靈とかや。三條院の御目も 御覽ぜられざりしは、寛算供奉が靈也。

[3.1.5] 門脇宰相か樣の事共傳聞いて、小松殿に申されけるは、「中宮御産の御祈樣々に候也。 何と申候とも非常の赦に過たる事有るべし共覺え候はず。 Above all, what merit or good roots could equal the recall of the exiles from Kikaigashima? When he said this, Lord Komatsu, seated before his father the Zen monk, said, "The Chancellor's insistent plea on behalf of that Tanba no Shōshō is pitiful." As for the matter of the Empress's illness, if it should come to pass, it is said to be especially the vengeful spirit of Lord Narichika. Even if you think to appease the Dainagon's vengeful spirit, you should recall the young captain who is still alive. If you ease people's resentment, your wishes will be fulfilled; if you grant people's prayers, your own prayers will soon be accomplished, and the Empress will immediately give birth to a prince, and the glory of your family will flourish even more. When he said such things, the Lay Priest Chancellor, unusually for him, was extremely gentle and said, "Well then, what about the matter of Shunkan and the monk Yasuyori?" "They too should be recalled in the same way." If even one person were to remain, it would surely be a grave sin. When he said this, [the Regent replied], "As for the monk Yasuyori, that is one thing, but Shunkan, through the intercession of the lay priest, became a person [of standing]. Moreover, there are many places, but he built a fortress at my mountain villa in Shishigatani, and on every occasion he behaved outrageously. Therefore, I cannot even think of sparing Shunkan." Moreover, there are many places, but he built a fortress at my mountain villa in Shishigatani, and on every occasion he behaved outrageously. Therefore, I cannot even think of sparing Shunkan. Thus he declared. Lord Komatsu returned and summoned his uncle, the Middle Counselor, saying, "The Lesser Captain has already been pardoned. Please set your mind at ease. When he said this, the Middle Counselor clasped his hands in joy. "Even when he was sent down, I thought I should have petitioned for him, and every time I saw Norimori I shed tears; it was pitiful. When he said this, Lord Komatsu replied, "Indeed, you must be thinking so." Since a child is sad no matter who it is, I will speak carefully. Saying this, he entered.

[3.1.6] Meanwhile, it was decided that the exiles on Kikaigashima should be recalled, and a letter was sent down to the Lay Priest Chancellor. The imperial messenger soon left the capital. In the Chancellor's joy, he sent a private messenger along with the imperial envoy. "Turn night into day and hurry down." Though it said so, because it was a sea route not following one's will, braving wind and waves on the journey, they left the capital in late July, but it was around the twentieth of the ninth month that they arrived at Kikaigashima.

[3.2.1] The imperial envoy was a man called Tanba no Saemon no Jō Motoyasu. He disembarked from the ship and said, "Is there the Tanba no Shōshō, Lord Hei no Hangan Nyūdō, who was exiled from the capital to this place?" Thus they asked in many voices. The two people had gone on their usual pilgrimage to Kumano and were not there. Shunkan, the only one left behind, heard this and said, "If I think about it too much, it might be a dream; or perhaps the heavenly demon, the Evil One, is trying to deceive my mind; it seems like a reality I cannot wake from." Saying this, he rushed about in confusion, not knowing whether he was running or falling, and hurried to the messenger, saying, "What is it? I am Shunkan, exiled from the capital." When he announced his name, the servant took out a letter from the lay priest prime minister from the letter case hung around his neck and presented it. When he opened it and looked, it said, "For the grave offense, the sentence of distant exile is remitted; you are to return to the capital soon." Because of the prayers for the safe delivery of the Empress, an extraordinary amnesty was proclaimed. In the meantime, the exiles on Kikaigashima, the Lesser Captain Naritsune and the monk Yasuyori, were pardoned. It was written thus, but the name "Shunkan" was not there. Thinking it might be on the attached sheet, he looked at the attached sheet, but it was not there either. They read from the end to the beginning, and from the beginning to the end, but only two people were written, and three people were not written.

[3.2.2] In the meantime, the minor captain and the lay priest magistrate also came out. When the minor captain took it and read it, and when the lay priest Yasuyori read it, only two names were written, and the three were not written. Such a thing happens only in a dream; when I try to think it is a dream, it is reality; when I think it is reality, it is again like a dream. Moreover, to the two men's places, there were many letters and messages from the capital, but to the monk Shunkan's place, there was not even a single letter of inquiry. Therefore, when he reflected that the things related to him had vanished without a trace from the capital, it was hard to endure. Now, the three of us share the same crime and the same place of exile. Why is it that at the time of pardon, two are recalled, while one should remain here? Is it a forgetting of the Heike's intention, or a mistake in the writing? What on earth has happened? Saying this, he looked up to heaven and fell to the ground, weeping and lamenting, but it was to no avail. Clinging to the young commander's sleeve, he said, "The reason Shunkan has come to this is because of the groundless rebellion of your father, the late Grand Counselor." Therefore, you should not think of it as someone else's affair. If there is no pardon, even if I cannot go as far as the capital, please put me on this ship and let me land in Kyushu. While each of them sat there, just as in spring the swallows and in autumn the wild geese bring news from the fields, they naturally heard tidings of their homeland. From now on, how will I be able to hear? Saying this, he writhed in anguish. The young captain said, "Indeed, you must be thinking so. The joy of our being recalled is indeed great, but seeing your condition, I cannot bear to leave. Even though they had boarded and set out, they said that the imperial envoy would not be able to come, and without any pardon, the three of them left the island, so when I heard that, it was all the more distressing. Naritsune will go up first, consult with everyone, observe the mood of the Lay Monk Prime Minister, and send someone to welcome you. Until then, please think of it as being just like these recent days and wait. No matter what, life is precious, so even if you are spared this time, in the end how could there not be a pardon? So he comforted them, but they wept and grieved without regard for others' eyes. When they said they should set sail at once and were bustling about, the bishop would get on board and then get off, and get off and then get on board, making a great fuss. As a keepsake of the young captain, they left a night quilt; as a keepsake of Yasuyori the monk, they left a copy of the Lotus Sutra. When the mooring rope was untied and the boat pushed off, the monk Shunkan clung to the rope, then to the gunwale, then to the side, and was dragged along until the boat was far out; when even the rope would not reach, he clung to the boat and cried, "So, my lords, will you finally abandon Shunkan?" I never thought it would come to this. The affection of many days now means nothing. Just bend the law and let him board. At least as far as the land of the nine provinces. Though he pleaded thus, the imperial envoy said, "It cannot possibly be granted." Saying so, he pulled away the hand that had been placed on him, and the boat finally set sail. The bishop, at a loss, climbed up onto the shore and fell prostrate; like a child longing for its wet nurse or mother, he stamped his feet and cried, "Take me with you! Take me along!" Even as they cried out, the boat, as is the way of departing vessels, left only white waves behind. Though the boat was not yet far away, his eyes were so blurred with tears that he could not see it, so the priest ran up to a high place and beckoned toward the offing. Even the way Matsura Sayohime, longing for the Chinese ship, waved her scarf, it seemed, could not surpass this. The boat rowed out of sight, and the sun set, but she did not return to her strange sleeping place; she washed her feet in the waves, wilted in the dew, and that night she passed the night right there. Still, since the lieutenant was a man of deep feeling, she trusted that he would surely speak well of her, and so she did not throw herself into those rapids—how fleeting was that heart of hers! Now I realize the sorrow of Sori, who was exiled to Kaiganzan in ancient times.

[3.3.1] Meanwhile, these people left Kikaigashima and arrived at Kasho-no-sho in Hizen Province, the domain of Taira no Saisho. The Chancellor sent a messenger from the capital, saying, "During the year the winds and waves are rough, and the roads are uncertain, so take good care of yourself there, and come up to the capital in the spring." So the Major Counselor spent the year at Kasho-no-sho.

[3.3.2] Meanwhile, on the twelfth day of the eleventh month of the same year, from the hour of the tiger, it was announced that the Empress was in labor, and the whole capital and Rokuhara were in an uproar. The place of the imperial birth was at Rokuhara Ikedono, and the Cloistered Emperor also made an imperial visit there. Beginning with the Chancellor, from the Grand Minister of State on down, all the court nobles and senior officials, everyone who was counted among people in the world, who had hopes for office and rank, and who held estates and offices—there was not a single one who was left out. There was also a precedent: when a consort or empress was about to give birth, a general amnesty was proclaimed. On the eleventh day of the ninth month of Daiji 2, at the time of Taikenmon-in's childbirth, there was a general amnesty. Following that precedent, this time too many serious offenders were pardoned, but it was regrettable that Shunkan, the monk, alone was not granted amnesty.

[3.3.3] If the imperial birth goes safely, she will make a pilgrimage to Hachiman, Hirano, Oharano, and such shrines, she vowed. The monk Sengan Hoin respectfully reported this. For the shrines, beginning with the Grand Shrine of Ise, sutra recitations were offered at more than twenty places; for the Buddhist temples, at sixteen places starting with Tōdaiji and Kōfukuji. The imperial messengers for the sutra recitations were chosen from among the courtiers of the palace who held official rank. Men wearing plain-patterned hunting robes and girded with swords carried the various sutra-offering items, the imperial sword and robes, in succession, crossing the southern courtyard from the eastern platform and emerging at the western middle gate. It was a splendid sight.

[3.3.4] Lord Komatsu, being a man who was not disturbed by good or evil as usual, after that, after a long time had passed, sent a succession of carriages of the nobles, beginning with his eldest son, the Minor Captain of the Right Gate Guards, and had forty robes of various colors, seven silver swords, placed on wide trays, and twelve horses led, and came to visit. It is said that at the time of the imperial birth of Jōtōmon-in in the Kankō era, the Midō Chancellor presented a horse, and this was cited as a precedent. This minister was the elder brother of the empress, and moreover, since they had the bond of parent and child, it was natural for him to present a horse. The Major Counselor of Fifth Rank, Lord Kunitsuna, presented two horses. People said, "Is this the utmost of sincerity, or the surplus of virtue?" Furthermore, starting from Ise and reaching as far as Itsukushima in Aki, he dedicated sacred horses to more than seventy shrines. Even in the palace, they attached shide to the horses of the imperial stables and led out several tens of them. The Cloistered Prince of Ninna-ji performed the rite of the Peacock Sutra; the Tendai Abbot Kakukai Hosshinnō performed the rite of the Seven Buddhas of Healing; the temple's head priest Enkei Hosshinnō performed the rite of the Vajra Youth; and besides these, they performed without omission the rites of the Five Great Void Treasures, the Six Kannon, the One-Syllable Golden Wheel, the Five Altars, the Six-Syllable Wheel, the Eight-Syllable Manjushri, and the Fugen Life-Extension. The smoke of the goma fire filled the palace, the sound of the bells echoed through the clouds, the voices of the ritual chanting made one's hair stand on end; whatever kind of possessing spirit it was, it did not seem as though one could face it. Furthermore, he ordered the Hoin of Bussho to begin making a statue of Yakushi equal to his own body and statues of the Five Great Kings.

[3.3.5] Even so, the Empress was only in constant pain, and the birth did not come quickly. 入道相國、 二位殿、胸に手を置て、こはいかにせんとぞあきれ給ふ。人の物申しけれども、唯と もかくも好樣にとぞ宣ける。さり共「軍の陣ならば、是程淨海は臆せじ物を。」とぞ 後には仰られける。御驗者は、房覺性運兩僧正、春堯法印、豪禪、實專兩僧都、各僧 伽の句どもあげ、本寺本山の三寶、年來所持の本尊達、責ふせ々々々もまれけり。誠 にさこそはと覺えて尊かりける中に法皇は、折しも新熊野へ御幸なるべきにて、御精 進の次なりける間、錦帳近く御座有て、千手經を打上遊されけるにこそ、今一際事替 て、さしも躍狂ふ御よりまし共が縛も、暫打靜けれ。法皇仰なりけるは、「如何なる 御物氣なり共、此老法師がかくて候はんには、爭か近附奉るべき。就中に今現るる所 の怨靈共は、皆我朝恩によて、人と成し者共ぞかし。縱報謝の心をこそ存ぜず共、豈 障碍を成すべきや。速に罷退き候へ。」とて女人生産し難からん時に臨で、邪魔遮障 し、苦忍難からんにも、心を致して大悲呪を稱誦せば、鬼神退散して、安樂に生ぜん と遊いて、皆水精の御數珠を推揉せ給へば、御産平安のみならず、皇子にてこそ坐け れ。

[3.3.6] 頭中將重衡卿、其時は未中宮亮にておはしけるが、御簾の内よりつと出て、御産平安、皇子御誕生候ぞや。 」と、高らかに申されければ、法皇を始參せて、關白殿以下の大臣、公卿、殿上人、各の助修、數輩の御驗者、陰陽頭、典藥頭、惣て堂上堂下、一同にあと悦あへる聲は、門外までどよみて、暫は靜りやらざりけり。 入道餘りの嬉さに、聲をあげてぞ泣ける。 悦泣とは是を云べきにや。 Lord Komatsu went to the Empress's quarters and placed ninety-nine coins by the prince's pillow, saying, "Take Heaven as your father and Earth as your mother." May your life be as long as that of the immortal Tōbōsaku, and may the spirit of Amaterasu Ōmikami dwell within you. Saying this, he had them shoot arrows of mulberry wood and bow of pampas grass to the four directions of heaven and earth.

[3.4.1] As for the wet nurse, the wife of the former Major Counselor of the Right Munemori had been appointed, but in the seventh month she had a difficult birth and passed away, so the wife of the Grand Counselor Taira no Tokitada served as wet nurse. Later she was called the Sochi no Suke. The Retired Emperor's returning palanquin was brought to a halt before the gate. The Lay Monk Chancellor, in his excess of joy, presented to the Retired Emperor a thousand ryō of gold dust and two thousand ryō of Fuji cotton. People privately whispered to one another that this was not right.

[3.4.2] At this birth there were many strange and amusing incidents. First, there was the matter of the Retired Emperor's spiritual protector, and then, at the time of the Empress's delivery, a rice-steamer rolled down from the ridge of the palace roof. At the birth of a prince, they would drop it to the south; at the birth of a princess, they would drop it to the north. But this one fell to the north, so everyone cried out, "What does this mean?" and picked it up and dropped it again to the south, but people said to one another that it was an evil omen. What was amusing was the astonishment of the Lay Monk Chancellor; what was splendid was the conduct of the Komatsu Minister; what was disappointing was that the former Major Captain of the Right, Lord Munemori, having lost his beloved wife, resigned both the offices of Major Counselor and Major Captain and secluded himself; if the brothers had both attended court, how splendid it would have been. Next, seven yin-yang masters were summoned, and when they performed the thousand-fold purification, among them was an old man called Kamon no Kami Tokiharu. Even his attendants were few. A great many people gathered, crowding together like rice plants, hemp, bamboo, and reeds. "It is an official! Open up!" 」とて、押分々々參る程に、右の沓を踏拔れて、そこにて些立休ふが、冠をさへ突落されぬ。 さばかりの砌に、束帶正しき老者が、髻放てねり出たりければ、若き殿上人こらへずして、一度にどと笑ひあへり。 陰陽師など云は、返陪とて足をもあだにふまずとこそ承れ。 其に懸る不思議の有けるを、其時は何共覺えざりしか共、後こそ思合する事共も多かりけれ。 御産によて、六波羅へ參らせ給ふ人々、關白松殿、太政大臣妙音院、左大臣大炊御門、右大臣月輪殿、内大臣小松殿、左大將實定、源大納言定房、三條大納言實房、五條大納言國綱、藤大納言實國、按察使資方、中御門中納言宗家、花山院中納言兼雅、源中納言雅頼、權中納言實綱、藤中納言資長、池中納言頼盛、左衞門督時忠、別當忠親、左宰相中將實家、右宰相中將實宗、新宰相中將通親、平宰相教盛、六角宰相家通、堀川宰相頼定、左大辨宰相長方、右大辨三位俊經、左兵衞督重教、右兵衞督光能、皇太后宮大夫朝方、左京大夫長教、太宰大貳親宣、新三位實清、以上三十三人、右大辨の外は直衣なり。 Among those who did not attend, the former Grand Minister Hanazono-in Tadamasa, the Major Counselor Ōmiya Takasue, and more than ten others below them, later donned plain clothes and went to the Lay Monk Chancellor's residence in Nishihachijō, it is said.

[3.5.1] At the conclusion of the ritual, rewards were given out. The Omuro of Ninna-ji was to have Tō-ji repaired. It was commanded that the Latter Seven-Day Rite, the Great Fundamental Ritual, and the Abhisheka should be performed. His disciple Kakushō Sōzu was promoted to Hōin. The head priest of the Tendai sect requested the imperial edict granting him the rank of Second Prince and the privilege of an ox-drawn carriage. Because the Omuro of Ninna-ji interceded and made the request, Hōgen Enryō was promoted to Hōin. It was said that there was no time even to enumerate all the other rewards and grants. When the Empress's days of purification were completed, she returned to the Imperial Palace from Rokuhara. When this daughter became Empress, the Nyūdō Prime Minister and his wife both said, "Oh, how we wish that an imperial prince would be born!" He prayed, saying, "If I ascend the throne, I will call you my maternal grandfather and maternal grandmother." He began monthly pilgrimages to Aki's Itsukushima, which he worshipped, and prayed. Then the Empress soon became pregnant, and as he had wished, she gave birth to a prince. How auspicious!

[3.5.2] Now, as for how the Heike came to believe in Aki's Itsukushima: during the reign of Emperor Toba, when Lord Kiyomori was still the governor of Aki, he was ordered to repair the great pagoda of Koya using the province of Aki, and Watanabe Endō Rokurō Yorikata was attached as the administrator. The repair was completed in six years. After the repairs were completed, Kiyomori went up to Mount Koya, worshipped at the Great Pagoda, and when he visited the Inner Shrine, an old monk, who had come from no one knew where, with frost hanging from his eyebrows and waves of wrinkles on his forehead, leaning on a staff with two prongs like deer antlers, appeared. They talked together for a while. "From ancient times until now, this [temple] has never declined in its esoteric Buddhist practice." There is no other like it in the whole realm. The great pagoda has already been completely repaired. Well then, the shrines of Itsukushima in Aki and Kehi in Echizen are both manifestations of the two realms, but while Kehi Shrine is flourishing, Itsukushima has fallen into ruin as if it were nothing. Next, please report this to the throne and have it repaired. If it is even so, there should be no one who can rank shoulder to shoulder with you in official rank and promotion. So saying, he departed. In the place where this old monk dwelt, a wondrous fragrance pervaded. When he sent someone to look, the man saw him for about three chō, and then he vanished as if wiped away. This was no ordinary person. Thinking that it was indeed the Great Master, he revered him all the more, and as a memento of this Sahā world, he had a mandala painted in the Golden Hall of Kōya; the Western Mandala he had painted by the artist Jōmyō Hōin. 東曼陀羅をば、清盛書んとて、自筆にかゝれけるが、何とかおもはれけん、八葉の中尊の寶冠をば我首の血を出いて、書かれけるとぞ聞えし。

[3.5.3] さて都へ上り、院參して、此由奏聞せられければ、君もなのめならず御感有り。 猶任を延られて、嚴島を修理せらる。 鳥居を立替へ、社々を造りかへ、百八十間の廻廊をぞ造られける。 修理畢て、清盛嚴島へ參り、通夜せられたりける夢に、御寶殿の 内より、鬟結たる天童の出て、「是は大明神の御使なり。汝此劔を以て一天四海をし づめ、朝家の御まもりたるべし。」とて、銀の蛭卷したる小長刀を賜ると云夢を見て、 覺て後見給へば。現に枕上にぞ立たりける。大明神御託宣有て、「汝知れりや忘れり や、或聖を以て言せし事は。但惡行有らば、子孫迄は叶ふまじきぞ。」とて、大明神 あがらせ給ぬ。 It was an auspicious event.

[3.6.1] During the reign of Emperor Shirakawa, the daughter of the Kyogoku Grand Minister became empress, and as Kenshi, the Chugu, she was deeply loved. The Emperor, desiring that a prince be born to this consort, summoned the Ajari Raigō of Miidera, who was renowned as a wonder-working monk, and said, "Pray that a prince be born to this consort; if your prayer is fulfilled, you shall have whatever reward you ask." Thus he spoke. Saying, "It shall be done," he returned to Miidera, and for a hundred days he prayed with all his might, so that the Empress conceived within those hundred days, on the sixteenth day of the twelfth month of Jōhō 1. The imperial birth was safe, and a prince was born. The lord was not indifferent, and was deeply moved; he summoned the Ajari Raigō of Miidera and said, "What is it that you desire?" When he was thus commanded, he petitioned for the establishment of an ordination platform at Miidera. The emperor said, "This is indeed an unexpected request." I thought you would request something like the rank of First-Rank High Priest. For the birth of an imperial prince and his succession to the throne is for the sake of peace throughout the realm. If your wish is granted now, the mountain monks will be enraged, and the world will not be at peace. If the two sects fight, the Tendai teachings will perish." And so, permission was not granted.

[3.6.2] Raigo, thinking it was a regrettable matter, returned to Miidera and tried to starve himself to death. The Emperor was greatly alarmed and summoned Masafusa, the Governor of Bizen, who was then known as the Governor of Mimasaka, saying, "You have a bond of master and disciple with Raigo." Go and prepare it and see. When he said this, Mimasaka no Kami, having received the imperial command, went to the lodging of the monk Raigō, and tried to convey the purport of the imperial decree, but Raigō had shut himself up in a soot-blackened Buddha hall, and in a fearful voice said, "There is no jest in the words of the Son of Heaven; I have heard that the imperial word is like sweat." If this request is not granted, since the prince was born through my prayers, I will take him and go to the realm of demons. Saying this, he did not meet him in the end. Mimasaka no Kami returned and reported this to the emperor. Raigo eventually died of starvation. The emperor was alarmed, wondering what to do. The prince soon fell ill, and although various prayers were offered, there was no sign that he would recover. An old monk with white hair appeared at the prince's pillow, holding a staff, and was seen in people's dreams and appeared as an apparition. Even fear is foolish.

[3.6.3] Meanwhile, on the sixth day of the eighth month of Jōryaku 1, the prince, at the age of four, finally passed away. He was Prince Atsufumi. The emperor grieved deeply. The emperor summoned to the palace the abbot of the western capital, the great bishop Ryōshin, who at that time was known as the monk of Enyū-bō and was renowned as a wonder-working priest, and said, "What shall be done about this?" When he said this, the priest replied, "Indeed, it is by the power of our mountain that such a prayer will be fulfilled." It was because the Kujō Minister of the Right had made a vow to the Great Bishop Jikei that Prince Reizei-in was born. It was an easy matter. Saying this, he returned to Mount Hiei and prayed to the Sannō Daishi, crushing his heart and liver for a hundred days. Then the Empress conceived within a hundred days, and on the ninth day of the seventh month of Jōryaku 3, she gave birth safely to a prince. This is Emperor Horikawa. Vengeful spirits were fearsome in ancient times as well. Although on this occasion, at such an auspicious birth, an extraordinary general amnesty was proclaimed, it was regrettable that the monk Shunkan alone was not pardoned.

[3.6.4] On the eighth day of the twelfth month of the same year. The prince was made Crown Prince. As his tutor, the Minister of the Left Komatsu, and as his chief, the Middle Counselor Ikeno Lord Yorimori, were appointed.

[3.7.1] When dawn broke, in the last ten days of the first month of the third year of Jishō, Tanba no Shōshō Naritsune set out from Kashinoshō in Hizen Province and hurried toward the capital, but the lingering cold was still severe and the sea was also terribly rough, so he went from bay to bay and island to island, and on about the tenth day of the second month he arrived at Kojima in Bizen. From there, when he sought out and entered the place where his father, the Dainagon, had lived, he saw the brushwork casually written on the bamboo pillars and old sliding doors, and said, "For a keepsake of a person, there is nothing that surpasses their handwriting." If he had not left this writing, how could we see it?" So saying, he and the priest Yasuyori, the two of them, read it and wept, and wept and read it. "On the twentieth day of the seventh month of Angen 3, I left home; on the twenty-sixth of the same month, Nobutoshi went down to the capital." was also written. It was only then that they knew that Minamoto no Saemon no Jō Nobutoshi had come. On the wall beside it was also written, "There is the coming of the Three Holy Ones to welcome us; there is no doubt of birth in the nine grades of the Pure Land." Seeing this memento, they realized, "Indeed, even he had the aspiration for the Pure Land." And so, amid endless lamentation, he spoke with a faint hint of hope.

[3.7.2] When he sought out the grave and looked upon it, there was a grove of pines, but no sign of a carefully built mound. At a place where the earth was slightly raised, the young captain, with sleeves pressed together, spoke as if to a living person, weeping: "That you have become a distant guardian, I heard faintly on the island, but being in this sorrowful world where nothing goes as one wishes, I could not hasten to come." Narinori, having been exiled to that island, did not let his dew-like life vanish, and after spending two years there, the joy of being summoned back—well, that is one thing, but if I could see you cross over to this world, then my long life would have meaning. Up until now I have been impatient, but from today onward, I do not feel like hurrying, she said, and sobbed, scratching at her mouth.
