Truly, if it were when he was alive, the Great Counselor Priest would surely say something, but the way of being separated by life—there is nothing more bitter than that. Under the moss, who could answer? Only the sound of pines rustling in the storm.

[3.7.3] After that, all night long, together with the lay monk Yasuyori, they walked around the grave performing circumambulation and chanting the Buddha's name. When dawn broke, they built a new earthen platform, had stakes driven in, erected a temporary hut in front, and for seven days and seven nights chanted the Buddha's name and recited sutras. At the concluding ceremony, they erected a large stupa and wrote on it: "May the departed spirit leave the cycle of birth and death and attain great enlightenment." Below the year, month, and day, they wrote: "Filial son Naritsune." Even the heartless people of the humble mountain village said, "There is no treasure that surpasses a child," and there was none who did not shed tears and wring their sleeves. Though years come and go, what is hard to forget is the kindness of nurturing in days gone by. It is like a dream, like an illusion. What is hard to exhaust is the tears of longing now. The holy assembly of Buddhas of the three worlds and ten directions also took pity, and the departed soul, too, how happy it must have felt. "Wait a little longer; though I should like to accumulate the merit of the nenbutsu, the people waiting in the capital must be anxious." I will come again. Saying this, he took leave of the departed spirit, and departed from there in tears. Even in the shadow of the grass, how reluctant he must have felt to part!

[3.7.4] On the sixteenth day of the third month, the Major Captain arrived at Toba. The late Grand Counselor's mountain villa, called Suhama-dono, is in Toba. As it had been left uninhabited for years, the earthen walls, though they existed, had no roof tiles, and the gates, though they existed, had no doors. When he entered the garden and looked, human traces had ceased and the moss was deep. When he looked around the edge of the pond, in the spring breeze of the autumn mountains, white waves frequently broke and mandarin ducks and white gulls wandered about. In longing for the person who had enjoyed this place, what never runs dry is tears. The house is there, but the gate is broken, and the latticed shutters and sliding doors are all gone. "Here is where the Great Counselor used to sit, through this door he used to go in and out, that tree he planted with his own hands." Saying such things, with words that clung to her father, she spoke of him with longing. It was the sixth day of the third month, so the blossoms still lingered. The branches of the willow, plum, peach, and pear trees were each in full bloom, as if showing off their beauty. 昔の主はなけれ共、春を忘れぬ花なれや。 少將花の下に立寄て、

lg.l: 桃李不言春幾暮、煙霞無跡昔誰栖。
故郷の花の言ふ世なりせば、如何に昔の事を問まし。

div.p:
[3.7.5] 此古き詩歌を口ずさみ給へば、康頼入道も折節哀に覺えて、墨染の袖をぞ濕しける。
暮る程とは待れけれ共、餘に名殘惜くて、夜更る迄こそ坐けれ。更行まゝに、荒たる 宿の習とて、古き軒の板間よりもる月影ぞ隈もなき。鷄籠の山明なんとすれ共、家路 は更に急がれず。さてしも有べき事ならねば、迎に乘物ども遣て、待らんも心なしと て、泣々洲濱殿を出つゝ、都へ歸り入給けん人々の心の中共、さこそは哀にも嬉しう も有けめ。康頼入道が迎にも乘物有けれ共其には乘らで、「今更名殘の惜に。」とて、 少將の車の尻に乘て、七條河原までは行く。其より行別れけるに、猶行もやらざりけ り。花の下の半日の客、月の前の一夜の友、旅人が一村雨の過行に、一樹の陰に立よ て、別るゝ名殘も惜きぞかし。 況や是は憂かりし島の栖、船の中、浪の上、一業所感の身なれば、前世の芳縁も不淺や思ひしられけん。

[3.7.6] The young commander entered the residence of his father-in-law, the Chancellor Taira. The young commander's mother, who was staying at Reizan, had been waiting at the Chancellor's residence since the previous day. Seeing the young commander enter, she said only, "If you are alive..." She lay down, pulling the covers over herself. The ladies-in-waiting and servants of the Chancellor gathered around, and all wept for joy. How happy must have been the heart of the young lord's wife and of the wet nurse Rokujō! Rokujō's hair, once black, had turned completely white from endless sorrow, and the wife, who had been so radiant and beautiful, had wasted away before anyone knew it, no longer recognizable as the same person. The young child who had been parted from the lieutenant when he was exiled, at the age of three, had grown up and now had her hair done up. Also, beside him sat a small child of about three, and the lieutenant said, "What about that one?" When he said this, Rokujo only said, "This is the one," and pressed her sleeve to her face and shed tears, and the lieutenant thought, "So this is the child I saw looking so pitiful when I left, and she has grown up without mishap." Even when he remembered it, he was sad. The minor captain was summoned to serve at the palace as before, and was promoted to Chancellor Middle Captain.
[3.7.7] The lay priest Yasuyori, because he had his own mountain estate at Tōzan Sōrinji, settled there and first continued his thoughts.

lg.l: 故郷の軒の板間に苔むして、思し程は洩ぬ月かな。

div.p: [3.7.8] Immediately he secluded himself there, continued to think of the sorrowful past, and wrote a tale called Hōbutsushū.

[3.8.1] Meanwhile, of the three men who had been exiled to Kikaigashima, two were recalled and returned to the capital. Shunkan, the monk, alone became the guardian of the island he had so hated—how wretched that was! There was a boy who, from a young age, had served the monk with compassion. His name was Ariō. When he heard that the exiles from Kikaigashima had already entered the capital, he went to Toba to meet them, but his master was not to be seen. When he asked, "How is it?" they replied, "He is still too sinful, so he has been left behind on the island." Hearing this, it is foolish to feel even sorrow. Usually I would go and stand around Rokuhara to listen, but I could not hear that there would be a pardon. I went to the place where the bishop's daughter was secretly staying, and said, "Even in this world you have not been allowed to remain, and you have not ascended to the capital. Somehow I have resolved to cross over to that island and seek your whereabouts. Please give me a letter. When he said this, she wrote it in tears and gave it to him. Even if she asked for leave, they would surely not permit it, so she did not tell her father or mother. The mooring ropes of the Chinese ship are untied even in the fourth and fifth months, so he must have thought that the departure for summer clothes was late. At the end of the third month he left the capital, and enduring many sea routes, he went down to Satsuma Bay. At the port where they crossed from Satsuma to that island, people became suspicious and stripped off the clothes he was wearing, but he did not regret it at all; only the princess's letter he would not show to anyone, and he hid it in his topknot. So, when the merchant boarded a ship and crossed over to that island to see, what he had vaguely heard about in the capital was not even worth mentioning. There are no rice fields. There are no fields. There are no villages. There are no hamlets. Although there are people, they do not understand the words I speak. If among those people there is someone who knows the fate of my master, I thought, and when I said, "May I speak?" they answered, "What is it?" "Do you know the fate of the priest called Hosshoji Shugyo, who was exiled from the capital to this place?" When I asked this, if they knew Hosshoji or Shugyo, they would have answered. They just shook their heads and said, "I don't know." Among them, someone realized, "Well now, there were three such people here, but two were summoned back and went up to the capital. The remaining one was left behind, and though he wanders about here and there, he does not know where to go. So they said. Anxious about the mountain side, they pushed far into it, climbed peaks and descended valleys, but white clouds buried the tracks, and even the path of coming and going was uncertain; the bright mist broke their dreams, and they could not see even that face. In the mountains they never found him, and when they reached the seashore and searched, apart from the gulls that leave their tracks on the sand and the plovers that gather on the white beaches of the coves, there was no one to ask about his traces.

[3.8.2] 或朝磯の方より、蜻蛉などの樣に痩衰たる者一人よろぼひ出來り。 本は法師にて有けりと覺て、髮は虚樣へ生あがり、萬の藻屑取附て、荊を戴たるが如し。 節見れて皮ゆたひ、身に著たる物は絹、布の分も見えず。 片手には荒海布を拾ひ持ち、片手には網人に魚を貰て持ち、歩む樣にはしけれ共、はかも行かず、よろ／＼として出來たり。
「都にて多くの乞丐人見しか共、かゝる者をば未見ず、『諸阿修羅等故在大海邊』と て、修羅の三惡四趣は深山大海の邊に有と、佛の説置給ひたれば、知らず、我餓鬼道 に尋來るか。」と思ふほどに、彼も此も次第に歩近づく「若か樣の者も、我主の御行 末知たる事や在ん。」と、「物申さう。」と言ば「何事」と答ふ。「是に都より流さ れ給し法勝寺の執行御房と申す人の御行末や知たる。」と問に、童は見忘たれ共、僧 都は何か忘べきなれば、「是こそ其よ。」と云も敢ず、手に持る物を投捨て、沙の上 に倒伏す。さてこそ我主の行末も知てけれ。軈て消入給ふを、膝の上に掻乘奉り「有 王が參て候。多くの浪路を凌て、是迄尋參りたる甲斐もなく、いかに軈て憂目をば見 せさせ給ふぞ。」と、泣々申ければ、良在て、少し人心地出來、扶起されて「誠に汝 が是まで尋來たる志の程こそ神妙なれ。明ても暮ても、都の事のみ思ひ居たれば、戀 き者共が面影は、夢に見る折も有り、幻に立つ時も有り。身も痛く疲弱て後は、夢も 現も思分かず。されば汝が來れるも唯夢とのみこそ覺れ。若この事夢ならば、覺ての 後は如何せん。」有王、「現にて候也。此有樣にて、今まで御命の延させ給て候こそ。 不思議には覺候へ。 When he said this, [the other] replied, "That is exactly why." Last year, after the young captain was abandoned by the lay monk Hōgan, his lack of means and the state of his heart can only be guessed at. When he was about to throw himself into that current, the frivolous young captain said, 'Wait just once more for word from the capital.' Saying such things, I consoled myself, foolishly hoping that I might still be young, and tried to endure; but on this island there is no food for people at all, so while I still had strength in my body, I climbed the mountain to gather a thing called sulfur, met merchants who came from the nine provinces, and exchanged it for goods; but as I grew weaker day by day, now I no longer do even that. In such peaceful days, I would go out to the shore, rub my hands together to beg from net-fishers and anglers, bend my knees, receive fish, gather shells at low tide, collect seaweed from the rough sea, and stake my dew-like life on the moss of the rocks—that is how I have lived until today. Otherwise, how would I have managed to get through this sorrowful world? The high priest said, "Though I would like to say many things here, come to my house." When he said this, how strange it was that even in such a state, he still maintained a household! Thinking this, as he went along, in a grove of pines, he made bamboo into pillars, tied reeds together, laid them across as beams, and covered them thickly with pine leaves above and below, so that wind and rain could not collect. In the past, as the temple administrator of Hosshoji, he had overseen more than eighty estates, and within his grand gates, he had been surrounded by four or five hundred servants and retainers. It was strange that he saw such a sorrowful sight before his very eyes. There are various kinds of karma. They are called present-life karma, next-life karma, and karma after next life. During the lifetime of the bishop, there was nothing that he used for himself that was not the property of the great temple or the Buddha. Therefore, because of that sin of shamelessly receiving offerings, it appeared that he was already experiencing retribution in this life.

[3.9.1] The bishop, thinking that it was indeed the young lord, said, "Well now, last year when the young lord and the lay priest Hangan came to welcome me, there was no letter from these people either." Now, in your case too, is it not the same that there is no message? Ariō choked with tears and hung his head, and for a while he could not say anything. Having recovered, he raised himself, suppressed his tears, and said, "When you went out to Nishi-Hachijō, immediately officials of the search and capture came, seized the people of your household, interrogated them about the circumstances of your alleged rebellion, and they perished." The lady of the north, unable to hide you, a small child, had you secretly stay in the depths of Kurama. Only this boy, Ario, came from time to time to serve you. Though there was nothing foolish in your lamentations, being a child, you longed for me excessively, and every time he came, you said, 'Ario, take me to Kikaigashima or wherever it is.' He was displeased, and in the second month that passed, he passed away from something called mogasa. The lady of the north, grieving over this and that, sank into deep sorrow, and as the days passed she grew weaker, until on the second day of the third month she finally passed away. Now only the young lady has gone over to her aunt's place in Nara. She has received a letter here. Saying this, she took it out and presented it. When he opened it and looked, it was written exactly as Ario had said. Inside, it said: "Why is it that, of the three people who were exiled, two have been summoned back, but you have not yet come up?" Alas, whether high or low, there is nothing more sorrowful than the lot of a woman. If I were a man, why would I not go to the island where you are exiled? With this Ario as your companion, please come up quickly. Thus it was written. "Look at this, Ariō. How fleeting is the way this child writes! It is hateful that he wrote, 'Come up quickly, bringing me with you.' If I were Shunkan, free to do as I pleased, why would I have spent three years of spring and autumn? This year he would turn twelve, she thought, but if he was to be so short-lived, how could he show himself to people, serve at court, and support himself?" So she wept, and indeed, a parent's heart is not darkness, yet it is lost in the path of thinking of one's child. "After being exiled to this island, there is no calendar, so I do not know the changing of months and days; only by seeing the flowers scatter and the leaves fall do I discern spring and autumn; when the cicadas' voices send off the wheat harvest, I know it is summer; by the snow piling up, I know it is winter. Watching the waxing and waning of the moon, counting the days of the month, and reckoning on their fingers, even a child who would have turned six this year has gone on ahead—how sad it is. When I went out to Nishi-Hachijo, this child followed me, saying 'I will go too,' but I soothed him, saying 'I will return soon.' Now it seems like a dream. If I had thought that was the end, why would I not have seen him even a little longer? Becoming parent, becoming child, and forming the bond of husband and wife—all these are bonds that do not end in this world alone. Why then, that they should have gone on ahead like that, and until now I never knew it even in a dream! Even though I am ashamed before others, I want to somehow keep my life, because I want to see these people once more. Only the matter of the princess is distressing, but since she is alive, she will probably endure it while grieving. If I keep thinking only of that and show myself a miserable sight, even I myself would seem to be putting on a brave face. Saying this, he stopped his own meals and devoted himself solely to chanting the name of Amida Buddha, praying for a peaceful death. When Ariō crossed over, on the twenty-third day, within that hermitage she finally passed away. Her age was thirty-seven, it was said. Ariō clung to the empty form, looked up to heaven and bowed down to earth, and wept and grieved, but it was of no avail. Having wept out all the feelings of his heart, he said, "I would like to accompany you at once in the afterlife, but in this world there is only the young lady to cross over with you. There is no one to mourn for you in the afterlife." Saying, 'Let me stay a while and perform the funeral rites,' he did not alter the sleeping room, but cut open the hermitage, covered it with dead pine branches and withered reeds, made it into smoke of seaweed salt, and when the cremation was finished, he gathered the white bones, hung them around his neck, and, taking passage on a merchant ship, arrived in the land of Kyushu.

[3.9.2] He went to the place where the bishop's daughter was sitting and told her in detail everything that had happened from the beginning. It was precisely when you read the letter that your grief grew even greater. Since there is neither inkstone nor paper, I cannot even write a reply. The feelings you had in your heart have vanished completely into nothingness. Even if we pass through life after life, and are separated by countless eons in other existences, how could we ever hear your voice or see your form again? When she said this, she prostrated herself and wept without restraint. Soon she became a nun at the age of twelve, went to Hokke-ji in Nara, and prayed for the repose of her parents' souls—how touching it was. Ariō hung the remains of Shunkan Sōzu around his neck, climbed Mount Kōya, placed them in the inner sanctuary, became a monk at Renge-dani, and traveled through all the provinces and seven circuits, praying for his master's afterlife. Thus the end of the Heike, where people's sorrows and laments accumulated, was indeed fearsome.

[3.10.1] Around noon on the twelfth day of the same fifth month, a whirlwind blew violently through the capital, overturning many houses. The wind arose from Nakamikado Kyogoku, blew toward the southwest, blew through ridge gates and flat gates, carried them four or five blocks, ten blocks, and scattered beams, rafters, pillars, and the like in the air. The cypress-bark shingles and the like were like winter leaves scattered by the wind. The tremendous roaring sound seemed as if it were the wind of karma from hell itself, or even worse. Not only were buildings damaged, but many people also lost their lives. Oxen and horses were killed in great numbers. This is no ordinary matter. Saying that there must be an imperial divination, they performed a divination at the Bureau of Divinities. "Within the next hundred days, there will be the caution of a minister who values rewards, and especially great affairs of the realm; both the Buddhist Law and the Imperial Law will decline, and warfare will continue." Thus both the Bureau of Divinities and the Bureau of Yin and Yang divined.

[3.11.1] Lord Komatsu, hearing such things, must have felt utterly forlorn. At that time, there was a pilgrimage to Kumano. Before the main shrine Shōjōden, he prayed all night: "Looking at the state of my father, the lay monk and chancellor, he is evil and lawless, and whenever he acts, he causes distress to the sovereign. As the eldest son, Shigemori repeatedly remonstrates with him, but because of his own unworthiness, his father does not heed him. Looking at his conduct, even the glory of a lifetime is still precarious. Since branches and leaves are continuous, it is difficult to reveal one's parent and make one's name known. At this time, Shigemori thought, however slightly. To be listed among them reluctantly and to rise and fall in the world is by no means the way of a good minister or a filial child. Rather, to escape from fame and withdraw one's body, to cast away the reputation of this life, and to seek the enlightenment of the next life— However, because ordinary people of shallow understanding are deluded by right and wrong, they still do not act as they please. O Gongen Kongō Dōji, I pray that if my descendants are to flourish unceasingly and serve at the imperial court, you will soften the priest's evil heart and grant peace to the realm. If glory is to last only one generation and bring shame upon my descendants, then shorten my own life and save me from the wheel of suffering in the next world. The two prayers earnestly sought divine aid. As he prayed with his heart torn apart, something like the light of a lantern emerged from the minister's body and vanished as if it had been extinguished. Many people saw it, but they were afraid and did not speak of it.

[3.11.2] Again, on the way down, when they were crossing the Iwata River, the young lords, with the heir Koremori, the Gon no Suke Shōshō, at their head, wore pale-colored robes under their white robes; and as it was summer, while they were somehow playing in the river water, the white robes got wet and the color showed through, looking exactly like the color [of the robes beneath]; Chikugo no kami Sadayoshi saw this and found it suspicious, saying, "What is this? That white robe of yours appears to be something the world would consider inauspicious." Should you not change them? When he said this, the Minister replied, "My wish has already been fulfilled. The white robe must not be changed at all." And so, he specially sent an offering of gratitude from the Iwata River to Kumano. People thought it strange, but they did not understand his intention. Then, before long, this young lord actually wore the color of sincerity—how mysterious it was!

[3.11.3] After returning to the capital, before many days had passed, he fell ill. Thinking that the deity had already accepted his prayer, he did not even seek medical treatment. He did not even have prayers offered. At that time, a famous physician surpassing those of Song China had crossed over and was staying in Japan. At that time, the Lay Monk Chancellor, who was at his villa in Fukuhara, sent Etchu no kami Moritoshi as a messenger to Lord Komatsu, saying, "I hear that your illness is becoming very serious. Moreover, a famous physician surpassing those of Song China has crossed over. At that time, he rejoiced. Summon him and have him administer medical treatment. Thus he sent word, and Lord Komatsu was helped to rise, summoned Moritoshi before him, and said, "First, regarding the medical treatment, you should say that you have respectfully received the order." But you too should listen. The Engi Emperor, though he was such a wise ruler, allowed a foreign physiognomist into the capital, and this has been seen as a mistake of a wise ruler and a disgrace to our country even to the end of time. How much more so for an ordinary person like Shigemori to bring a foreign physician into the imperial palace—is that not a disgrace to the country? Emperor Gaozu of Han, though he raised a three-foot sword and governed the realm, when he went to attack Qing Bu of Huainan, was struck by a stray arrow and suffered a wound. The Empress Dowager Lü invited a good physician and had him examine it. The physician said, "This wound can be healed. However, if you give me fifty catties of gold, I will heal it." So he said. Gaozu said, "As long as I have been a strong warrior, I have encountered many battles and received wounds, but there was no pain. His luck had already run out. Life is in the hands of Heaven. Even if you were Bian Que, what good would it do? In that case, it is like begrudging the gold. Saying this, he gave fifty catties of gold to the physician, but in the end he could not be cured. The words of the ancients are in my ears; even now I am satisfied. Shigemori, though unworthy, has been ranked among the nine ministers and has risen to the three highest offices. When I consider my fate, it is entirely in the hands of Heaven. Why, without discerning Heaven's will, would I foolishly trouble myself with medical treatment? If it is fixed karma, even if I apply medical treatment, would there be no benefit? If it is not a fixed karma, even without applying medical treatment, one can be saved. That Jivaka's medical skill was insufficient, and the Great Enlightened World-Honored One proclaimed his extinction on the bank of the Hiranyavati River. This is to show that the illness of fixed karma cannot be cured. If fixed karma were to be affected by medical treatment, how could the World-Honored One have entered extinction? It is clear that fixed karma cannot be cured. The one who governs is the Buddha's body. The one who heals is Jivaka. Therefore, Shigemori's body is not the Buddha's body. The famous physician also cannot reach Jivaka. Even if one examines the four books and excels in a hundred treatments, how could one seek healing for this impure body subject to impermanence? Even if one were to master the teachings of the Five Classics and heal all illnesses, how could one cure the karmic diseases from past lives? If one were to survive by means of that medical art, the medical tradition of our country would be as nothing. If the medical treatment is ineffective, there is no point in meeting him. Above all, to receive a wandering guest from a foreign land in the capacity of a minister of state of our own country would be both a national disgrace and a decline of the Way. Even if Shigemori's life should perish, how could he not harbor a heart that thinks of the nation's shame? Report this matter. Thus he said.

[3.11.4] When Moritoshi returned to Fukuhara and reported this matter in tears, the Lay Monk Chancellor said, "I have never heard of a minister who has brought such shame upon the country even in ancient times, let alone in this latter age. Since he is a minister unfit for Japan, he will surely be ruined this time. So saying, he hurried up to the capital in tears.

[3.11.5] On the twenty-eighth day of the same seventh month, Lord Komatsu took the tonsure. His religious name was Jōren. Then, on the first day of the eighth month, he remained in right mindfulness at his final moment and passed away. He was forty-three years old; his life seemed to be at its peak, but it was a sorrowful affair.

[3.11.6] The reason that the Lay Monk Prime Minister had been so overbearing was that this man had soothed and pacified him; thus the world was at peace. After this, wondering what might happen in the realm, high and low in the capital all lamented together. The people of the household of the former Udaishō, Lord Munemori, rejoiced, saying, "The world will now surely come to the General's side." The way of a parent's love for a child is such that even the death of a foolish one is sorrowful, indeed. How much more so, since he was the pillar of the family and a wise man of the age, the parting of love and the decline of the house were sorrowful beyond measure. Thus, in the realm they lamented the loss of a good minister, and in the house they grieved the decline of military strategy. In general, this minister was elegant in writing, kept loyalty in his heart, excelled in talents and arts, and combined virtue with his words.

[3.12.1] By nature, this minister was a mysterious person, and perhaps because he had also perceived future events, the dream he had on the seventh day of the fourth month was indeed mysterious. For example, while he was walking along a long, unfamiliar beach road, there was a large torii gate by the side of the road, and he asked, "What torii gate is that?" When he asked, they said, "It is the sacred torii gate of Kasuga Daimyojin." they said. Many people were gathered in a crowd. Among them, a monk's head was pointed out. "Well, what about that head?" "When he asked, [the answer was]: 'This is because the head of the Taira Prime Minister Nyūdō committed evil deeds beyond measure, and the great deity of this shrine has taken it.'" "He said, and it seemed, and he woke from the dream." Since the Hōgen and Heiji eras, our family has repeatedly subdued the enemies of the court, and rewards have exceeded our merits; as the maternal relatives of the sovereign of all under heaven, more than sixty members of our clan have been promoted. For more than twenty years, our prosperity was beyond compare, but because the Novice's evil deeds have exceeded all bounds, the fate of our clan is now at an end—so thinking, she continued to reflect on the past and the future, and choked with tears.

[3.12.2] Just then, someone knocked loudly on the side door. "Who is it?" "Listen to that!" When he said this, [the messenger] said, "Seo Taro Kanesada has come." He said. "What is it?" When he said this, [the messenger] said, "Just now, a strange thing has happened, and I felt that the dawn was slow to come, so I have come to tell you. Please dismiss the people before you." Please dismiss the people before you. When he said this, the minister had people withdraw far away and met with him. Now, the dream that Kaneyasu had seen, he related in detail from beginning to end, and it did not differ in the slightest from the dream the minister had seen. Thus, the Minister also felt that Seo no Taro Kaneyasu was a man who could even communicate with the gods.

[3.12.3] That morning, when the heir, Gon no Suke Shōshō Koremori, was about to go to the Imperial Palace, the Minister called him and said, "As a parent, it is extremely foolish of me to say such a thing, but among my children, you seem to be the best." But I feel anxious about what will become of this world. Is Sadayoshi not here? Serve sake to the young lord. When he said this, Sadayoshi came to serve the sake. This cup should first be given to the young lord, but since he would never drink before his father, I, Shigemori, will first raise it and offer it to him. Saying this, he received it three times and then offered it to the young lord. When the young lord received it three times in turn, he said, "Well then, Sadayoshi, give a gift." When he said this, [the attendant] respectfully received [the command], and took out the sword that was placed in a brocade bag. "Ah, is this the sword called Kogarasu, which has been passed down in the family?" While he was thinking joyfully, it turned out not to be so; it was a plain sword used at the time of the minister's funeral. At that time, the young captain's expression did not change, but he looked very displeased, so the minister shed tears and said, "How is this, young captain? This is not Sadanaga's fault." The reason is, if you ask why, this sword is a plain sword used at the time of the minister's funeral. When the Novice was in any way present, Shigemori had carried it with him to attend upon him, but now, since Shigemori is to die before the Novice, he presents it to you. Thus he said. The young captain heard this and could not even reply. Choked with tears, he lay face down, and that day he did not attend court, but remained lying down. After that, the minister went down to Kumano on pilgrimage, fell ill, and before long passed away; only then did I truly realize it.

[3.13.1] Because this minister's aspiration for extinguishing sins and producing good was deep, lamenting the ups and downs of the future, at the foot of the Eastern Hills, in imitation of the forty-eight great vows, he built a hall of forty-eight bays, and in each bay hung one lantern, forty-eight lanterns in forty-eight bays, so that they shone before the eyes of the nine grades of lotus pedestals, and their brilliance was like a polished mirror of a phoenix, as if facing the pure land. On the fourteenth and fifteenth of every month, he would light the lamps, and from the households of both his own family and others, he would invite and gather many beautiful, young, and flourishing ladies-in-waiting. In each of the forty-eight rooms, six at a time, making two hundred eighty-eight in all, he appointed them as the assembly of devotees. During those two days, their single-minded invocation of the Buddha's name never ceased. Truly, it seemed that the compassionate vow of the Buddha's descent to welcome and draw in beings manifested itself here, and that the light of never abandoning sentient beings shone upon this minister. On the fifteenth day, at noon, as the great nembutsu was being performed, the minister himself joined the procession, faced west, and said, "Hail to Amida, the teacher of the Land of Bliss, who saves all beings in the three realms and six paths!" As he thus made his vow of dedication, those who saw him were moved to compassion, and those who heard him shed tears. Because of this, people called this minister the Lantern Minister.

[3.14.1] Moreover, even if a minister has performed great good deeds in our court, it is rare for descendants to continue and hold memorial services. Thinking that he would have memorial services performed in another province, around the Angen era he summoned from Kyushu a boatman called Myōten, and met with him after keeping others far away. He summoned three thousand five hundred ryō of gold and said, "Since you are a man of great honesty, I give you five hundred ryō. Send three thousand ryō to the Song court, go to Mount Yuwang, give one thousand ryō to the monks, present two thousand ryō to the imperial gate, and request the fields for Mount Yuwang, and have them pray for my afterlife. Thus he said. Receiving this sacred scripture, he braved the misty waves of ten thousand leagues and crossed over to the land of Great Song China. He met the abbot of Yuwangshan, Zen Master Fozhao Deguang, and told him of this matter. The master rejoiced and praised him, giving one thousand taels to the monk and presenting two thousand taels to the emperor. When he reported in detail the message that the minister had conveyed, the emperor was deeply moved and bestowed five hundred chō of rice fields upon Yuwangshan. Therefore, the prayers for the afterlife of the Japanese minister, Taira no Shigemori, are still offered to this day.

[3.15.1] The Lay Monk Chancellor, having been left behind by Lord Komatsu, must have felt utterly forlorn; he galloped down to Fukuhara and shut himself up in his residence. On the night of the seventh day of the eleventh month of the same year, around eight o'clock in the evening, the earth shook violently for a long time. 陰陽頭安倍泰親、急ぎ内裏へ馳參て、「今夜の地震、占文の指す所其愼輕からず。 當道三經の中に、坤儀經の説を見候に、『年を得ては年を出ず、月を得ては月を出ず、日を得ては日を出 ず。』と見えて候。以の外に火急候。」とて、はらはらとぞ泣ける。傳奏の人も色を 失ひ、君も叡慮を驚せ坐ます。若き公卿殿上人は「怪からぬ泰親が今の泣樣や、何事 の有るべき。」とて、笑合れけり。され共此泰親は、晴明五代の苗裔を請て、天文は 淵源を窮め、推條掌を指が如し。一事も違はざりければ、指神子とぞ申ける。雷の落 懸りたりしか共、雷火の爲に、狩衣の袖は燒ながら、其身は恙も無りけり。上代にも 末代にも、有がたかりし泰親なり。

[3.15.2] 同十四日、相國禪門此日比福原におはしけるが、何とか思ひなられたりけん。 數千騎の軍兵をたなびいて、都へ入給ふ由聞えしかば、京中何と聞わきたる事は無れ共、上下怖れおののく。 何者の申出したりけるやらん。 The Lay Monk Chancellor made a public announcement that he bore a grudge against the imperial court. The Chancellor, having heard of this privately, hurried to the palace and said, "This time, the Lay Monk Chancellor's entry into the capital is a scheme solely to destroy Motofusa." What kind of misfortune will I meet? He reported this, and the Emperor was greatly alarmed and said, "Whatever misfortune befalls you will be as if it befell me alone." Saying this, he shed tears, which was deeply moving. Truly, the governance of the realm is by the sovereign's regent's plan, but what have you done? The divine will of Amaterasu Omikami and Kasuga Daimyojin is hard to fathom.

[3.15.3] On the same fifteenth day, when it was heard that the Lay Monk Chancellor would certainly bear a grudge against the imperial court, the Cloistered Emperor was greatly alarmed and sent the late Lesser Counselor Shinzei's son, Jōken Hōin, as an envoy to the Lay Monk Chancellor. "In recent years the court has not been at peace, people's hearts are unsettled, and the world seems not to have settled down. Although you lament this above all, if you are there, I rely on you for everything. It may be that you cannot pacify the whole realm, but to hear that you are in a state of distress and moreover bear resentment against the court—what is this?" " he sent word. The Dharma Seal Jōken, as an imperial messenger, headed toward the residence in Nishihachijō. Although he waited from morning until evening, there was no response, so thinking it was useless, he had Minamoto no Daibu Hangan Kanesada convey the imperial decree and said, "I take my leave." When he said that and went out, the Lay Monk said, "Call the Dharma Seal." Saying that, he went out. He called him back and said, "Hey, Dharma Seal, is what Jōkai says a mistake?" The fact that the late Lord Kiyomori has passed away—even the Lay Priest, when he considers the fate of our house, must have held back his tears of grief as he passed by. Please understand this in your own heart as well. Since the Hogen era, rebellions have occurred one after another, and the sovereign could not have peace of mind; the Lay Priest merely carried out the general administration. It was the Inner Minister who took action and worked tirelessly, calming the sovereign's repeated anger. Besides that, for extraordinary imperial matters and daily governmental affairs, a meritorious retainer like the Inner Minister is rare indeed. Thus, when I recall the past, Emperor Taizong of Tang, after the death of Wei Zheng, in his grief wrote with his own hand an inscription saying, 'The ancient Yin sovereign obtained a good minister in a dream; I, the present emperor, after waking, have lost a worthy subject,' and had it erected at his tomb—how deeply he must have grieved. He wrote the inscription with his own hand and had it erected at the tomb—how deeply he must have grieved. In our own court as well, this is something I have seen with my own eyes. When Minamoto no Akisato, the Minbu-kyō, passed away, the Retired Emperor was especially grieved, and the imperial visit to Hachiman Shrine was postponed, and there were no musical entertainments. In general, when a vassal dies, successive emperors have all grieved. Indeed, it is said that the relationship between lord and vassal is more affectionate than that of parent and child, and more intimate than that of parent and child. However, during the mourning period for the Inner Minister, there was an imperial visit to Hachiman Shrine, and there was music. There was no sign of grief at all. Even if you do not have compassion for the priest's grief, how could you forget the loyalty of the Inner Minister? Even if you forget the loyalty of the Inner Minister, how could you not have compassion for the priest's grief? Both father and son have now lost face by going against the imperial will. That is one. Next, regarding Echizen Province, although you had promised that it would never be altered for generations to come, after the Inner Minister, it was soon confiscated. What fault was that? That is one. Next, when the position of Middle Counselor was vacant, the Second Rank Captain requested it, and although the Novice did his utmost to recommend him, in the end it was not granted, and the Chancellor's son was appointed. How is that? Even if the lay priest should make some unreasonable claim, why would you not once listen to it? Should I say it? As for being the heir, as for rank, to have it reversed when it is beyond reason—this is truly an unintended plan, I think. This is one. Next, the matter of the new Dainagon Narichika and others gathering at Shishigatani and plotting rebellion was not at all a private scheme. It was entirely because of the lord's permission. Though it is a presumptuous thing to say, how could you possibly abandon this clan for seven generations? Moreover, the priest has reached seventy years of age, and within the short remainder of his life, he has made plans to destroy [the clan] at the slightest opportunity. How much more so that descendants should succeed one another and be employed by the imperial court is rare indeed. In general, losing a child in old age is no different from a withered tree losing its branches. Now, in this fleeting world, even if I exhaust my heart, what would come of it? I have come to think, 'Let it be however it may.' Saying this, he was both angry and weeping, and the Hōin felt both fear and pity, and broke out in a sweat. At such a time, no one could manage a single word in reply. Moreover, I myself am a close attendant. Since I had clearly seen and heard the matter of the gathering at Shishigatani, thinking that they would surely summon and confine me even now as one of that number, I felt as if I were stroking a dragon's whiskers and treading on a tiger's tail, but the priest was also such a fearless person that he was not at all disturbed, and he said, "Truly, your repeated services are not shallow." The reason for your momentary resentment is understandable. But as for official rank and stipend, for you personally they are entirely satisfactory. Therefore, it is only because of the lord's appreciation that such a great merit exists. However, the saying that close retainers disturb affairs and the lord permits it is surely the harm of scheming ministers. Believing the ears and doubting the eyes is a common failing of the vulgar. To give weight to the frivolous words of petty men and, when the imperial favor is extraordinary, to turn against the lord and depart—considering both the visible and invisible worlds, that fear is not small. The will of heaven is vast and unfathomable; the imperial mind must surely be set on this course. For a subordinate to rebel against a superior—how could that be the proper conduct of a retainer? You should consider this very carefully. In the end, it is this intention that I should report. Saying this, he left, and all the people sitting in rows exclaimed, "How frightening!" To answer without any fear, even though the priest was so angry, and to stand up—what a thing! Saying this, there was no one who did not praise the priest.

[3.16.1] When the Hōin went to the palace and reported this matter, the Cloistered Emperor also deemed it entirely reasonable, and there was no way to issue a command. On the same sixteenth day, the Lay Monk Chancellor, since this was a matter he had resolved upon, beginning with the Regent, stripped forty-three nobles—the Grand Minister of State and below, courtiers, and senior officials—of their offices and confined them. The Regent was transferred to the governorship of Dazaifu and exiled to Kyushu. Saying that in such a world it mattered not either way, he took the tonsure at a place called Furukawa in the vicinity of Toba. He was thirty-five years old. 禮儀能く知めし、曇なき鏡にて渡せ給ひつる者をとて、世の惜奉る事斜ならず、遠流の人の道にて出家したるをば、約束の國へは遣ぬ事である間、初は日向國と定られたりしか共、御出家の間、備前の國府の邊、井ばさまと云ふ所に留め奉る。
[3.16.2] 大臣流罪の例は、左大臣蘇我赤兄、右大臣豐成、左大臣魚名、右大臣菅原、左大臣高明公、右大臣藤原伊周公に至る迄、既に六人。 され共攝政關白流罪の例は、是始めとぞ承る。

[3.16.3] 故中殿の御子二位の中將基通は入道の婿にておはしければ、大臣關白になし奉らる。
圓融院の御宇、天禄三年十一月一日、一條攝政謙徳公失給しかば、御弟堀川の關白忠 義公、其時は未從二位中納言にてましましけり。其御弟法興院の大入道殿其比は大納 言の右大將にておはしける間、忠義公は、御弟に越られ給しか共、今又越返し奉り、 内大臣正二位にあがて、内覽の宣旨蒙らせ給ひたりしをこそ、人皆耳目を驚したる御 昇進とは申しに、是は其には猶超過せり、非參議二位中將より大中納言を經ずして、 大臣關白になり給ふ事いまだ承り及ばず。普賢寺殿の御事也。上卿の宰相、大外記、 大夫史に至る迄、皆あきれたる樣にぞ見えたりける。

[3.16.4] The Grand Minister of State Moronaga was stripped of his office and exiled to the east. In the past Hogen era, because of the guilt by association with his father, the Minister of the Left, the four brothers were sentenced to exile, but the three—his elder brother, the Major General of the Right Kanenaga; his younger brother, the Middle Captain of the Left Takanaga; and the Zen master Hannen—did not wait for their return to the capital and died at their places of exile. This was in Tosa Province, where he spent nine years in exile, and in the second year of Chōkan (1164) he was recalled, restored to his former rank, and in the first month of the following year promoted to Senior Second Rank, and in the tenth month of Nin'an 1 (1166) he was raised from former Middle Counselor to Provisional Major Counselor. At that time, since the Major Counselor was not present, he was added beyond the regular number. This was the first time that there came to be six Major Counselors. Moreover, as for becoming Gondainagon from the former Chunagon, except for the later Yamashina Minister Konomi and Uji Dainagon Takakuni, I have not heard of it. Because he was accomplished in the way of music and excelled in arts, his promotions were not delayed, and he rose to the rank of Grand Minister; then, as retribution for what sin, I wonder, was he exiled again? In the old days of the Hōgen era, he was exiled to Tosa in the southern sea; now in the Jishō era, he is again sent to Owari Province in the eastern barrier region, or so they say. Since he was originally without crime, to say that he would gaze at the moon from his place of exile is something that a person of sensibility would wish for; therefore the Minister did not particularly make a fuss about it. Recalling the ancient times when that Tang dynasty Crown Prince's guest Bai Letian lingered by the banks of the Xunyang River, he gazed far off at the distant tide road of Narumi, constantly admired the bright moon, whistled into the sea breeze, played the biwa, composed waka poems, and idly passed the days and months. Once, the third prince of that province made a pilgrimage to Atsuta Myojin. That night, for the sake of the sacred music, he played the biwa and recited poetry, but since the place was originally a realm of ignorance, there was no one who understood the sentiment. Old men of the village, village women, fishermen, and old rustics bowed their heads and pricked up their ears, but none could distinguish the clear from the muddy or understand the musical modes. Yet when Hu Ba played the lute, fish scales leaped and danced; when Duke Yu sang, the dust on the rafters stirred and moved. When one reaches the ultimate in an art, it is natural that it evokes a response; so all the people felt their hair stand on end, and the whole assembly was filled with wonder. Gradually, as the night deepened, in the melody of the fragrant breeze, the flowers carried a rich perfume, and in the tune of the flowing spring, the moon vied in brightness. He recited the poem, "Would that I might use the errors of worldly letters and wild words and specious phrases in this life," and played the secret piece; the gods, unable to bear the divine response, caused the sacred hall to tremble greatly. If the Heike had not committed evil deeds, how could we now behold this auspicious sign? So saying, the minister shed tears of emotion.

[3.16.5] The son of Azechi Dainagon Sukekata, Ukon no Shōshō and Sanuki no Kami Minamoto no Suketoki, was stripped of both offices. Sangi Kōtaigōgū no Gon no Daibu and Uhyōe no Kami Fujiwara no Mitsuyoshi, Ōkurakyō Ukyō no Daibu and Iyo no Kami Takashina no Yasutsune, and Kurōdo Sashōben and Chūgū no Gon no Daishin Fujiwara no Motochika were all three stripped of their offices. The Azechi Dainagon Sukekata, his son the Ukon no Shōshō, and his grandson the Ushōshō Masakata—these three were to be expelled from the capital immediately, and so the matter was entrusted to the senior noble Tō Dainagon Sanekuni and the hakase hangan Nakahara no Norisada, and that very day they were expelled from the capital. The Dainagon said, "Though the three worlds are vast, there is no place to lay down this five-foot body." Though a lifetime is said to be short, a single day is hard to pass. So saying, in the middle of the night he slipped out of the ninefold palace and fled beyond the clouds that rise in layers. He came to that Mount Oe and the road of Ikuno, and rested for a while at a place called Muragumo in Tanba Province, but in the end he was sought out and, it is said, was in Shinano Province.

[3.17.1] Among the retainers of the former Chancellor Matsudono, there was a man called E no Daifu Hangan Tōnari. Because the Heike were also displeased with him, when it was heard that they would soon come from Rokuhara to seize him, he took his son, E no Saemon no Jō Ienari, and fled without any particular destination. They went up to Inariyama, dismounted from their horses, and the father and son said to each other, "I think we should flee toward the east and rely on the exiled former Hyōe no Suke Yoritomo in Izu Province, but he too is currently a person under imperial censure, and even alone it would be difficult for him to manage." In the land of Japan, is there any place that is not a Heike estate? Since I cannot escape anyway, it would be shameful to show people the place where I have lived for years. It would be better to return from here and, if summoned by Rokuhara, to cut open my belly and die. Saying this, he turned back, saying he was going to the residence at Kawarasaka. As expected, from Rokuhara, Minamoto no Daibu Hangan Kiyosada, Settsu Hangan Morizumi, with over three hundred mounted warriors in full armor, pressed upon the residence at Kawarasaka, and raised a war cry with a great shout. E no Daibu Hangan came out to the veranda and said, "Look at this, all of you! In Rokuhara, please report it in this manner." Saying this, he set fire to the mansion, and father and son together cut open their bellies and died in the flames.

[3.17.2] Now, as for why so many people, high and low, perished and came to ruin, it is said to be because of the dispute between the Middle Counselor and the Second Rank Middle Captain, who had become Chancellor, and the Third Rank Middle Captain, son of the former Chancellor. Then, as for the Regent himself, what kind of terrible fate might he meet? Could the forty or so others possibly escape disaster? Last year, although the posthumous title of Sanuki-in and the posthumous rank and office of Uji no Aku Safu were granted, the world was still not at peace. It seemed that things would not end with just this. When it was heard that a heavenly demon had entered the mind of the Lay Monk Chancellor and that he could not contain his anger, everyone in the capital, high and low, trembled with fear, wondering what further calamity might befall the realm.

[3.17.3] At that time, the man known as Saki no Sashōben Yukitaka was the eldest son of the late Nakayama Chūnagon Akitoki. In the reign of Emperor Nijō, he had been added to the ranks of the Benkan and was held in awe, but for these ten-odd years he had been stripped of his office, unable even to change his clothes for summer and winter, his morning and evening meals not as he wished, living as if he were neither alive nor dead, when the Nyūdō Prime Minister said, "I have something to tell you. Come quickly. When he was thus commanded, Yukitaka thought, "For these ten years and more I have kept aloof from all affairs, and now someone has slandered me," and he was greatly alarmed and agitated. His wife and children also wept and grieved, saying, "What kind of fate will befall us?" As they were weeping and grieving, a messenger came from Nishi-Hachijo, and unable to resist, they borrowed a carriage from someone and went out to Nishi-Hachijo. Contrary to his expectations, the priest immediately came out and met him face to face. "Your father, the lord, was a person with whom I consulted on all matters great and small, so I do not think of you as foolish. Although I have felt sorry for your long seclusion, I could do nothing about it while the Cloistered Emperor was in charge of government. Now, please come to court. I will also see to it that you receive a government post. Then return quickly. Saying this, he entered. When he returned, the ladies-in-waiting at the lodging felt as if the dead had come back to life, and gathering around, they all wept for joy together.

[3.17.4] The Taira Chancellor sent many documents of estate grants to be administered through Minamoto no Daifu Hangan Kanesada. First, thinking it would be so, they sent a hundred rolls of silk and a hundred ryō of gold loaded with rice. Saying it was for the purpose of going to court, he had even the miscellaneous servants, ox-drivers, and ox-carts arranged and sent. He could not even remember where to place his feet in the dance steps of the expert performer; startled, he wondered, "Is this a dream? Is it a dream?" On the same seventeenth day, he was appointed to the Fifth Rank, to the Chamberlain's office, and was promoted to Minor Captain of the Left. This year he was fifty-one, and now he was rejuvenated. It seemed like the glory of just a moment.

[3.18.1] 同廿日、院御所法住寺殿には、軍兵四面を打圍む。 平治に信頼が、仕たりし樣に、火をかけて、人をば皆燒殺さるべしと聞えし間、上下の女房女童、物をだに打被かず、 遽て噪で走出づ。法皇も大に驚かせおはします。前右大將宗盛卿、御車を寄て、「と う／＼めさるべう候。」と奏せられければ、法皇「こはされば何事ぞや。御とがある べし共思召さず。成親俊寛が樣に遠き國遙の島へも、遷遣んずるにこそ。主上さて渡 せ給へば、政務の口入する計也。其もさるべからずば、自今以後さらでこそ有め。」 と仰ければ、宗盛卿「其儀では候はず。世を靜ん程、鳥羽殿へ御幸成參せんと、父入 道申候。」「さらば宗盛やがて御供に參れ。」と仰けれ共、父の禪門の氣色に畏を成 て、參られず。「哀れ是に附ても、兄の内府には事外に劣たる者かな。一念もかゝる 御目に逢べかりしを内府が身に代て制し停てこそ今日迄も心安かりつれ。 諫むる者無しとて、か樣にするにこそ。 行末とても憑しからず。 」とて御涙を流させ給ふぞ忝けなき。

[3.18.2] Then he was summoned to the imperial carriage. Not a single court noble or senior official accompanied him. Only a low-ranking retainer of the Northern Guard, and then a man of strength called Kaneyuki, came. At the rear of the imperial carriage, a single nun was in attendance. This nun, known as the former nurse, was the wet nurse of the cloistered emperor, Kii no Nii. The imperial procession went west along Shichijo and south along Suzaku. Even lowly men and women wept, saying, "Alas, the cloistered emperor is being sent into exile!" and there was none who did not wring their sleeves with tears. "The great earthquake of the night of the seventh day was surely an omen of this, and even the depths of the sixteen lakhs responded, and the firm earth deity was startled and alarmed—how reasonable!" So people said.

[3.18.3] Now, when he entered the Toba Palace, the Daizen no Daibu Nobunari, who had somehow slipped in, was summoned because he was near the imperial presence, and [the emperor] said, "In any case, I intend to be killed tonight." He thinks he would like to have a bath, but what is he to do? When he said this, Nobunari, who even without this had been in a daze since morning, his spirit not with him, out of gratitude for receiving this command, tied up his hunting robe with a cord, broke down the brushwood fence and the pillars of the great floor, and, like a water-drawing servant, prepared the bath and presented it.

[3.18.4] Again, the Dharma Seal Jōken went to the Lay Monk Chancellor's residence in Nishihachijō and said, "I hear that last evening His Cloistered Eminence went to the Toba Palace, and that there is not a single person before him. This seems too pitiful. What harm could there be? Please grant permission for at least Jōken to go. I will go and attend him." When he said this, the Chancellor replied, "Well, well, you are a monk who would not make a mistake in such matters," and permitted him. The Dharma Seal went to the Toba Palace, got down from his carriage before the gate, and entered within. Just then, the Cloistered Emperor was chanting sutras aloud, and his voice sounded especially awe-inspiring. When the Master of Discipline came in, he saw that tears had fallen onto the sutra that the Emperor had been reading, and the Master of Discipline, in his overwhelming grief, pressed the sleeve of his fur robe to his face and came weeping before the Emperor. Before the Emperor there was only the nun. "How is it, Master of Discipline? Since His Majesty partook of his meal at Hojuji-dono yesterday morning, he has not taken any food, neither last night nor this morning. All through the long night he has not slept. His life already seems to be in danger. When he said this, the Master of Discipline, pressing back his tears, said: "All things have their limits; the Heike have flourished in their pleasures for over twenty years. But their evil deeds have exceeded the law, and they are already on the verge of ruin. How could the Sun Goddess and the Great Bodhisattva Hachiman abandon you? Above all, if the vow of the seven shrines of Hie Sanno, which you especially rely upon, and the vow of the One Vehicle's protection have not lost their power, then the eight scrolls of the Lotus Sutra will surely fly up and protect you. Therefore, the government will become the reign of the lord, and the rebels will vanish like bubbles on the water. When he said such things, the Emperor was somewhat consoled by these words.

[3.18.5] The Emperor lamented that the Regent had been exiled and many of his vassals had perished, but after he heard that the Cloistered Emperor had been confined in the Toba Palace, he no longer took any food at all. Saying he was ill, he always had [people] enter only into the night chamber. Beginning with Empress, the court ladies in attendance could not even imagine what would become of them.

[3.18.6] After the Cloistered Emperor was confined in Toba Palace, in the palace, saying it was an extraordinary divine service, the Emperor every night at the white plaster platform of the Seiryōden worshiped the Grand Shrine of Ise. This is solely the Cloistered Emperor's prayer. As for Nijō-in, although he was a wise ruler, because it is said that the emperor has no parents, and because he always had the Cloistered Emperor's words changed, perhaps that is why he did not become the heir to the throne. Therefore, the Rokujō-in, who had received the abdication, also passed away on the fourteenth day of the seventh month of the second year of Angen, at the age of thirteen. It was a pitiful event.

[3.19.1] "Among the hundred conducts, filial piety is put first." The wise king governs the realm through filial piety. ” he said. Thus, Emperor Yao cherished his aged mother, and Emperor Shun respected his stubborn father, it appears. How admirable is the depth of the imperial consideration that must have followed the precedents of those wise kings and sage rulers! At that time, a letter was secretly sent from the imperial palace to the Toba Palace. In a world like this, even if I were to leave my mark in the imperial court, what would it avail me? I would visit the ancient times of Kanpyō, inquire into the old days of Kazan, leave my house, flee the world, and become a wandering ascetic in mountains and forests. In ancient times, too, there were people who hid among the clouds of Mount Shang and purified their hearts in the moonlight of the Ying River; is this not indeed a case of broad learning and purity, and of having fled the world? Among them, the Chancellor Monk Narichika, who had retired to Mount Koya, heard of such matters and said, "Ah, what a noble man, who has fled the world even in his illness!" And so, even if I were to hear of it and it were the same, if I could meet him face to face, how sad it would be! He thought the Hogen and Heiji disturbances were dreadful, but in these latter days such things have come to pass. After this, what further things will come to pass? I wish I could go up through the clouds and enter beyond the mountains. Thus he spoke. It does not seem to be a world where people of true heart would leave their mark.

[3.19.2] The same, on the twenty-third day. Because the Tendai abbot, Imperial Prince Kakukai, repeatedly declined, the former abbot Myoun Daisojo was reinstated. The Lay Monk Chancellor, though he had been so thoroughly defeated, was still the father of the Empress. The one called the Chancellor (Kampaku) is also his son-in-law. How at ease he must have felt! "The affairs of state should be entirely at the discretion of the Emperor." Saying this, he went down to Fukuhara. The former Minister of the Right, Lord Munemori, hurried to the palace and reported this matter. The Emperor said, "If it were a world where the Retired Emperor had abdicated, then indeed. Just go and consult with the Regent, and arrange things with Munemori one way or another." But he did not heed the report.

[3.19.3] The Retired Emperor was at the detached palace south of the capital, and as winter was more than half over, the sound of the wind in the mountains and fields was fierce, and the moonlight on the cold garden was clear. In the garden, only snow had piled up, and there was no one to tread a path; in the pond, ice had formed in layers, and the birds that had gathered there were no longer to be seen. The sound of the great temple's bell startles one from hearing at Yiai Temple; the color of the snow on the western mountains evokes the view of Xianglu Peak. The sound of fulling blocks, cold in the night frost, faintly reached his pillow; the tracks of carriages grinding over dawn ice stretched far across the gate. The appearance of hurried war-horses among passersby on the road, and the manner of people crossing this fleeting world, were perceived by him and seemed sorrowful. Even the barbarians who guard the palace gates, performing their night and day guard duty—what kind of bond from a previous life could it be that they now form a connection with me?—so His Majesty spoke, and it was awe-inspiring. There was nothing that did not wound His Majesty's heart, as he encountered all things and followed all events. In such circumstances, recalling those occasional excursions, the pilgrimages to various places, and the auspicious celebrations, His Majesty could not hold back tears of nostalgia. Years passed and years came, and Jishō too became its fourth year.

[4.1.1] On the first day of the first month of the fourth year of Jishō, at the Toba Palace, since the Chancellor did not permit it and the Cloistered Emperor was also afraid, during the three days of the New Year, no one entered. However, only the late Lesser Counselor Shinzei's son, the Middle Counselor of Sakura-machi Shigenori, and his younger brother, the Mayor of the Left Capital District Nagamori, were permitted to enter. On the twentieth day of the same first month, there were auspicious events such as the Crown Prince's first wearing of the hakama and the first offering of fish, but the Cloistered Emperor, being at Toba Palace, heard of them only as things far from his ears.

[4.1.2] On the twenty-first day of the second month, they forced the Emperor, who had no particular illness, to abdicate, and the Crown Prince ascended the throne. This was the doing of the Lay Monk Chancellor, who had everything as he wished. Saying that the time had come, they crowded together. They handed over the sacred mirror and the sacred sword of the Naishidokoro. The high court nobles gathered in the camp, and following precedents and old customs, when they were about to proceed, Ben no Naishi came forward with the sacred sword. At the western side of the Seiryōden, Yasumichi Chūjō received it. The Naishi of Bitchū took out the box with the mark. Takafusa's captain receives it. The box of the sacred jewel of the Naishidokoro—tonight, at least, I thought I might lay hands on it, and in the heart of the Naishi, who had been thinking so, it seemed indeed to be so, and there was much pathos; but as for the box of the sacred jewel, the Shōnagon Naishi was supposed to take it out, but hearing someone say that if she laid hands on it tonight, she would never become a new Naishi for long, she declined at that time and did not take it out. He was already advanced in years. Since it was not a time when one could expect a second prime of life, everyone disliked it, but Bitchū no Naishi, at the age of sixteen, still a young girl, voluntarily sought the occasion and went out; it was an admirable thing. The various treasures that had been handed down were received by the respective officials and presented to the new emperor's palace, the Gojō Palace. At the Kangi-in, the light of the fires was dim, the voices of the rooster-callers were stilled, and the roll-call at the Takiguchi guard post had ceased, so the old retainers felt forlorn and, amid the auspicious congratulations, shed tears and grieved in their hearts. The Minister of the Left went out to the encampment and, upon hearing the words concerning the abdication, those with feeling shed tears and wet their sleeves. Even when one thinks, 'I will yield the throne to the Crown Prince and live quietly in the mountains of Magu,' such thoughts themselves are full of sorrow—this is the way of the world. How much more so in this case, when it was not His Majesty's own will but he was forced to abdicate—the sorrow of it is beyond words.

[4.1.3] The new emperor was only three years old this year. 'Alas, what a pitiful abdication!' people of the time said to one another. The Great Counselor Taira no Tokitada, being the husband of the nurse of the Emperor and of the assistant governor of Dazai, said, "Who would dare to criticize this abdication, saying it is too soon?" In foreign lands, King Cheng of Zhou was three years old, Emperor Mu of Jin was two; in our court, Emperor Konoe was three, Emperor Rokujo was two. All of them were wrapped in swaddling clothes and did not wear belts properly, yet some were carried by regents to ascend the throne, and some were held by empress dowagers to face the court. Emperor Xiao Shang of the Later Han ascended the throne when he was just one hundred days old. The precedents of ascending to the imperial throne are like this in both Japan and China. When he said this, the courtiers of that time said, "How frightening! Do not say such things." So, that is a good example, isn't it? So they muttered to each other. When the Crown Prince ascended the throne, the Lay Monk Chancellor and his wife, as maternal grandfather and grandmother, received the imperial decree of Junior Third Rank, were granted annual official posts and court ranks, and employed servants of the highest rank. Servants with painted and flowered garments came in and out, and it was just like the palace of an emperor or retired emperor. Even after becoming a monk, his glory was not exhausted, it seemed. The receiving of an imperial decree of junior third rank for a person who has left the household is the precedent of the Great Lay Monk Lord Kaneie of Hōkō-in.

[4.1.4] In the first ten days of the same third month, it was heard that the Retired Emperor would make an imperial visit to Itsukushima in Aki Province. When the emperor has abdicated and makes imperial visits to various shrines, he goes to Hachiman, Kamo, Kasuga, and the like, but people wonder why he would go as far as Aki Province. A certain person said, "Emperor Shirakawa made an imperial visit to Kumano, and Emperor Go-Shirakawa made an imperial visit to Hiyoshi Shrine. We already know that it is in the imperial mind. Deep in his heart he had a profound vow. Moreover, as for this Itsukushima, the Heike were not indifferent, and while they worshipped it, above, the Cloistered Emperor was in sympathy with the Heike, and below, he was somehow confined in Toba-dono; it was said that this was for the sake of prayers to soften the heart of the Lay Monk Chancellor, who was plotting rebellion. The monks of the mountain temple were indignant. "If it is not to Iwashimizu, Kamo, or Kasuga, then the imperial visit should be to the Sanno of our mountain." What precedent is there for an imperial visit to Aki Province?" If that is the case, let us lower the sacred palanquin and stop the imperial procession. When they deliberated thus, because of this, the imperial procession was postponed for a while. When the Lay Monk Chancellor gradually calmed them down, the monks of Enryakuji became quiet.

[4.1.5] On the same seventeenth day, as the departure for the imperial visit to Itsukushima, he entered the Lay Monk Chancellor's Nishihachijo mansion. At dusk that day, he summoned the former Major Counselor Munemori and said, "Tomorrow, after the imperial procession, I intend to go to Toba Palace and have an audience with the Retired Emperor. What do you think?" If you do not inform the Chancellor, it will surely be bad. When he said this, Lord Munemori shed tears and said, "What matter could there be?" When he said this, the other replied, "Then, Munemori, go and tell that to the Toba Palace tonight." So he said. The former Right Grand General Lord Munemori hurried to the Toba Palace and reported this matter. The Cloistered Emperor, thinking it too strange, said, "Is it a dream?"

[4.1.6] On the same nineteenth day, the Great Minister of the Palace, Takasue, came while the night was still deep, and the imperial procession was urged on. The imperial visit to Itsukushima, which had been spoken of these days, has already been accomplished from Nishi-Hachijo. Though the third month has already half passed, the dawn moon, dimmed by haze, is still hazy. The wild geese returning, heading for the Koshi region, send word from the clouds, and even that is heard with sorrow at this time. Before the night was over, the imperial procession arrived at Toba Palace. At the gate, he alighted from his carriage and entered within the gate; the place was deserted and the trees were dark, and the dwelling seemed desolate; he felt sorrowful at first. Spring was already about to end, and the trees had become summer foliage. The color of the blossoms on the treetops had faded, and the voice of the warbler in the palace had grown old. On the sixth day of the first month last year, when His Majesty went to Hōjūji Palace for the morning service, musicians played discordant music in the music room, the nobles stood in rows, the guards drew up their formations, the officials of the In no Chō approached, opened the curtained gate, the Kadenokōji laid out the matting for the path, and not a single ceremony was performed properly. Today, it seems like only a dream.

[4.1.7] When the Middle Counselor Shigekiyo reported the Emperor's mood, the Retired Emperor went to the space under the stairs of the main hall and waited in attendance. The Retired Emperor was twenty years old this year, and as he appeared in the light of the moon at dawn, his august person looked even more beautiful. Because he closely resembled his mother, Kenshunmon-in, the Cloistered Emperor recalled the late Empress and could not hold back his tears. The seats of the two retired emperors were placed close together. Their conversation was beyond what anyone could hear. Before them, only the nun was in attendance. For a long while he conversed with him. After the day had grown late, he took his leave and boarded a boat from Kusatsu in Toba. The Retired Emperor, seeing the Cloistered Emperor's detached palace, a quiet and lonely dwelling, felt pity for him; and the Cloistered Emperor, in turn, felt anxious about the Retired Emperor's temporary lodging, a traveling palace on the waves, in a boat. Indeed, leaving behind the imperial shrines, Hachiman, Kamo, and the like, and going all the way to Aki Province—how could the gods not accept such a pilgrimage? It was evident that his prayer would be fulfilled without doubt.

[4.2.1] On the twenty-sixth of the same month, they arrived at Itsukushima, and the residence of the beloved lady-in-waiting of the Lay Monk Chancellor became the imperial lodging. After staying for two days, a sutra recitation and music and dance performance were held. As for the officiating monk, it was said to be the Monk-Prince Kōken of Miidera. He ascended the high seat, struck the bell, and in the words of the declaration said, "How gracious is the intention of leaving the ninefold capital and making your way through the eightfold sea routes to come here!" When he had declared this in a loud voice, both lord and vassals were moved to tears. The Empress Dowager, beginning with the guest, made pilgrimages to all the shrines and places. About five chō from the Empress Dowager's palace, going around the mountain, they made a pilgrimage to the Waterfall Shrine. The monk Kōken composed a poem and it was written on a pillar of the worship hall.

lg.l: 雲居よりおちくる瀧のしらいとに、ちぎりをむすぶ事ぞうれしき。

div.p: [4.2.2] The priest Saeki Kagehiro was promoted in rank to Senior Fifth Rank, and the provincial governor Fujiwara no Ari Tsuna was raised in rank and promoted to Junior Fourth Rank, and was granted access to the retired emperor's palace. The head priest Zōmyō was made a hōin. It seemed that the divine will was moved, and the heart of the Taira no Nyūdō was also stirred.

[4.2.3] On the same twenty-ninth day, the Retired Emperor decorated his boat and returned. Because the wind was strong, the boat was rowed back and stayed at Ari-no-ura in Itsukushima. The Retired Emperor said, "Compose a poem out of regret for the Great Deity." When he said this, the Lesser Captain Takafusa...

lg.l: 立かへる名殘もありの浦なれば、神もめぐみをかくる白浪。

div.p: [4.2.4] Around midnight, when both the waves and the wind had calmed, the boat was rowed out, and that day they arrived at the port of Shikina in Bingo Province. This place had a palace built by the provincial governor Fujiwara no Tamenari at the time of the retired emperor's visit in the past Ōhō era, and although the lay monk chancellor had it prepared for him, the retired emperor did not go up to it.

[4.2.5] Today being the first day of the fourth month, the day of the changing of robes, they all turned their thoughts toward the capital and were amusing themselves, when a wisteria of deep color was blooming over a pine tree on the bank. The Retired Emperor saw it and summoned the Major Counselor Takasue, saying, "Send someone to break off that flower." When he said this, he summoned the Left Secretary Nakahara no Yasusada, who was crossing in front of the imperial presence in a bridge boat, and sent him to break off the flower. He broke off the wisteria flowers, attached them to a pine branch, and brought them. He was praised for his thoughtfulness, and the Emperor was deeply moved. "There should be a poem about this flower." When he said this, the Great Counselor Takasue...

lg.l: 千年へん君がよはひに藤なみの、松の枝にもかゝりぬる哉。

div.p: [4.2.6] After that, when many people were gathered before the Emperor and they were amusing themselves, the Retired Emperor said, "The court lady wearing white robes has set her heart on Lord Kunitsuna." When he said this and laughed, the Great Counselor strongly protested, and just then a serving woman carrying a letter arrived and said, "This is for the Great Counselor of Fifth Avenue." Saying this, he pointed upward. As expected, everyone in the hall found it amusing and talked about it. When the Grand Minister took it and looked at it,

lg.l: 白浪の衣の袖をしぼりつゝ、君故にこそたちもまはれね。

div.p: [4.2.7] The Retired Emperor said, "How gracious you are." There should be a reply to this. Saying this, he immediately had an inkstone brought down. The Dainagon, in his reply,

lg.l: おもひやれ君がおもかげ立つ浪の、よせくる度に濕るゝ袂を。

div.p: [4.2.8] From there he arrived at the harbor of Kojima in Bizen Province.

[4.2.9] On the fifth day, the sky was clear and the wind was calm, and the sea was also tranquil, so starting with the ship of the imperial residence, all the people's ships were launched one after another, and they sailed through clouds of waves and smoke of billows, and at the hour of the rooster on that day they arrived at the bay of Yamada in Harima Province. From there he was placed in a palanquin and entered Fukuhara. On the sixth day, the attendants, though they wished to hurry back to the capital even one day sooner, the Retired Emperor remained, and viewed various places in Fukuhara. He viewed the mountain villa of Ike no Chunagon Yorimori, as far as Arata.

[4.2.10] On the seventh day, when he departed from Fukuhara, the Dainagon Takasue received the imperial decree, and rewards were bestowed upon the house of the Lay Priest Chancellor. The Lay Priest's adopted son, Tanba no Kami Kiyokuni, was raised to Senior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade; and the Lay Priest's grandson, Echizen no Shosho Sukemori, was raised to Junior Fourth Rank, Upper Grade, it was said. That day he arrived at Terai. When he returned to the capital on the eighth day, the court nobles and senior officials who came to meet him went as far as Kusatsu in Toba. On the return journey, he did not go to the Toba Palace, but went to the Nishihachijo residence of the Lay Priest Chancellor.

[4.2.11] On the twenty-second day of the fourth month of the same year, the new emperor's enthronement ceremony took place. It should have been held at the Daigokuden, but after the fire the previous year, it had not yet been rebuilt. It was decided that it should be held at the Daijōkan, but the then Kujō-dono said, "The Daijōkan is a place that, if compared to a commoner's house, is like an office." Since there is no Daigokuden, the enthronement should be held at the Shishinden. When he said this, the enthronement was held at the Shishinden. The enthronement of Emperor Reizei at the Shishinden on the first day of the eleventh month of Koho 4 was because the emperor, due to an evil spirit, could not go to the Daigokuden. What precedent could there be for that? Just follow the fine precedent of Emperor Go-Sanjo's Enkyu era and hold it at the Daijokan. Although everyone agreed, saying so, they could not go against Lord Kujō's plan. The Empress moved from the Kokiden to the Jijūden, and the sight of her proceeding to the Takamikura was splendid. While all the Heike people were attending court, the young lords of Komatsu-dono had been staying at home in mourning since the previous year when the minister passed away.

[4.3.1] Kurōdo Saemon no Gon no Suke Sadanaga wrote down in great detail on about ten sheets of thick paper how auspicious and without incident this imperial accession was, and presented it to the wife of the Nyūdō Prime Minister, the Lady of Hachijō, who received it with a smile of delight. Although there were such splendid and auspicious events, the world was still not at peace.

[4.3.2] At that time, the second prince of the Retired Emperor, called Prince Mochihito, was the daughter of his mother, the Great Counselor of Kaga, Lord Suenari. Because he lived in Sanjo Takakura, he was called Takakura no Miya. On the sixteenth day of the twelfth month of Eiman 1, at the age of fifteen, he secretly underwent his coming-of-age ceremony at the Omiya Palace in Konoe Kawara. His handwriting was beautiful and refined, and his learning and talents were superior, so he should have ascended to the throne, but because of the jealousy of the late Kenshunmon'in, he was confined, and in spring outings beneath the flowers he wielded a purple brush and wrote poems in his own hand, and at autumn banquets before the moon he played the jeweled flute and personally performed elegant music. Thus he passed his days and nights, and in the fourth year of Jishō, he reached the age of thirty.

[4.3.3] At that time, the Gen Sanmi Nyūdō Yorimasa, who was living at Kawara in the vicinity of the capital, secretly visited this prince's palace one night and said something terrifying. You are the seventy-eighth generation from Emperor Jimmu, the forty-eighth descendant of Amaterasu Omikami. Though you should become crown prince and ascend the throne, do you not think it sad that you have passed your time in the palace until the age of thirty? When I observe the state of the world today, although outwardly they seem to obey, are there not those who secretly resent the Heike? You should raise a rebellion, destroy the Heike, and also put to rest the Cloistered Emperor's heart, which is always confined in Toba-dono; and you should ascend the throne. This is indeed the height of filial piety. 若思召し立せ給ひて、令旨を下させ給ふ物ならば、悦をなして馳參らむずる源氏共こそ多う候へ。 」とて申續く。 「先京都には、出羽前司光信が子共、伊賀守光基、出羽判官光長、出羽藏人光重、出羽冠者光能、熊野には、故六條判官爲義が末子、十郎義盛とて隱て候。 攝津國には多田藏人行綱こそ候へども、新大納言成親卿の謀反の時、同心しながら返り忠したる不當人で候へば申に及ばず。 さりながら、其弟多田次郎朝實、手島冠者高頼、太田太郎頼基、河内國には、武藏權守入道義基、子息石河判官代義兼、大和國には、宇野七郎親治が子ども、太郎有治、次郎清治、三郎成治、四郎義治、近江國には、山本、柏木、錦古里、美濃、尾張には山田次郎重廣、河邊太郎重直、泉太郎重光、浦野四郎重遠、安食次郎重頼、其子太郎重資、木太三郎重長、開田判官代重國、矢島先生重高、其子太郎重行、甲斐國には、逸見冠者義清、其子太郎清光、武田太郎信義、加々美次郎遠光、同小次郎長清、一條次郎忠頼、板垣三郎兼信、逸見兵衞有義、武田五郎信光、安田三郎義定、信濃國には、大内太郎維義、岡田冠者親義、平賀冠者盛義、其子の四郎義信、故帶刀先生義方が次男、木曽冠者義仲、伊豆國には流人前右兵衞佐頼朝、常陸國には、信太三郎先生義教、佐竹冠者正義、其子太郎忠義、同三郎義宗、四郎高義、五郎義季、陸奧國には故左馬頭義朝が末子、九郎冠者義經、是皆六孫王の苗裔、多田新發意滿仲が後胤也。 Although in quelling the enemies of the court and achieving long-cherished ambitions, neither the Minamoto nor the Taira was superior or inferior, now the distance between them is like that between clouds and mud, and even in the etiquette of lord and vassal, they are still inferior. In the provinces, they obey the provincial governors; in the manors, they are employed by the estate proprietors; they are driven about for public and miscellaneous duties, and have no peace of mind. How sorrowful it must be! If you, my lord, should resolve to rise and grant me an imperial command, I would gallop up night and day, and the destruction of the Taira would not take even a day. Although I am old, I will bring my children and come to serve. Thus he said.

[4.3.4] The prince, thinking how this matter should be, for a while did not consent, but Akomaru Dainagon Munetō's grandson, Bingo former governor Suetō's son, Shōnagon Korenaga, was a skilled physiognomist, so people called him the physiognomist of the time. That person saw this prince and said, "You have the physiognomy of one who should ascend to the throne. You must not abandon the affairs of the realm.
