When he said this, and Gen Sanmi Nyūdō also spoke in the same way, the prince thought, "Then it must be so." Was it a divine message from Amaterasu Omikami? So saying, He firmly resolved in his heart. He summoned Yoshimori, the tenth son of Kumano, and made him a Kurodo. He changed his name to Yukiie and was sent down to the eastern provinces as a messenger of the imperial command.

[4.3.5] On the twenty-eighth day of the same fourth month, he left the capital, and starting from Ōmi Province, he gradually contacted the Genji of Mino and Owari along the way; on the tenth day of the fifth month, he arrived at Hōjō in Izu and delivered the imperial command to the exiled former Hyōe no Suke. Shida Saburō Senjō Yoshinori, being the elder brother, intended to take him, and went down to the floating island of Shida in Hitachi Province. Kiso no Kanja Yoshinaka, being the nephew, intended to help him, and set out along the mountain road.

[4.3.6] At that time, the Kumano bettō Tansei had deep loyalty to the Heike, but somehow he got wind of it: Shingū no Jūrō Yoshimori received the imperial command of Prince Takakura, stirred up the Genji of Mino and Owari, and had already raised a rebellion. The people of Nachi and Shingū will surely side with the Genji. Tanzō, having received the favor of the Heike as vast as Mount Tenzan, how could he possibly turn against them? He shot a single arrow at the men of Nachi Shingū, and saying he would report the details to the Heike, he set out for the harbor of Shingū with a thousand men in armor. At Shingū were the hōgen Torii and the hōgen Takabō; among the samurai were Ui, Suzuki, Mizuya, and Kikkō; at Nachi, from the shugyō hōgen on down—in all, their force numbered more than two thousand men. With war cries and exchanges of arrows, on the Genji side they shot as if to say, "Shoot like this!", and on the Heike side, "Shoot like this!", and without any pause in the shouting voices or any gap in the whistling of the arrows, they fought for about three days. Kumano Betto Tanzo had many of his retainers and followers killed, was himself wounded, and barely escaped with his life, fleeing up to the main shrine.

[4.4.1] Meanwhile, the Cloistered Emperor said, "Will I be exiled to a distant province, or will I be moved to a far-off island?" He said this, but in the detached palace south of the capital, this year became the second year of his residence. On the twelfth day of the fifth month of the same year, around noon, many weasels ran about noisily in the imperial palace. The Cloistered Emperor was greatly startled, and divined the omens. He summoned Nakakane, the governor of Omi, who was then still called Tsuru no Kurando, and said, "Take this divination result to Yasuchika's place, have him examine it carefully, and bring back a written report." Thus he spoke. Nakakane received this and went to the house of Abe no Yasuchika, the Director of the Bureau of Yin and Yang, but he happened not to be at home. When he was told that he was at a place called Shirakawa, he went there to look for him, met Yasuchika, and conveyed the imperial command, whereupon Yasuchika immediately presented a written report. Nakakane returned to the Toba Palace and tried to enter through the gate, but the guarding warriors would not allow it. He knew the way in; he climbed over the earthen wall, crawled under the raised floor, and from the cut-out plank he presented Yasuchika's letter. When the Retired Emperor opened it and looked, it said: "Within the next three days there will be both joy and sorrow." So he said. The Retired Emperor said, "Your joy is only natural. Having become a person of such high rank, what sorrow could there possibly be? So he said.

[4.4.2] Meanwhile, when the former Major Counselor Munemori reported the Retired Emperor's situation to him, the Lay Monk Chancellor gradually reconsidered, and on the thirteenth of the same month he had the Retired Emperor moved from Toba Palace to the residence of Bifukumon-in at Hachijo-Karasuma. It was Yasuchika who declared that the joy within three days was this.

[4.4.3] At such a place, when Kumano Betto Tanzo sent a courier to the capital to report the rebellion of Prince Takakura, the former Udaisho Munemori was greatly alarmed, and when he reported this to the Nyudo Prime Minister, who happened to be at Fukuhara, the latter, without even listening, immediately galloped up to the capital, saying, "It cannot be helped." Seize Prince Takakura and exile him to Hata in Tosa. Thus he declared. The senior noble was Sanjō Dainagon Sanefusa, and the steward was Tō no Ben Mitsumasa, it was said. Minamoto no Daibu Hōgan Kanetsuna, receiving the order from Dewa Hōgan Mitsunaga, headed toward the prince's palace. This Minamoto no Daibu Hōgan was the second son of Sanmi Nyūdō. The reason he was included among these people was that the Heike did not know that the Third Rank Novice had advised Takakura-no-miya's rebellion.

[4.5.1] The Prince was composing a poem on the moon seen through a break in the clouds on the night of the fifteenth of the Fifth Month, and had no inkling of what was to come, when a messenger from the lay monk of the Third Rank arrived in haste bearing a letter. The Prince's wet nurse's son, Rokujō no Suke no Tayū Munenobu, took it, brought it before the Prince, and opened it to read: "Your Highness's rebellion has come to light, and they are sending you into exile to the province of Tosa; officials have come to take you into custody. Leave the palace at once and go to Mii-dera. The lay monk will also come soon. So he said. What shall we do about this? While they were making a commotion, there was a man named Nobutsura, a samurai of the palace. There is no other way. Please go out in court lady's attire. When he said that, "That is appropriate." Saying that, she disheveled her hair, and over her layered robes she put on an ichimegasa (a lady's hat). Rokujō no Suke no Tayū Munenobu, holding a Chinese umbrella, attended her. A page named Tsurumaru carried things in a bag on his head. She set out like a nobleman going to fetch a wife, and when she went north along Takakura, she lightly jumped over a large ditch. A passerby stopped and said, "How indecent! The way that court lady jumps over a ditch!" Saying this, he looked suspiciously, and passed by even more quickly.

[4.5.2] Chōbei no Jō Nobutsura was left behind to guard the palace. He made the few court ladies who were there hide here and there, and while looking around to put away any unsightly things, he noticed that the flute called Koeda, which the prince had so treasured, had just now been left behind on the pillow in the usual room. He wanted to go back and get it. Nobutsura saw this and said, "How shameful!" The flute that His Highness treasures so much!" Saying this, he pursued him within five cho and arrived. The prince was deeply moved and said, "When I die, put this flute in my coffin." Thus he said. "Attend me at once." When he said this, Nobutsura replied, "Just now, officials are coming to the palace to welcome you, and there is not a single person before you; it would be terribly lonely." That Nobuyori is in this palace is known to all, high and low; if he is not here tonight, people will say that he too fled that night. For a man who takes up bow and arrow, his reputation, even if only for a moment, is what he must cherish. The officials will deal with him for a while, then break through and come at once. Saying this, he ran back.

[4.5.3] For that day's attire, Chōbei wore a light blue hunting robe over a yellowish-green laced haramaki, and girded on a sword of the Imperial Guard. They opened both the main gate on Sanjō and the small gate on Takakura, and lay in wait. Minamoto no Daibu Hogan Kanetsuna, Dewa Hogan Mitsunaga, with a force of over three hundred horsemen in all, pressed upon the prince's palace at the hour of the rat on the night of the fifteenth. Minamoto no Daibu Hogan, thinking that there was something he wished to say, stayed outside the distant gate. Dewa Hogan Mitsunaga, riding on horseback, forced his way inside the gate, and halting in the courtyard, raised his voice loudly and said, "Because word of your rebellion has reached us, the officials, receiving the command of the betto, have come to escort you." Come out quickly. When he said this, Choheie stood up on the raised floor and said, "This is not the palace now." I am going on a pilgrimage. What is it? Explain the details of the matter. When he said this, [the other] replied, "Why, if not to this palace, where would you have him go?" Don't say such a thing. Servants, come and search for him! So he said. Nagabei no Jō heard this and said, "What a thing for these senseless officials to say! Even for me to come inside the gate on horseback is strange enough, but to say that the servants should come in and search—how can you say such a thing? It is I, Sahyōe no Jō Hasebe Nobutsura. Come closer and do not let him pass. So he said. Among the lower officials of the agency, a man of great strength named Kanetake, a brave warrior, set his eyes on Chohei and leaped up onto the raised floor. Seeing this, the companions, fourteen or fifteen of them, followed. Chōbei, as he tore off the cord of his hunting robe and threw it away, drew the sword he had had made for his own use, though it was a Palace Guard's sword, and cut them to pieces. Though the enemy fought with great swords and long halberds, they were cut down by Nobuyori's Palace Guard sword, and fell to the garden like leaves scattered by a storm.

[4.5.4] When the moon of the fifteenth night of the fifth month appeared from between the clouds and shone, the enemy was unfamiliar with the terrain, while Nobutsura knew the lay of the land. Pursuing them into that open road, he struck them down with a thud; driving them into this dead end, he cut them down with a slash. "How can you do this to an imperial messenger?" When he said this, [the other] replied, "What is an imperial messenger?" Saying this, he danced back with his sword bent, straightened his stance, and struck down fourteen or fifteen of the enemy who were standing there. When he tried to cut his own belly, the tip of his sword was broken off about three inches, and when he felt for his waist, the scabbard had fallen off and was gone. His strength failing, he opened the main gate wide and tried to flee through the small gate on the Takakura side, but a man with a long sword came at him. Nobutsura tried to leap onto the long sword, but missed and was pierced through the thigh. Though his heart was fierce, he was surrounded by many and taken alive.

[4.5.5] After that, they searched the palace, but the prince had not crossed over. They bound Nobutsura and took him to Rokuhara. The lay monk Prime Minister was seated within the blinds. The former Right Grand General Lord Munemori stood on the broad veranda and had Nobutsura brought to the great courtyard, saying, "Truly, you fellow, what is an imperial decree?" Saying that, did he cut him down? Moreover, he has wounded and killed a servant of the office. In short, interrogate him thoroughly, inquire into the details of the matter, and after that, take him out to the riverbank and behead him. Thus he said. Nobutsura, without being flustered at all, laughed scornfully and said, "During these nights, when someone was spying on that palace, I thought something must be happening, and so I was not on guard, when men in armor burst in. 'Who are you?'" When he asked, "Who goes there?", they answered, "An imperial messenger." Bandits, pirates, robbers, and such fellows sometimes say, "A nobleman is coming!" Sometimes they say, "An imperial messenger!" and such, as I have heard before, so they say, "What is an imperial decree?" And with that, they cut them down. If we had all the equipment we wanted and good iron swords, we would not let a single official return safely. And where has the Prince's residence been moved to? I do not know. Even if I did know, would a mere servant, having resolved not to tell, be likely to confess under interrogation? So saying, after that he said nothing more.

[4.5.6] The many Heike warriors who were lined up there said, "What a brave man!" What a pity that such a fine man should be cut down! they said. Among them, one person said, "That man, even in the past when he was in the province, was the one who, when the great guard company could not hold back six robbers, alone chased them, cut down four, captured two alive, and at that time became the Sahyōe-no-jō. He is indeed the one." He is indeed a warrior worth a thousand. When they all lamented him in this way, the Lay Monk Chancellor, perhaps thinking something, had him exiled to Hino in Hōki. When the Genji came to power, he went down to the eastern provinces, and following Kajiwara Heizo Kagetoki, he reported the origin of the matter in full detail, so the Kamakura lord, thinking it admirable, bestowed upon him a favor in Noto Province, it is said.

[4.6.1] The Prince crossed Takakura to the north, Konoe to the east, and the Kamo River, and went to Nyoigatake. Long ago, when Emperor Kiyomihara was still Crown Prince, he was attacked by rebels and fled into Mount Yoshino; it was then that he disguised himself as a maiden. The present condition of this prince is not in the least different from that. As he made his way all night along unfamiliar mountain paths, the blood from his feet—what could he be accustomed to?—dyed the sand crimson. Even the dew on the summer grass must have felt oppressive to him. Thus at dawn he entered Miidera. "Because I value my worthless life, I have relied on the monks and entered [the temple]." When he said this, the monks respectfully rejoiced, prepared a residence in the Horin-in, and served him food as usual.

[4.6.2] When dawn broke on the sixteenth, the news that Prince Takakura had raised a rebellion and been killed caused an uproar in the capital beyond compare. The Cloistered Emperor heard this and said, "Your leaving the Toba Palace is a joy to me." And also a lament. And Yasuchika's divination report that he presented said this. Thus he spoke.

[4.6.3] Now, if the lay monk Gen Sanmi had been alive all these years and days, it would have been so. When asked, "What was in your mind this year that you raised a rebellion?", it was because the second son of the Heike, the former Major General of the Right, Lord Munemori, did what should not be done. Therefore, just because one is in the world, to do what should not be done, and to say what should not be said even in private, one must be a person of deep forethought.

[4.6.4] For example, at the residence of Nakatsuna, the eldest son of the lay monk Gen Sanmi, there was a famous horse whose reputation had reached the imperial palace. It did not seem that there could be another horse, a chestnut with no equal, that would run and turn as this one did. Its name was called Kinoshita. The former Major General of the Right heard of this and sent a messenger to Nakatsuna's place, saying, "I would like to see the famous horse I have heard about." When he sent word saying this, the reply of the Governor of Izu was: "I do have such a horse, but since I have recently overworked it, I have sent it to the countryside to rest for a while." "If that is so, it cannot be helped." "Saying this, after that there was no further word, but the many Heike warriors who were lined up said, "Alas, that horse was here until the day before yesterday, and yesterday too, and this morning it was ridden in the garden." "When they said this, he replied, "Then you must be regretting it. Very well, ask for it." "It is bad; ask for it." Saying this, he had him ride it, and sent letters and such, and when he was asked five or six times, seven or eight times in a single day, the Novice of the Third Rank heard of this, summoned the Governor of Izu, and said, "Even if it were a horse made of solid gold, how could one begrudge something that people ask for to that extent?" Send that horse to Rokuhara immediately. Thus he said. The Governor of Izu, unable to resist, wrote a poem and attached it, and sent it to Rokuhara.

lg.l: 戀くば來ても見よかし、身にそへるかげをばいかゞ放ちやるべき。

div.p: [4.6.5] Lord Munemori did not write a reply to the poem, but said, "Alas, the horse! The horse was truly a fine horse." But because it is hateful that the master is so reluctant, immediately brand the master's name on it. So saying, he branded it with the name Nakatsuna and stood it in the stable. A guest came and said, "I would like to see the famous horse I have heard about." When he said this, [the master] said, "Put a saddle on that Nakatsuna and lead him out." Ride that Nakatsuna! Strike Nakatsuna! Now! When he said this, the Governor of Izu heard it and thought, "Even though it is a horse I value more than my life, and even if it is taken by authority, it is unbearable that because of a horse Nakatsuna should become a laughingstock of the whole world." And when he was greatly angered, the Third Rank Novice heard this and said to the Governor of Izu, "Thinking that nothing could happen, the Heike people are saying such foolish things." If that is the case, what use is it to remain alive? We should watch for an opportunity. And so, without even thinking of it privately, he urged the Prince, and later it was heard.

[4.6.6] Even in this, the people of the realm mourned the late Lord Komatsu. Once, when Lord Komatsu was attending the palace, as he was going to the quarters of the Empress, a snake about eight feet long crawled around the left leg of the Minister's sashinuki. Shigemori thought that if he made a fuss, the court ladies would also make a fuss, and the Empress would be startled. So he pressed the snake's tail with his left hand, took its head with his right hand, drew it into the sleeve of his court robe, and without any disturbance, called out, "Is there a Sixth Rank official? Is there a Sixth Rank official?" When he was summoned, the Governor of Izu, who was at that time still a Chamberlain of the Imperial Guard, came forward and announced his name as Nakatsuna, and was given the snake. He gave it to him, and passing through the Yubadono, he went out to the small garden of the palace, and summoning the young servant of the storehouse, said, "Take this." When he said this, the snake shook its head violently and fled. Unable to resist, he summoned his retainer Takiguchi and gave it to him. He gave it and threw it away. That morning, Lord Komatsu saddled a fine horse and sent it to the Governor of Izu, saying, "Indeed, yesterday's entertainment was truly splendid. This is a horse for riding. When night falls and you go from outside the camp to your beloved's place, you should use it. So saying, he sent it. The Governor of Izu, since it was a reply from the Minister, said, "I have respectfully received the horse." And indeed, yesterday's entertainment was just like the Genjōraku dance. So he said. Why was it that Lord Komatsu was so noble, while Lord Munemori was not so, and moreover, by taking a horse that others regretted losing, he brought about a great national calamity—how regrettable!

[4.6.7] On the night of the sixteenth, Minamoto no Yorimasa, the lay monk of the Third Rank, together with his eldest son Nakatsuna, the governor of Izu, his second son Kanetsuna, the Minamoto no Tayu hogan, Nakatsuna's son Nakamitsu, the Kurodo no Taro, and the rest, with a force of over three hundred horsemen, set fire to their mansion and went to Mii-dera. Among the retainers of the lay monk of the Third Rank was a man named Watanabe no Genzo Takiguchi no Kioi. When he had galloped after them and stopped, the former Major General of the Right summoned Kiso and said, "Why did you not accompany the Novice of the Third Rank, but stayed behind?" When he said this, Kiso, in fear, replied, "If something unexpected should happen, I have always thought to be the first to rush forward and give my life, but for some reason you have not said so." "Do you intend to side with the enemy, Yorimasa?" He is also a person who serves both sides. Thinking of future glory, does he intend to serve this house? Tell it as it is. Thus he said. Shedding tears, he said, "Although it is a matter of inherited friendship, how could I side with someone who has become an enemy of the court?" I will serve you in the palace. When he said that, the other replied, "Then serve me." I will not be inferior in the least to the favors that Priest Yorinori has shown me. Saying this, he went inside.

[4.6.8] "Is there a samurai to compete?" "Yes." "Is there a contest?" "Yes." Saying so, he waited in attendance from morning until evening. When the day had gradually darkened, the general came out. The contestant, in fear, said, "Is it true that the Third Rank Novice Lord is at Mii-dera?" Surely they will send a punitive force against us. It is not at all pleasant. It must be the monks of Miidera, or perhaps those close fellows from Watanabe. We should have chosen and attacked them, but the horse that we should have ridden to meet the situation was stolen by that close fellow. Would you kindly lend us a horse? When he said this, the general deemed it reasonable, and on a white-roan horse called 'Nanten' that he kept as a treasure, he had a fine saddle placed and gave it to him. Returning to the boat-shaped carriage, he said, 'Would that the day would end soon! I will mount this horse, gallop to Mii-dera, and be the first to charge at the Lay Monk of the Third Rank, dying in battle.' Thus he spoke. As the day gradually darkened, he secretly sent his wife and children away in various directions, and the feelings in his heart as he set out for Mii-dera were truly pitiful.

[4.6.9] Wearing a plain-patterned hunting robe with large chrysanthemum fastenings, a hereditary armor of scarlet braided cords, a helmet with white-starred crest and tied chin-cord, a great sword of fine workmanship at his side, carrying twenty-four black-feathered arrows, and as if not forgetting the archery skills of the Takiguchi guards, he had a single arrow fletched with hawk feathers ready in his quiver. Taking up his bow of Shigetō, he mounted his horse in the warm court, took along a spare horse, had a servant carry his sidearm, set fire to the mansion and burned it up, and galloped off to Mii-dera. At Rokuhara, they were in an uproar, saying that a fire had broken out from the residence of Kiō. Lord Munemori hurried out and asked, "Is Kiō there?" When he asked, they replied, "He is not here." They said. "Oh no! That fellow has stretched out his hand and deceived us!" "Chase after him and strike him down!" He said this, but Kioi was by nature a superior archer with a strong bow, skilled in rapid shooting, and a man of great strength and courage; with twenty-four arrows he would first shoot dead twenty-four men. Saying "Don't make a sound," there was no one to face him. At Miidera, at that time, there was talk of Kioi. The Watanabe band said, "We should have brought Kioi along, but he stayed behind at Rokuhara. What misfortune might he have met?" When they said this, the Novice Sanmi, knowing their hearts, said, "Surely that man will not be rudely seized and bound. He is a man deeply loyal to the Novice. Watch now. He will come right now. He had hardly finished speaking when Kioi came rushing out. "That is why." Thus he said. The one who respectfully reported said, "Lord Izu's retainer, at the foot of the tree, has brought the brazier from Rokuhara." I will bring it. So saying, he drove Izu-no-kami into the gate around midnight. When they entered the stable and the horses bit each other, the grooms were startled and said, "Nantei has come to visit." They said. When the general hurried out and looked, there was a brand that said, "Formerly Nantei, now Taira no Munemori, the lay priest." The general said, "This is not reassuring. It is regrettable that I was tricked by extending my hand to the horse. When we go to Mii-dera this time, by all means first capture the scout alive. Cut off his head with a saw. Saying this, he jumped up and up, and though he was scolded, Nuan Ting grew tail hair, and the brand also did not disappear.

[4.7.1] At Miidera, the bell rang, and the monks held a council. "When I consider the state of the world in recent times, the decline of the Buddhist Law and the weakening of the Imperial Law are exactly at this moment. If we do not now admonish the atrocities of the Novice Kiyomori, what day should we wait for? The Prince's entry into this temple—is it not the protection of the Great Hachiman Shrine and the divine aid of the Shinra Myōjin? How could it be that the heavenly beings and earthly spirits do not manifest themselves, and that the power of the Buddhas and gods does not bring about his subjugation? Now, the Northern Peak is the place of learning of the one-flavor of the Perfect Teaching, and the Southern Capital is the ordination platform for receiving the precepts after the summer retreat." Why should we not join in sending the dispatch? So they all agreed unanimously and sent the dispatch to both the mountain and Nara. First, the letter to the mountain said:Onjo-ji Temple sends this letter to the office of Enryaku-ji Temple.We earnestly request your assistance to save our temple from destruction. The lay monk Jokai has arbitrarily violated the imperial law and seeks to destroy the Buddhist law.In the midst of boundless grief, on the night of the fifteenth of the past month, the second prince of the Retired Emperor secretly entered the temple.Here, although there was an order to the effect that he should be produced under the name of an imperial decree, they were unable to produce him.Therefore, there was a report that government troops would be dispatched.The destruction of this temple was exactly at this moment.How could the monks not lament?Above all, the two temples of Enryaku and Onjō, though divided into two monzeki, the things they study are the same in the one-flavor teaching of perfect and immediate enlightenment.They are like the left and right wings of a bird.Also, they are like the two wheels of a cart.If one side is missing, how could there be no lament? Therefore, if you especially join forces and help the destruction of this temple, we will quickly forget the longstanding resentment and return to the old days of dwelling in the mountain.The monks' council was like this.Thus the document was sent as stated.
[4.7.2] Jishō 4th year, 5th month, 18th day, the assembly of monks
[4.7.3] Thus it was written.

[4.8.1] The monks of the mountain gate, upon reading this letter, said, "What is this? Though it is a branch temple of this mountain, to write that it is like the wings of a bird or the two wheels of a cart is outrageous." Saying this, they did not send a reply. Moreover, when the Lay Monk Chancellor conveyed to the Tendai Abbot Myōun, the Archbishop, that he should pacify the monks, the Abbot hurriedly climbed the mountain and calmed the assembly. During that time, they reported to the Prince's side that it was uncertain. Also, the Lay Monk Chancellor sent twenty thousand koku of rice from Ōmi and three thousand bolts of silk from the northern provinces to the monks. When these were distributed to the various valleys and peaks, it was a sudden event, and there were monks who each took a large amount. Also, there were monks who came away empty-handed and took nothing. By whose doing was it? They wrote a lampoon.

lg.l: 山法師織延衣うすくして、恥をばえこそかくさざりけれ。

div.p: [4.8.2] Also, was it composed by the monks who are not even worth silk?

lg.l: 織延を一きれも得ぬわれらさへ、薄恥をかくかずに入哉。

div.p: [4.8.3] Also, in the letter to Nanto, it says:Onjo-ji Temple sends a document to the office of Kofuku-ji Temple.We earnestly request your assistance to save our temple from destruction. The excellence of Buddhism is for the protection of the royal law, and the longevity of the royal law depends on Buddhism.Here, the former Grand Minister of State, Taira no Ason Kiyomori, whose Buddhist name was Jōkai, arbitrarily usurped the authority of the state, disturbed the government, and both at home and abroad caused resentment and lamentation. On the night of the fifteenth of this month, the second prince of the First Retired Emperor, in order to escape an unexpected calamity, suddenly had himself enter the temple.Here, although it was said that there was an imperial decree to be issued, the monks all regretted this.Therefore that lay monk is about to bring warriors into this temple.Both the Buddhist Law and the Imperial Law are about to be destroyed at once.Long ago, when Emperor Wuzong of Tang used military force to destroy Buddhism, the monks of Mount Qingliang fought a battle and defended it.Even royal authority is like this.How much more so for those who commit rebellion and treason?In particular, in Nanjing, without precedent, an innocent elder was exiled.If it is not this time, on what day will we achieve our revenge?I pray that if the monks, within, assist in the destruction of the Buddhist Law, and without, repel the evil companions, then this unity of purpose will surely fulfill our long-cherished desire.The deliberation of the monks was like this.Therefore, the document was sent as stated.
[4.8.4] Jishō 4th year, 5th month, 18th day, the great assembly
[4.8.5] Thus it was written.

[4.8.6] The great assembly of the Southern Capital opened this letter and immediately sent a reply. In the reply letter it said:Kofukuji sends this letter: it is recorded in one sheet of the letter that came from Onjoji.Regarding the matter that the lay monk Nyudo Jokai intends to destroy the Buddhist teachings of your esteemed temple, we send this letter. Although you speak of establishing the doctrines of the two schools of Gyokusen and Gyoka, the golden chapters and golden phrases alike have come forth from the teaching gate of the one lifetime.Both the southern capital and the northern capital alike are disciples of the Tathagata.Our own temple and other temples should mutually subdue the demonic hindrances of Devadatta.Now, the lay monk Kiyomori was the dregs of the Taira clan and the dust of the warrior houses.His grandfather Masamori served the house of Kurōdo no Goi and took up the whip of provincial governor.Ōkura-kyō Tamefusa was appointed to the Kebiishi when he was the governor of Kashū, and Shuri no daibu Akisue was appointed to the post of Muma no Bettō when he was the governor of Harima.However, when his father Tadamori was granted access to the imperial palace, young and old in the capital and countryside all lamented the flaw in the jeweled vase, and the fortunes of those inside and outside the court all wept at the oracle of the land of horses.Although Tadamori brushed the wings of his ambition toward the blue clouds, the people of the world still despised the seed of the humble cottage.A young samurai who values his reputation does not seek to serve in that household.However, since the first year of Heiji, in the twelfth month, when the Retired Emperor, in recognition of his service in a single battle, bestowed upon him an extraordinary reward, he rose to the rank of Chancellor and was also granted the privilege of bearing arms.His sons either disgraced the high ministerial ranks or joined the imperial guards.His daughters either served in the office of the empress's household or received the title of quasi-empress.All his brothers and illegitimate sons walked the thorny path of officialdom, and his grandsons and nephews all divided the bamboo tallies of provincial governors.Moreover, he ruled Kyushu, appointed and dismissed all officials, and made all servants his followers.If even a hair's breadth went against his will, he would imprison even princes and marquises; if a single word offended his ears, he would bind even court nobles.Because of this, some, to prolong their lives for a while, and some, to escape momentary humiliation, even the sovereign of ten thousand chariots flattered with a sycophantic smile, and the hereditary lord instead performed the courtesy of approaching on his knees.Even when they were said to seize hereditary family estates, they feared the imperial judgment and rolled up their tongues; even when they were said to take the manors inherited by the temples, they were awed by the authority and said nothing.Riding on their victories too far, in the winter of the previous year, in the eleventh month, they arrested the retired emperor in his residence and exiled the Chancellor.The extremity of the rebellion was truly unprecedented in all ages.At that time, although we said that we should go to meet the rebel forces and interrogate their crimes, some were wary of the divine will, and some relied on what was called an imperial edict, so while we suppressed our frustration and passed the time, they again raised troops and surrounded the second prince of the Retired Emperor's palace, whereupon the three shrines of Hachiman and Kasuga Daimyojin secretly manifested their divine presence, and reverently bearing the imperial palanquin, sent it to your noble temple and entrusted it to the gate of Shiragi.It was clear that the royal law would never be exhausted.Accordingly, who among sentient beings would not rejoice at the fact that your noble temple has abandoned its own life to protect and serve [the emperor]?While we, being in a distant region, were moved by that sentiment, the lay monk Kiyomori again became angry and, hearing that he intended to enter your noble temple, we have made preparations in advance.At the hour of the dragon (8 a.m.) on the eighteenth day, they roused the great assembly, sent dispatches to all the temples, issued orders to the branch temples, and, having secured soldiers, were about to send out guides when a blue bird flew in and dropped a fragrant letter.The gloom of many days was dispelled in an instant.Even the bird Chū of the Qingliang Mountain in that Tang land turned back Emperor Wuzong's government troops.How much more should the monks of the two gates, north and south, of our land of Japan not sweep away the wicked sort of traitorous ministers?Fortify well the encampments on the left and right of the Ryoen, and await the announcement of our departure.Perceive the situation, and do not harbor doubts.Hereby [we] send this document.
[4.8.7] On the twenty-first day of the fifth month of the fourth year of Jishō, the great assembly [of monks]
[4.8.8] Thus [they] wrote, it is said.

[4.9.1] At Miidera, the great assembly also rose up and held a council. The mountain temple has changed its mind; the southern capital has not yet come. If this matter drags on, it will be bad. They will press on to Rokuhara and make a night attack. If that is the plan, divide into two groups, old and young; the old monks should head toward the rear gate from Nyoi Peak. Four or five hundred foot soldiers go first, and when they set fire to the houses in Shirakawa and burn them up, the people in the capital and the warriors of Rokuhara will say, "Oh, something has happened!" Saying this, they would rush toward them. At that time, while Iwasaka and Sakuramoto were holding out for a while, fighting, the main force, with Izu no Kami as commander, would press upon Rokuhara with the wicked monks, set fire to the windward side, and attack in one fell swoop; how could the Nyūdō Prime Minister fail to be burned out and killed? Thus they deliberated.

[4.9.2] Among them, the monk Ichinyo-bō Ajari Shinkai, who had been praying for the Heike, came forward into the council hall with several tens of disciples and fellow monks, and said, "If I speak thus, you may think I am a partisan of the Heike. Even if it is so, let it be. How could I possibly break the monks' cause and not care about the name of our temple? In the past, the Minamoto and the Taira contended on the left and right, and were the protectors of the imperial court, but recently the fortunes of the Minamoto have declined, and the Taira have held the realm for over twenty years; there is not a plant or tree that does not bow to them. The state of the inner mansion is such that with a small force it would be difficult to attack and capture it easily. We should carefully devise a plan outside, gather forces, and perhaps attack on a later day. Thus, in order to delay the time, they deliberated at great length.

[4.9.3] Here there was an old monk named Jōen-bō Ajari Keishū. Under his robe he wore a belly band, thrust a large sword into his front apron, wrapped his head, and leaning on a long-handled sword with a white hilt, he advanced into the council courtyard and said, "You must not take the evidence outside." The founder of our temple, Emperor Tenmu, when he was still Crown Prince, was opposed by Prince Ōtomo, and so he left the depths of Yoshino and passed through Uda District in Yamato Province. At that time his force was only seventeen horsemen, but he crossed over into Iga and Ise, and with the forces of Mino and Owari he destroyed Prince Ōtomo, and finally ascended the throne. "A bird in distress flies into a man's bosom. People take pity on it," says the text. As for the rest, I do not know; but as for Keishū's followers, tonight let us press upon Rokuhara and die fighting! Thus they deliberated. Enman-in no Daibu Gengaku stepped forward and said, "There is too much deliberation; the night is deepening—hurry, advance!" Thus he said.

[4.10.1] The old monks who faced the rear attack as commanders-in-chief were Genzanmi Nyūdō Yorimasa, Jōenbō Ajari Keishū, Ritsujōbō Ajari Nichiin, Sotsu Hōin Zenchi, Zenchi's disciple Gihō, and Zenyō, and altogether their force numbered one thousand men, each with a burning pine torch, and they headed toward Nyoigatake. As the great general of the main force, his eldest son Izu no kami Nakatsuna, second son Gen-dayū hōgan Kanetsuna, Rokujō Kurōdo Nakai, his son Kurōdo Tarō Nakamitsu; among the warrior monks, Enman-in Daisuke Gengaku, Jōki-in Aratosā, Risshō-bō Iga no Kō, Hōrin-in Oni-Sado — these men, in strength and with bow, arrow, and striking weapons, were warriors each a match for a thousand, of whom it was said they would meet even demons or gods. At Byōdō-in were Inaba Tateja Ara-dayū, Kaku Rokurō-bō, Shima Ajari, Tsutsui Hōshi, Gō Ajari, Aku Shōnagon; at Kitain were Kinkō-in no Roku Tengu, Shikibu no Tayū, Noto, Kaga, Sado, Bingo, and others. Among the sixty men, including Matsui Higo, Shōnan'in Chikugo, Kaya Chikuzen, Ōya Toshinaga, Gochiin Tajima, and the monk Jōen-bō Ajari Keishū's attendant, in the priestly group none was equal to Ikkai Hōshi, nor to Gyōbu Shunshū. Among the temple clergy, Tsutsui Jōmyō Meishū, Kozō Sonzuki, Son'ei, Jikei, Rakujū, and Tekken Gen'ei; among the warriors, Watanabe no Shō Harima no Jirō, Sazuke Satsuma no Hyōe, Chōshichi, Kiso no Takiguchi, Yoemon no Suke, Zoku Genta, and Kiyoshi took the lead, and with a total force of over fifteen hundred men, they set out from Miidera.

[4.10.2] After the prince entered, they cut off the great barrier and the small barrier, and dug moats and set up abatis, so while they were building bridges over the moats and removing the abatis, time passed and the roosters at the barrier road crowed. The Governor of Izu said, "If the birds sing here, the Rokuhara will surely attack in broad daylight; what shall we do?" When he said this, Enman-in Daisuke Genkaku again stepped forward as before and deliberated: "Long ago, in the time of King Zhao of Qin, when Lord Mengchang was imprisoned, thanks to the queen's help, he led three thousand soldiers and escaped, and reached Hangu Pass. As long as the rooster had not crowed, the gate of the pass was not opened. Among Lord Mengchang's three thousand guests, there was a soldier called Tenkatsu. Because he was skilled at imitating the rooster's crow, he was also called Keimei (Rooster Crow). He climbed up to a high place where roosters crow, and when he imitated the crowing of a rooster, the roosters along the barrier road heard it and all crowed. At that time, the barrier keeper was deceived by the false crowing of the bird, and opened the barrier gate and let them pass. This too may be the enemy's trick; just come closer. So he said. While this was happening, the short summer night dawned faintly. The Governor of Izu said, "I thought it would surely be a night attack, but in a daytime battle we cannot possibly win. Call them back! Saying this, he called back the rear guard from Nyoi Peak. The main force turned back from Matsuzaka. The young monks said, "It was because of Ichinyo-bo Ajari's long deliberation that dawn broke." They pressed in and cut the monk's quarters to pieces. The disciples and fellow monks who were defending the place, several tens of them, were killed. Ichinyo-bo Ajari fled in a panic to Rokuhara and, with tears streaming from his aged eyes, reported this matter, but at Rokuhara, although tens of thousands of mounted warriors had gathered, there was no disturbance.

[4.10.3] At dawn on the twenty-third of the same month, the Prince thought that this temple alone would not suffice, that the mountain monks had changed their minds, and that the southern capital had not yet arrived. Thinking that it would be bad if it became later, he left Mii-dera and entered Nara. This prince had two flutes of Chinese bamboo, known as Semiore and Koeda. That Semiore: long ago, in the time of Emperor Toba, when a thousand ryō of gold was sent to the gate of the Song dynasty, as a return gift, a flute bamboo with joints like a living cicada was presented, one joint. Wondering how he could possibly set aside such a precious treasure, he summoned the high priest Kakushu of Miidera, had him stand on the altar, perform seven days of consecration, and carve it. This is the flute he had made. Once, when the Middle Counselor Takamatsu no Sanesada came and played this flute, he forgot it was an ordinary flute and placed it below his knees, and the flute, as if to say 'how regrettable!', broke at that moment. That is why it was named 'Semi-ori' (Cicada-fold). Because of the flute's excellence, it was passed down in this prince's family. However, thinking perhaps this was the end, he offered it to Maitreya in the Golden Hall. It seemed as if it was for the sake of encountering Maitreya at the dawn of the Dragon Flower Assembly, and it was a moving thing.

[4.10.4] The old monks were all given leave, and were made to stay behind. The appropriate young monks and wicked monks came. The Gen Sanmi Nyudo's whole clan was brought along, and their force was said to be a thousand men. The Ajari Keishu of the Jōen-bō, leaning on a pigeon-headed staff, came before the Prince, and with tears streaming from his aged eyes, said: "Though I would serve you to the end, I am already over eighty, and walking has become difficult." I will send my disciple, the Hōkyō-bō Shunshū. He is the son of Yamanauchi Sudō Gyōbu no Jō Toshimichi, a resident of Sagami Province, who, during the Heiji War, was in the service of the late Sama no Kami Yoshitomo and died in battle at Rokujō-gawara. Since he has some connection with me, I have taken care of him, and I know him to the bottom of his heart. Please take him with you wherever you go. 」とて、涙を抑て留りぬ。 宮もあはれに思召て、何の好にかうは申らんとて、御涙せきあへさせ給はず。

[4.11.1] 宮は宇治と寺との間にて、六度迄御落馬有けり。 これは去ぬる夜、御寢の成ざりし故也とて、宇治橋三間引きはづし、平等院に入奉て、暫御休息有けり。 六波羅には、 「すはや宮こそ南都へ落させ給ふなれ。追懸て討奉れ。」とて、大將軍には左兵衞督 知盛、頭中將重衡、左馬頭行盛、薩摩守忠教、侍大將には、上總守忠清、其子上總太 郎判官忠綱、飛騨守景家、其子飛騨太郎判官景高、高橋判官長綱、河内判官秀國、武 藏三郎左衞門尉有國、越中次郎兵衞尉盛繼、上總五郎兵衞忠光、惡七兵衞景清を先と して、都合其勢二萬八千餘騎、木幡山打越て、宇治橋の詰にぞ押寄たる。敵平等院に と見てんげれば、閧を作る事三箇度、宮の御方にも、同う閧の聲をぞ合せたる。先陣 が、「橋を引いたぞ、過すな。」とどよみけれども、後陣に是を聞つけず、我先にと 進程に、先陣二百餘騎押落され、水に溺れて流けり。 They stood at both ends of the bridge and exchanged arrows.

[4.11.2] On the prince's side, the arrows shot by Ōya Toshinaga, Gochi-in Tajima, Watanabe Shōju, and Zoku Genta pierced through without catching on armor or shield. Gen Sanmi Nyūdō wore a long silk hitatare under armor laced with leather strips. Did he think that day would be his last? He deliberately did not wear a helmet. The eldest son, Izu no kami Nakatsuna, wore a red brocade hitatare under black-laced armor. Intending to draw his bow strongly, he too had not put on his helmet. Here Tajima of Gochi-in removed the scabbard of his great halberd and advanced alone onto the bridge. The Heike side saw this and said, "Shoot him down, men!" and their skilled archers selected arrows, nocked them, drew their bows, and shot furiously. Tajima was not disturbed at all; he ducked under the arrows that came high, leaped over those that came low, and cut down with his halberd those that came straight at him. Both enemies and allies watched. From that time on, he came to be called Yagiri no Tajima.

[4.11.3] Among the hall monks, Tsutsui no Jōmyō Meishū, wearing a brown hitatare and armor laced with black leather, tying the cords of a five-plate helmet, girding a black-lacquered sword, carrying twenty-four black-feathered arrows, taking up a black-lacquered rattan-wrapped bow and his favorite white-handled long sword, advanced onto the bridge. Raising a loud voice, he announced his name: "You have surely heard of me by reputation; now see me with your own eyes. At Mii-dera, there is no hiding for him. Among the hall monks there was one called Tsutsui Jōmyō Meishū, a warrior worth a thousand men. Those who think themselves brave, come forward and let us see you! So saying, he took up his twenty-four arrows, fitted them one after another, drew his bow to the full, and shot them in rapid succession. In an instant he shot dead twelve men and wounded eleven, leaving only one arrow in his quiver. He threw away his bow with a clatter, untied his quiver, and cast it aside. He took off his sandals and went barefoot, and ran across the bridge's beams with a clatter. People were afraid and did not cross, but to Jōmyō's mind, it was as if he were walking along First Avenue or Second Avenue. With his long sword he mowed down five enemies facing him, and when he met an enemy who was the sixth, he struck his long sword in the middle, broke it, and threw it away. After that, drawing his sword and fighting, the enemy was numerous; he cut them in all directions—spider-hand, corner-rope, cross-shape, dragonfly-return, water-wheel—without leaving any opening. In an instant he cut down eight men, and when he struck the helmet bowl of the ninth enemy too hard, his sword broke off right at the base of the hilt ornament; he pulled it out and jumped into the river with a splash. Trusting in his short sword, he went mad, determined to die.

[4.11.4] Here there was a man of great strength and quick action called Ikkai Hōshi, a servant of Jōen-bō Ajari Keishu. Continuing to fight behind him, the passage was narrow, and there was no way to pass by his side. Putting his hand on the front of Jōmyō-bō's helmet, he said, "That's bad, Jōmyō-bō," and leapt over his shoulder to fight. Ikkai Hōshi was struck down and killed. Jōmyōbō crawled back, and on the grass in front of the gate of Byōdō-in, he stripped off his armor and counted the arrowheads stuck in it: sixty-three, with five arrows that had pierced through to the back. But since none of the wounds were serious, he cauterized them here and there, tied up his head, put on a white robe, broke his bow to use as a staff, put on flat straw sandals, invoked Amida Buddha, and departed toward Nara.

[4.11.5] Taking Jōmyōbō's crossing as an example, the monks of Mii-dera and the Watanabe band rushed on one after another, each vying to cross the bridge. Some divided the spoils and went home, and some, gravely wounded, cut open their bellies and threw themselves into the river; the battle on the bridge was fought with such intensity that it seemed as if fire was bursting forth. Seeing this, the Heike side's commander of samurai, Kazusa no Suke Tadakiyo, came before the great general and said, "Look at that! The battle on the bridge is intense. Now we should cross the river, but since it is the season of the fifth-month rains, the water has risen. If we cross, many horses and men will surely be lost. Should we go to Yodo to wash the potatoes, or should we go to the Kawachi road? When he said this, Ashikaga Matatarō Tadatsuna, a resident of Shimotsuke Province, stepped forward and said, "As for the Yodo potato-washing and the Kawachi road, would you summon warriors from India and China to face them? It is we who will face them. If you enter the southern capital without striking down the enemy before your eyes, the forces of Yoshino and Totsukawa will surely gather and it will be an even greater crisis. On the border between Musashi and Kozuke, there is a great river called the Tone River. Chichibu and Ashikaga were at odds, and while they were constantly fighting, the main force attacked from the Nagai ford and the rear force from the Kogasugi ford. At that time, a resident of Kozuke Province, Nyudo Nitta, was persuaded by Ashikaga and prepared boats to cross from the Sugi ford, but Chichibu's side destroyed all the boats. He said, "If we do not cross here now, it will be a lasting disgrace to our bows and arrows." "If we drown in the water, we die; come, let us cross!" So saying, they made a raft of horses and crossed. As is the custom of Bando warriors, in a battle separated by a river with the enemy in sight, would they avoid deep or shallow places? How much this river's depth and swiftness are inferior or superior to the Tone River—surely there is no such thing. Follow, gentlemen! Saying so, he was the first to plunge in. The men who followed—Ōgo, Ōmuro, Fukasu, Yamagami, Nawa Tarō, Sanuki Hirotsuna Shirōdayū, Onodera Zenshi Tarō, Hen'yagoshi Shirō, and among their retainers, starting with Ubukata Jirō, Kiriu Rokurō, and Tanaka Sōta—three hundred and more riders followed. Ashikaga raised his voice loudly: "Put the strong horses upstream, and put the weak horses downstream." As far as the horse's legs can reach, give it the reins and let it walk. If it stumbles, row it across. Attach the lower ones to the bow tip. Take each other's hands, line up shoulder to shoulder, and cross. Sit firmly in the saddle and press hard on the stirrups. If the horse's head sinks, pull it up. Pull hard and don't let it be pulled over your head. If water collects, ride on top of the three horses. Be weak with the horse, but strong with the water. Do not shoot a bow in the middle of the river. Do not shoot at the enemy together. Always tilt your helmet. Do not tilt it too much and shoot at the sky. Do not cross over to the metal fittings and get pushed off. Cross over in the water! Cross over! So he commanded, and all three hundred-odd horsemen, without a single one being swept away, crossed swiftly to the opposite bank.

[4.12.1] Ashikaga, wearing a twilled hitatare of russet-brown, donning armor laced with red leather, fastening the cords of a helmet with high crest, girding on a gold-mounted sword, shouldering arrows fletched with spotted feathers, holding a bow wrapped in many layers of rattan, mounted on a dappled gray horse, sat upon a gold-rimmed saddle decorated with oak-leaf and ear-shaped metal fittings. He braced himself in the stirrups, stood up, raised his voice, and announced his name: "You have heard of me from afar by reputation, and now you see me close at hand." I am the tenth-generation descendant of Tawara Tōta Hidesato, who long ago destroyed the imperial enemy Masakado and received rewards, and the son of Ashikaga Tarō Toshitsuna: Matatarō Tadatsuna, seventeen years of age. Though I am a man without rank or office, I have come before the Prince and drawn my bow and shot arrows. I am deeply in awe of Heaven, but both my bow and arrows and my good fortune are surely due to the exalted virtue of the Heike. Let those who consider themselves warriors on the side of the Lay Monk Prime Minister come forward and present themselves! Saying this, they charged into the gate of Byodoin and fought.

[4.12.2] Seeing this, the great general, the Middle Captain of the Left Gate Guards, Tomomori, said, "Let them cross! Let them cross!" When he gave this order, all of the more than twenty-eight thousand horsemen charged in and crossed. Blocked by horses and men, the water of the swift Uji River piled up on top. In the water that overflowed by itself, nothing could withstand the current and was swept away. The common soldiers, clinging to the downstream side of the horses, crossed over, and many of them did not even get wet above the knees. Somehow, the government soldiers of Iga and Ise provinces had their horse-raft broken through, and more than six hundred riders were drowned and swept away. The armors of various colors—light green, scarlet-laced, red-laced—now floating, now sinking, were tossed about, just like the autumn leaves of Mount Kannabi, blown by the storm from the peaks, and caught in the weir at the end of autumn on the Tatsuta River, unable to flow on. Among them, three warriors wearing scarlet-laced armor were caught in the net and were being pulled along; when the Governor of Izu saw this,

lg.l: 伊勢武者はみなひおどしの鎧きて、宇治の網代にかゝりぬるかな。

div.p: [4.12.3] These three are all residents of Ise Province. They were men called Kuroda no Goshiro, Hino Juro, and Otobe Yashichi. Among them, Hino Juro, being an old hand, wedged the tip of his bow into a crevice in the rock, climbed up, and pulled up the other two men as well, saving them—so it is told. All the troops crossed over, and inside the gate of Byōdō-in, they fought, taking turns. In this confusion, they sent the prince ahead to Nara, and the family of Gen Sanmi Nyūdō remained behind and shot arrows in defense.

[4.12.4] Sanmi Nyūdō, over seventy years old, fought, and had his left knee shot; since it was a serious wound, he withdrew inside the gate of Byōdō-in to calmly take his own life. When the enemy attacked, his second son, Gen Daibu Hangan Kanetsuna, wearing a dark blue brocade hitatare and armor laced with Chinese twill, mounted on a white roan horse, turned back again and again to fight, to protect his father. When Kazusa no Tarō Hōgan shot an arrow, it pierced Kanetsuna's helmet lining and he was in pain; then Kazusa no kami's page, a strong fellow called Jirōmaru, pressed in and grappled with him, and they fell down together with a thud. Minamoto no Tayū Hōgan, though his helmet lining was also wounded, was known for his great strength, so he grabbed the page, pinned him down, and cut his throat; just as he was about to stand up, the Heike warriors, fourteen or fifteen riders, piled on top of each other with a crash and killed Kanetsuna. Izu no kami Nakatsuna, too, having received many severe wounds, killed himself at the fishing pavilion of Byōdō-in. Shimokōbe no Tōsaburō Kiyochika took that head and threw it under the great floor. Rokujō Kurōdo Nakaie and his son Kurōdo Tarō Nakamitsu fought fiercely, took many trophies, and finally died in battle. This Nakayoshi was the legitimate son of the late Tachi no Sensei Yoshikata. He was an orphan, but the Sanmi Nyudo adopted him and treated him with compassion; yet without changing their long-standing bond, they died together—how pitiful! The Novice of the Third Rank summoned Watanabe no Chōshō and said, "Cut off my head." The retainer, saddened at the thought of taking his lord's living head, shed tears and said, "I cannot bring myself to do it. Please take your own life, and then I will receive your head." So saying, he faced west, recited the ten invocations in a loud voice, and his final words were truly moving.

lg.l: 埋木の花さく事もなかりしに、みのなる果ぞかなしかりける。

div.p: [4.12.5] With these as his final words, he thrust the tip of his sword into his belly and fell forward upon it, and so he died. At that time, although he was not one to compose poems, since it was a path he had loved intensely from his youth, even at his final moment he did not forget it. Taking that head, weeping, he tied it to a stone, slipped out through the midst of the enemy, and sank it in a deep place of the Uji River.

[4.12.6] The Heike warriors tried in every way to capture Kiso no Yoshinaka alive, but he, anticipating their intent, fought fiercely, and after receiving a mortal wound, cut open his own belly and died. Enman-in no Tayu Genkaku thought, "The prince must have already fled far away." Holding a great sword and a long halberd in his left and right hands, he broke through the enemy, jumped into the Uji River, and without discarding a single piece of armor, dived to the bottom of the water, reached the opposite bank, climbed to a high place, and raising his voice in a great shout, said, "How is it, lords of the Heike? Is this not a great matter?" Saying this, he returned to Mii-dera.

[4.12.7] Hida no kami Kageie, being an old warrior, thought that in this confusion the prince must have fled toward Nara, so he did not engage in battle, but with his force of over five hundred horsemen, he spurred on in pursuit. As expected, the Prince fled with about thirty horsemen, but they caught up with him before the torii of Kōmyōzan and shot arrows like falling rain; though no one knew whose arrow it was, one arrow struck the Prince's left side, and he fell from his horse and was beheaded. Seeing this, the attendants who were with him—Oni Sado, Ara Tosa, Ara Dayū, Iga no Kimi of Richijōbō, Gyōbu Shunshū, and the Six Tengu of Konkōin—cried out, “Why should we spare our lives?” and, shouting, fought to the death.

[4.12.8] Among them, the prince's foster brother, Rokujō no Suke no Daifu Munenobu, with the enemy in pursuit and his horse exhausted, plunged into the Niino Pond, covered himself with floating weeds, and lay trembling; the enemy passed by in front of him. After a while, as four or five hundred mounted warriors were returning with a clamor, someone noticed a corpse dressed in white robes, without a head, lying under a latticed shutter. When they looked to see who it was, it was the Prince. "If I die, put this flute in my coffin," he had said. The flute known as Koeda was still at his waist. He thought he would run out and take it, but he was too afraid, so he could not. After all the enemies had gone, he came up from the pond, wrung out his wet clothes and put them on, and weeping went up to the capital. There was no one who did not hate him.

[4.12.9] Meanwhile, the great monks of Nanto, seven thousand or more in all, came to meet the Prince. The vanguard advanced to Konotsu, while the rear guard was still wavering at the South Gate of Kōfuku-ji. When it was heard that the Prince had been killed before the torii of Kōmyōzan, all the monks, unable to do anything, held back their tears and remained. How pitiful was the fate of the prince, who, without waiting even about fifty chō, was struck down!

[4.13.1] The Heike warriors, together with the prince and the lay monk Sanmi, pierced the heads of the Miidera monks, more than five hundred in all, on the tips of their swords and halberds, raised them high, and returned to Rokuhara as evening fell. The clamor of the warriors was tremendous. Even being afraid is foolish. Among them, the head of Gen Sanmi Nyudo was taken by Chōshichi and sunk in a deep place of the Uji River, so that one was not seen. The children's heads were all searched out from here and there. Among them, as for the prince's head, since there was no one who had come to serve him over the years, there was no one who could recognize it. In previous years, the Director of the Bureau of Medicine, Sadanari, had been summoned for the prince's medical treatment, so thinking that he would be the one to recognize it, they summoned him, but he did not come, saying he was currently ill. A lady-in-waiting who had always been in the prince's service was found and brought to Rokuhara. Because she had been so deeply loved and had borne a child, how could she fail to recognize him? Only when she had one look, pressed her sleeve to her face, and shed tears, did she realize it was the prince's head.

[4.13.2] This prince had many children by various consorts. By a lady-in-waiting called Sanmi no Tsubone, daughter of Iyo no Kami Morinori, who served at Hachijo-in, there was a seven-year-old prince and a five-year-old princess. The Lay Monk Chancellor, through his younger brother, the Middle Counselor Lord Ikeno Yorimori, sent word to Hachijō-in: "It is said that many of the children of Prince Takakura have come over to you." As for the princess, needless to say, but the young prince, please send him out quickly. When she said this, the Retired Empress replied, "On the dawn when such a rumor arose, did the wet nurse and others, with little heart, take the child and lose him? He was never brought to this palace." When she said this, Lord Yorimori, unable to do anything, reported this matter to the Lay Priest Chancellor. Why, unless it is that palace, where would he be taken? If that is the case, let the warriors come and search for me. Thus he spoke. This middle counselor, having been accompanied by the lady-in-waiting called Saishō no Tsubone, the wet nurse of the Empress Dowager, used to come and go regularly, so in recent days she had been thinking fondly of him, but when he came to speak about the young prince's matter, she now felt estranged from him as if he were a different person. The young prince said to the Empress Dowager, "Since it has come to such a grave matter, in the end I will not be able to escape. Please come out at once. When he had them say this, the Retired Empress shed tears in streams and said, "A child of seven or eight is at an age when he cannot yet understand anything." It is pitiful that you say such a thing, thinking it is shameful that a great matter has arisen because of me. Having tamed for these six or seven years a person who was of no account, now see this bitter sight! Saying this, she could not hold back her tears. When Lord Yorimori repeatedly requested that the prince be sent out, the Empress was unable to resist, and finally sent the prince out. The mother, Sanmi no Tsubone, since this was the final parting, must have felt how very reluctant she was to part. Weeping, she dressed him in his clothes, stroked his hair, and sent him off, but it all felt like nothing but a dream. When the Empress was first brought in, from the ladies of the chamber down to the young girls, there was none who did not shed tears and wring their sleeves.

[4.13.3] Lord Yorimori received the Prince, helped him into the carriage, and escorted him to Rokuhara. The former Right Grand General, Lord Munemori, saw this Prince, sat before his father, the Chancellor and Zen monk, and said, "What is it? Seeing this Prince, I feel too much pain." Bending justice, please give the life of this prince to Munemori. When he said this, the novice monk replied, "Then quickly make him take the tonsure." So he said. When Lord Munemori reported this to Hachijo Nyoin, the Nyoin said, "There is nothing to be done; just quickly." So saying, she made him a monk, had him receive the Buddhist name, and made him a disciple of the Omuro of Ninna-ji. Later, the one who was called the First Chief Abbot of Toji, Yasui-no-miya's monk-prince Dōson, was this prince himself.

[4.14.1] Also in Nara, there was one place where he sat. His wet nurse, Sanuki no kami Shigehide, had him take the tonsure, and taking him along, they fled down to the northern provinces. When Kiso no Yoshinaka came up to the capital, intending to make him their lord, he brought him up to the capital and had him undergo his coming-of-age ceremony, and so he was called Kiso no Miya. He was also called the Genzoku no Miya (the Prince who returned to secular life). Later, when he moved to Noyori in the Saga area, he was also called Noyori no Miya.

[4.14.2] There was a physiognomist named Tsūjō. He had said that Uji-dono and Nijō-dono would both be regents for three generations and live to be eighty, and it was not wrong. He had said that the Sochi no Naidaijin had the physiognomy of exile, and it was not wrong. Prince Shōtoku had said that Emperor Sushun had the physiognomy of a violent death, and he was killed by Minister Umako. Even for such worthy people, though they were not necessarily physiognomists, how splendid it was! Is this not the oversight of the Lesser Counselor Aishō? In the middle period, Prince Kaneakira and Prince Tomohira were called the Former and Latter Prince of the Chancellery, and though both were sons of wise kings and holy rulers, they did not ascend to the throne. But why would he have caused a rebellion? Also, the third prince of Emperor Go-Sanjo, Prince Sukehito, was outstanding in learning, so when Emperor Shirakawa was still Crown Prince, Emperor Go-Sanjo left a will saying, "After my reign, you should place this prince on the throne." But Emperor Shirakawa, for some reason, did not place him on the throne, and as a last resort, he granted the surname Minamoto to Prince Sukehito's son, promoted him from no rank to the Third Rank at once, and immediately made him a Middle Captain. It is said that among the Genji of the first rank, the promotion from no rank to the Third Rank was unprecedented except for the son of Emperor Saga, the Dainagon of Yōin, Sadakata. This was the matter of the Minister of the Left of Hanazono, Lord Arihito.

[4.14.3] During the rebellion of Prince Takakura, rewards were given to the high priests who had performed the rites of subjugation. The son of the former Major General of the Right, Lord Munemori, the chamberlain Kiyomune, was promoted to the Third Rank, and was called the Third Rank Chamberlain. He was only twelve years old this year. Even your father, at this age, was only a Hyōe no Suke, was he not? To suddenly rise to the rank of a senior noble—apart from the sons of the highest-ranking courtiers, I have never heard of such a thing. It was as a reward for the pursuit and destruction of Minamoto no Mochihito and the monk Yorimasa, father and son, that this was written in the appointment record. Minamoto no Mochihito was the name given to Prince Takakura. Even to strike down a prince of the Retired Emperor is already outrageous; to do so to a mere commoner is utterly deplorable.

div.head: 4.15. ぬえ[_][1]]

div.p: [4.15.1] Now, the one called Gen Sanmi Nyūdō Yorimasa was the fifth-generation descendant of Settsu no Kami Yorimitsu, the grandson of Mikawa no Kami Yoritsuna, and the son of Hyōgo no Kami Nakamasa. At the time of the Hōgen War, although he was the first to charge on the side of the court, he received no special reward; and in the Heiji Rebellion too, although he abandoned his relatives and came to serve, the rewards were meager. Although he had been the guard of the imperial palace for many years, he was not permitted to enter the court. After he grew old and his years declined, he composed a poem of lamentation, and only then was he permitted to enter the court.

lg.l: 人しれず大内山の山守は、木隱てのみ月を見るかな。

div.p: [4.15.2] Because of this poem, he was permitted to enter the court, and for a while he was at the rank of Senior Fourth Rank, Lower Grade, but he kept wishing for the Third Rank.

lg.l: のぼるべき便無き身は木の下に、しゐをひろひて世をわたるかな。

div.p: [4.15.3] And so, he finally attained the Third Rank. He soon became a monk, and as the lay monk Gen Sanmi, this year he turned seventy-five. The most famous deed of this man's life was that during the reign of Emperor Konoe, around the Ninpei era, the emperor was frightened night after night. They commanded high priests of proven efficacy to perform great rites and secret rituals, but there was no effect. The emperor's affliction occurred around the hour of the ox, and when a mass of black clouds came from the direction of the forest of Higashi Sanjo and covered the palace, he was invariably frightened. Because of this, the court nobles held a council. In the past, during the Kanji era, when Emperor Horikawa was on the throne, there was an occasion when His Majesty was frightened night after night. At that time, the general Yoshiie Ason, who was waiting in attendance on the great floor of the Southern Hall, when the time of His Majesty's distress arrived, after sounding his bowstring three times, announced in a loud voice, 'Former Governor of Mutsu, Minamoto no Yoshiie,' whereupon everyone's hair stood on end, and His Majesty's distress subsided. Therefore, following precedent, they decided to appoint a warrior to guard the palace, and when they selected from among the warriors of the Minamoto and Taira clans, it was heard that this Yorimasa was chosen. At this time, he was still called the Director of the Bureau of Horses. Yorimasa said, "Since ancient times, the reason warriors have been placed in the imperial court is to repel rebels and destroy those who disobey imperial orders." I have not yet heard of any command that I should serve as an invisible supernatural being. So saying, since it was an imperial command, he obeyed the summons and went to the palace. Yorimasa had with him only one attendant, I no Hayata, a resident of Tōtōmi Province, a retainer who had served him through thick and thin, and he had him carry arrows with the tips cut off in a holly-leaf pattern. I, wearing a double-layered hunting robe, with two arrows fletched with pheasant tail feathers, fitted to a bow wrapped in rattan, attend upon the great floor of the Southern Hall. The reason Yorimasa held two arrows in his hand was that, at that time, Lord Masayori was still a Junior Secretary and had not yet been promoted, and when it was said that the one who would deal with the monster was Yorimasa, he thought that if he missed the monster with the first arrow, he would shoot Masayori's neck bone with the second. Just as people had been saying, when the time of his illness arrived, a single mass of black clouds came rising from the direction of the forest of Higashi Sanjō and hung over the palace. When Yorimasa looked up sharply, there was the form of a strange creature in the clouds. If he were a man who would miss this shot, he would not be worthy to live in the world. Nevertheless, he took an arrow and nocked it, prayed in his heart to Hachiman Daibosatsu, drew the bow fully, and shot with a whiz. He felt a response in his hand, and it struck with a thud. "Got it!" they cried, raising a battle shout. Ihaya quickly approached, and saying, "I'll hold down the place where it falls," he pinned it down and stabbed it nine times in succession. At that time, the people above and below lit fires in their hands and looked at it: its head was a monkey, its body a raccoon dog, its tail a snake, and its limbs were those of a tiger. Its cry resembled that of a thrush. Even to call it frightening is foolish. In the excess of His Majesty's admiration, he bestowed upon him the imperial sword called Shishiō. After the Uji Minister of the Left received this, intending to give it to Yorimasa, when he had descended about halfway down the steps before the throne, as it was the time after the tenth of the fourth month, a cuckoo in the distant sky called out two or three notes as it passed. At that time, the Minister of the Left said:

lg.l: 時鳥名をも雲井にあぐるかな。

div.p: [4.15.4] When he said this, Yorimasa knelt on his right knee, spread out his left sleeve, and with the moon slightly in his side glance,

lg.l: 弓はり月のいるにまかせて。

div.p: [4.15.5] he recited, received the sword, and withdrew. Not only is he peerless in archery, but he also excels in the art of poetry. So saying, both lord and vassals were deeply moved. Then, that transformed creature was put into an empty boat and set adrift, so it is said.

[4.15.6] In the Ōhō era, during the reign of Emperor Nijō, a monster bird called nue cried in the imperial palace and often disturbed the emperor's heart. Following precedent, Yorimasa was summoned. It was still early evening on the twentieth day of the fifth month, and the nue cried only once, not twice. It was a darkness in which one could not even see one's hand, and since the figure could not be seen, it was difficult to determine the target. Yorimasa, as a strategy, first took a large kabura arrow and nocked it, and shot it up toward the palace where the nue had cried. The nue, startled by the sound of the kabura arrow, hovered in the air for a while. With the second arrow, he took a small kabura arrow and nocked it, and shot it through with a whiz, and the nue and the kabura arrow fell down together in front of him. The palace was in an uproar, and the emperor's admiration was extraordinary. When he bestowed a robe upon Yorimasa, at that time, the Great Minister of the Right, Ōinomikado no Kinnō, received it and then had it put on Yorimasa, saying, "The ancient Yang You shot a wild goose beyond the clouds; the present Yorimasa has shot a nue in the rain." Thus he was praised.

lg.l: 五月闇名をあらはせる今宵哉。

div.p: [4.15.7] When he had said this, Yorimasa,

lg.l: たそがれ時もすぎぬとおもふに。

div.p: [4.15.8] he said, and placing the imperial robe on his shoulder, he withdrew. After that, he was granted Izu Province, his son Nakatsuna was made a zuryō, he himself became a Third Rank official, and he held the five shōen of Tanba and the Tōgū River in Wakasa. And yet, this man who should have been sitting peacefully, for no reason raised a rebellion, caused the prince to be lost, and brought ruin upon himself and his descendants—how hateful it is!

div.note: [_] [1] The kanji in our copy-text is New Nelson 6976 or Nelson 5357.

div.p: [4.16.1] Usually it is the monks of the mountain gate who make noisy appeals, but this time they are keeping quiet, thinking it prudent. The monks of Nanto and Mii-dera either receive the prince, or go to meet him. Therefore, he is an enemy of the court. Therefore, saying that they would attack both Miidera and Nanto, on the twenty-seventh day of the same fifth month, the great general was the lay monk's fourth son, the Middle Captain Shigehira, and the vice-general was the Governor of Satsuma, Tadanori; with a total force of more than ten thousand horsemen, they set out for Onjoji. At the temple too, they dug moats, set up shields, and pulled in abatis, waiting in readiness. At the hour of the hare (around 6 a.m.), they exchanged arrows, and fought all day. The defending monks and all the priests, more than three hundred in number, were killed. It became a night battle; the darkness was dark, and the imperial forces attacked into the temple grounds and set fire. The places that burned: Hongaku-in, Jōki-in, Shinnyo-in, Hanazono-in, Fugen-dō, Daihō-in, Seiryū-in, the main residence of the monk Kyōtai, and the principal images; the great lecture hall of eight bays by four bays, the bell tower, the sutra repository, the abhisheka hall, the shrine of the guardian deities, the sacred hall of Ima-Kumano; in all, 637 temple buildings and pagodas, 1,853 houses in the town of Ōtsu, over 7,000 scrolls of the complete scriptures that Chishō had transmitted, and over 2,000 Buddhist images—all suddenly turned to smoke, how sorrowful it was! The music of the five wonders of the heavens, too, at this time ceased forever, and the suffering of the three heats of the dragon king, too, seemed to grow ever more intense.

[4.16.2] Now, Mii-dera was originally the private temple of the great administrator of Omi, but it was offered to Emperor Tenmu and made into an imperial vow temple. The principal image was also that emperor's personal object of worship, but the living Maitreya, the priest Kyotai, after practicing for one hundred and sixty years, entrusted it to the great master. He descended from the Mani Treasure Hall in the Tushita Heaven above, and I heard that he was waiting for the dawn of the descent of Maitreya at the Dragon Flower Tree, but what is this that has happened? Because the Great Master made this place a sacred site of the Dharma-transmission abhisheka and scooped up water from the well, it was named Mii-dera. Although it is such an auspicious sacred site, now it is nothing. The exoteric and esoteric teachings were lost in an instant, and the temple buildings have no trace left. Since there is no place for the three mysteries practice, the sound of the bell is not heard either. Even the flowers of the whole summer were gone, and the sound of the water offering was no longer heard. The venerable masters of high virtue neglected their practice and learning, and the disciples who had received the transmission of the teachings turned away from the scriptures. The temple's chief administrator, Prince Enkei, was dismissed from his post as the head priest of Tennoji. In addition, thirteen monks of the sōgō were stripped of their ranks and all were handed over to the kebiishi. The evil monks, up to Tsutsui Jōmyō Meishū, more than thirty people were exiled. Such disturbances of the realm and upheavals of the land did not seem to be mere trifles; people said that they were surely an omen that the end of the Heike's age had come.

[5.1.1] On the third day of the sixth month of the fourth year of Jishō, it was said that there would be an imperial visit to Fukuhara, and the whole capital was in an uproar. Although it had been heard that there would be a transfer of the capital someday, it was not thought that it would be so sudden as today or tomorrow; everyone, wondering what this was, was in an uproar. Moreover, although it had been set for the third day, it was moved up by one day and became the second day. At the hour of the rabbit on the second day, when the imperial palanquin was already brought near, the emperor, being only three years old and still very young, was summoned without any concern. When the emperor was young and being carried in the same palanquin, the empress dowager would ride with him, but this time there was no such arrangement. It was the wet nurse, the wife of Taira no Dainagon Tokitada, the Suke no Tsubone, who rode in the same palanquin. The Empress, the Cloistered Emperor, and the Retired Emperor made an imperial progress. Beginning with the Regent, the Grand Minister and all the court nobles and senior courtiers vied with one another to attend in the imperial procession. On the third day they entered Fukuhara. The residence of Ike no Chunagon Yorimori became the imperial palace. On the same fourth day, as a reward for the house of Yorimori, he was granted the rank of Senior Second Rank. The son of Kujō-dono, the Right General Yoshimichi, was able to cross over. It is said that this was the first time that the son of a regent or chancellor was promoted in rank over the second son of a commoner.

[5.1.2] In the meantime, the Lay Monk Chancellor gradually relented toward the Retired Emperor, had him released from Toba Palace, and brought him back to the capital. But because of Prince Takakura's rebellion, he became greatly enraged again, had the Retired Emperor taken to Fukuhara, boarded up all four sides, built a three-bay plank hut inside with only one opening, and confined him there. As for the guard warriors, only Harada no Tayū Tanenao was in attendance. Since there was no way for people to come and go easily, the children called it the Cage Palace. These were events so dreadful and terrifying that even hearing of them was abhorrent. The Retired Emperor had not the slightest thought of governing the realm now; he only wished to practice religious austerities in various mountains and temples, and to find solace as his heart desired, so he said. As for the evil deeds of the Heike, they have all reached their limit. Since the past Angen era, they have exiled or killed many court nobles and officials, exiled the regent, made their own son-in-law regent, moved the retired emperor to the detached palace in the south of the capital, attacked and killed Prince Takakura, the second prince, and now, because it is a matter of moving the capital, people said that they would do such a thing.
