[5.1.3] Moving the capital is not without precedent. The one called Emperor Jimmu was the emperor of the fifth generation of earthly deities, the fourth prince of Hikohohodemi no Mikoto, whose mother was Tamayori-hime, a daughter of the sea people. He inherited the legacy of the twelve generations of the age of the gods, and was the founding emperor of the hundred kings of the age of men. In the year Kanoto-tori, in Miyazaki District of Hyūga Province, he succeeded to the imperial throne, and in the year Tsuchinoto-hitsuji, said to be the fifty-ninth year, he made an expedition to the east, stayed in Toyoashihara no Nakatsukuni, selected the mountain of Unebi, which at this time was named Yamato Province, established the imperial capital, cleared the land of Kashihara, and built a palace. This was named the Palace of Kashihara. From that time onward, the emperors of successive generations moved the capital to other provinces and other places more than thirty times, reaching forty times. From Emperor Jimmu to Emperor Keikō, for twelve generations, they established capitals in the various districts of Yamato Province, and never moved to another province. However, in the first year of Emperor Seimu, they moved to Ōmi Province and established a capital in Shiga District. In the second year of Emperor Chūai, they moved to Nagato Province and established the capital in Toyoura District. When the Emperor passed away in that capital of that province, Empress Jingū took over the reign, and as a woman, she subjugated even the demon world, Goryeo, and the Khitan. After she pacified the foreign armies and returned to Japan, in Mikasa District of Chikuzen Province, the prince was born, and that place is called Umi Palace. It is awe-inspiring even to speak of it: this is the matter of Hachiman. When he ascended to the throne, he was called Emperor Ōjin. After that, Empress Jingū moved to Yamato Province and resided in the Iware no Wakazakura Palace. Emperor Ōjin resided in the Karushima no Akari Palace in the same province. In the first year of Emperor Nintoku's reign, he moved to Naniwa in Tsu Province and resided in the Takatsu Palace. In the second year of Emperor Richū, [the capital] was moved to Yamato Province, and a capital was established in Toichi District. In the first year of Emperor Hanzei, [the capital] was moved to Kawachi Province, and [the emperor] resided in Shibagaki Palace. In the forty-second year of Emperor Ingyō, [the capital] was again moved to Yamato Province, and [the emperor] resided in the Asuka Palace of Asuka. In the twenty-first year of Emperor Yūryaku, [the emperor] resided in Hatsuse Asakura in the same province. In the fifth year of Emperor Keitai, [the capital] was moved to Tsuzuki in Yamashiro Province, and in the twelfth year, after that, [the emperor] resided in Otokuni. In the first year of Emperor Senka, he returned again to Yamato Province and resided at Hinokuma Iri no Miya. In the first year of Taika of Emperor Kōtoku, he moved to Nagara in Settsu Province and resided at Toyosaki Palace. In the second year of Empress Saimei, he returned again to Yamato Province and resided at Okamoto Palace. In the sixth year of Emperor Tenji, he moved to Ōmi Province and resided at Ōtsu Palace. In the first year of Emperor Tenmu, he returned again to Yamato Province and resided at the palace south of Okamoto. This was called the Kiyomigahara no Mikado. The sacred reigns of Empress Jitō and Emperor Monmu were at Fujiwara Palace in the same province. From Emperor Genmei to Emperor Konin, seven generations resided in the capital of Nara. However, Emperor Kanmu, on the second day of the tenth month of Enryaku 3, moved from Kasuga no Sato in the capital of Nara to Nagaoka in Yamashiro Province, and in the first month of the year called 'ten years', he sent Dainagon Fujiwara no Koguromaru, Sangi Sadaiben Ki no Kosami, Daisozu Genkei and others to inspect Uda Village in Kadono District of that province; both men reported together, saying, 'Looking at the lay of this land, it is a place where the four gods correspond: Blue Dragon on the left, White Tiger on the right, Vermilion Bird in front, Black Tortoise behind.' It is said that it is truly worthy of establishing the imperial capital. Therefore, after reporting to the great deity Kamo Daimyojin, who resides in Atago District, and after being transferred from the capital of Nagaoka to this capital on the twenty-first day of the eleventh month of the thirteenth year of Enryaku, thirty-two generations of emperors have passed, and the years have seen three hundred and eighty-odd springs and autumns come and go. Since ancient times, successive emperors have established many capitals in various provinces and places, but there is no scenic spot like this one, so Emperor Kanmu especially cherished it in his heart, consulted with ministers, nobles, and scholars of various arts, and, saying that it should be everlasting, made a human figure eight shaku tall out of earth, clad it in iron armor, gave it an iron bow and arrows, and buried it standing on the ridge of Higashiyama facing west. If in a later age this capital should be moved to another province, he would become its guardian deity—so it was promised. Therefore, whenever something was about to happen in the realm, this mound would surely rumble and shake. It is called the General's Mound and remains to this day. The one called Emperor Kanmu is the founder of the Heike clan. In particular, this capital was named Heian-kyō, written as 'the peaceful and tranquil capital.' It is indeed a capital that the Heike should revere. To move the capital, which the ancestral emperors had so deeply cherished, to another province or another place without any reason is truly deplorable. In the reign of Emperor Saga, when the former emperor Heizei, at the urging of the Naishi-no-kami, threw the realm into disorder, and was about to move this capital to another province, the ministers, nobles, and people of all the provinces opposed him, and so the move was not carried out and came to nothing. Even the sovereign of the realm, the lord of ten thousand chariots, could not move the capital; yet the Lay Monk Chancellor, a mere subject, moved it—how dreadful!

[5.1.4] The old capital was a lovely and splendid capital, indeed! The guardian shrines protecting the royal city softened their light in all directions, and the temples of wondrous efficacy lined up their roof tiles above and below; the common people and all the masses were free from trouble, and the five home provinces and seven circuits were also at peace. However, now they have dug up all the crossroads, and even carts cannot easily pass through. Even those who travel by chance ride in small carts and pass along the roads. The dwellings of people who competed for eaves are abandoned day by day and fall into ruin. Houses are broken down and thrown into the Kamo and Katsura rivers, assembled into rafts and floated, with materials and miscellaneous goods loaded onto boats, and transported down to Fukuhara. It is truly sad that the capital of flowers becomes a countryside. What kind of deed was this? On the pillars of the old capital's palace, two poems were written.

lg.l: 百年を四かへり迄に過來にし、愛宕の里のあれやはてなん。
さきいづる花の都をふりすてて、風ふく原の末ぞあやふき。

div.p: [5.1.5] On the same ninth day of the sixth month, saying that the construction of the new capital should begin, they appointed as the chief official the Middle Counselor Tokudaiji Sanesada, and as the assistant official the Consultant Tsuchimikado Michichika; and as the magistrate, the Chamberlain and Junior Secretary Yukitaka, together with other officials, were summoned, and they marked out the western field of Wada no Matsubara and divided the land of Kujō; from Ichijō down to Gojō the sites were allotted, but below Gojō there was none. The officials returned and reported this matter to the throne. So, was it to be Harima's Inamino, or perhaps Settsu Province's Koyano? Such deliberations were held among the court nobles, but it did not appear that the matter would be carried out.

[5.1.6] The old capital has already been abandoned, and in the new capital things have not yet been settled. Everyone, without exception, feels as if they are floating clouds. Those who had long dwelt in this place lost their land and grieved, while the people now moving in lamented the toil of construction. All these events were just like a dream. The Middle Counselor Tsuchimikado Michichika said, "In foreign lands, it is recorded that they opened three great avenues and erected twelve gates." 況や五條迄有ん都に、などか内裏を立ざるべき。
且々里内裏造るべき由、議定有て、五條大納言國綱卿、臨時に周防國を賜て、造進せ らるべき由、入道相國計ひ申されけり。此國綱卿は大福長者にておはすれば、造出れ ん事、左右に及ばねども、如何が國の費え民の煩ひ無るべき。指當る大事、大嘗會な どの行はるべきを差置いて、かゝる世の亂に遷都造内裏、少も相應せず。古の賢き御 代には、即内裏に茨を葺き、軒をだにも調へず、煙の乏きを見給ふ時は、限有る御貢 物をも許れき。是即民を惠み、國を扶け給ふに依て也。楚、章華臺を立て黎民をあら け、秦、阿房殿を起して、天下亂ると云へり。茅茨剪ず、采椽けづらず、舟車飾ず、 衣服文無ける世も有けん物を。 されば唐の太宗は、驪山宮を造て、民の費えをや憚せ給けん、遂に臨幸なくして、瓦に松生ひ、墻に蔦茂て止にけるには、相違かなとぞ人申ける。

[5.2.1] 六月九日、新都の事始、八月十日上棟、十一月十三日遷幸と定めらる。 舊き都は荒行ば、今の都は繁昌す。 The dreadful summer passed, and autumn had already arrived. As autumn gradually reached its midpoint, the people residing in the new capital at Fukuhara, wishing to view the moon at famous places, some traced the traces of the Minamoto general of old, traveling along the coast from Suma to Akashi, crossing the strait of Awaji, and viewing the moon over the beach of Ejima. Some people composed poems about the dawn moon over Shirahama, Fukiage, Waka Bay, Sumiyoshi, Naniwa, Takasago, and Onoe, and then returned. The people who remained in the old capital view the moon over Fushimi and Hirosawa.

[5.2.2] Among them, the Great Minister of the Left Tokudaiji Sanesada, longing for the moon of the old capital, went up from Fukuhara on the tenth day of the eighth month. Everything has changed utterly; the few houses that remain have grass growing deep before their gates and dew lying thick in their gardens. The mugwort has become a thicket, the low bamboo grass a field; it has fallen into ruin as a roosting place for birds, and with the voices of insects lamenting, it has become a moor of yellow chrysanthemums and purple orchids. As for the remains of the old capital, only the Great Palace at Kangi Kawara remained. The Commander went to that palace, and first had his attendant knock on the main gate, when from inside a woman's voice said, "Who is it, in this place where no one even brushes away the dew on the mugwort?" "When she reproved them, they said, 'The Commander has come from Fukuhara.'" he said. The main gate is locked. Please enter through the small gate on the east side. When he said this, the general said, "Very well," and entered through the east gate. The Empress, perhaps recalling the past with her attendants, opened the lattice on the south side and was playing the biwa when the general arrived. "Is this a dream or reality? Come here, come here," she said. Thus he spoke. In the Uji chapter of the Tale of Genji, the daughter of the lay priest, regretting the passing of autumn, tuned her lute and played all night with a pure heart; when the dawn moon appeared, unable to bear it, she beckoned it with her fan—now I truly understand that feeling.

[5.2.3] The lady-in-waiting called Matsuyoi no Koshōjō was also in attendance at this palace. The reason this lady was called Matsuyoi was that once, at the palace, someone asked, "Matsuyoi, on the morning of your return, which is more moving?" When he asked this,

lg.l: 待宵のふけゆく鐘の聲聞けば、歸るあしたの鳥はものかは。

div.p: [5.2.4] It was because he had read it that it came to be called 'Matsuyoi' (Waiting Evening). The general called out the woman, and as they talked of old times and new, and the night deepened, he sang in the imayo style about the old capital falling into ruin.

lg.l: 舊き都を來て見れば淺茅が原とぞ荒にける、 月の光はくまなくて秋風のみぞ身にはしむ。

div.p: [5.2.5] When he had sung the three songs, beginning with the Empress Dowager, all the court ladies in the palace wet their sleeves with tears.

[5.2.6] When dawn broke, the general took his leave and returned to Fukuhara. He summoned the chamberlain who was in attendance and said, "Since the chamberlain seems so reluctant to part, you go back and say something to him." The chamberlain ran back and said, "He says, 'I respectfully decline.'" So saying,

lg.l: 物かはと君が云けん鳥の音の、今朝しもなどか悲かるらん。

div.p: [5.2.7] The lady-in-waiting, holding back her tears,

lg.l: またばこそ深行く鐘も物ならめ、あかぬわかれの鳥の音ぞうき。

div.p: [5.2.8] The Chamberlain returned and reported this matter, whereupon [the General] said, "That is exactly why I sent you." So saying, the General was greatly impressed. From that time on, he was called the Chamberlain of the Leather Bag.

[5.3.1] 福原へ都を移されて後、平家の人々夢見も惡う、常は心噪ぎのみして、變化の者共多かりけり。 或夜入道の臥給へる所に、一間にはゞかる程の物の面出來て、覗奉る。 入道相國ちとも噪がず、ちやうとにらまへておはしければ、只消に消失ぬ。 岡の御所と申は、新しう造られたれば、然べき大木もなかりけるに、或夜大木の倒るゝ音して、 人ならば二三十人が聲して、どと笑ふ事ありけり。是は如何樣にも天狗の所爲と云ふ 沙汰にて、蟇目の當番と名附て、夜百人晝五十人番衆をそろへて蟇目を射させらるる に、天狗の在る方へ向いて射たる時は、音もせず、又無い方へ向いて射たるとおぼし き時は、はと笑などしけり。

[5.3.2] 又或朝入道相國帳臺より出で、妻戸をおしひらいて、坪の内を見給へば、死人の髑髏共が幾らと云ふ數も知らず、庭にみち／＼て、上に成り、下に成り、轉合轉退き、端なるは中へ轉び入り、中なるは端へ出づ。 When they clattered together in great numbers, the Lay Monk Prime Minister called out, "Is anyone there?" He called out, but at that moment no one came. Thus the many skulls gathered together into one mass, and within the courtyard they became so numerous as to be overwhelming, forming a mountain that seemed to be fourteen or fifteen jo tall. From that one great skull, eyes like those of a living person, countless eyes, appeared and glared fixedly at the Lay Monk Prime Minister without blinking. The Lay Monk was not disturbed in the least. He glared at him with a fixed stare. That large-headed man, being glared at too intensely, vanished without a trace, like frost or dew melting in the sun. Moreover, in the first stable, a horse that was kept with many attendants and fed without pause morning and evening had a mouse build a nest in its tail overnight and give birth to young. Saying this was no ordinary matter, they had a diviner perform a divination, and it was declared to be a serious ritual abstinence. This horse was presented to the Lay Monk Chancellor by Oba Saburo Kagechika, a resident of Sagami Province, as the finest horse in the eight eastern provinces. The black horse had a white blaze on its forehead. It was named Mochizuki. The Yin-Yang master Abe no Yasuchika received it. In ancient times, during the reign of Emperor Tenji, when a mouse made a nest in the tail of a horse from the imperial stables and gave birth to offspring in a single night, it was recorded in the Nihon Shoki that foreign rebels rose up in revolt.

[5.3.3] Also, the dream that a young servant who served at the residence of the Middle Counselor Minamoto no Masayori saw was frightening. For example, in what seemed to be the Jingikan (Office of Deities) within the Imperial Palace, many courtiers in formal attire were present, and when there was something like a council meeting, a person seated at the lowest seat, who appeared to be a supporter of the Heike, was driven out from among them. That young servant thought in his dream, "What kind of high-ranking person could that be?" When he asked an old man, he replied, "The Great Deity of Itsukushima." After that, a venerable elder of noble appearance was seated in the upper seat, and he said, "The sword of authority that the Heike have been keeping until today shall now be bestowed upon the exile of Izu Province, Yoritomo." When he said this, another venerable elder who was still beside him said, "After that, give it to my grandson as well." He dreamed that [the deity] said this, and he asked about it in order. The one who said, 'Grant the sword of authority to Yoritomo,' was Hachiman Daibosatsu; the one who said, 'After that, grant it also to my descendant,' was Kasuga Daimyojin; and the old man who spoke thus was Takeuchi no Sukune. He saw in a dream that [the deity] said, "..." and while he was telling this to people, the Lay Monk Chancellor overheard it, and sent Minamoto no Daifu Hōgan Kagesada to Lord Masayori's place with the message, "The young samurai who had the dream, come here at once." When he sent this message, the young samurai who had the dream immediately fled. Lord Masayori hurried to the Lay Monk Chancellor and said, "There is absolutely no such thing." When he reported this, after that there was no further action taken. Among these strange things, when Kiyomori was still the governor of Aki, on the occasion of a shrine visit, he received a divine dream from the Great Deity of Itsukushima, and in reality was given a silver-mounted short halberd, which he kept always by his pillow; but one night it suddenly disappeared—how strange! The Heike had long been the guardians of the imperial court and protected the realm, but now, if they disobey the imperial command, even the sword of authority will be taken back from them, and they feel uneasy. Among them, the priest and former governor Narichika, who was staying at Mount Koya, heard about these events and said, "Ah, the Heike's era has finally come to an end. The reason why the Great Deity of Itsukushima is said to have been a supporter of the Heike is this." However, since she is the third princess of the dragon king Sagara, I have heard that she is a female deity. It was reasonable that the Emperor said he would grant the sword of Hachiman Daibosatsu to Yoritomo. It is incomprehensible that Kasuga Daimyojin said, "After that, grant it to my descendant as well." After the Heike have perished and the age of the Genji has come to an end, will the descendants of the Great Minister of the Left, the young lords of the regent's house, become the generals of the realm? Thus he spoke. Again, a certain monk who happened to come by said, "Now, the gods, in their various manifestations of the light and the trace, appear sometimes in secular form and sometimes as goddesses." Truly, although the Great Deity of Itsukushima is called a goddess, since she is a divine spirit possessing the three kinds of supernatural knowledge and the six supernatural powers, it would not be difficult for her to manifest in a secular form. Thus he said. Having grown weary of this fleeting world and entered the true path, one should have no worldly concerns other than the afterlife and enlightenment; yet when hearing of good governance one is moved, and when hearing of sorrow one grieves—these are all the ways of human beings.

[5.4.1] On the second day of the ninth month, Ōba Saburō Kagechika, a resident of Sagami Province, sent a fast messenger to Fukuhara, saying: "On the seventeenth day of the eighth month past, the exile of Izu Province, the former Assistant Captain of the Right Division of Outer Palace Guards, Yoritomo, dispatched his father-in-law Hōjō Shirō Tokimasa, and in a night attack at the Yamaki mansion they slew the deputy governor of Izu, Izumi no Hangan Kanetaka." After that, beginning with Doi, Tsuchiya, and Okazaki, over three hundred horsemen barricaded themselves in Ishibashiyama. When Kagechika led over a thousand horsemen who were loyal to our side and attacked them, the Assistant Captain was beaten down to seven or eight horsemen, fought with his topknot undone, and fled into the Sugiyama of Doi. After that, Hatakeyama, with more than five hundred horsemen, served the imperial side. The sons of Miura no Ōsuke Yoshiaki, with more than three hundred horsemen, fought for the Genji side at the bay of Yui and Kotsubo, but were defeated by Hatakeyama's army and retreated to Musashi Province. After that, Hatakeyama's clan, including Kawagoe, Inage, Oyamada, Edo, and Kasai, and in all the warriors of the seven bands besides, with more than three thousand horsemen, attacked and fought at the castle of Miura Kinugasa. Ōsuke Yoshiaki was killed. The children all boarded boats from the bay of Kurihama and crossed over to Awa and Kazusa. Thus it was said.

[5.4.2] The Heike people quickly lost interest in the capital move. The young court nobles and palace officials said, "Alas, how sad! If only something would happen, we would face the punitive force." Such things they said, but it was all in vain. Hatakeyama Shoji Shigeyoshi, Oyama Betto Arishige, and Utsunomiya Saemon Tomotsuna, being on guard duty in the capital, happened to be in Kyoto at that time. Hatakeyama said, "It must be a mistake. Since I have become a parent, Hojo does not know. The rest of the men would never serve as allies of the imperial enemy. He will soon hear and correct it. When he said this, some said, "Indeed," and others said, "No, no, it will soon become a great matter for the realm." And there were many who whispered so. The Lay Monk Chancellor's anger was extraordinary. "Yoritomo should have been put to death, but because the late Lord Ike pleaded so earnestly, his sentence was reduced to exile. Yet, forgetting that kindness, he has now turned his bow against our house. How could the gods and the Three Treasures ever forgive him? It is Yoritomo who is about to incur the punishment of heaven right now. Thus he declared.

[5.5.1] Now, when we seek the beginning of enemies of the court in our land, in the fourth year of the reign of Emperor Jimmu, in Kii Province, Nagusa District, Takao Village, there was a spider. Its body was short, its legs and arms were long, and its strength surpassed that of humans. Because the people suffered great damage, the imperial army set out, read the imperial edict, tied nets of kudzu, and finally surrounded and killed them. From that time onward, those who harbored ambition and sought to overthrow the imperial authority—Ōishi no Yamamaru, Ōyama no Ōji, Moriya no Ōomi, Yamada no Ishikawa, Soga no Iruka, Ōtomo no Matori, Funya no Miyata, Tachibana no Hayanari, Hikawa no Kawatsugu, Iyo no Shinnō, Dazai no Shōni Fujiwara no Hirotsugu, Emi no Oshikatsu, Sawara no Taishi, Inoue no Kōgō, Fujiwara no Nakanari, Taira no Masakado, Fujiwara no Sumitomo, Abe no Sadatō, Tsushima no Kami Minamoto no Yoshichika, Akusafu, and Akue-mon no Kami—numbered in all more than twenty. Yet not a single one of them fulfilled his true desire. Their corpses were exposed on mountains and fields, and their heads were hung at the prison gate.

[5.5.2] In this world, even the imperial throne is utterly worthless. In ancient times, when an imperial edict was read aloud, even withered trees and grasses blossomed and bore fruit, and flying birds followed it. It was an event of the middle era: Emperor Engi went to Shinsen'en, and when a heron was perched on the edge of the pond, he summoned a man of the sixth rank and said, "Catch that heron and present it to me." When he said that, although he thought, "How could I possibly catch it?", since it was an imperial command, he walked toward it. The heron also preened its feathers and was about to stand. "It is an imperial command." When he said that, it prostrated itself and did not fly away. He took it and returned. "You have come in obedience to the imperial decree; that is most admirable." Promote him to the Fifth Rank at once. So saying, he promoted the heron to the Fifth Rank. "From today onward, you shall be the king of the herons." He had a plaque made saying this, hung it around the heron's neck, and released it. It is not at all for the sake of the heron; it is solely to make known the extent of the royal authority.

[5.6.1] Again, when seeking precedents in foreign lands, there was a man called Prince Tan of Yan, who was imprisoned by the First Emperor of Qin and suffered punishment for twelve years. Prince Tan shed tears and said, "I have an aged mother in my homeland; grant me leave that I may see her." When he said this, the First Emperor laughed scornfully and said, "As for granting you leave, you must wait until horns grow on a horse and the head of a crow turns white." Yan Dan looked up to heaven and bowed down to the earth, saying, "I pray that you will wait until horns grow on a horse and the head of a crow turns white." Yan Dan looked up to heaven and bowed down to the earth, saying, "I pray that you will wait until horns grow on a horse and the head of a crow turns white." I will return to my hometown and see my mother once more. Thus he prayed. Myōon Bodhisattva went to the Pure Land of Vulture Peak and admonished the unfilial; Confucius and Yan Hui appeared in China and initiated the way of loyalty and filial piety. Because the Three Treasures of the visible and invisible worlds took pity on his filial devotion, a horse grew a horn and came to the palace, and a crow's head turned white and it perched on a tree in the front garden. The First Emperor, startled by the omen of the crow's head and horse's horn, believed that an imperial edict cannot be retracted, and pardoned Crown Prince Dan, sending him back to his homeland. The First Emperor still regretted it, and on the border between the land of Qin and the land of Yan, there was a country called Chu. A great river flowed. The bridge that was built over that river was called the Bridge of Chu. The First Emperor dispatched government troops, and when Yan Dan was about to cross, he had the bridge in the middle of the river rigged so that if he stepped on it, he would fall, and he made Yan Dan cross, but how could he not fall in? He fell into the middle of the river. However, he did not drown in the water at all, and as if walking on level ground, he reached the opposite shore. Wondering what this was, he looked back, and there were turtles, countless in number, floating up on the water, lining up their shells and making him walk. This too was because the unseen and the visible worlds pitied his filial devotion.

[5.6.2] Prince Tan, harboring resentment, again did not submit to the First Emperor. When the First Emperor sent government troops to strike Prince Tan of Yan, Prince Tan, terrified and trembling, persuaded a warrior named Jing Ke and made him his chief minister. Jing Ke also consulted with the warrior Tian Guang. That master said, "Do you, knowing that I am no longer in my prime, still rely on me?" A qilin can run a thousand li, but once it grows old, it is inferior even to a nag. Now, no matter what, it will not be possible. Let me go and consult with the warrior. As he was about to return, Jing Ke said, "This matter is secret; do not disclose it to anyone." He said. The master said, "There is no greater shame than being suspected by people." If this matter leaks out, I will be suspected. Saying this, he struck his head against a plum tree in front of the gate and smashed it, and died. There was also a soldier named Fan Yuqi. He was a man of the state of Qin. Because of the First Emperor, his father, uncles, and brothers were destroyed, and he fled and hid in the state of Yan. The Emperor of Qin issued an imperial edict throughout the realm: "To the one who cuts off Fan Yuqi's head and presents it, I will give five hundred kin of gold." Thus he proclaimed. Jing Ke heard this and went to Fan Yuqi's place, saying, "I have heard..." Your head will be rewarded with five hundred catties of gold. Lend me your head, and I will take it and present it to the First Emperor. When he is pleased and grants you an audience, it will be easy to draw a sword and stab his chest. When he said this, Fan Yuqi jumped up, sighed deeply, and said, "My parents, uncles, and brothers were destroyed by the First Emperor. Day and night I think of this, and it pierces my bones and marrow; I cannot bear it." Indeed, if I were to destroy the First Emperor, giving you my head would be easier than [giving you] a speck of dust. Saying this, he cut off his own head and died.

[5.6.3] There was also a warrior named Qin Wuyang. He too was a man of the land of Qin. At the age of thirteen, he killed an enemy and fled to the land of Yan. He is a peerless warrior. When he gets angry and faces you, even a big man faints. And when he smiles and faces you, even a baby is held by him. As he told this to a guide of the capital of Qin and took him along, one night when they lodged near a certain remote mountain, he heard someone playing wind and string instruments in a village nearby, and divined his original intention by the musical mode: the enemy's side was water, his own side was fire. Meanwhile, the sky had not yet dawned. A white rainbow pierced the sun but did not pass through. "It is unlikely that our wish will be fulfilled." So they said.

[5.6.4] However, since he could not return, he arrived at the capital of the First Emperor, Xianyang Palace. When he reported that he had come bearing Yan's maps and Fan Yuqi's head, the emperor tried to have his retainers receive them. "I will not send anyone; I will go up myself directly." "Then," he said, "so be it." So saying, he prepared the ceremonies of the seasonal festival and summoned the swallow's messenger. The Xianyang Palace was built with a circumference of 18,380 li around the capital. The imperial palace was built three li higher than the ground, and stood upon that. There is a Chōshōden (Palace of Long Life) and a Furōmon (Gate of Eternal Youth); they made the sun out of gold and the moon out of silver. They spread sand of pearls, sand of lapis lazuli, and sand of gold. On all four sides he built an iron wall forty jo high, and over the palace too he stretched an iron net. This was to keep out the messengers of the underworld. In autumn, when the wild geese in the rice fields, and in spring, when they return to the northern shores, because there was an obstacle to their free flight, he named the wall 'Ganmon' (Goose Gate), and opened the iron gate to let them pass. Among them there was also a palace called Abōden, where the First Emperor always went in imperial progress and conducted the affairs of state. Its height was thirty-six jō; it extended nine chō east to west and five chō north to south; beneath the great floor, a flagpole of five jō was erected, but even that did not reach the top. Above, it was roofed with lapis lazuli tiles; below, it was polished with gold and silver. Jing Ke carried Yan's map, and Qin Wuyang carried Fan Yuqi's head as they climbed the jade steps. Seeing the palace's extreme splendor, Qin Wuyang trembled violently, and the courtiers, suspicious, said, 'Wuyang has a rebellious heart.' Do not place a criminal beside the ruler; a gentleman does not approach a criminal; to approach a criminal is the way of making light of death. Thus he said. Jing Ke returned and said, "Wuyang has absolutely no intention of rebellion. It is only that, being accustomed solely to the humble ways of the countryside, he is bewildered by the imperial palace. When he said this, all the retainers fell silent. Therefore he was allowed to approach the king. When the map and Fan Yuqi's head were presented, at the bottom of the box containing the map, a sword like ice appeared. The First Emperor saw it and immediately tried to flee. Jing Ke grabbed the king's sleeve firmly and thrust the sword at his chest. It appeared that now it was all over. Although tens of thousands of soldiers lined up in the courtyard, they were powerless to rescue him. They only grieved that the lord would be harmed by the traitor. The First Emperor said, "Grant me a moment's leisure." I want to hear once more the sound of the koto of my most beloved consort. When he said this, Jing Ke did not attack for a while. The First Emperor had three thousand consorts. Among them was Lady Huayang, a master of the koto. From then on, when one heard the sound of this koto, even the anger of fierce warriors would soften, birds would fall from the sky, and plants and trees would bend. How much more so when she played, weeping, intending this moment to be her last before the emperor's ears—surely it must have been profoundly moving. Even Jing Ke lowered his head and pricked up his ears, and the thoughts of the scheming ministers also slackened. At that time, the empress for the first time played one more piece. "Even if the seven-foot folding screen is high, if one jumps, why would one not clear it?" Even if a single thread of thin silk is strong, if you pull it, why would it not break? So saying, he played. Jing Ke did not know this, but the First Emperor knew it, and cutting off his sleeve, he leaped over a seven-foot screen and hid behind a bronze pillar. Jing Ke, enraged, hurled his sword at the Emperor. At that moment, the imperial physician on duty threw his medicine bag at Jing Ke's sword. While carrying the sword and medicine bag, he cut the six-foot copper pillar only halfway. Jing Ke, again, since he had no sword, threw it as well. The king returned, summoned his own sword, and cut Jing Ke into eight pieces. Qin Wuyang was also killed. He dispatched government troops to destroy Yan Dan. Because blue heaven did not forgive him, the white rainbow did not pierce the sun, and Qin Shi Huang escaped, while Prince Dan of Yan ultimately perished. Therefore, people wondered if the present Yoritomo would also be like that, and there were those who showed concern.

[5.7.1] Now, this Yoritomo, because of the rebellion of his father, the Left Horse Bureau Director Yoshitomo, in the twelfth month of the first year of Heiji, was exiled to Hirugashima in Izu Province on the twentieth day of the third month of the first year of Eiryaku, at the age of fourteen, and has passed more than twenty years there. If it had been for many years, it might have been understandable, but what kind of mind made him raise a rebellion this year? It is said that the learned monk of Takao advised him to do so. This learned monk, originally the son of Watanabe no Endō Sakon no Shōgen Moritō, was called Endō no Musha Moritō, and was a retainer of Jōsaimon-in. At the age of nineteen, he awakened the aspiration for enlightenment and became a monk. When he was about to set out on ascetic practice, he thought, "What great matter is this thing called ascetic practice? Let me test it." Saying this, in the sixth month, when the grass was burning under the blazing sun, he crawled into a thicket on a remote mountain, lay down on his back, and although horseflies, mosquitoes, bees, ants, and other poisonous insects swarmed onto his body and bit and stung him, he did not move his body at all, and did not get up for seven days. On the eighth day he sat up and asked, "Is religious practice such a great matter as this?" When he asked someone, "If it is to that extent, how could even life survive?" While saying this, "Then it is peaceful and safe." Saying this, he immediately set out on his ascetic journey.

[5.7.2] He went to Kumano, intending to seclude himself at Nachi, but as a trial of his practice, he went down to the waterfall, thinking to be struck by the famous falls for a while. It was around the tenth day of the twelfth month, so snow had fallen and piled up, icicles hung, even the small streams in the valleys made no sound, the wind from the peaks blew freezing, the white threads of the waterfalls became icicles, everything was spread out in pure white, and even the treetops in all directions could not be distinguished. However, the scholar submerged himself in the waterfall basin, with the water up to his neck, and recited the Jiku spell. For two or three days he endured, but when it came to four or five days, he could bear it no longer and floated up. Since it is a waterfall that plunges down thousands of fathoms, how could it possibly be still? He was swept away and, like the blade of a sword, through the forbidding rocky crags, now sinking, now floating, he was carried for five or six hundred yards. Then a beautiful young boy came and, taking Monjō's left and right hands, pulled him up. People thought it was a miracle, and built a fire and warmed him, so since it was not his fixed karma to die, he soon began to breathe again. Monjō, having somewhat regained his senses, opened his eyes wide in anger and said, "I have a great vow to be beaten by this waterfall for twenty-one days and to complete the thirty thousand recitations of the Jikushu. Today is only the fifth day. Even seven days have not passed, and who has come here? When he said this, the people who saw him had their hair stand on end and could not speak. Again he returned to the waterfall basin and was struck down.

[5.7.3] On the second day, eight young boys came and tried to pull him up, but they pinched him all over and could not raise him. On the third day, the scholar finally passed away. Perhaps to avoid defiling the waterfall basin, two heavenly youths with their hair in buns descended from above the waterfall, and from the top of his head to the tips of his fingers and toes, they seemed to stroke him down with hands fragrant and warm beyond compare. He felt as if in a dream and could not breathe. "What kind of person are you, that you show me such compassion?" " he asked respectfully. "We are the two attendants, Kongara and Seitaka, sent by the Great Holy Immovable Wisdom King." By the command of the Wisdom King, we have come to join forces with you, who have made the supreme vow of learning and undertake courageous practice. Thus they replied. Raising his voice in anger, he said, "Well then, where is the Wisdom King?" "In the Tushita Heaven." He answered, and ascended far into the clouds. He pressed his palms together and worshipped him. "Indeed, even the Great Holy Immovable Wisdom King knows of my practice." " he said, and feeling reassured, he returned again to the waterfall basin and was struck down. Indeed, because there were auspicious signs, the wind that blew did not enter his body, and the water that fell was like hot water. Thus, when the great vow of twenty-one days was finally fulfilled, he confined himself at Nachi for a thousand days, went three times to Ōmine, twice to Katsuragi, and also to Kōya, Kokawa, Kinpusen, Hakusan, Tateyama, the peak of Fuji, Izu, Hakone, Shinano's Togakushi, and Dewa's Haguro; in short, he traveled around leaving no place in Japan unvisited, and yet, perhaps still longing for his old home, he returned to the capital. He was renowned as a miracle-worker whose prayers could even bring down flying birds.

[5.8.1] Later, he lived in the depths of a mountain called Takao, devoting himself to religious practice. At that Takao there is a mountain temple called Jingoji. It is a temple that Wake no Kiyomaro built in the time of Empress Shōtoku. As it had not been repaired for a long time, in spring it was enveloped in haze, in autumn it mingled with fog; its doors were blown down by the wind and rotted beneath fallen leaves; its roof tiles were eroded by rain and dew, and the Buddhist altar was all the more exposed. Since there was no resident priest, the only occasional offerings were the light of the moon and sun. Bungaku, resolving to repair it by any means, made a great vow, and carrying a subscription list, he went around soliciting donations from donors in all directions. On one occasion, he went to the retired emperor's palace, Hōjūji-dono. He reported that there should be an imperial donation, but as it was during a musical entertainment, the emperor did not listen. Mongaku was by nature the most fearless and wild of holy men. Not knowing the inner thoughts of the court, he thought only that he had not been allowed to enter, and so, having no choice, he broke into the palace grounds and cried out in a loud voice, "You are a lord of great mercy and compassion—why will you not listen to me?" Saying this, he spread open the fundraising appeal and read it aloud in a clear voice. The novice Mongaku respectfully states.In particular, having received the support of high and low, clergy and laity, I have built a temple on the sacred ground of Mount Takao, and I request a fundraising appeal to perform the great rite for the peace of this world and the next. Thus, the true reality is vast and great.Though it is said that he severed the provisional name of the living Buddha, since the time when, with the clouds of delusion following the Dharma-nature thickly covering him, he sat side by side on the peak of the twelve-linked chain of causation, the light of the moon of the originally existent lotus of the mind has been dim, and it has not yet manifested in the great void of the three virtues and four mandalas.Alas!The sun of the Buddha has long since set, and the crossroads of birth-and-death transmigration are utterly dark.They merely indulge in lust and indulge in wine.Who will apologize for the delusions of the mad elephant and the leaping monkey?In vain they slander people and slander the Dharma.How could they escape the punishment of the hell wardens?Here, although they say that learning has shaken off the dust of the secular world and adorned itself with the Dharma robe, evil deeds still run rampant in their hearts, being created day and night, and good sprouts, going against their ears, are abandoned morning and evening.How painful!Alas, that they must return again to the fiery pit of the three evil paths and forever revolve on the wheel of suffering of the four forms of birth!For this reason, the countless scrolls of the peerless sutras, each scroll clarifying the seed of Buddhahood, and the teaching of utmost sincerity according to conditions—there is not one that does not reach the far shore of enlightenment.Therefore, shedding tears at the gate of contemplation on impermanence in literature, urging both high and low, clergy and laity, to move their steps to the lotus pedestal of the highest grade, and to build the sacred site of the King of Equal and Wonderful Enlightenment.Now, Mount Takao is high and steep, showing the treetops of Vulture Peak; the valley is quiet, spreading the moss of Mount Shang.The spring among the rocks gurgles and stretches like cloth; the monkeys on the ridge cry and play among the branches.The human habitation is far away and there is no worldly dust; the place is near at hand and there is only faith.The terrain is excellent; indeed, one should revere the Buddhas and gods.The contribution is small; who would not help?I hear in the wind: 'Gathering sand to make a Buddha stupa, the merit suddenly evokes the Buddha's cause.'How much more so for the precious wealth of a single sheet of paper or half a coin?I pray that the construction may be completed, the imperial vow fulfilled, and that throughout the capital and countryside, near and far, neighbors and strangers alike may sing of the reign of Yao and Shun, and open smiles of reunion under the camellia leaves.Especially, the holy spirits and hidden rites, whether earlier or later, greater or lesser, will quickly reach the platform of the one Buddha's true gate, and will surely enjoy the moon of the three bodies and myriad virtues.Therefore, the purport of the exhortation and practice is probably like this.
[5.8.2] Third year of Jishō, third month, [day], written by [name].
[5.8.3] Thus it was read aloud.

[5.9.1] At that moment, before the emperor, the Grand Minister Myōon-in played the biwa and chanted a rōei, making it splendid. The Azechi Dainagon Sukekata took the beat and sang fūzoku and saibara. Uma no kami Tokitada, Shii no jijū Morisada plucked the wagon, sang imayō in turns, and inside the jeweled blinds and brocade curtains there was a lively commotion; it was truly delightful, so the retired emperor also composed an accompanying song. Then a loud voice from the literary scholar rang out, and both the melody and the rhythm were thrown into complete disarray. "Who is it?" Cut off his head! Thus he commanded, and just then— Among the young warriors who vied with one another to advance, a man called Sukeyuki no Hōgan ran out and said, "What is this you are saying?" Come out! When he said this, the other replied, "Unless a manor is granted to the Jingo-ji of Takao, I will never study letters." So saying, he did not move. When he tried to thrust at his neck, he snatched back the kanjinchō, struck off the hat of the judge Sukeyuki with a slap, clenched his fist, thrust at his chest, and knocked him flat on his back. Judge Sukeyuki, with his topknot undone, fled shamefacedly up onto the dais. After that, from within his robe, he drew a sword whose hilt was wrapped with horse tail and whose blade was like ice, and he stood waiting to thrust at anyone who came near. With the subscription list in his left hand and a drawn sword in his right, he ran about; it was an unexpected sudden event, and it looked as if he held swords in both hands. The court nobles and senior officials all clamored, "What is this? What is this?" and the musical performance was soon thrown into disorder. The commotion in the palace was extraordinary. Andō Musha Uemune, a resident of Shinano Province, who was at that time a guard in the office of the samurai-dokoro, said, "What is it?" Saying this, he drew his sword and ran out. The scholar rejoiced at this, but thinking that to cut him would be bad, he reversed his sword and struck the scholar's elbow, which held the sword, hard. Being struck, he felt a slight pain, dropped his sword, and said, "Well done!" Saying this, they grappled. While being grappled, Bungo no Andō no Musha thrust at his right elbow. While being thrust at, he held him down. As they were both of equal great strength, they went up and down, and in the midst of their tumbling, with a knowing look, they closed in on each other, and Bungo took advantage of a moment when he moved. However, he did not mind it at all, and all the more heaped abuse and wild words. They dragged him out through the gate and beat him in the courtyard of the office. They dragged him along. While being dragged and standing, he glared toward the imperial palace and raised a loud voice, saying, "You will surely not make a donation!" Since you have made me suffer such hardships in my studies, I will make you realize it! The three worlds are all a burning house. Even if it is called a royal palace, one cannot escape that difficulty. Even if you pride yourself on the throne of the ten good deeds, after you depart on the journey to the Yellow Springs, you will not escape the tortures of the horse-headed and ox-headed demons. So saying, he leaped up again and again. Saying this priest is strange, he was immediately imprisoned. The magistrate Sukeyuki, having his eboshi knocked off, was so ashamed that for a while he did not even attend court. Andō no Musha, for his literary merit, without passing through the first rank, was made Umanosuke. Meanwhile, around that time, Bifukumon'in passed away, and because there was a general amnesty, Bungaku was soon pardoned. For a while he should have gone somewhere, but instead of doing so, he again presented a kanjinchō and solicited donations, but then, without any result, he said, "Alas, in this world, right now there is disorder, and both lord and vassal will all perish." Saying such frightening things, he went around, and so they said, "This monk must not be left in the capital; exile him far away." And so he was exiled to Izu Province.

[5.9.2] Because the eldest son of Gen Sanmi Nyūdō, Nakatsuna, was at that time the governor of Izu, as a matter of course they were to send it down by ship from the Tōkaidō, and when they took it to Ise Province, two or three police officers were attached to it. These men said, "It is the custom of the office's lower officials to show favoritism in such matters." How is it, holy monk? When you are exiled to a distant province after such an event, do you have no acquaintance? Please beg even for things like provisions for the journey. When he said this, the scholar replied, "I have no such important acquaintance to speak of; my acquaintance is in the Higashiyama area." Well then, let us send a letter. When he said this, they searched for a strange paper and gave it to him. There is no way to write things on this kind of paper. Saying this, he threw it back. Then, saying 'if that's the case', they searched for thick paper and gave it to him. The scholar laughed and said, 'A monk cannot write things, so then you all write.' And so he wrote, saying: "It was for the sake of the vow to build and consecrate the Jingo-ji temple on Mount Takao that I urged and solicited contributions; and now, having met with such a reign as this, my long-cherished wish will not be fulfilled." I was imprisoned, and moreover exiled to Izu Province. It is a long journey. Even things like provisions for the journey are precious. Please give them to this messenger. When he said, "Write it like this," he wrote it as told, and then said, "Now, to whom shall I address it?" "Write it to the Kannon-bo of Kiyomizu." "This is to deceive the servants of the office." When he said this, the other replied, "If that is so, then it is Kannon whom you have deeply trusted." Otherwise, to whom would you speak of your business? So he said.

[5.9.3] They boarded a boat at the harbor of Anotsu in Ise Province and sailed down, but at the Tenryū Rapids in Tōtōmi Province, a sudden gale blew and great waves rose, and it seemed about to capsize the boat. The sailors and helmsmen, trying somehow to save themselves, chanted the name of Kannon or recited the ten final invocations, but the wind and waves only grew more violent. But the scholar paid no attention to it. He had been sleeping soundly, snoring loudly, but then, as if struck by a thought, he suddenly woke up, stood at the bow of the ship, glared toward the stern, and shouted in a loud voice, "Is the Dragon King here? Is the Dragon King here?" So they cried out. "How can you try to pass a ship on which a holy man who has made such a great vow is riding?" You dragon gods will soon incur divine punishment! So they said. Perhaps because of that, the wind and waves soon calmed down, and they arrived in Izu Province. From the day he left the capital, he made a vow. "If I return to the capital and build and dedicate the Jingo-ji Temple on Mount Takao, I shall not die. If this vow is in vain, I shall die on the road. So saying, from the capital until he reached Izu, because there was no favorable wind at any time, he went along the shores and from island to island, and for thirty-one days he fasted completely. Yet his strength did not diminish at all; he walked on and sat. Indeed, there were many things that did not seem like the deeds of an ordinary person. He was entrusted to a man named Kondo Shiro Kunitaka, and lived in the inner part of Nagoya in Izu Province.

[5.10.1] In the meantime, he often went to Lord Hyoe no Suke's residence, and while he was telling stories of old and new to console himself, one day a scholar said, "In the Heike, Lord Komatsu no Daijin was indeed firm in spirit and superior in strategy." Perhaps because the Heike's fortunes had come to an end, he passed away in the eighth month of last year. Now, among the Minamoto and the Taira, there is no one who has the appearance of a general like you. Quickly raise a rebellion and take control of Japan! "Hyōe no Suke said, 'What an unexpected thing you say, holy priest!' I was saved from a worthless life by the late Ike no Ama, and so, to pray for her afterlife, I do nothing but recite one chapter of the Lotus Sutra every day. Thus he spoke, but the scholar said again, "If you do not take what Heaven gives, you will instead receive its punishment. There is a text that says, 'If you do not act when the time comes, you will instead receive its calamity.' If I speak thus, it is because I wish to see your heart, and so I speak, thinking it over. Please show me the color of your deep devotion. Saying this, he took out from his bosom a skull wrapped in white cloth. Lord Hyōe no Suke said, "What is that?" When he said this, "This is the head of your father, the late Lord Sama no Kami." After the Heiji disturbance, it was buried beneath the moss in front of the prison, and there was no one to pray for his afterlife; but the scholar, having a thought to preserve it, begged it from the jailer and has worn it around his neck for these ten-odd years, visiting mountains and temples to worship and pray for him, so now surely he must have been saved even for a kalpa. Therefore, the scholar is indeed a loyal servant to the late Lord. When he said this, Lord Hyōe no Suke, though he could not be certain, hearing that it was his father's head, overcome with longing, first shed tears. After that, they relaxed and conversed. If Yoritomo had not been pardoned from the imperial censure, how could he have raised a rebellion? When he said this, [the other] replied, "That is an easy matter; I will go up at once and request [your pardon] and present it to you." "Well, well," [said the other], "you, a monk, are also under imperial censure, yet you say you will intercede for someone; your arrangement seems most insincere." "If I were to ask pardon for my own censure, that would indeed be wrong. But to intercede for you, what hardship could there be? To go up to the new capital, Fukuhara, the present capital, it will not take more than three days. If I ask for an imperial decree, there will be a stay of one day. In total, it must not exceed seven or eight days. Saying this, he pushed him out. He returned to Nagoya, and told his disciples that he had a secret intention to confine himself in prayer for seven days on the mountain of Izu, and so he departed. Indeed, on the third day, he went up to the new capital at Fukuhara, and because he had some slight connection with the former Major General of the Right Guards, Lord Mitsuyoshi, he went to his residence and said, "The exile from Izu Province, the former Lieutenant of the Right Guards, Yoritomo, has been pardoned of his imperial censure, and if he could but receive an imperial decree, he would summon the warriors of eight provinces, destroy the Heike, and pacify the realm." "Well, well," said the Hyōe-no-suke, "I too have been suspended from all three offices at this time, and it is a painful moment." The Cloistered Emperor has also been confined and sent away; what will become of him? Nevertheless, I must go and see him. So saying, he secretly reported this matter, and the Cloistered Emperor immediately issued an imperial decree. The holy man hung it around his neck, and on the third day arrived in Izu Province. Hyōe no Suke said, "Alas, this holy man has unnecessarily brought up a groundless matter; what kind of misfortune will Yoritomo meet with now?" While he was thinking about this without any particular concern, the messenger arrived at around noon on the eighth day and said, "Here is the imperial decree." Saying this, he presented it. Hyōe no Suke, in awe at hearing it was an imperial decree, washed his hands, rinsed his mouth, put on a new eboshi and white robes, bowed three times to the decree, and opened it. Since the years of the Shigetada disturbance, the Heike have despised the imperial rule and have shown no restraint in their governance.They intend to destroy the Buddhist Law and bring ruin to the imperial authority.Now, our court is a land of the gods; the ancestral shrines stand side by side, and the divine virtue is ever new.Therefore, since the founding of the court, for more than several thousand years, there has never been a case where those who sought to overturn the imperial rule and endanger the state did not all end in defeat.If so, then on the one hand relying on the divine protection of the gods, and on the other hand observing the purport of the imperial edict, quickly destroy the entire Heike clan and drive away the enemies of the imperial house.Inherit the military strategies of your ancestral bow and arrow, excel in the loyal service of successive generations of your forebears, and establish yourself and raise your family—so the imperial edict says.The writ was issued as stated.
[5.10.2] In the fourth year of Jishō, on the fourteenth day of the seventh month, the former Captain of the Right Palace Guards, Mitsuyoshi, respectfully presents
[5.10.3] Respectfully presented to the former Assistant Captain of the Right Palace Guards.
[5.10.4] Thus it was written. This imperial decree was placed in a brocade bag, and even during the Battle of Ishibashiyama, the Assistant Captain of the Right Palace Guards wore it around his neck.

[5.11.1] Meanwhile, in Fukuhara, before the troops could gather, the court nobles held a council and decided to send a punitive force quickly. As commander-in-chief, Komatsu no Gon no Suke Shōshō Koremori; as deputy commander, Satsuma no Kami Tadanori; altogether their forces numbered more than thirty thousand horsemen. They left the new capital on the eighteenth day of the ninth month, arrived at the old capital on the nineteenth, and on the twentieth they set out for the eastern provinces. The commander-in-chief, Gon no Suke Shōshō Koremori, was twenty-three years old. His appearance and bearing were such that even if one tried to paint them or describe them in writing, it would be difficult to do them justice. The heirloom armor called Karakawa was put in a Chinese chest and carried. On the way, he wore a red brocade hitatare and armor laced with light green thread, and rode a dappled gray horse with a gold-fringed saddle. The vice-commander Satsuma no kami Tadanori wore a dark blue brocade hitatare and armor laced with black thread, and rode a stout black horse with a gold-lacquered saddle. Even down to the horse saddles, armor, helmets, bows and arrows, swords, and daggers, they were outfitted so that they shone brilliantly, and it was a splendid sight. Satsuma no kami Tadanori had for years been visiting the residence of a certain lady-in-waiting of imperial birth, but on one occasion when he was sitting there, a noble lady came as a guest to that lady's residence, and they conversed for a long time. The night had grown late, and still the guest had not returned. Tadanori paused for a while at the eaves, and when he rustled his fan, a court lady of the Miyahara said, "The sound of insects gathering in the fields..." When she recited this gracefully and gently, the Satsuma governor immediately stopped sending the fan and returned. After that, when he was sitting again, a court lady from the palace asked, "Why did you stop using your fan that day?" When she asked this, he replied, "Well, since it was said to be noisy, I stopped using it." Thus he said. From that lady's place, to Tadanori's place, she sent a single-layer robe, and in the sadness of parting, she sent a poem.

lg.l: 東路の草葉をわけん袖よりも、たゝぬ袂の露ぞこぼるゝ。

div.p: [5.11.2] Satsuma no kami's reply:

lg.l: 別路を何かなげかんこえて行く、關もむかしの跡とおもへば。

div.p: [5.11.3] The poem that says 'the barrier too is a trace of the past' was composed when Taira no Sadamori, on his way down to the eastern provinces to subdue Masakado, recalled the past and recited it; it sounded most excellent.

[5.11.4] In the past, a general who was to proceed to foreign lands to subdue enemies of the court would first have an audience with the emperor and receive a ceremonial sword. The Emperor went out to the Southern Hall, the Imperial Guards drew up their ranks below the steps, the court nobles of the Inner and Outer Guards assembled, and the ceremony of the Middle Rite was performed. The Great General and the Deputy General each straightened their attire and received it. The precedents of the Jōhei and Tengyō eras had become too old to serve as a model, so this time, following the example of Sanuki no kami Masamori, who had gone down to Izumo Province to subjugate the former Tsushima no kami Minamoto no Yoshichika, they gave only a bell, put it in a leather bag, and had a servant hang it around his neck as he departed. A general who leaves the capital to destroy an old enemy of the court has three things to keep in mind. On the day he receives the sword of commission, he forgets his family; when he leaves his home, he forgets his wife and children; when he fights the enemy on the battlefield, he forgets his own life. Therefore, the present Taira commanders Koremori and Tadanori must surely have been aware of such things. It was a pitiful thing.

[5.11.5] On the same twenty-first day, the Retired Emperor again made an imperial visit to Itsukushima in Aki Province. There had also been an imperial visit in the past March. Perhaps because of that, for one or two months the world was governed auspiciously and the people had no troubles, but due to the rebellion of Prince Takakura, the realm was again thrown into disorder and the world was not peaceful. Because of this, it was said to be partly for the peace of the realm and partly for prayers for the emperor's recovery from illness. This time, since it was an imperial visit from Fukuhara, there was no trouble of dust and dirt. He personally composed the prayer text, and had the Regent write the fair copy. I have heard that the clouds of the Dharma nature are serene.The moon of the fourteenth and fifteenth nights shines high and clear, and the wind of yin and yang blows from the side, as the wisdom of the provisional manifestations is deep.Now, the shrine of Itsukushima is a place where the invocation of the name is widely heard, a site of unparalleled efficacy.The shrine buildings encircling the distant ridge manifest the towering height of the great compassion, and the shrine edifices extending to the vast sea express the depth and breadth of the great vow.Thus, with a humble and ignorant body, I have reverently ascended to the throne of the emperor.Now I enjoy the wise plans among the crowd of the sacred realm, and take pleasure in leisurely freedom in my dwelling on the mountain.However, secretly I offered my sincere heart, visited the secluded shrine on the solitary island, looked up for divine grace beneath the auspicious fence, concentrated my earnest thoughts and shed sweat, and received a divine message within the sacred palace.There is something engraved in my heart about that message.Among these, especially when it points to a time of fear and reverence, it corresponds precisely to the season of late summer and early autumn.Illness suddenly attacks, and there is no way to apply the effectiveness of medicine.Duckweed and laurel constantly shift.More and more, I know that divine response is not in vain.Though I seek through prayer, mist and dew are hard to dispel.Rather, I will draw forth the aspiration of my heart and plan anew the practice of ascetic discipline.At the bottom of the vast cold wind, I lie in a traveler's lodging and my dreams are broken; before the faint, lonely sunlight, I face the distant road and strain my eyes.At last, arriving at the garden of his home, he reverently spread out a pure seat and copied the Lotus Sutra in colored paper and ink, one complete set, together with the opening and closing sutras, the Amida Sutra, the Heart Sutra, and other sutras, one volume each.He personally copied in gold paint the Devadatta chapter, one volume.At that time, under the shade of the green pines and cypresses, together they added the seeds of good reason; the ebb and flow of the tide harmonized with the sound of Buddhist chanting in the sky.Although it is said that the disciple left the clouds of the northern palace and not many years passed, he crossed the waves of the western sea twice, and deeply knew that his karmic connection was not shallow.The visitors who pray in the morning are not just one.Those who cast lots in the evening number a thousand.However, though the reverence of the noble is great, visits to the temple by the court have never been heard of.The Cloistered Emperor Zenjo first performed that ceremony.His disciple, of humble body, deeply pursued that aspiration; before the moon of that lofty mountain, Emperor Wu of Han had not yet worshipped the shadow of the harmonious light.Even at the bottom of the clouds of Penglai Cave, the heavenly immortals vainly separated the dust of their manifested traces.I humbly pray, O Great Deity, and prostrate myself in supplication: shine your divine favor anew upon the Lotus Sutra, and grant us your sole miraculous response.
[5.11.6] On the twenty-eighth day of the ninth month of the fourth year of Jishō, the Retired Emperor
[5.11.7] Thus he composed [the poem].

[5.11.8] Meanwhile, these people left the capital of the nine-fold palace and set out for the Eastern Sea, a thousand leagues away. The prospect of returning safely was truly perilous: sometimes they lodged in the dew of the fields, sometimes they slept on the moss of high peaks, crossing mountains and fording rivers; and as the days passed, on the sixteenth day of the tenth month they arrived at Kiyomigaseki in Suruga Province. Although he had left the capital with over thirty thousand horsemen, gathering soldiers along the way, it was said to be over seventy thousand horsemen. The vanguard advanced to Kambara and Fuji River, while the rear guard held at Tegoshi and Utsuya. The Grand General, Assistant Captain Koremori, summoned the Staff General, Governor of Kazusa Tadakiyo, and said, "In my opinion, we should cross over Ashigara and fight in the Bando region." When he said this, the Governor of Kazusa replied, "When you departed from Fukuhara, the Lay Monk's command was that you should entrust the military affairs to Tadakiyo. Since the soldiers of the eight provinces have all sided with the Assistant Governor of Bizen, how many tens of thousands of horsemen might there be? Although it is said that our side's forces number seventy thousand horsemen, they are warriors gathered from various provinces. Both horses and men are exhausted. The forces of Izu and Suruga, who should be coming, have not yet appeared. Should we just wait for our forces with the Fuji River in front of us? When he said this, they could not resist and wavered.

[5.11.9] Meanwhile, Hyōe no Suke crossed over Mount Ashigara and arrived at the Kise River in Suruga Province. The Genji of Kai and Shinano came riding up and joined forces. At Ukishima-ga-hara, there was a review of the troops. It was recorded as two hundred thousand horsemen. A servant of Satake Tarō, a Genji of Hitachi, was going up to the capital carrying a letter as a messenger of his master, when the Heike vanguard, Kazusa no Suke Tadakiyo, stopped him, snatched the letter he was carrying, opened it, and saw that it was a letter to a lady. Thinking it would not be painful, he had it taken. "Well, how large is the force of the Assistant Commander?" When he asked, "For about eight or nine days' journey, they are packed together, and fields, mountains, seas, and rivers are all filled with warriors." As for the low-ranking ones, up to four or five hundred thousand, I know the number, but beyond that I do not know. Whether they are many or few, I do not know. Yesterday at Kise River, someone said that the Genji forces number two hundred thousand horsemen. Hearing this, Kazusa no Suke said, "Alas, while the great general's mind is so relaxed, there is nothing regrettable. If he had sent out the punitive force even one day earlier, and crossed over Ashigara Mountain and gone out to the eight provinces, would Hatakeyama's clan and the Oba brothers not have come to join us? If even these were to come, there would be no plant or tree in the Bando region that would not submit. Thus he regretted it, but it was in vain.

[5.11.10] Again, the Grand General, the Assistant Commander Koremori, summoned Nagai Saitō no Bettō Sanemori, saying he was a guide to the eastern provinces: "Hey, Sanemori, how many strong archers and elite soldiers like you are there in the eight provinces?" When he asked this, Saitō no Bettō laughed scornfully and said, "If that is so, do you, my lord, think of Sanemori as a great arrow?" I can only manage thirteen bundles. There are any number of archers like Sanemori in the eight provinces. Those who are called great archers do not draw a bow of less than fifteen bundles; the bow's strength is such that five or six strong men string it. When such elite warriors shoot, they can easily pierce even two or three layers of armor. A single great commander, as they say, is one whose forces are few; he never has fewer than five hundred horsemen. Once mounted on horseback, they do not know the path of falling. Even when they gallop through rough terrain, they do not let their horses stumble. In battle, let parent be struck down, let child be struck down; when they die, they fight on, trampling over the dead. As for the armies of the western provinces, if a parent is killed, they perform filial duties and, after the mourning period ends, they attack; if a child is killed, they do not attack because of their grief and lamentation. When provisions run out, in spring they work the fields, in autumn they harvest and then attack; in summer they say it is hot, in winter they dislike the cold. In the eastern provinces, such things do not happen at all. The Genji of Kai and Shinano know the lay of the land. They will probably go around by the rear of Mount Fuji. If I say this, would you think that I am saying it to make you remember me? It is not that. It is said that war does not depend on numbers but on strategy. Sanemori does not think that he will survive this battle and return to the capital again. When he said this, the Heike warriors heard it and all trembled and shook.

[5.11.11] In the meantime, it became the twenty-third day of the tenth month. On the next day, when they had decided to exchange arrows at the Fuji River between the Genji and the Heike, as night fell, when the Heike side looked out over the Genji camp, they saw the fires of the encampments of the people and peasants of Izu and Suruga, who, fearing the battle, had either gone into the fields and hidden in the mountains, or boarded boats and floated on the sea and rivers. The Heike warriors said, "Oh, how numerous are the distant fires of the Genji camp!" Indeed, truly, fields, mountains, seas, and rivers were all enemies. What shall we do? So they panicked. Around midnight that night, a great flock of waterfowl that had gathered in the Fuji marshes suddenly took flight all at once, startled by something; the sound of their wings was like a great wind or thunder, and when the Heike warriors heard it, they cried, "Ah! The Genji are attacking in force!" As Saito Betto said, surely the rear guard is also coming around. If we are surrounded, we will be unable to escape. Let us withdraw from here and defend the Owari River and Sunomata! So saying, they fled, each trying to be first, without even taking their belongings. Those who hastily take up bows in the confusion do not know arrows, those who take up arrows do not know bows; they mount other men's horses, and their own horses are mounted by others. Some, mounting tethered horses, endlessly circled around stumps. The courtesans and prostitutes who had been invited from nearby lodgings and were amusing themselves: some had their heads kicked and broken, their hips trampled and fractured, and many were crying out.

[5.11.12] At the hour of the rabbit (6 a.m.) on the following day, the twenty-fourth, the great Minamoto army of two hundred thousand horsemen pressed forward to the Fuji River, and with a war cry that made heaven resound and the earth shake, they raised their battle cry three times.

[5.12.1] On the Heike side, there was not a sound. When he sent someone to look, [the report came back]: "They have all fled." He said. There were also those who came carrying armor the enemy had forgotten. There were also those who came carrying large curtains the enemy had discarded. "In the enemy camp, not even a fly is stirring." he said. Hyōe no Suke dismounted from his horse, removed his helmet, performed the ritual washing of hands and rinsing of mouth, prostrated himself toward the imperial palace, and said, "This is by no means Yoritomo's personal glory; it is the divine plan of Hachiman Daibosatsu." he declared. Since it was a place to be captured immediately, Suruga Province was entrusted to Ichijō Jirō Tadayori, and Tōtōmi Province to Yasuda Saburō Yoshisada. Although the Heike could have continued to attack, they felt uneasy about their rear, so they withdrew from Ukishimagahara and returned to Sagami Province. The courtesans and prostitutes of the post stations along the coast said, "How dreadful!" How shameful that the great general of archers fled without shooting even a single arrow! In battle, even the act of overlooking an enemy is considered a shameful thing, but this is fleeing upon hearing [the enemy]. They laughed together. There were many lampoons. 都の大將軍をば宗盛と云ひ、討手の大將をば權亮と云ふ間、平家をひら屋によみなして、

lg.l: ひらやなるむねもりいかにさわぐらん、柱とたのむすけをおとして。
富士河の瀬々の岩こす水よりも、はやくもおつるいせ平氏かな。

div.p: [5.12.2] 上總守たゞきよが、富士河に鎧を捨たりけるを讀めり。

lg.l: 富士河に鎧はすてつ、墨染の衣たゞきよ後の世のため。
たゞきよはにげの馬にぞのりにける、上總鞦かけてかひなし。

div.p: [5.12.3] 同十一月八日、大將軍權亮少將維盛、福原の新都へ上りつく。 入道相國大に怒て、 「大將軍權亮少將維盛をば鬼界が島へ流すべし、侍大將上總守忠清をば死罪に行へ。」 とぞ宣ひける。同九日平家の侍共、老少參會して、「忠清が死罪の事、いかゞ有ら ん。」と評定す。中に主馬判官盛國進出でて申けるは、「忠清は昔より不覺人とは承 り及ばず、あれが十八歳と覺え候、鳥羽殿の寶藏に五畿内の惡黨二人、迯籠て候しを、 寄て搦めうと申す者候はざりしに、此忠清白晝に唯一人築地を越え、はね入て、一人 をば討取り、一人をば生捕て、後代に名を揚たりし者にて候。今度の不覺は、徒事と も覺え候はず。 是に附ても、能々兵亂の御愼候べし。 Thus he said.

[5.12.4] On the same tenth day, the Great General, Gon no Suke Shōshō Koremori, became Middle Captain of the Right Palace Guards. "Although he was known as the commander of the punitive force, he has done nothing particularly noteworthy. What kind of reward is this? Thus the people whispered to one another.

[5.12.5] Long ago, for the purpose of hunting down Masakado, Taira no Shogun Sadamori and Tawara no Tota Hidesato received the imperial command and set out for the Bando region, but since Masakado was not easy to destroy, it was decided in a council of nobles to send a punitive force again, and Uji Minbukyo Tadafumi and Kiyohara no Shigefuji were given the office of gunkan (army inspector) and sent down. On the night when they lodged at Kiyomi Barrier in Suruga Province, that Shigefuji, gazing far over the vast sea, recited aloud a Chinese poem: "The fishing boat's firelight is cold and burns the waves; the post road's bell sound passes through the night mountains." Tadafumi was deeply moved and shed tears of admiration. In the end, Sadamori and Hidesato killed Masakado. As they were going up carrying his head, they met at Kiyomi Barrier. After that, the generals before and after went up to the capital together. When rewards were being granted to Sadamori in Hidezato, there was a council of nobles as to whether rewards should also be given to Tadabumi and Shigefuji. The Right Minister Kujō Morosuke said, "Although it is said that a punitive force was sent to the east, Masakado was not easy to destroy, and when these men received the imperial command and went to the east, the imperial enemy had already been destroyed." Therefore, why should there be no reward? " he said, but the regent at that time, Ononomiya-dono, said, "In the Book of Rites it is written, 'Do not do what is doubtful.' " and in the end did not grant it. Tadabumi, considering this a regrettable matter, said, "I will make the descendants of the Ononomiya lord into slaves." For the descendants of the Kujō lord, I will become a guardian deity for all ages. Thus he swore, and died of starvation. Therefore, although the descendants of the Kujō lord prospered splendidly, among the descendants of the Ononomiya lord there was no worthy person, and now they have completely died out.

[5.12.6] In the meantime, the fourth son of the Nyūdō Prime Minister, the Middle Captain Shigehira, became a Middle Captain of the Left Palace Guards. On the thirteenth day of the eleventh month, at Fukuhara, a palace was built, and the emperor moved there. Although there should have been a Great Thanksgiving Festival, the Great Thanksgiving Festival was held at the end of the tenth month, when the emperor went to the Eastern River and performed purification. In the northern field of the great palace, they built a purification site and prepared the sacred garments and utensils. In front of the Great Audience Hall, below the Dragon Tail Walkway, they erected the Kairyūden and drew the sacred water. Next to the same platform, they built the Daijōgū and prepared the sacred offerings. There was an imperial banquet. There was an imperial musical performance. There was a grand ceremony at the Daigokuden. There was a sacred kagura performance at the Seishodō. There was a banquet at the Burakuin. However, in this new capital of Fukuhara, since there is no Daigokuden, there is no place to perform the grand ceremony. Since there is no Seishodō, there is no way to perform the sacred music. Since the Buraku-in was also gone, the banquets were not held either. This year, it was decided by the court nobles that only the Niiname-sai and the Gosechi should be held, and so the Niiname-sai was performed at the Jingikan in the old capital.

[5.12.7] During the reign of Emperor Tenmu, at the Yoshino Palace, on a night when the moon was bright and the wind was fierce, as he was playing the koto with a serene heart, a heavenly maiden descended and fluttered her sleeves five times. This is the beginning of the Gosechi festival.

[5.13.1] Regarding this recent transfer of the capital, both lord and vassals lamented. Starting with the temples of Nara, down to all the shrines and temples, they all filed complaints saying it was unacceptable, and even the Prime Minister, who usually broke through all opposition, said, "Then let the capital be returned," and the whole capital was in an uproar.

[5.13.2] On the second day of the twelfth month of the same year, the capital was suddenly returned. The new capital was high in the north, bordering the mountains, and low in the south, near the sea. The sound of the waves is always loud, and the salt wind is fierce—such is this place. Therefore, the Retired Emperor, without knowing when, was troubled only by illness, and so he hurriedly departed from Fukuhara. Beginning with the Regent, the Chancellor and all the court nobles and senior officials below him vied with one another to accompany him. Beginning with the Lay Monk Chancellor, the nobles and senior officials of the Heike clan vied to be first to go up. Who would remain even for a moment in the new capital that had become so hateful? Since the sixth month, they had dismantled the houses, carried down the materials and miscellaneous goods, and rebuilt them in proper form, but then, because the capital was again in turmoil, they could not attend to any arrangements and abandoned everything and fled. Each of them, having no place to live, stayed in the corridors of temples and the worship halls of shrines, in the vicinity of Hachiman, Kamo, Saga, Uzumasa, Nishiyama, and Higashiyama, even people of high rank.

[5.13.3] When asked what the true purpose of this capital relocation was, the old capital was close to the southern capital (Nara) and the northern peak (Mount Hiei), and even for trivial matters, they would bring out the sacred tree of Kasuga or the portable shrine of Hiyoshi, causing disturbances. Fukuhara, being separated by mountains and layered with rivers, was after all far away, so such things would not easily happen, and thus it was planned by the Lay Priest Chancellor.

[5.13.4] On the twenty-third day of the twelfth month of the same year, to attack the Omi Genji who had rebelled, the great general was Tomomori, the Left Palace Guard Commander, and Tadanori, the Governor of Satsuma, with a total force of over twenty thousand cavalry, they departed for Omi Province, and attacked and defeated the so-called overflow Genji at Yamamoto, Kashiwagi, Nishikikori, and other places one by one, and then crossed over into Mino and Owari.

[5.14.1] In the capital, when Prince Takakura entered Onjō-ji, the monks of Nara joined forces and even went to welcome him; this made them enemies of the court.
