So it was said that both Nara and Mii-dera should be attacked, and the monks of Nara rose up in great numbers. From the Regent came the message: "If you have any intention, you should report it to the throne as many times as necessary." But they did not comply at all. When the official bettō Tadanari was sent as an envoy, they said, "Drag him out of the palanquin and pull him down! Cut off his topknot!" While they were making a commotion, Tadanari lost his composure and fled. Next, they sent down Uemon no Suke Chikamasa. For him too, "The topknot is cut!" When the monks clamored, "Cut it!" he fled without taking anything. At that time, the two servants of Kangakuin had their topknots cut.

[5.14.2] Also in Nanto they made a large ball for the stick-ball game, named it 'the head of the Heike Chancellor,' and said, 'Hit it, trample it.' they said, and so on. A word that leaks easily is a medium that invites calamity. A word that is not guarded is a path that brings ruin. so it is said. This Nyūdō Sōkō, to speak of him, is awe-inspiringly the maternal grandfather of the present emperor. That the monks of Nanto spoke in such a way was, it seemed, entirely the work of the heavenly demon.

[5.14.3] When Nyūdō Sōkō heard of such matters, how could he possibly think it good? In order to quell the outrages of Nanto, he appointed Seto Tarō Kaneyasu, a resident of Bitchū Province, to the office of police commissioner in Yamato Province. Kaneyasu set out for Nanto with over five hundred horsemen. 「相構て、衆徒は狼藉を致すとも、汝等は致すべからず。 物具なせそ。 弓箭な帶しそ。 」とて向はれたりけるに、大衆かゝる内議をば知らず、兼康が餘勢六十餘人搦取て、一々に皆頸を斬て、猿澤の池の端にぞ懸竝べたる。 入道相國大に怒て、 「さらば南都を攻よや。」とて、大將軍には頭中將重衡、副將軍には中宮亮通盛、都 合其勢四萬餘騎で南都へ發向す。大衆老少嫌はず七千餘人甲の緒をしめ、奈良坂、般 若寺、二箇所の路を掘切て、堀ほり垣楯かき、逆茂木引て待かけたり。平家は四萬餘 騎を二手に分て、奈良坂、般若寺、二箇所の城郭に押寄て、鬨をどとつくる。大衆は 皆歩立打物なり。官軍は馬にてかけまはしかけまはし、あそここゝに追懸／＼指つめ 引つめ散々に射ければ、防ぐ所の大衆數を盡いて討れにけり。卯刻に矢合して一日戰 ひ暮す。夜に入て、奈良坂、般若寺、二箇所の城郭共に破れぬ。落行く衆徒の中に、 坂四郎永覺と云ふ惡僧あり。打物持ても弓箭を取ても力の強さも七大寺十五大寺に勝 たり。萌黄威の腹巻の上に、黒絲威の鎧を重てぞ著たりける。帽子甲に五枚甲の緒を しめて、左右の手には茅の葉の樣に反たる白柄の大長刀、黒漆の大太刀持つまゝに、 同宿十餘人前後にたて、てがいの門より打て出でたり。 This was a temporary support. Many government soldiers had their horses' legs cut down and were killed. However, the government forces were numerous, and as they attacked in waves, all of Eikaku's fellow monks who defended him on all sides were killed. Eikaku alone fought fiercely, but when his rear became exposed, he fled toward the south.

[5.14.4] It became a night battle; the darkness was deep. The Commander-in-Chief, Middle Captain Shigehira, stood before the gate of Hannya-ji Temple and ordered, "Set fire!" It was just as he said. Among the Heike forces, a man named Jirō Tayū Tomokata, the local official of Fukui Manor, a resident of Harima Province, broke his shield into pieces and made a torch of it, and set fire to the houses. It was the night of the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth month; the wind was fierce, and though there was but one source of fire, the gusting wind blew it onto many temple buildings. Those who cared about shame or valued their reputation died fighting at Narazaka, or were killed at Hannya-ji. Those who were able to walk fled toward Yoshino and Totsukawa. Even old monks who could not walk, ordinary scholars, children, and young girls fled into the Great Buddha Hall and Yamashina-dera, each trying to be first. More than a thousand people climbed up to the second floor of the Great Buddha Hall, and pulled up the stairs so that the enemy could not follow them up. The fierce flames pressed in upon them. The voices crying out, the sinners at the bottom of the flames of the Hell of Scorching Heat, the Hell of Great Scorching Heat, and the Hell of No Interval, even these would not surpass this.

[5.14.5] Kofuku-ji is the temple founded by the vow of Tankaiko and the temple of the Fujiwara clan for generations. The statue of Shakyamuni, the first Buddha, seated in the Eastern Golden Hall; the Kannon that spontaneously appeared, seated in the Western Golden Hall; the four-sided corridors lined with lapis lazuli; the two-story tower painted with red lead; the two pagodas whose nine rings shone in the sky—all suddenly turned to smoke, how sorrowful it is. Todaiji was thought to be eternal and indestructible, the living body of the Buddha in the Land of Actual Reward and Tranquil Light. Emperor Shomu himself carved and erected the sixteen-jō gilt-bronze statue of Vairocana. Its ushnisha rose high, hidden among the clouds of mid-sky; its white curl between the eyebrows, the full-moon countenance newly worshipped, also—its head burned off and lies on the ground, its body melted together like a mountain. The eighty-four thousand marks of a Buddha are early hidden by the fivefold clouds of the autumn moon, and the jeweled ornaments of the forty-one stages are vainly tossed by the winds of the ten evils in the night sky. Smoke fills the sky, and flames leave no gap in the air. Those who saw it with their own eyes could not bear to look, and those who heard of it from afar lost their wits. Of the sacred scriptures of the Hossō and Sanron schools, not a single scroll remained. Needless to say in our own country, even in India and China, one would not think that such a destruction of the Dharma could occur. Even the gold of King Udayana, polished, and the red sandalwood carved by Vishvakarman, were only life-sized images of the Buddha. How much more so this one, in the southern continent of Jambudvipa, the only unparalleled Buddha, who was thought to be free from decay for a long time, but now, mixed with the dust of poisonous karma, has long left behind sorrow. Brahma, Indra, the Four Heavenly Kings, the eight kinds of dragon gods, and the judges and multitudes of the underworld all seemed to be astonished and agitated. What could Kasuga Daimyojin, protector of the Hossō sect, have been thinking? And so the dew on Kasuga Field changed color, and the sound of the wind in the pines of Mount Mikasa seemed to be heard as a voice of resentment. When they recorded the number of people who had burned to death in the flames, it was more than 1,700 on the upper floor of the Great Buddha Hall, more than 800 at Yamashina-dera, more than 500 in one hall, more than 300 in another hall; when they had recorded them all, it was more than 3,500 people. More than a thousand monks were killed on the battlefield; some were cut down at the gate of Hannya-ji, and some had their heads taken and were brought up to the capital.

[5.14.6] On the twenty-ninth, the Middle Captain destroyed Nanto and returned to the northern capital. Only the Lay Monk Chancellor felt his anger clear and rejoiced. The Empress, the Retired Emperor, the Regent, and all those below them lamented, "Even if we destroy the evil monks, should we destroy the temple buildings?" Thus they lamented. It was said that the heads of the monks should be carried across the main avenue and hung on the prison gate, but because of the dreadful destruction of Todaiji and Kofukuji, the matter was not even discussed. They were thrown away into ditches and moats here and there. In the imperial writing of Emperor Shōmu, it is written: "If our temple prospers, the realm will prosper; if our temple declines, the realm will decline." Thus it was written. Therefore, there is no doubt that the realm will decline. The dreadful year came to an end, and it became the fifth year of Jishō.

[6.1.1] On the first day of the first month of the fifth year of Jishō, at the imperial palace, because of the warfare in the eastern provinces and the fire at the southern capital, the New Year's audience was cancelled, and there was no imperial procession. No musical instruments were sounded, no court dances were performed, the Kuzu of Yoshino did not come, and not a single court noble of the Fujiwara clan attended, because their family temple had been destroyed by fire. On the second day, there was no banquet in the palace hall. Men and women kept silent, and the imperial palace appeared gloomy and ominous. Both the Buddhist Law and the Imperial Law have come to an end—how deplorable! The Retired Emperor said, "By virtue of the lingering blessings of the ten good deeds, I have maintained the imperial rank of the ten-thousand-chariot sovereign." The emperors of four generations, when I think of it, are my children and grandchildren. Why should I abandon the myriad affairs of state and idly pass the months and years? Thus he lamented.

[6.1.2] On the fifth day of the same month, the high-ranking monks of the southern capital were dismissed from their offices, their official invitations were suspended, and their positions were confiscated. Of the monks, both old and young, some were shot to death, some were cut down, some did not escape from the smoke and choked on the flames, and many died; the few who remained mingled with the mountain forests, and not one stayed behind. When the Kofukuji betto, the archbishop of Karin-in, Eigen, saw the smoke of the Buddhist images and scriptures rising, he thought, "How dreadful!" and his heart was disturbed; from the time his heart was broken, he fell ill, and before long he finally passed away. This archbishop was a person of exceptional depth of feeling. Once, hearing the cry of a cuckoo,

lg.l: 聞く度にめづらしければほとゝぎす、いつも初音の心地こそすれ。

div.p: [6.1.3] He composed the poem that goes, and so he was called Hatsune no Sojo.

[6.1.4] However, even if it were to be held in some form, the imperial memorial service should take place, and when there was discussion of the monks' names, the monastic officials of Nara had been dismissed, so the court nobles deliberated whether it should be conducted using the monastic officials of the northern capital (Kyoto). However, since he could not abandon Nara entirely, the student of the Sanron school, Jōhō Ikō, who had been hiding in Kajū-ji, was summoned, and the memorial service was conducted in due form. The Retired Emperor, because he had been grieved in his heart by such events as the matter of the Cloistered Emperor's having been confined in the Toba Palace two years before, the sight of Prince Takakura's having been killed the previous year, and the disturbance of the realm when the capital was moved—an ignominious affair—fell ill, and although he had always been in poor health, when he heard that the Tōdaiji and Kōfukuji temples had been destroyed, his illness grew all the more severe. While the Cloistered Emperor grieved deeply, on the fourteenth day of the first month of the same year, at the Ikedono in Rokuhara, the Retired Emperor finally passed away. His reign lasted twelve years; he revived the neglected ways of poetry, calligraphy, benevolence, and righteousness, and carried on the legacy of good government and peace that had been interrupted. Even arhats with the three insights and six supernatural powers cannot escape it, and even sages of illusion and transformation cannot avoid this path; though it is the way of all conditioned things, it seemed to surpass reason. Immediately that night they moved him to Seikanji at the foot of the eastern hills, and he rose like evening smoke and like spring haze. Chōgen, the Dharma Seal, hurried down from the mountain to attend the funeral, but when he saw that the smoke had already become empty, he composed this poem.

lg.l: 常に見し君が御幸をけふ問へば、かへらぬ旅ときくぞ悲き。

div.p: [6.1.5] Another lady-in-waiting, hearing that the lord had gone into hiding, composed this poem in her grief.

lg.l: 雲の上に行末遠く見し月の、光きえぬときくぞかなしき。

div.p: [6.1.6] He was twenty-one years old. He kept the ten precepts within, did not violate the five constant virtues without, and caused propriety and righteousness to be correct. Because he was a wise king of the latter age, the world's regretting him was like losing the light of the sun and moon. In this way, the realm of humans where people's wishes are not fulfilled and the people's fortune is poor is indeed sorrowful.

[6.2.1] "Even if one were to say that the emperor of Engi and Tenryaku was excellent, how could he surpass this?" Thus people said. Generally, the raising of the name of a wise king and the performance of benevolent deeds are things that come about only after the sovereign has come of age and distinguished between the pure and the impure; but this lord, from the time he was a mere child, was endowed with a gentle nature. In the past, around the Jōan era, at the beginning of His Majesty's reign, when he was about ten years old, he loved autumn leaves so much that he had a small hill built in the northern court and had sumac and maple trees with beautifully colored leaves planted there, naming it the Mountain of Autumn Leaves; yet even viewing it all day long, he was still not satisfied. However, one night a storm blew violently, scattering all the autumn leaves, and the fallen leaves were in great disorder. The palace guard Tomo no Tsukuri, saying he would clean up in the morning, swept all of them away. The remaining branches and scattered leaves were gathered up, and because it was a morning when the wind was cold, they were used as firewood to warm sake at the guard station of the Nuido. The commissioner, thinking to go before the imperial procession, hurried there and looked, but there was no trace of it. "What is this?" When he asked, "It is..." He said. The courtier was greatly astonished and said, "How dreadful!" How deplorable that you have treated the autumn leaves, which His Majesty cherished so deeply, in this manner! You do not realize that you may soon be imprisoned or exiled, and I myself may incur His Majesty's wrath. As she lamented, the Emperor, unable to bear staying in the palace at night, went to that place, and when he viewed the autumn leaves, they were gone. "What is this?" When he asked, the Chamberlain had no way to report, so he reported the truth as it was. The Emperor smiled with great delight and said, "Who taught you the meaning of the poem, 'Warm the wine in the woods and burn the autumn leaves'?" How excellently he has served! Saying this, and having received imperial favor, there was no imperial censure at all.

[6.2.2] Moreover, in the Angen era, when there was an imperial excursion for a directional taboo, even without that, the rooster's crowing at dawn would have startled the emperor from sleep, so he was prone to waking and could not sleep at all. How much more so on a bitterly cold frosty night, recalling how Emperor Daigo in the Engi era, wondering how cold the people of the land must be, took off his own robe in the middle of the night, the emperor lamented that his own virtue had not reached such heights. As the night deepened, a voice crying out from afar was heard. 供奉の人々は聞附られざりけれども、主上聞召て、 「今叫ぶ者は何者ぞ。きと見て參れ。」と仰ければ、上臥したる殿上人、上日の者に 仰す。走り散て尋ぬれば、或辻に、怪の女童のながもちの蓋提て泣にてぞ有ける。「いかに。」と問へば、「主の女房の、院の御所に侍はせ給ふが、此程やうやうにし て、したてられつる御裝束が持て參る程に、只今男の二三人詣來て、奪取て罷りぬる ぞや。今は御裝束が有ばこそ、御所にもさぶらはせ給はめ。はかばかしう立宿せ給ふ べき親い御方も坐さず。此事思ひつゞくるに泣也。」とぞ申ける。さて彼女童を具し て參り、此由奏聞しければ、主上聞召て、「あな無慚。如何なる者のしわざにてか有 らん。堯の代の民は、堯の心のすなほなるを以て心とするが故に皆すなほ也。今の代 の民は、朕が心を以て心とするが故に、かたましき者朝に在て罪を犯す。此吾恥に非 ずや。」とぞ仰ける。「さて取られつらん衣は何色ぞ。」と御尋あれば、「然々の 色。 」と奏す。 建禮門院の未中宮にておはしましける時なり。 其御方へ、「さやうの色したる御衣や候。 」と仰ければ、先のより遙に美きが參たりけるを、件の女童にぞ賜せける。 "The night is still deep; perhaps I might again meet with such a sight." Saying this, he sent a man from the previous day to escort her to the lady's chamber, which was a gracious act. Therefore, from the lowliest men and women, all prayed for this lord's long life of a thousand autumns and ten thousand years.

[6.3.1] Among these, a particularly touching event was when a page girl, whom a lady-in-waiting serving the Empress had employed, unexpectedly came into the presence of the Emperor. It was not even plain white cloth, but the Emperor always wore it. Because his devotion was so sincere, the mistress did not treat her as a servant, but rather cherished her as if she were the mistress herself. There is a saying from that time in a song. "Do not spoil a girl when she is born. Do not rejoice when a boy is born. A boy is not even made a lord, while a girl becomes a queen. Saying this, she stood behind the empress. This person was treated as an imperial consort and empress, and was revered as the mother of the nation and a retired emperor. Thinking what a fortunate person she was, they called her Aoi no Mae, and privately whispered about her as Aoi no Nyogo. The emperor heard this, and after that he did not summon her. It was not that his affection had run out, but because he feared the criticism of the world. Therefore, he was constantly composing poems, and entered only the night chamber.

[6.3.2] The Chancellor Matsudono at that time must have felt it was a painful matter. Thinking to console him, he hurried to the palace and said, "Why should you let such a thing weigh on your mind? I think you should summon the court ladies quickly. There is no need to inquire about his lineage; Motofusa will immediately become your adopted son. When he respectfully reported this, the Emperor said, "Well, now." What you say is reasonable, but after abdicating the throne, there is no precedent for such a thing. If I were properly on the throne, such a thing would be a disgrace for future generations. Saying this, he did not heed the request. The Chancellor, unable to prevail, held back his tears and withdrew. After that, when the emperor was deeply moved by the green willow-colored robe, though it was an old story, he remembered it and recited it.

lg.l: しのぶれど色に出にけり我戀は、物や思ふと人のとふまで。

div.p: [6.3.3] When Reizei Shōshō Takafusa received this calligraphy practice and sent it to the aforementioned Aoi no Mae, she blushed, felt an unusual emotion, returned home, lay down for five or six days, and finally passed away. "For the sake of your one day's favor, I have ruined my hundred years' life." "Should one say such things?" In ancient times, when Emperor Taizong of Tang tried to take Zheng Renji's daughter into the inner palace, Wei Zheng said, "That girl is already betrothed to the Lu family." When he remonstrated, saying, "...", he was made to stop entering the palace, but his heart did not deviate in the least.

[6.4.1] The Emperor was sunk in longing thoughts of love. To console him, from the Empress's side a lady-in-waiting called Kogō no Tsubone was sent. This lady was the daughter of the Middle Counselor Shigeyori of Sakura-machi, the most beautiful woman in the palace, and an expert on the koto. She was the lady whom the Major Counselor Takafusa of Reizei had first fallen in love with when he was still a minor captain. At first the young captain composed poems and wrote letters, grieving in love, but she showed no sign of yielding; yet, perhaps because her heart was weakened by sorrow, in the end she yielded. But now, summoned by you, I am helpless in my sorrow; at the tears of our unsatisfying parting, my sleeves are soaked and cannot dry. The young captain, hoping that even from a distance he might catch a glimpse of Lady Kogō, was always coming to the palace. He would walk back and forth near the room where she was staying, by the bamboo blinds, and stand still, but Lady Kogō, thinking that since she had been summoned by His Majesty, no matter what the young captain might say, she could not exchange words with him or even look at a letter, did not even show him the slightest sign of affection. The young captain, thinking it might be so, composed a poem and tossed it inside the bamboo blinds where Lady Kogō was staying.

lg.l: 思かね心は空にみちのくの、ちかの鹽釜近きかひなし。

div.p: [6.4.2] Lady Kogō, though she thought she would like to reply at once, perhaps felt uneasy for the sake of the Emperor, and did not even take the letter in her hand to look at it. She immediately had a page girl take it and threw it out into the courtyard. The captain felt heartless and resentful, but fearing that someone might see, he felt uneasy, so he hastily took it, put it in his bosom, and left. Still, he turned back,

lg.l: 玉章を今は手にだにとらじとや、さこそ心に思ひすつとも。

div.p: [6.4.3] Now, since it would be difficult to meet again in this world, rather than living and worrying, he wished only to die.

[6.4.4] The Lay Monk Chancellor heard this and said, "The Empress is also my daughter, and the Reizei Lesser Captain is also my son-in-law." Having had two sons-in-law taken by Lady Kogō, he said, "No, no, as long as Kogō exists, the world is not to my liking. I will summon her and have her killed." Thus he spoke. Lady Kogō heard of this secretly and said, "As for my own fate, it matters not; but for His Majesty's sake, I am distressed." Saying this, one evening he left the palace, and disappeared without a trace. The emperor's grief was extreme. By day he would enter the night chamber and weep only in tears; by night he would go out to the south hall and gaze at the moonlight, finding consolation. The priest chancellor heard this and said, "The emperor is sunk in grief because of Kogo. If that is so... Saying this, he did not even allow the court ladies who attended the emperor to visit him, and he was suspicious of the nobles who came to court, so that, fearing the priest's authority, no one came and went. The imperial palace seemed increasingly ominous.

[6.4.5] Thus it became the tenth day of the eighth month and more. Though the sky was so cloudless, the Emperor, with his tears dimming his eyes, viewed even the moonlight as hazy. When it grew quite late at night, he called out, "Is anyone there?" He called out, but there was no one to answer him. Nakatsukasa no Shōyū Nakakuni, who was on night duty that very night, was standing at a distance, and when the Emperor called out, "Nakakuni," he replied, "Come closer." There is something I must tell you. Wondering what it could be, he came before the Emperor, who asked, "Do you know where Kogō has gone?" Nakakuni replied, "How could I possibly know?" I absolutely do not know. "Is it true? There is someone who says that Kogō is in a house with a half-folded door in the vicinity of Saga." "Even if you do not know the master's name, will you not go and search for her?" "If I do not know the master's name, how could I possibly go and search for her?" "Indeed." And so saying, he shed tears from his august face.

[6.4.6] As Nakakuni pondered, "Indeed, Lady Kogo was the one who played the koto." In this moonlight, remembering His Majesty, she would surely play the koto. When he played at the palace, Nakakuni was summoned to play the flute, so no matter what the sound of that koto was, he would surely recognize it. How many houses are there in Saga? Thinking that if he went around searching, how could he not find it, he said, "If that is so, even if I do not know your name, I will go and look for you." However, even if I should meet him and speak, if I do not receive a letter from you, he may think it is all empty talk. I will receive your letter and go to meet him. When he said this, the other replied, "Indeed," and wrote a letter and gave it to him. "Ride the horse from the imperial stables and go." Thus he commanded. Having been granted a horse from the Nakakuni stable, he raised his whip in the bright moonlight and wandered off, not knowing where he was going. The poem 'The young deer cries in this mountain village' must have been composed in the autumn around Saga; how moving it must have been! When he saw a house with a half-open door, he would stop and listen, thinking, 'Is she inside here?' but there was no sound of a koto being played. Thinking she might have gone to a temple, he started with the Shaka-do and looked around hall after hall, but not even a lady-in-waiting resembling Kogo no Tsubone appeared. To return empty-handed would be worse than not having come at all. Though I think I would like to wander off anywhere from here, there is no place that is not the king's land, and no lodging where I could hide myself. He agonized over what to do. Indeed, since the temple is near, perhaps he has come drawn by the moonlight; so he urged his horse toward that direction.

[6.4.7] Near Kameyama, in a place where there was a grove of pines, faintly a koto was heard. Is it the wind from the peaks, or the wind through the pines, or the sound of a koto played by someone seeking? Though uncertain, as he urged his horse onward, inside a half-closed gate, someone was playing the koto beautifully. When he listened to it, it was the sound of Lady Kogō's koto, with not the slightest mistake. When he asked what the piece was, it was the piece called Sōfuren, which is about longing for one's husband. That is why, thinking of His Majesty, there are many pieces, but how elegant it was that she played this piece! Thinking it was wonderful, he drew his sword from his waist, chirped a little, and when he knocked on the gate, she immediately stopped playing. In a loud voice, he said, "I have come as an imperial messenger from the palace, Nakakuni. Please open the gate." 」とて、たゝけども／＼、咎る人も無りけり。
やゝ有て、内より人の出る音のしければ嬉う思て待つ所に、鎖子をはづし、門を細目 に開け、いたいけしたる小女房、顏ばかり指出いて、「門違にてぞ候らん。是には、 内裏より御使など給はるべき所にても候はず。」と申せば、中々返事して門たてられ、 鎖子さゝれては惡かりなんと思ひて、押開てぞ入にける。妻戸の際の縁に居て、「い かにか樣の所には御渡候やらん。君は御故に思召沈ませ給ひて、御命も既に危うこそ 見えさせ御坐し候へ。只うはの空に申とや思召され候はん。御書を給て參て候。」と て、取出て奉る。 有つる女房取次で、小督殿に參せたり。 開て見給へば、誠に君の御書也けり。 軈て御返事書き引結び、女房の裝束一重添て出されたり。 Nakakuni, having thrown the lady's robe over his shoulder, said: "If I were an ordinary messenger, I would not presume to say anything beyond delivering your reply; but when you held musical gatherings at the palace in those days, I was summoned to serve as a flute player. How could you forget that service?" It would be truly regrettable if I were to return without receiving your direct reply." When he said this, Lady Kogo, thinking it was indeed so, replied herself. You must have heard of that as well. When I heard that the Chancellor was saying nothing but terrifying things, I was so shocked that I fled from the palace. Since I have been living in such a place as this, I have not played the koto or anything, but as it cannot be helped, from tomorrow I intend to go deep into Ohara. The lady of the house, lamenting that this is the last night, urged me, saying, 'The night is already late, and there will be no one listening,' so, indeed, even the memories of the past are moving, and as I played the koto I was accustomed to, I was heard playing it with ease. Saying this, unable to hold back her tears, Nakakuni too wet his sleeves. After a while, Nakakuni, holding back his tears, said, "From tomorrow, you intend to go deep into Ohara; that would be to change your appearance." It absolutely must not be. Then, what will you do about your grief? Please take this out. Saying this, he left behind the horse-keeper Kichijō and others he had brought along, had them guard the building, mounted the imperial horse from the Bureau of Horses, and returned to the palace; dawn was breaking faintly. Now the emperor must have retired. Who should announce it? Saying this, he had the imperial horse from the Bureau of Horses tethered, threw the court lady's robe over the sliding door of the stable, and went to the Southern Hall, where the emperor was still in his night chamber. It is hard to entrust the cold and warmth to the autumn hawk, whether it flies south or faces north. It rises in the east and flows to the west, and I entrust my distant gaze to the moon at dawn. As he was gazing out, Nakakuni came running in. He presented the reply of Lady Kogō. The Emperor was deeply moved and said, "You, bring her along this very evening." When he said this, although he feared what the Lay Monk Chancellor would hear, since it was an imperial command, he prepared a clean ox-carriage with a servant and an ox-driver, went toward Saga, and though he repeatedly said that he should not come, he contrived in various ways, helped her into the carriage, and when he brought her to the palace, he hid her in a secluded place, and as she was summoned night after night, a princess was born. This 'Princess' refers to the Empress Dowager of Bomon. How did the Lay Priest Chancellor come to hear of it? "That Kogo has disappeared is a baseless lie." Saying this, he seized Lady Kogo and forced her to become a nun. Though Lady Kogo's becoming a nun was her long-held wish, she was forced against her will to take the tonsure at the age of twenty-three, and she lived in seclusion near Saga, clad in dark ink-black robes. These were dreadful events. The Emperor, distressed by such events, finally passed away, it was heard.

[6.4.8] The Cloistered Emperor's grief only increased continuously. In the past Eiman era, his first son, Emperor Nijo, passed away. In the seventh month of the second year of Angen, his grandson, Emperor Rokujo, passed away. If we dwell in heaven, we shall become birds with wings joined; if we dwell on earth, we shall become trees with branches intertwined—so they had vowed, pointing to the stars of the Heavenly River. The late Kenshunmon'in, whose bond with the Emperor was not shallow, was attacked by the autumn mist and vanished like the morning dew. Though months and years piled up, the Emperor still felt as if the parting had been yesterday or today, and his tears had not yet dried when, in the fifth month of Jishō 4, the second prince, Takakura-no-miya, was killed. Even the Retired Emperor, who had placed his hopes for this world and the next in you, has passed away before you, so there is nothing but tears of helpless grief. "Of all sorrows, the most sorrowful is to be left behind by one's child after growing old; there is no sorrow greater than this." "Of all regrets, the most regrettable is to die before one's parents while still young; there is no regret greater than this." And now, at last, the traces of the brush with which that Lord Asaomi had written, following after his son Sumiaki, were recognized by the Emperor. And so, without neglecting the recitation of that Lotus Sutra, and without ceasing to accumulate the merits of the three mysteries, he continued his practice. When the realm entered imperial mourning, even the courtiers, jostling together, must have grown haggard in their flowery sleeves.

[6.5.1] The Lay Monk Chancellor, having behaved so cruelly and heartlessly, must have felt some fear after all, and so, to console the Retired Emperor, he presented to him his daughter by the lady of Itsukushima in Aki, a girl of eighteen, who was graceful and beautiful. High-ranking court ladies were selected in abundance and sent to attend her. Many court nobles and senior officials attended in procession, and it was just like the procession of an imperial consort. After the Retired Emperor had passed away, barely even two weeks had not yet passed when people privately whispered to one another that this was not proper.

[6.5.2] Meanwhile, at that time in Shinano Province, there was a Minamoto warrior called Kiso no Kanja Yoshinaka, as was heard. He was the son of the late Rokujō Hangan Tameyoshi's second son, Tachi no Oi no Kata Yoshikata. His father Yoshikata was killed by Kamakura's Akugenta Yoshihira on the sixteenth day of the eighth month of Kyūju 2. At that time, Yoshinaka was two years old; his mother, weeping, carried him and crossed into Shinano, went to Kiso Chūzō Kanetō's place, and said, "Please raise him somehow, and let him become a person." When she said this, Kanetō took him in and raised him carefully for over twenty years. As he gradually grew up, his strength was also outstanding in the world, and his spirit was also peerlessly brave. Even if you mention the rare strong bows and elite soldiers, mounted warriors, foot soldiers, all the ancient heroes like Tamura, Toshihito, Yogo Shogun, Muneyori, Yasumasa, the ancestor Yorimitsu, and Yoshiie Ason, how could they surpass this man? people said.

[6.5.3] At one time, he summoned his wet nurse Kaneto and said. Minamoto no Yoritomo, the Assistant Captain of the Right Division of Outer Palace Guards, has already raised a rebellion, subjugated the eight provinces of the East, and is now advancing along the Tokaido to overthrow the Heike. Yoshinaka has also subjugated the two routes of the Tosan and Hokuriku, and now, if he can defeat the Heike even one day earlier, it would be as if there were two generals in Japan. When he hinted at this, Nakasaburo Kaneto was greatly overjoyed and said, "It is for that very purpose that I have been raising you until now." Indeed, that you speak thus makes me feel that you are truly a descendant of Hachiman. Saying this, he immediately began plotting a rebellion.

[6.5.4] Accompanied by Kanetō, he would always go up to the capital and observe the behavior and circumstances of the Heike people. When he came of age at thirteen, he went to Hachiman and before the great bodhisattva Hachiman said, "My great-great-grandfather Yoshiie Ason became the son of this deity and was called Hachiman Tarō." And we should pursue his tracks. Saying this, before the sacred image of Hachiman Daibosatsu, he took up his topknot and was named Kiso Jiro Yoshinaka. Kaneto, thinking he should first send a letter, summoned Nei no Koyata Shigeno Yukichika in Shinano Province, and there was no refusal. Beginning with this, the warriors of the entire province of Shinano submitted, so that not even the grasses and trees failed to bend. In the province of Kōzuke, because the late Tachihaki no Senjō Yoshikata had been on good terms with them, the warriors of Tagō District all attached themselves to him. Seizing the opportunity that the Heike were coming to an end, they intended to fulfill the long-cherished desire of the Genji.

[6.6.1] The place called Kiso, even within Shinano, is at the southern edge, and since it borders Mino, it is not at all far from the capital. The Heike people heard of this and said, "Even if the eastern provinces are in rebellion, now the northern provinces too—what is this?" Thus they clamored. The Lay Monk Chancellor said, "That man is not unattractive." If you think about it, among the warriors of Shinano Province, even if they are said to be followers, in Echigo Province there are the descendants of Yogo Shogun, Jotaro Sukenaga and Shiro Sukemochi; these are brothers and both have many troops. If you send down an order, they will easily defeat them and come to serve. When he said that, "What will happen?" There were many who whispered privately, "What will happen?"

[6.6.2] On the first day of the second month, a resident of Echigo Province, Jōtarō Sukenaga, was appointed Governor of Echigo. This was heard to be a plot to hunt down and destroy Kiso. On the seventh day of the same month, at the houses of the ministers and below, the Sonshō Dhāraṇī and Fudō Myōō were copied and offered. This was also a precaution against military disturbances.

[6.6.3] On the ninth day of the same month, Musashi no Gon no Kami Nyūdō Giki, who was living in Ishikawa District of Kawachi Province, and his son Ishikawa Hangan Dai Yoshikane turned against the Heike, communicated with Hyōe no Suke Yoritomo, and it was heard that they were about to flee to the eastern provinces, so the Nyūdō Prime Minister immediately sent a punitive force. As the commander of the attacking force, Minamoto no Daibu Hangan Suekata and Settsu Hangan Morizumi set out with a total force of over three thousand horsemen. Inside the castle, Musashi no Gon no Kami Nyudo Yoshimoto and his son Hangan-dai Yoshikane led the way, and their force did not exceed about a hundred horsemen. They raised a war cry, exchanged arrows, and fought for hours, entering and retreating repeatedly. The warriors inside the castle fought desperately, and many were killed in battle. Musashi no Gon no Kami Nyudo Yoshimoto was killed in battle. His son, Ishikawa Hōgan-dai Yoshikane, was gravely wounded and taken alive. On the eleventh of the same month, the monk Yoshimoto entered the capital and was paraded along the main avenue. The parading of a rebel's head during the imperial mourning was said to have a precedent in the case of the head of Minamoto no Yoshichika, the former governor of Tsushima, which was paraded at the time of Emperor Horikawa's death.

[6.6.4] On the twelfth of the same month, an express messenger arrived from the western provinces. The report of Usa Daigūji Kōtsū was: "The warriors of Kyushu, beginning with Ogata Saburō, and extending to the Usuki, Hegi, and Matsuura clans, have all turned against the Heike and joined the Genji." Hearing this, they said, "Even with the eastern and northern provinces in revolt, what is this?" So saying, they clapped their hands and sneered at each other.

[6.6.5] On the sixteenth of the same month, a courier arrived from Iyo Province. Since last winter, beginning with Kōno Shirō Michikiyo, all the warriors of Shikoku had turned against the Heike and sided with the Genji. Because the priest Nukada no Nyūdō Saijaku, a resident of Bingo Province, was deeply loyal to the Heike, he crossed over to Iyo Province and killed Kōno Shirō Michikiyo at Takanao Castle on the border between Dōzen and Dōgo. When his father was killed, his son Kōno Shirō Michinobu, because Nuta Jirō, a resident of Aki Province, was his maternal uncle, went over to him but did not meet him. He is a man who killed his father, Michinobu, and is not at peace. Somehow, he was watching for an opportunity to kill Saijaku. After Nukui no Nyūdō Saijaku killed Kōno Shirō Michikiyo, he subdued the outrages in Shikoku, and on the fifteenth day of the first month of this year, he crossed over to Tomo in Bingo, gathered together courtesans and prostitutes, and was enjoying himself drinking sake, when, without knowing what was before or behind, he fell asleep drunk; then Kōno Shirō, with more than a hundred determined men, conspired together and suddenly attacked. At Saijaku's place too there were more than three hundred men, but because it was a sudden event, they were unprepared and panicked; those who stood against them were shot down and cut down, and first Saijaku was captured alive, taken across to Iyo Province, brought to Takanao Castle where his father had been killed, and it was heard that his neck was cut with a saw. It was also heard that he was crucified.

[6.7.1] After that, the men of Shikoku all followed Kono Shiro. Kumano Betto Tanzo, who had been a recipient of great favors from the Heike, also turned against them and it was heard that he sided with the Genji. Generally, the eastern and northern provinces all turned against them. The southern seas and western seas are like this. The uprisings of the barbarians startle the ears, and omens of rebellion are frequently reported. The barbarians of the four directions have suddenly risen up. Saying that the world is about to be lost, even those who are not of the Heike clan, people with feeling, all grieved and lamented.

[6.7.2] On the same twenty-third day, there was a council of court nobles. When the former Major Captain of the Right, Lord Munemori, said, "Although it is said that a punitive force has been sent to the East, there has been no deed worthy of note." This time, when he said that he would accept the role of great general and go forth, the assembled nobles changed color and said, "That would be ominous." They said. The court nobles and senior officials, as well as those who would serve in military posts and take up bows and arrows, were ordered that Lord Munemori, as great general, should pursue and subdue the rebels of the eastern and northern provinces.

[6.7.3] On the twenty-seventh of the same month, it was heard that the former Major Captain of the Right, Lord Munemori, had already set out for the East to subdue the Genji, but because the Lay Monk Chancellor was said to be unwell, he remained behind. From the 28th day of the month, he was said to have fallen gravely ill, and throughout the capital and Rokuhara people whispered, "Now it has happened." they whispered. From the day the Novice Chancellor fell ill, he could not even let water pass his throat, and the heat inside his body was like burning fire. The place where he lay: anyone who came within four or five ken could not bear the heat. The only thing he said was, "Hot, hot." It did not seem at all like a trivial matter. From Mount Hiei, they drew water from the Senju Well, filled a stone boat with it, and when they poured it down and cooled it, the water gushed up abundantly, and before long it became hot water. When they splashed water from the bamboo pipe, thinking to revive him, the water scattered like stones or iron heated red-hot, and would not come near. The water that hit him turned into flames and burned, so black smoke filled the hall, and the flames swirled upward. This was the place where long ago the monk Hōzō, when he went at the invitation of King Enma to seek the place of his mother's rebirth, was pitied by King Enma, who sent him with a hell-warden to the Hell of Scorching Heat. When it was thrust inside the iron gate, flames rose up into the sky like shooting stars, and it must have reached many hundreds of yojanas—now I realize it.

[6.7.4] The dream that the Nyudo Prime Minister's wife, the Lady of Nii, saw was truly terrifying. For example, it was like sending a cart blazing with fierce fire inside the gate. Those standing in front and behind included some with horse-like faces and some with ox-like faces. In front of the cart stood an iron placard on which only the character for 'nothing' was visible. In a dream, the Lady of Second Rank asked, "What is that over there?" When she asked, "I have come from the palace of King Enma to welcome the Lay Monk Chancellor of the Taira." " he said. "Well then, what kind of placard is that placard?" " he asked, and [the other] said, "Because of the sin of the burning down of the sixteen-jō gilt-bronze Vairocana Buddha of Jambudvīpa, it has been decided in the court of King Yama that you are to fall to the bottom of the Avīci hell; but the character 'mu' has been written, and the character 'ken' has not yet been written." Thus he said. The Second Rank Nun was startled, broke out in a sweat, and when she told this to people, everyone who heard it got goosebumps. They threw gold, silver, and the seven treasures into the sacred Buddhist temples and Shinto shrines, and brought out and offered up even horse saddles, armor, helmets, bows and arrows, and swords, and prayed, but there was no sign of any effect. The young lords and ladies gathered at the pillow of the deceased, and lamented, saying, "What shall we do?" but it did not seem that their wishes could be fulfilled.

[6.7.5] On the second day of the intercalary second month, the Lady of the Second Rank, though she could hardly bear it, drew near to the pillow and said through her tears, "As I look upon your condition, day by day you seem to grow weaker and less hopeful." If there is anything you wish to leave behind in this world, please give your instructions now, while you are still able to think clearly. Thus he spoke. The Lay Monk Prime Minister, though he had seemed so formidable in recent days, now truly appeared to be in pain, and he said in a faint voice: "Since the Hogen and Heiji eras, I have subdued many enemies of the court, and my rewards have exceeded my station. I have been graciously raised to the rank of Grand Minister of State, and my glory extends to my descendants. There is nothing left that I desire in this life. However, the one thing I regret is that I have not seen the head of the exile from Izu Province, the former Assistant Captain of the Right Military Guards, Yoritomo. After I have died, you must not build a pagoda or perform memorial services for me. Immediately send a punitive force, cut off Yoritomo's head, and hang it before my grave. That is what will be a memorial service for me. That he said this was indeed sinful.

[6.7.6] On the fourth day of the same month, tormented by illness, as a last resort, he had water poured on a board and lay rolling on it, but he could not feel any relief. He fell to the ground in agony, and at last died a sudden death. The sound of the horses and carriages passing each other made the heavens resound and the earth shake. Even if the sovereign of the whole realm, the lord of ten thousand chariots, were to do something, it would not surpass this, it seemed. This year he became sixty-four. Though it is not an age to be called death from old age, when his allotted fate suddenly came to an end, the efficacy of the great and secret teachings was lost, the power of the gods and the Three Treasures vanished, and the heavenly beings no longer protected him. How much more so for ordinary minds! The tens of thousands of soldiers who, resolved to give their lives in place of their lord, stood in ranks above and below the hall, could not for even a moment fight back against the invisible, powerless demon of impermanence. And to the mountain of death from which none return, the River of Three Crossings, the sky of the journey through the intermediate state of the Yellow Springs, to that one place alone did he go. The sins you have committed day after day have surely become hell's wardens and come to meet you. These were all pitiful events. Since it could not be helped, on the same seventh day, they cremated him at Atago, and the priest Enjitsu Hogen hung the bones around his neck, went down to Settsu Province, and placed them on Kyo Island. Although he was a man who had raised his name and wielded power throughout the land of Japan, his body became a momentary smoke and rose into the capital's sky, and his corpse, resting for a while, played with the sands of the shore, and became empty earth.

[6.8.1] That very night of the funeral, there were many strange occurrences. The Nishi-Hachijo-dono, which had been built with polished jewels and inlaid gold and silver, suddenly burned down that night. The burning of people's houses is a common occurrence, but these events were dreadful. Whose deed could it have been? It was said to be arson. Again that night, toward the south of Rokuhara, there was a voice as of twenty or thirty people, if they were human, singing "How delightful! The water sound is the waterfall's water," and they danced and leaped, and there was a sound of loud laughter. In the past first month, the Retired Emperor passed away, and the realm entered a period of mourning. Scarcely a month or two had passed when the Lay Monk Chancellor passed away. Even down to the lowly men and women of the strange affair, how could they not grieve? This was rumored to be the work of tengu in any case, and among the Heike samurai, when more than a hundred young men, laughing at the sound, went to investigate, they found that at the imperial palace Hōjūji-dono, the Retired Emperor had not visited for the past two or three years, and there was a man named Motomune, the former governor of Bizen, who was the caretaker of the palace. The men who were acquaintances of that Motomune, twenty or thirty of them, came gathering under cover of night, and drank sake. At first, saying 'Don't make noise at such a time,' they drank, but gradually they became drunk and danced about like this. They rushed in, seized all the drunken men, about thirty of them, without letting one escape, and brought them to Rokuhara, and made them sit in the courtyard where the former Udaishō Munemori was. Having carefully inquired into the details of the matter, they said that even if he was truly drunk to that extent, he should not be cut down, and so they all pardoned him. After a person has passed away, it is customary for mysterious beings to ring the bell morning and evening and to recite the regular repentance, but after this Zen monk died, there was no longer any activity of offering to the Buddha and giving alms to monks. Morning and evening, there was nothing else but strategies for battle.

[6.8.2] Although the manner of his final illness was indeed dreadful, there were many things that did not seem like those of an ordinary person. Even when he went to worship at Hiyoshi Shrine, many court nobles of both the reigning and retired emperor's families accompanied him, and people said that even the Kasuga pilgrimage of the Fujiwara regent or the Uji visit could not surpass this. And more than anything, the fact that the harbor island of Fukuhara was built and, down to the present age, ships going back and forth between the capital and the provinces have no trouble is truly auspicious. That island was first built in the early part of the second month of the first year of Ōhō, but in the eighth month of the same year a great wind suddenly blew and great waves rose, and it was entirely washed away. In the latter part of the third month of the third year of the same era, Awa no Minbu Shigeyoshi was put in charge of the construction, but although there was a council of nobles about whether a human pillar should be erected, it was deemed a sin, and the entire Buddhist canon was written on the surface of the stones, and so it was built; therefore it was named the Sutra Island.

[6.9.1] An old person said, "Although I think Lord Kiyomori is a villain, in truth he is the reincarnation of the high priest Jikei." The reason is that there is a mountain temple called Kiyosumi-dera in Settsu Province. The resident monk of that temple, called Jishinbō Songe, was originally a scholar-monk of Mount Hiei and for many years a devotee of the Lotus Sutra. However, he aroused the aspiration for enlightenment, left the mountain, and spent months and years at this temple, so everyone came to have faith in him. On the night of the twenty-second day of the twelfth month of the previous Jōan 2 [1172], as he was leaning on an armrest and reciting the Lotus Sutra, around the hour of the ox, neither in a dream nor in reality, a man of about fifty years old, wearing a pure robe and a lacquered cap, with straw sandals and leggings, came carrying a letter. "Where are you from?" asked Songui. When he asked, [the messenger] said, "I am a messenger from the palace of King Enma." "I have an imperial decree." Saying this, he handed a letter to Songui. When Songui opened it and looked,A summons: The monk Jishinbō Sonkai of Kiyosumi Temple in Settsu Province, Japan, in Jambudvīpa, is to come on the 26th and recite the Lotus Sutra of 100,000 copies with 100,000 sutra-holders at the Great Hall of the Palace of King Yama.Therefore, you should attend.By the decree of King Yama, the summons is as stated.
[6.9.2] Jōan 2, 12th month, 22nd day, at the court of King Yama.

[6.9.3] Thus it was written. Since it was not a matter that Sonne could refuse, he wrote a letter of acceptance without hesitation, thinking he would present it, and so he did. Thinking only of death, he told this matter to the temple head Kōyōbō. Everyone thought it was wondrous. Sonne chanted the name of Amida with his mouth, and in his heart he meditated on the compassionate vow of salvation. Gradually, as the night deepened on the twenty-fifth day, he went before the eternal Buddha, and as usual, leaning on an armrest, he chanted the Buddha's name and recited sutras. Because it was late at night and he was fast asleep, he returned to his lodging and lay down. Around the hour of the Ox (2 a.m.), two demons dressed in white robes came again as before, and urged him, saying, "Come quickly, quickly!" When he tried to decline the command of King Enma, he felt great fear. When he tried to go to worship, he had no robe or bowl at all. When he thought this, a Buddhist robe naturally wrapped itself around his body and hung on his shoulders, and a golden bowl descended from heaven. Two young attendants, two accompanying monks, ten lower-ranking monks, and a great cart of the seven treasures appeared in front of the temple building. Sonkai was overjoyed and immediately got into the carriage. The attendant monks flew through the sky toward the northwest, and before long arrived at the palace of King Enma.

[6.9.4] When he looked at the appearance of the royal palace, the outer walls were vast and boundless, and the interior was spacious and empty. Inside it there was a great hall made of the seven treasures. It was tall, wide, and golden, not a place that ordinary people could praise. After the ceremony of that day ended, when all the invited monks were returning, Sonkai stood at the southern middle gate and looked far off at the Great Hall of State; the dark officials and dark multitudes all feared before King Enma's presence. Sonkai thought it was a rare and wonderful pilgrimage. Thinking to ask about the afterlife next, he went to the Great Hall of State. Meanwhile, two young boys pointed the way, two attendant monks carried boxes, and ten lower-ranking monks formed a line; as they gradually approached, King Enma and all the dark officials and multitudes came down to greet them. Tamonten and Jikokuten appeared as the two young boys, and Yakuo Bosatsu and Yuse Bosatsu transformed into the two attendant monks. The ten rakshasa women appeared as ten low-ranking monks and attended upon him. King Yama asked, "The other monks have all returned home. Why have you come here?" "I have come to ask about the place of my next life." "However, whether one is reborn in the Pure Land or not depends on whether one has faith or not," and so on. Then King Yama again commanded the dark officials, saying, "The box of writings of this monk's good deeds is in the treasure house of the south." Take it out and show him the record of his life's deeds and the inscription of the monument of benefiting others. The dark official received the order, went to the treasure house of the south, took out one box of writings, and returned. Immediately he opened the lid and read all of it aloud. Sonei grieved, lamented, and wept, saying, "I only pray that you will have compassion on me, teach me the method of escaping birth and death, and show me the direct path to attaining great enlightenment." At that time, King Yama, out of compassion, taught and recited various verses. The clerk of the underworld dipped his brush and wrote these down one by one. Wife, children, royal rank, wealth, and retainers—when death comes, not one of them follows. Always accompanied by the demon of karma, I am bound and suffer torment, crying out without end.

[6.9.5] King Yama finished reciting this verse, and immediately entrusted that document to Sonkei. Sonkei was overjoyed and said, "The person called the Great Minister of Japan selected Wada-no-misaki in Settsu Province, built houses over an area of more than ten cho on all four sides, invited many sutra-holders as in today's assembly of one hundred thousand monks, seated them one by one in each hall, and had them perform sermons and sutra recitations with great devotion." When he said this, King Yama rejoiced and admired him, saying, "That lay priest is not an ordinary person; he is the incarnation of the holy priest Jie." He has been reborn in Japan to protect the Buddhist teachings of the Tendai sect. Therefore, there is a text that says to worship that person three times every day. You should present this text to that person. And so saying,Reverence to the compassionate and wise Great Archbishop, protector of the Tendai Buddhist Law, who manifested first as a general; may evil-karma beings all share in the benefit.

[6.9.6] When Sonkei received this and was leaving through the middle gate on the south side of the Daigokuden, ten officials stood outside the gate, helped him into a carriage, and followed before and behind. Again, he flew through the sky and returned. Feeling as if in a dream, he awoke with a start. With this, Sonkei went to Nishi-Hachijo and visited the Lay Monk Chancellor; the Chancellor was exceedingly pleased, entertained him in various ways, gave him various gifts, and as a reward he was made a Risshi, so it is said. Thus people came to know that Lord Kiyomori was the reincarnation of the holy priest Jikei.

[6.10.1] Again, someone said: Lord Kiyomori was not Tadamori's son, but in truth the son of Emperor Shirakawa. The reason was that, in the Eikyū era, there was a favored lady known as Gion no Nyōgo. The residence of that lady was at the foot of the eastern mountains, near Gion. Emperor Shirakawa often made imperial visits there. Once, when the Emperor made a secret excursion accompanied by one or two courtiers and a few of the Northern Guards, it was the twentieth day of the Fifth Month and still early evening, so it was a darkness in which one could not see one's hand before one's face; moreover, the long rains of the Fifth Month had made it overcast, and it was truly gloomy, when near the lodging of that lady-in-waiting there was a chapel. Beside the chapel, a luminous object appeared. Its head glittered as if silver needles had been polished and set upright, and what appeared to be its left and right hands were raised; in one hand it held something like a mallet, and in the other it held a shining object. Both lord and vassals cried, "How dreadful! This must truly be a demon." The thing it holds in its hand must be the famous Uchide no Kozuchi (the mallet of fortune). What shall we do? While they were making a commotion saying this, Tadamori, who at that time was still a low-ranking retainer of the North Guard, was summoned, and the emperor said, "You are the one here, aren't you? Shoot that fellow dead, or cut him down, and stop this." When the emperor said this, Tadamori respectfully obeyed and went forward. He thought to himself, "This fellow does not look like such a fierce person." It must be a fox or a badger or something. If I shoot and kill him, or cut him down, it would be utterly regrettable. Thinking to capture him alive, he approached on foot. Thinking thus, he flashed; thinking thus, he flashed, two or three times, and Tadamori ran up and grappled him tightly. Being grappled, he said, "What is this?" He cried out in confusion. It was not a monster; it was actually a human being. At that time, the people above and below lit torches in their hands and looked at him: he was a monk of about sixty years old. For example, there was a temple servant of the hall; intending to offer a light, he put oil into a vessel called a hand-jar, and in one hand he carried a fire in an earthenware dish. The rain was falling heavily; thinking he would get wet, he tied wheat straw over his head like a hat and carried it; the wheat straw shone in the fire of the earthenware dish, and it looked like silver needles. The circumstances were revealed one by one. If he had shot him dead or cut him down, how heartless that would have been! Tadamori's conduct was indeed deeply thoughtful. A man who takes up bow and arrow is excellent indeed! So saying, he gave to Tadamori, as a reward, the Gion consort, who was said to be his most beloved.

[6.10.2] Now, when that lady became pregnant with the Retired Emperor's child, he said, "If the child born is a girl, I will make her my own child. If it is a boy, make him a son of Tadamori and raise him to be a man who takes up the bow and arrow. When he said this, she immediately gave birth to a boy. He sought to report this matter to the throne, but there was no suitable opportunity. Then one time, when the retired Emperor Shirakawa made an imperial visit to Kumano, at a place called Itosaka in Kii Province, the palanquin bearers set down the palanquin and he took a brief rest. There were many wild yams in the thicket. Tadamori gathered them into his sleeve and came before the emperor.

lg.l: いもが子は這ふ程にこそ成にけれ。

div.p: [6.10.3] When he said this, the retired emperor immediately understood.

lg.l: たゞもりとりてやしなひにせよ。

div.p: [6.10.4] Thus he had it attached. From that time on, he treated him as his own son. Because this young lord cried excessively at night, the Retired Emperor heard of it and composed a poem, which he graciously sent.

lg.l: 夜啼すとたゞもりたてよ末の代は、清く盛る事もこそあれ。

div.p: [6.10.5] Thus he came to be called Kiyomori. At the age of twelve, he became Hyōe no Suke. At the age of eighteen, he held the Fourth Rank and was called the Assistant Captain of the Palace Guards of the Fourth Rank; people who did not know the details said, "It is precisely a person of noble lineage who is like this." When they said this, Emperor Toba also came to know of it and said, "Kiyomori's noble lineage is not inferior to others." Thus he spoke.

[6.10.6] Long ago, when Emperor Tenchi gave a pregnant court lady to Ōshikōchi, he said, "If the child this court lady bears is a girl, I will make her my child; if it is a boy, make him your child." When he said this, she immediately gave birth to a boy. The founder of Tōnomine is Jōe Kashō. Since there was such a precedent even in ancient times, in the latter age too, the Grand Minister Taira, truly being a son of Emperor Shirakawa, must have conceived such an extraordinary undertaking as moving the capital.

[6.11.1] On the twentieth day of the same intercalary second month, the Major Counselor from Fifth Avenue, Lord Kunitsuna, passed away. He was a person who had a deep bond and not shallow intentions with the Grand Minister Taira. Perhaps because of the depth of their bond, he fell ill on the same day and passed away in the same month. This Dainagon, as he is called, is the eighth-generation descendant of the Chunagon Kanesuke, and the son of the former Umaryo no suke Morikuni. He did not even become a Kurando, but served as a Zoshiki of the Shinshi. During the reign of Emperor Konoe, around the Ninpei era, a fire suddenly broke out in the Imperial Palace. The Emperor went out to the South Hall, but not a single member of the Konoefu came, and as he stood there in astonishment, this Kunitsuna came carrying a palanquin on his shoulders, saying, "At such a time, you should ride in such a palanquin." When he said this, the Emperor rode in it and went out. "Who is it?" When he asked, "Who are you?", he announced his name: "Fujiwara no Kunitsuna, a miscellaneous servant of the shinshi." "Such a splendid fellow! I should take him into my service." And when he was taken into the service of the Chancellor of that time, the Hosshoji-dono, he was given a fief and employed, and during the reign of that same emperor, when there was an imperial visit to Hachiman, the nincho got drunk, fell into the water, soaked his costume, and the sacred music was delayed; then this Kunitsuna said, "Though I am not worthy, let me wear the nincho's costume." And when he took out a set, he put it on and performed the sacred music in tune. Although a little time had passed, the voice of the song rose clear, and the dance sleeves matched the rhythm and were delightful. When something deeply moves one, both gods and humans share the same feeling. Now, for the first time, I truly understand even the events of the age of the gods, when the heavenly rock door was pushed open.

[6.11.2] Now, in the ancestry of this Kunitsuna, there was a person called Yamakage no Chunagon. As his son, there was a monk called Nyomu Sozu, whose wisdom and talent were more than enough, a monk of virtuous conduct and observance of precepts. In the Shōtai era, when Emperor Kōkō made an imperial visit to the Ōi River, the son of the Inner Minister of Kanjūji, Lord Takafuji, the General of Izumi, Sadakuni, had his eboshi blown into the river by the wind from Mount Ogura, and holding his topknot with his sleeve, he stood there helplessly, when this Nyomu Sozu took out an eboshi from his robe box, it is said. When that monk's father, the Middle Counselor Yamakage, was appointed Dazai no Daini and went down to Kyushu, the boy was two years old. His stepmother, out of malice, pretended to embrace him and tried to throw him into the sea to kill him. But his real mother, who had died, had once, while alive, taken off the small-sleeved robe she was wearing and exchanged it for a turtle that a cormorant fisherman of Katsura was about to kill to use as food for his cormorants, and released the turtle. To repay that kindness, the turtle rose to the surface of the water with the young lord on its shell and saved him. That is a matter of ancient times, so how could it have been? In this latter age, the fame of Lord Kunitsuna is a rare thing indeed. In the reign of the Hosshoji Regent, he became a Middle Counselor. After the Hosshoji Regent passed away, the Lay Monk Chancellor, having some intention, approached this man. Because he was a man of great wealth, he always sent one kind of gift every day to the Lay Monk Chancellor. Saying that no one in this world could surpass this man as a benefactor, he adopted one son, had him take the name Kiyokuni, and also the Lay Monk Chancellor's fourth son, the Middle Captain Shigehira, became that Dainagon's son-in-law.

[6.11.3] When the Gosechi festival of the fourth year of Jishō was held at Fukuhara, courtiers made an uninvited visit to the Empress's quarters, and a certain nobleman recited the poem 'Bamboo is mottled on the shores of Xiang.' When he recited the poem, this Grand Minister overheard it and said, 'How shameful! I have heard that this is taboo.' Even if I hear such a thing, I will not listen. Saying this, he slipped away and fled. For example, the meaning of this poem is that in ancient times, Emperor Yao had two princesses. The elder sister was called Ehuang, and the younger sister was called Nüying. Both were consorts of Emperor Shun. After Emperor Shun passed away, when they escorted him to the fields of Cangwu and cremated him, the two consorts, grieving over his remains, followed as far as a place called Xiangpu, weeping and lamenting, and their tears fell on the bamboo by the shore and stained it with spots. After that, he often went to that place and played the koto to console himself. Now, when I look at that place, the bamboo on the bank stands mottled. Clouds trail over the place where he played the koto, and the Chancellor Tachibana composed a poem expressing his deep emotion. This Dainagon was not particularly gifted in literary talent or poetry, but being such a wise person, he was even reproved for things of that sort. This person had never even dreamed of becoming Dainagon, but his mother made a pilgrimage to Kamo Grand Shrine and prayed, "If only my son Kunitsuna could serve even for a day, let him become Kurodo no To." And so, for a hundred days he prayed with all his heart and soul, and one night in a dream he saw a carriage of betel palm wood come and stand at the entrance of his house. When he told this to someone, the person said, "That means you will become the wife of a high-ranking noble." When the person said this, the man replied, "I am already advanced in years. I do not think I could behave in such a way now. But his son, Kunitsuna, the Chamberlain, was a fine young man. It would be splendid if he were promoted to Senior Second Rank and became a Great Counselor.

[6.11.4] On the twenty-second of the same month, the Cloistered Emperor made an imperial visit to the Hōjōji-dono, the palace of the retired emperor. That palace had been built on the fifteenth day of the fourth month of the Ōhō 3rd year, and new Hiei and new Kumano shrines had been invited and enshrined nearby; even the landscape and trees were as the Cloistered Emperor wished, but for the past two or three years, because of the Heike's evil deeds, imperial visits had not taken place. When the former General of the Right, Lord Munemori, reported that the palace should be repaired and an imperial visit arranged, there was no alternative, and so, saying 'just so, just so,' the imperial visit took place. When he viewed the former residence of the late Kenshunmon'in, the pines on the shore and the willows by the water's edge seemed to have aged with the years, and as they had grown tall, how could tears not well up when facing the lotus of the Taieki Pond and the willows of the Miei Palace? Now he realized the traces of the past at the Southern Palace and the Western Palace.

[6.11.5] On the first day of the third month, the monastic officials of Nanto were restored to their former offices, and it was decreed that they should administer their branch temples and estates as before. On the third day of the same month, the construction of the Great Buddha Hall was begun. The official in charge of the commencement ceremony was said to be the Chamberlain and Minor Controller of the Left, Yukitaka. This Yukitaka, in a previous year, had gone to Hachiman and kept a night-long vigil, and in a dream, from within the sacred hall, a heavenly child with hair tied in loops came forth and said, "This is a messenger of the Great Bodhisattva. When you are in charge of the Great Buddha Hall, you should carry this. He dreamed that he was given a shaku with the words, "...", and when he woke up and looked, it was actually there. "How strange! What could be happening now? I am to be appointed as the official in charge of the Great Buddha Hall." Saying this, he put it in his bosom and returned to his lodging, and stored it away deeply. But because of the evil deeds of the Heike, when the southern capital was burned, this Yukitaka was chosen among the Ben and went as the official in charge of the beginning of the affair—how auspicious was the karma of his former life!

[6.11.6] On the tenth day of the third month of the same year, the deputy governor of Mino Province sent a fast messenger to the capital, saying that the Genji of the eastern provinces had already advanced as far as Owari Province, blocking the roads and not letting people pass. When this was reported, an attacking force was immediately dispatched. As commander-in-chief, the Left Captain of the Palace Guards Tomomori, the Middle Captain Kiyotsune, and the Lesser Captain Arimori of Komatsu set out with a total force of over thirty thousand horsemen. After the Lay Monk Chancellor passed away, although barely fifty days had not even passed, even though it was an age of such disorder, these were shocking events. On the Genji side, Jūrō Kurōdo Yukiie, the younger brother of Hyōe no Suke, Lord Gien, and altogether their force of over six thousand horsemen, with the Owari River between them, took up positions on both the Genji and Heike sides.

[6.11.7] Around midnight of the same sixteenth day, the Genji forces, over six thousand horsemen, crossed the river and charged shouting into the midst of the Heike's thirty thousand horsemen. When dawn broke, from the hour of the tiger on the seventeenth day they exchanged arrows, and fought until daylight, but on the Heike side there was not the slightest disturbance. "The enemy has crossed the river, so their horses and armor are all wet. Use that as a marker and strike!" Saying this, they surrounded them in great numbers, crying, "Leave none alive! Let none escape!" Saying this, they attacked, and the Genji forces were struck down, leaving only a few; the great general Yukiie barely escaped with his life and retreated eastward across the river. The courtier Kōmyō Gien advanced too deeply and was killed. The Heike immediately crossed the river and pursued the Genji, shooting them down with arrows. The Genji turned and fought back here and there, but the enemy was numerous while their own side was few. He did not see it as something that could be fulfilled. Do not put the swamp behind you. Thus it is said, but the Genji's strategy this time is foolish. Thus people said.

[6.11.8] Meanwhile, the great general Jūrō Kurō Hangan Yukitsuna crossed over into Mikawa Province, pulled up the bridge over the Yahagi River, and set up a shield fence, waiting in readiness. When the Heike immediately pressed the attack, unable to withstand it, they lost that place as well. If the Heike had immediately continued the attack, the forces of Mikawa and Totomi would have followed them, but the great general Tomomori, the Sama no kami, returned from Mikawa Province because of illness. This time too, although they broke through a single battle line, since they did not attack the remnants, it was as if they had accomplished nothing. The Heike: the year before last, Lord Komatsu passed away. This year, the Lay Monk Chancellor also passed away. Since it was clear that this was the end of his fate, except for those who had long enjoyed his favor, there was no one who followed him. In the eastern provinces, both grasses and trees all bowed to the Genji.

[6.12.1] In the meantime, Jōtarō Sukenaga, a resident of Echigo Province, was appointed Governor of Echigo. Grateful for the imperial favor, for the purpose of hunting down Kiso, he set out on the fifteenth day of the sixth month with a force of over thirty thousand horsemen, and at dawn on the sixteenth, just as he was about to depart, around midnight a great wind suddenly blew, heavy rain fell, and thunder roared violently; after the sky cleared, a great hoarse voice from the clouds said, "Here is one who sides with the Heike, who have burned down the sixteen-foot gilt-bronze statue of Vairocana Buddha of Jambudvipa. Seize him!" So it cried out three times and passed by. Starting with Jōtarō, all who heard this felt their hair stand on end. The retainers said, "Since such a terrifying divine warning has appeared, please simply bend the law and stay." Though he said this, they replied, "There is no way for a warrior to rely on that," and at the hour of the rabbit on the sixteenth, as it grew light, they left the castle and had gone only a little over ten chō. A mass of black clouds rose up and seemed to cover Sukenaga, and suddenly his body stiffened, his mind failed, and he fell from his horse. They carried him in a palanquin back to his residence, and after he lay down for about three hours, he finally died. When a courier was sent to the capital to report this, the Heike people were greatly alarmed.

[6.12.2] On the fourteenth day of the seventh month of the same year, there was a change of era name, and it was called Yōwa. On that day, Sadayoshi, the governor of Chikugo, was granted the two provinces of Chikuzen and Higo, and set out for the western provinces to quell the rebellion in Kyushu. On the same day, a great amnesty was also proclaimed, and those who had been exiled in the third year of Jishō were recalled. The Lay Monk Regent Matsudono came up to the capital from Bizen Province, and the Grand Minister Myōon'in came up from Owari Province. It was reported that the Consultant Grand Counselor Sukekata returned to the capital from Shinano Province.

[6.12.3] On the twenty-eighth of the same month, the Myōon-in lord visited the retired emperor. On his return to the capital in the past Chōkan era, he played 'Celebrating the Sovereign's Favor' and 'Return to the Palace Music' on the veranda before the emperor; but on this return to the capital in the Yōwa era, he played 'Autumn Wind Music' at the Sentō Palace. How admirable was the depth of his heart, which in everything discerned the appropriate mood for the occasion! The Consultant Grand Minister Sukekata also visited the retired emperor that day. The Retired Emperor said, "How is it? It seems like a dream." Though you may think that, having grown accustomed to a rustic life, even such elegant arts as popular songs have now left no trace, I would like to hear just one imayo song. When he said this, the Major Counselor took up the rhythm and sang, 'The Kiso River that is in Shinano.' The imayo song he sang, 'The Kiso River that was in Shinano,' was a brilliant improvisation, for he had seen the original version.

[6.13.1] On the seventh day of the eighth month, the Great Benevolent Kings Assembly was held at the Bureau of Divination. This was said to be in imitation of the precedent of the punitive expedition against Masakado. On the first day of the ninth month, saying it was the precedent of the punitive expedition against Sumitomo, he offered iron armor to the Grand Shrine of Ise. The imperial envoy, the priestly official and Senior Assistant Head of the Department of Divinities, Ōnakatomi no Sadataka, left the capital, fell ill at the post station of Kōga in Ōmi Province, and died at the detached palace in Ise. The Great Ajari of Gōzanze, who had undertaken the five-altar rite for the subjugation of the rebels, died in his sleep at the Higanjo of the Great Officiant. It is evident that neither the gods nor the Three Treasures accepted (the prayers). Moreover, when the scrolls of the Ajari Jitsugen of Anshōji, who had undertaken the Great Original Rite, were presented and opened, it was terrifying that he had reported the subjugation of the Heike. "What is this?" When he said this, [the monk] replied, "You have commanded me to subdue the enemies of the court. When I observe the state of the present world, the Heike appear to be the enemies of the court. Therefore I subdue them; what fault could there be? Thus he spoke. "This monk is strange." Is it death penalty or exile? So it was said, but in the confusion of urgent matters, it was forgotten, and after that there was no further inquiry. After it became the era of the Genji, the Kamakura lord thought, "He is admirable." So he thought with admiration, and as a reward, it is said that he was made a great archbishop.

[6.13.2] On the twenty-fourth day of the twelfth month of the same year, the Empress was granted the title of In, and she was called Kenreimon-in. It is said that this was the first time a mother of an infant emperor received the title of In. In the meantime, this year too came to an end, and the Yōwa era became its second year.

[6.13.3] On the twenty-first day of the second month, Venus invaded the Pleiades. The Tenmon Yōroku says, "If Venus invades the Pleiades, barbarians from all directions will rise up." He said, "..." Also, "The general received the imperial command and left the province's border." It also appeared as "..."

[6.13.4] On the tenth day of the third month, the appointment ceremony was held, and the Heike family members were generally promoted in rank. On the tenth day of the fourth month, the former Gon no Shōsōzu Kenshin, at Hiyoshi Shrine, performed a ritual reading of ten thousand copies of the Lotus Sutra according to the proper method. For the sake of forming a karmic bond, the Cloistered Emperor also made an imperial visit. Someone must have proposed it: the Retired Emperor commanded the monks of Enryakuji to attack the Heike, and when word of this spread, warriors came to the palace and guarded the four gates. All the members of the Taira clan gathered at Rokuhara. The Middle Captain of the Third Rank, Lord Shigehira, went to Hiyoshi Shrine with a force of more than three thousand horsemen to meet the Cloistered Emperor. When it was heard at the monastery that the Taira were climbing the mountain with a force of several hundred horsemen to attack the mountain, the monks all descended to East Sakamoto and said, "What is this?" " they deliberated. The commotion in the mountains and the capital was extraordinary. The court nobles and senior officials in attendance lost their composure, and among the men of the Northern Guard, many were so flustered they panicked and lost control of their bowels. Lord Shigehira, the Middle Captain of the Third Rank, met the retired emperor at Anou and escorted him back to the capital. "If it is only like this, from now on, even pilgrimages and such will no longer be at your own discretion, will they?" Thus he said. In truth, there was no plan for the monks of Mount Hiei to attack the Heike. There was also no plan for the Heike to attack Mount Hiei. These are all groundless matters. It is because the heavenly demons are so violent. Thus people said. On the twentieth day of the fourth month of the same year, there was an extraordinary offering to the gods. This was because of famine and epidemic.

[6.13.5] On the twenty-fourth day of the fifth month of the same year, there was a change of era name, and it was called Juei. On that day, also, Shiro Sukemochi, a resident of Echigo Province, was appointed Governor of Echigo.
