During the mourning for his elder brother Sukenaga, he repeatedly declined, saying it was inauspicious, but since it was an imperial command, he could not refuse. He changed his name from Sukeshige to Nagashige.

[6.13.6] On the second day of the ninth month of the same year, Jō Shirō Nagashige, for the purpose of attacking Kiso, led the warriors of the four districts of Echigo, Dewa, and Aizu, with a total force of over forty thousand horsemen, and set out for Shinano Province. On the ninth day of the same month, he set up camp at Yokota-gawara in that province. Kiso was at Yoda Castle, but hearing this, he left Yoda Castle and rode out with over three thousand horsemen. Shinano Genji, following the stratagem of Inoue Kuro Mitsumori, suddenly made seven red banners, divided their three thousand horsemen into seven units, and from that peak and this valley raised the red banners in their hands as they approached. Shiro, the castle commander, saw this and said, "Alas, even in this province there are allies of the Heike!" and took courage. Saying this, as they gradually approached the place where the enemy was shouting, they agreed on a signal, and the seven units became one and raised a war cry all at once. They quickly raised the white banners they had prepared. The Echigo forces saw this and said, "The enemy must have hundreds of thousands of horsemen. What shall we do?" What shall we do? They lost their color, panicked and flustered; some were driven into the river, some were forced down into bad places; few were saved, and many were killed. The renowned warriors called Echigo no Yamatarō and Aizu no Jōtanbō, whom Shirō Jō had relied upon, were all killed there. Wounded in body, barely clinging to life, he crossed the river and retreated to Echigo Province.

[6.13.7] On the sixteenth of the same month, in the capital the Heike made no particular fuss about it; the former Commander of the Right, Lord Munemori, was restored to the office of Grand Counselor, and on the third day of the Tenth Month he became Minister of the Interior. On the seventh of the same month there was a congratulatory audience. Twelve court nobles of the Fujiwara family accompanied him, and sixteen courtiers, from the Chamberlain down, rode ahead. The Genji of the eastern and northern provinces were rising up like bees, and just as they were about to attack the capital, the Heike, appearing as if they did not know whether waves were rising or wind was blowing, had been so splendid—but now it all seemed utterly futile.

[6.13.8] In the meantime, it became the second year of Juei. The seasonal court banquets and other ceremonies were as usual. The Inner Palace Guards were performed by the Heike Inner Minister Munemori. On the sixth day of the first month, the Emperor made an imperial visit to the Retired Emperor's palace, Hōjūji-dono, for the New Year's audience. It was said that Emperor Toba, at the age of six, made an imperial visit for the New Year's audience, and that was the precedent. On the twenty-second day of the second month, Lord Munemori was promoted to Junior First Rank. Immediately on that day, he submitted a memorial resigning from the office of Inner Minister. It was said that this was because of the taboo against military disturbances. The monks of Nanto and Hokurei, the priests of Kumano and Kinpusen, and even the chief priests and shrine officials of the Grand Shrine of Ise all turned against the Heike and communicated with the Genji. Although imperial decrees were sent out in all directions and cloistered edicts were dispatched to the provinces, everyone took both the cloistered edicts and the imperial decrees as merely the orders of the Heike, and there was no one who followed them.

[7.1.1] In the first ten days of the third month of Juei 2, there was a falling-out between the Assistant Captain of the Military Guards and Kiso no Kanja Yoshinaka. The Assistant Captain of the Military Guards, for the purpose of pursuing and destroying Kiso, set out for Shinano Province with an army of over a hundred thousand horsemen. Kiso was in Yoda Castle, but hearing this, he left Yoda Castle and took up a position at Kumakayama, on the border between Shinano and Echigo. The Assistant Captain of the Military Guards arrived at Zenkoji in the same Shinano Province. Kiso sent his foster brother Imai no Shiro Kanehira as a messenger to the Assistant Captain of the Military Guards. What reason is there that you say you will kill Yoshinaka? You have subdued the eight provinces of the east, and are advancing from the Tokaido to drive out the Heike. Yoshinaka, too, having brought the two provinces of Tōsan and Hokuriku under his command, is determined to attack the Heike even one day sooner. For what reason would you think to break with Yoshinaka and be laughed at by the Heike? But Lord Jūrō Kurōdo, saying that he had a grudge against you, went over to Yoshinaka; and if even Yoshinaka were to treat him coldly, what would happen? So they went together. As for Yoshinaka, he bears no grudge against Your Highness at all. he sent word. In Hyōe no Suke's reply, he said, "Although you say so now, there are people who report that there is certainly a plot of rebellion to attack Yoritomo." You should not rely on that. Saying this, he sent Doi and Kajiwara ahead, and when it was heard that he had already dispatched a punitive force, Kiso, in order to prove that he truly had no such intention, sent his eldest son, Shimizu no Kanja Yoshishige, a young page who was eleven years old, accompanied by renowned warriors such as Unno, Mochizuki, Suwa, and Fujisawa, to Hyōe no Suke. Hyōe no Suke said, "Now indeed there is no resentment. Yoritomo has no child who has come of age. Well then, let me make you my son. So saying, he took Shimizu no Kanja with him and returned to Kamakura.

[7.2.1] Meanwhile, when it was heard that Kiso had subdued the two routes of Tōsan and Hokuriku and was about to attack the capital with an army of over fifty thousand horsemen, the Heike, since the previous year, had been saying, "Next year, with the grass-feeding of horses, there will be war." When this was proclaimed, the warriors of San'in, San'yō, Nankai, and Saikai came rushing in like clouds and mist. On the Tōsandō, the warriors of Ōmi, Mino, and Hida came, but on the Tōkaidō, those east of Tōtōmi did not come, while those to the west all came. From the Hokuriku region, north of Wakasa, not a single warrior came to join. First, they sent a punitive force to the Hokuriku road to subjugate Kiso no Kanja Yoshinaka, and after that, to attack the Assistant Commander of the Military Guards. As the great generals, they appointed Komatsu no Sanmi Chūjō Koremori, Echizen no Sanmi Michimori, Tajima no Kami Tsunemasa, Satsuma no Kami Tadanori, Mikawa no Kami Tomonori, Awaji no Kami Kiyofusa; as the samurai commanders, they appointed Etchū no Zenji Moritoshi, Kazusa no Daibu Hōgan Tadatsuna, Hida no Daibu Hōgan Kagetaka, Takahashi Hōgan Naganori, Kawachi Hōgan Hidekuni, Musashi Saburō Saemon no Jō Arikuni, Etchū Jirō Hyōe Moritsugu, Kazusa Gorō Hyōe Tadamitsu, and Aku Shichibyōe Kagekiyo as the vanguard. In total, there were six great generals, about three hundred and forty worthy samurai, and altogether their force numbered more than one hundred thousand horsemen. On the seventeenth day of the fourth month of the second year of Juei, at the hour of the dragon (around 8 a.m.), they departed the capital and headed toward the northern provinces. Having received the road, starting from the Osaka Barrier, without fearing the official tax goods of powerful families they met along the way, they seized everything one by one. As they pursued and passed along the roadsides of Shiga, Karasaki, Mikawajiri, Mano, Takashima, Shiozu, and Kaizu, the people could not endure it and all fled to the mountains and fields.

[7.3.1] The great generals Koremori and Michimori advanced, but the vice-generals Tsunemasa, Tadanori, Tomomori, and Kiyofusa were still holding back at Shiotsu and Kaizu in Ōmi Province. Among them, Tsunemasa, being a person skilled in poetry, music, and wind and string instruments, even in such a disturbance, cleared his mind, went out to the edge of the lake, and gazing far off at the island in the offing, summoned Fujibe no Yūkyō, who had accompanied him, and asked, "What is that called?" When he asked, "That is the famous Chikubushima, I believe." he said. "Indeed, such a thing exists. Come, let us go. Saying this, Fujibei no Arikata, Yasumon no Morikata, and five or six retainers boarded a small boat and crossed over to Chikubushima. Since it was the eighth day of the fourth month, the treetops that appeared green seemed to retain the feelings of spring, and the warbler's voice in the valley had grown old, while the cuckoo, with its first song so dear, announced the season as if it knew the time. The wisteria blooming in waves over the pines was truly delightful, so they hurriedly disembarked from the boat, climbed ashore, and viewed the scenery of this island, but neither words nor feelings could do it justice. That Qin Shi Huang and Han Wu, sometimes sending young boys and girls, sometimes ordering alchemists to seek the elixir of immortality, said that if they did not see Penglai they would not return, and so they aged in vain aboard their ships; the vast blue sea stretched endlessly and they could not obtain what they sought—the appearance of the Penglai grotto must have been just like this. In a certain sutra it is said: "Within Jambudvipa there is a lake, and in it there is a mountain of crystal that has arisen from the Golden Wheel, where heavenly maidens dwell." Thus it is said. This is exactly that island. Tsunemasa, sitting down before the deity, said: "Now, the great goddess Benzai-kudoku-ten is an ancient Tathagata, a great bodhisattva of the Dharma-body." Although the names of the two deities Benzai and Myōon are different, their original ground is one and the same, and they save sentient beings. I have heard that those who make a pilgrimage there once have their wishes fulfilled. It is indeed awe-inspiring. Saying this, he made offerings for a while; gradually the sun set, the moon of the seventeenth day rose, the sea shone all around, and the shrine hall glittered even more. It was truly beautiful, so the resident monks said, "This is a matter worth hearing." So saying, he presented the biwa to Tsunemasa. When Tsunemasa played it, the secret piece "Kamihara Ishigami" made the palace itself resound, and the deity, unable to contain his divine response, appeared as a white dragon upon Tsunemasa's sleeve. Overwhelmed with awe and joy, he could not help but continue to compose this poem, weeping.

lg.l: ちはやぶる神にいのりの叶へばや、しるくも色のあらはれにけり。

div.p: [7.3.2] Therefore, having subdued the enemy before their eyes and being about to punish the rebels at once, they rejoiced without doubt, and boarding the ship again, they departed from Chikubushima.

[7.4.1] Kiso no Yoshinaka, while being in Shinano, built a castle in Echizen Province called Hiuchi Castle. The forces holed up in that castle, beginning with Heisenji Chōri Saimyō Igishi, Inazu Shinsuke, Saitō Tarō, Hayashi Rokurō Mitsuaki, Togashi Nyūdō Busshō, Tsuchida, Takebe, Miyazaki, Ishiguro, Nyūzen, and Sami, numbered more than six thousand horsemen. It is a fortress more secure than any other. Great rocks stand towering around, and mountain peaks are ranged on all four sides. It has mountains behind it and mountains in front of it. In front of the fortress flow the Nomi River and the Shindo River. At the confluence of the two rivers, they cut down large trees and dragged them into an abatis, and when they had built up a palisade thickly, it was as if the water was dammed up at the roots of the mountains on east and west, facing a lake. The shadow soaks the southern mountains, turning them blue, and shimmers broadly. The waves sink the western sun, turning it crimson, and vanish into the depths. At the bottom of that Anavatapta Lake, they spread sand of gold and silver; on the shores of Kunming Lake, they floated boats of tokusei. At the constructed pond of this Hiuichi Castle, they built a dike, muddied the water, and deceived people's hearts. Since there were no boats and no way to cross easily, the large Heike forces lodged on the opposite mountain and idly passed the days.

[7.4.2] 城の内に在ける平泉寺長吏齋明威儀師、平家に志深かりければ、山の根を廻りて、 消息を書き、蟇目の中に入れて忍びやかに平家の陣へぞ射入たる。「彼湖は往古の淵 に非ず、一旦山川を塞上て候。夜に入、足輕共を遣て柵を切落させ給へ、水は程なく 落べし。馬の足立好所で候へば急ぎ渡させ給へ。後矢は射て參らせむ。是は、平泉寺 長吏齋明威儀師が申状。」とぞ書たりける。大將軍大に悦び、やがて足輕どもを遣し て、柵を切落す。おびたゞしう見えつれども、げにも山川なれば水は程なく落にけり。 平家の大勢暫の[_][1]遲々にも及ばす、さと渡す。 城の内の兵共暫し支へて防ぎけれ共、敵は大勢也、御方は無勢也ければ、叶べしとも見えざりけり。 平泉寺長吏齋明威儀師、平家に附て忠をいたす。 稻津新介、齋藤太、林六郎光明、富樫入道佛誓こゝをば落て、猶平家を背き加賀國に引退き、白山河内に引籠る。 平家やがて加賀に打越て、林、富樫が城郭二箇所燒拂ふ。 He could not see how he could face anyone. They dispatched couriers from nearby lodgings and reported this to the capital, whereupon the Minister and all the members of his clan who had remained behind rejoiced beyond measure.

[7.4.3] On the eighth day of the same fifth month, there was a review of troops at Shinohara in Kaga Province. They divided their army of more than one hundred thousand horsemen into two forces and advanced toward the main gate and the rear gate. The commander-in-chief of the main gate force was Komatsu no Sammi Chūjō Koremori, with Echizen no Sammi Michimori, and as the chief of staff, Etchū no Zenji Moritoshi led the way; altogether their force numbered more than seventy thousand horsemen, and they advanced toward Mount Tonami, which lies on the border between Kaga and Etchū. The commander of the rear guard was Satsuma-no-kami Tadanori, with Mikawa-no-kami Tomonori; as the captain of the samurai, Musashi Saburozaemon was placed at the head, and altogether their force numbered more than thirty thousand horsemen, and they advanced to Mount Shiho, which is on the border of Noto and Etchū. Kiso was at the provincial capital of Echigo, and hearing this, he rode out to meet them with more than fifty thousand horsemen. Saying that it was the auspicious custom of his army, he divided them into seven divisions. First, his uncle Jūrō Hangan Yukiyasu advanced toward Mount Shiho with more than ten thousand horsemen. Nishina, Takanashi, and Yamada Jirō were dispatched to the rear guard at Kitagurosaka with more than seven thousand horsemen. Higuchi Jirō Kanemitsu and Ochiai Gorō Kaneyuki were sent to South Kurozaka with seven thousand horsemen. They hid more than ten thousand horsemen at the mouth of Tonamiyama, the foot of Kurozaka, Matsunaga's Yanagihara, and the Gumiki forest. Imai Shirō Kanehira crossed the Washinosu ford with six thousand horsemen and took up a position in the Hinomiya forest. Kiso himself, with more than ten thousand horsemen, crossed the Oyabe ford and took up a position at the northern edge of Tonamiyama, at Haniu.

[7.5.1] Kiso said, "Since the Heike are certainly a large force, they will cross over Tonamiyama and come out into the open, and it will be a battle of meeting engagement." However, in a pitched battle, victory depends on the number of forces. If they attack with a large force and surround us, it will be bad. First, send out the flag-bearer, and if we raise the white flag, the Heike will see it and say, 'Ah, the Genji vanguard is facing us!' Surely they are a large force. Without hesitation, they will come out to the open field; the enemy knows the terrain, we do not; if we are surrounded, we cannot win. This mountain is rocky on all sides, so they will surely not go around to the rear; let us dismount for a while and rest the horses. So saying, they dismounted in the mountains. At that time Yoshinaka, pretending to be at ease for a while, waited for the sun to set, intending to drive the great force of the Heike into the Kurikara valley. So saying, he first raised thirty white banners and set them up on Kurozaka. As expected, the Heike saw this and said, "Ah, the vanguard of the Genji is facing us; surely they must be a great force. If we go out into the open without hesitation, the enemy knows the terrain, while we do not." If we are surrounded, it will be bad. This mountain is rocky on all sides. They will surely not go around to the rear attack force. The grass for the horses and the water supply are both good; let us dismount for a while and rest the horses. Saying this, they dismounted in the mountains of Tonamiyama, at a place called Saru no Baba. Kiso set up camp in Haniu, and when he looked around in all directions, he saw a vermilion sacred fence faintly visible through the green trees on the summer mountain peaks, and there was a shrine built in the katasogi style. In front of it stood a torii gate. Lord Kiso summoned a local guide and asked, "What shrine is that over there, and what deity is worshipped there?" "That is Hachiman Shrine." And this place is the estate of Hachiman Shrine." " he said. Lord Kiso was greatly pleased, and summoning the priest Kakumyo, who was in attendance, he said, "It is fortunate that I, Yoshinaka, have come near the sacred hall of the new Hachiman Shrine, and I am about to engage in battle." It seems certain that we will win this battle, no matter what. If that is to be, then partly for the sake of future generations, and partly as a prayer for the present, I think I should write a votive petition and offer it—what do you think? "That would be most appropriate," said Kakumyō. So saying, he dismounted from his horse and tried to write. Kakumyō's appearance: he wore a red-braided hitatare with black-laced armor, carried a black-lacquered sword, bore twenty-four black-feathered arrows, held a lacquered rattan bow under his arm, removed his helmet and hung it on the high cord, took out a small inkstone and folded paper from his quiver, and respectfully wrote the petition before Lord Kiso. Ah, he appeared to be a master of both the literary and military arts. This Kakumyō was originally a Confucian scholar. He was called Kurōdo Michihiro, and while he was at the Kangakuin, he became a monk and took the name Saijōbō Shinkyū. He often went to Nara as well. Once, when Prince Takakura entered Onjō-ji, he sent a letter to Yamato and Nara, and the monks of Nara had this Shinkyū write the reply. "Kiyomori is the dregs of the Heike, the dust of the warrior houses." "When he wrote that, the Nyudo Daijo was greatly angered and said, 'How can that Shingon priest write that Jokai is the dregs of the Heike and the dust of the warrior houses?' Seize that priest and put him to death! While he was saying this, the priest fled from the southern capital to the northern provinces, wrote a letter to Lord Kiso, and called himself Daibu-bo Kakumyo. In that petition he wrote:I bow my head in reverence. The Great Bodhisattva Hachiman is the original lord of the imperial court of Japan, the distant ancestor of generations of wise rulers.In order to protect the imperial throne and to benefit the people, he manifested his golden body of the three bodies and pushed open the provisional gates of the three shrines.Now, in recent years, there is a man called the Chancellor of the Heike, who governs the whole realm and torments the people.He is already an enemy of the Buddhist Law and a foe of the imperial law.Yoshinaka, though born into a family of warriors, has barely continued the dust of his ancestors' bow and arrow.When I consider that violence, I cannot turn my thoughts to prudence.Entrusting my fate to the way of heaven, I throw my body into the nation.I wish to raise a righteous army as a trial and drive away the weapons of war.However, although it is said that the two armies joined battle, while the soldiers had not yet gained unified courage, in the place where their hearts were filled with various fears, suddenly on the battlefield where a flag was raised, they worshipped the shrine of Sanjo Wako.The ripening of the response to the divine influence is clear.There is no doubt that the rebels will be punished and killed.Tears of joy overflow, and longing soaks into the heart.Above all, since the time when his great-grandfather, the former Governor of Mutsu, Minamoto no Yoshiie, attached himself to the clan of the imperial shrine and was called Hachiman Taro, there has been no one among the family members who did not pay reverence.Yoshinaka, as his descendant, has bowed his head for many years.Now, to accomplish this great deed is like a baby measuring the vast ocean with a shell, or a mantis raising its axe in anger against a great carriage.However, for the sake of the country and for the sake of the lord, he launches this; for the sake of his house and for the sake of himself, he does not initiate it.The sincerity of the will reaches the gods and heaven.How trustworthy!How joyful!Prostrating myself, I humbly pray: may the visible and invisible gods lend their power, may the divine spirits exert their strength, decide the victory in a single moment, and drive away the enemy in all directions.If, then, my sincere prayers accord with the divine will and the dark mirror grants its protection, first show me an auspicious sign.
[7.5.2] Respectfully submitted by Minamoto no Yoshinaka on the eleventh day of the fifth month of the second year of Juei.

[7.5.3] Writing thus, beginning with himself, thirteen men drew the whistling arrows from their upper quivers, attached them to the written vow, and offered them at the sacred hall of the Great Bodhisattva. Surely the great bodhisattva Hachiman, seeing from afar that this was not his true will, sent three mountain doves flying out of the clouds to flutter above the white banners of the Genji.

[7.5.4] Long ago, when Empress Jingu attacked Silla, our side's fighting was weak and the enemy's army was strong, and just when it seemed that things would go badly, the Empress made a vow to heaven, and three sacred doves flew down and appeared on the face of her shield, and the enemy's army was defeated. Moreover, when the ancestor of these people, Yoriyoshi no Ason, attacked Sadatō and Munetō, his own side's fighting was weak and the rebels' army was strong, so Yoriyoshi no Ason, facing the enemy's camp, said, 'This is by no means a private fire; it is a divine fire,' and set fire to it. The wind suddenly blew over toward the barbarians, and Sadatō's mansion, Kuriyagawa, burned down. After that, the army was defeated, and Sadatō and Munetō perished. Kiso-dono, not forgetting the precedent of that kind, dismounted from his horse, removed his helmet, performed the hand-washing and cormorant-fishing ritual, and now, the heart with which he worshipped the sacred dove—how trustworthy it was!

[7.6.1] Meanwhile, the Minamoto and Taira forces joined battle. The two battle lines had drawn close to within a mere three chō of each other. Neither the Genji nor the Heike advanced. From the Genji side, fifteen elite warriors advanced in front of the shields, and shot whistling arrows into the Heike camp. The Heike, not knowing it was a stratagem, sent out fifteen riders and shot back fifteen whistling arrows. When the Genji sent out thirty riders and shot, the Heike sent out thirty riders and shot back thirty whistling arrows. If they sent out fifty riders, the other side sent out fifty riders to meet them; if they sent out a hundred riders, the other side sent out a hundred riders to meet them; both sides advanced a hundred riders each to the front of the formation. They tried to fight each other, but the Genji side restrained them and did not let them fight. The Genji spent the day in this manner, and although they had planned to drive the large Heike force into the Kurikara valley, the Heike, not realizing it in the least, exchanged greetings and spent the day with them—how fleeting it was.

[7.6.2] As it gradually grew dark, the rear-guard force of over ten thousand horsemen, who had come around from the north and south, assembled at the Kurikara temple, struck their quiver frames, and raised a war cry. When the Heike looked back, white banners were raised like clouds. Because this mountain is rocky on all sides, they thought the rear approach would surely not be passable, but wondering what this could be, they were thrown into an uproar. Meanwhile, Lord Kiso raised a war cry from the main gate. The force of ten thousand horsemen stationed at Matsunaga's willow field and the forest of Gumi, and the more than six thousand horsemen of Imai Shiro at Higuromi forest, likewise raised a war cry. The shouting voices of forty thousand horsemen in front and behind sounded as if mountains and rivers were collapsing all at once. As expected, the Heike. 次第に闇うはなる、前後より敵は攻來る、「きたなしや返せや返せ。 」 と云ふ族多かりけれ共、大勢の傾立ちぬるは、左右なう取て返す事難ければ、倶利迦 羅谷へ、我先にとぞ落しける。ま先に落したる者が見えねば、此谷の底に、道の有に こそとて、親落せば子も落し、兄落せば弟も續く。主落せば家子郎等落しけり。馬に は人、人には馬、落重り落重りさばかり深き谷一つを、平家の勢七萬餘騎でぞ填たり ける。巖泉血を流し、死骸岳を成せり。されば其谷の邊には、矢の穴刀の瑕殘て今に 有りとぞ承はる。平家には宗と憑まれたりける上總大夫判官忠綱、飛騨大夫判官景高、 河内判官秀國も、此谷に埋もれて失にけり。備中國住人瀬尾太郎兼康といふ聞ゆる大 力も、そこにて加賀國住人藏光次郎成澄が手に懸て、生捕にせらる。越前國火打が城 にて、返忠したりける平泉寺の長吏齋明威儀師も捕はれぬ。木曾殿「あまりに憎きに 其法師をば先切れ。 」とて、切られけり。 平氏の大將維盛、通盛、希有の命生て加賀國へ引退く。 七萬餘騎が中より、僅に二十餘騎ぞ遁たりける。

[7.6.3] On the twelfth day, from the residence of Hidehira in Oku, two horses were presented to Lord Kiso. One was a black horse with white mane and tail, and the other was a dappled gray. Immediately, a mirror saddle was placed on it, and it was dedicated to Hakusan Shrine as a sacred horse. Lord Kiso said, "Now there is nothing to worry about. But the battle of Shiho with Lord Juro Kurando is indeed uncertain." Come, let's go and see. Saying so, from among the forty thousand horsemen, they spurred their horses and men, and with twenty thousand horsemen they galloped toward the enemy. When they tried to cross Himi inlet, the tide happened to be full, and they did not know the depth, so they drove in about ten saddled horses. With the saddle pommels submerged, they reached the opposite shore without mishap. "It was shallow! Cross over!" With that, the great force of over twenty thousand horsemen all charged in and crossed. As expected, Jūrō Kurō Hangan Yukishige was fiercely attacked, and as he was retreating, at the place where his horse was resting, Kiso no Yoshinaka said, "That's exactly why," and with a fresh force of over twenty thousand horsemen, he charged back in, and with a shout, he galloped into the midst of the Heike's over thirty thousand horsemen, and they fought and fought until sparks flew, attacking fiercely. The Heike warriors resisted for a while and defended, but unable to hold out, they were finally driven from that place. On the Heike side, the Great General, Governor of Mikawa, Tomonori, was killed. He was the youngest son of the Lay Monk Chancellor. Many samurai died. Lord Kiso crossed over Mount Shio and took up a position before the tomb of the Prince at Kodanaka in Noto.

[7.7.1] Thereupon he donated shrine estates to all the shrines. To Hakusan Shrine he donated Yokoe and Miyamaru; to Sugō Shrine, Nōmi no Shō; to Tada Hachiman, Chōya no Shō; to Kehi Shrine, Iihara no Shō. To Heisenji he donated Fujishima Shichigō.

[7.7.2] The warriors who had shot at Lord Hyōe no Suke at the battle of Ishibashiyama a year earlier fled up to the capital and were on the side of the Heike. Among the leaders were Matano Gorō Kagehisa, Nagai Saitō Bettō Sanemori, Itō Kurō Suketsune, Ukishima Saburō Shigechika, and Mashimo Shirō Shigenao. These men, thinking to rest for a while until there was another battle, gathered together day after day, and amused themselves with circulating cups of sake. On the day when they had gathered at Sanemori's place, Saitō Bettō said, "When I look carefully at the state of this world, the Genji side is strong, and the Heike side appears to be losing." Come, everyone, let us go to Lord Kiso. When he said this, everyone agreed, saying, "Indeed so." The next day, when they had gathered at Ukisaburō's place, Saitō Bettō said, "Well then, what about the matter we discussed yesterday, everyone?" Among them, Matano Gorō stepped forward and said, "We, after all, are known by everyone in the eastern provinces and are men of name." To go over there or come over here following one's fancy would be unsightly. We do not let people know. As for Kagehisa, being on the side of the Heike, he may become anything. When he said this, Saitō Bettō laughed and said, "Indeed, it was to draw out each of your intentions that I spoke." Moreover, Sanemori has resolved to die in this battle. He has told everyone that he will not return to the capital a second time. He has also reported this to the Minister. When he said this, everyone agreed with this proposal. Thus, did they break that promise? All those who were present at that time, without a single one remaining, died in the northern provinces—how pitiful it is!

[7.7.3] Meanwhile, the Heike rested their men and horses and set up camp at Shinohara in Kaga Province. On the twenty-first day of the same fifth month, at the hour of the dragon (around 8 a.m.), Kiso attacked Shinohara and raised a war cry. On the Heike side, Hatakeyama Shoji Shigeyoshi and Oyamada Betto Arishige, who had been confined since the Jisho era until now, were told, "You are old retainers. You should also decide the manner of battle." Saying this, he set off toward the northern provinces. These brothers, with more than three hundred horsemen, advanced to the front of the battle line. From the Minamoto side, Imai no Shiro with more than three hundred horsemen came out to meet them. Imai no Shiro and Hatakeyama at first sent out five or ten horsemen at a time to fight, and later both sides fell into confusion and fought. On the twenty-first day of the fifth month, at the hour of the horse, under a blazing sun that did not stir even the grass, as they fought, each striving not to be outdone, sweat poured from their entire bodies, no different from flowing water. Many soldiers also died on Imai's side. Hatakeyama, with his retainers and sons, was reduced to a small number and, unable to resist, retreated. Next, from the Heike side, Takahashi no Hangan Nagatsuna advanced with over five hundred horsemen. From the Kiso side, Higuchi Jiro Kanemitsu and Ochiai Goro Kaneyuki galloped to meet them with over three hundred horsemen. They fought for a while, but since Takahashi's forces were warriors from various provinces, not a single one of them stayed to fight; they all fled, each trying to be first. Though Takahashi's heart was fierce, because his rear had become exposed, he was unable to exert his strength and retreated. As he fled alone, a resident of Etchū Province, Kotarō Yukishige of Nyūzen, saw him as a worthy opponent, spurred his horse, and came galloping; they grappled fiercely with each other. Takahashi grabbed Nyūzen, pressed him against the front of the saddle, and said, "Who are you? Tell me your name!" When he said this, the other replied, "I am a resident of Etchū Province, Kotarō Yukishige of Nyūzen, eighteen years old." He announced his name. "Alas, how pitiful! If the son of Nagatsuna, who died last year, were alive this year, he would be eighteen years old." "I should twist off your neck and throw you away, but I will spare you." So saying, he pardoned him. He himself dismounted from his horse and rested for a while, waiting for the allied forces. Nyūzen said, "Though he spared me, alas, what an enemy! I wish I could kill him somehow." As he was thinking this, Takahashi loosened his armor and began to tell a story. Nyūzen, a warrior of superior quick skill, drew his sword, attacked, and stabbed Takahashi's inner thigh twice. Meanwhile, three horsemen of Nyūzen's retainers came riding up from behind and joined the battle. Though Takahashi's spirit was fierce, his luck must have run out; the enemy was many, he had received a deep wound, and there he was finally slain.

[7.7.4] Again from the Heike side, Musashi Saburōzaemon Arikuni, with about three hundred horsemen, shouted and attacked. From the Genji side, Nishina, Takanashi, and Yamada Jirō rode out to meet them with over five hundred horsemen. They fought holding them off for a while, but many of the forces on Arikuni's side were killed. As Arikuni fought deep into the enemy, he used up all his arrows, had his horse shot, and became a foot soldier. Drawing his sword, he fought on, but the enemy killed many and shot him with seven or eight arrows, and he died standing. When their general came to such an end, all his forces fled.

[7.8.1] Also, Nagai Saitō Bettō Sanemori, a resident of Musashi Province, though all his side fled, alone turned back again and again, fighting to hold them off. As he had a thought, he wore a red-ground brocade hitatare, put on armor laced with yellow-green, tied the cords of a helmet with a gilt-copper crest, girded on a gold-mounted long sword, shouldered arrows with clipped feathers, took a bow of black-lacquered rattan, and mounted a dappled gray horse with a gold-rimmed saddle. From the direction of Kiso-dono, Tezuka Taro Mitsumori fixed his eyes on him as a worthy opponent and said, "Ah, how admirable!" What kind of person are you, that while all your side's forces have fled, you alone remain? That is admirable! Tell me your name! When he called out, "Who are you who speaks thus?" "I am Tezuka Taro Kanasashi no Mitsumori, a resident of Shinano Province," he announced his name. "Well then, we are good opponents for each other!" However, I am not trying to find out who you are; since I have something in mind, I will not announce my name. Come on, grapple with me, Tezuka! Saying this, as they were about to clash, Tezuka's retainers came galloping up from behind, and to prevent their master from being killed, they interposed themselves and grappled fiercely with Saito Betto. "Alas, I am grappling with the mightiest warrior in Japan—what a joy!" So saying, he seized him, pulled him close, pressed him against the front rim of his saddle, cut his throat, and threw him away. Tezuka Tarō, seeing his retainer being struck down, circled around to the left, lifted the skirt of the armor, stabbed twice, and grappled with him where he was weakening, and they fell. Saitō Bettō, though his heart was fierce, was not accustomed to battle, and moreover he was an old warrior, so he ended up beneath Tezuka. Also, Tezuka's retainer, who had come late, took the head, and hastened to Kiso-dono's presence, and said, "Mitsumori, indeed, is a strange fellow; I grappled with him and struck him down." When I looked, thinking he might be a samurai, he was wearing a brocade hitatare. Again, when I looked, thinking he might be a great general, there were no troops following him. Though I urged him repeatedly, saying, "Identify yourself! Identify yourself!", he never identified himself. His voice was in the Bando dialect. When I said this, Lord Kiso said, "Ah, this is Saito Betto, isn't it?" If so, when Yoshinaka crossed into Kozuke, I saw him briefly; he had white hair and a thin tail. Now surely he must have become white-haired, but his sideburns and beard being black is strange. Higuchi Jiro is a familiar companion; he will recognize him. Summon Higuchi. So saying, he was summoned. Higuchi Jiro took one look and said, "Alas, how pitiful! It is Saito Betto." Lord Kiso said, "If that is so, he must now be over seventy, and his hair must have turned white; how is it that his beard and sideburns are black?" When he said this, Higuchi Jiro shed tears in streams and said, "If that is so, I was about to report that matter, but it was so sad that tears of inadvertence fell." A bow-and-arrow taker should always prepare in advance, even for a trivial occasion, the words of remembrance. Saito Betto, meeting Kanemitsu, said as he always did in conversation: 'When I am over sixty and go to face the battle camp, I will dye my beard and sideburns black and try to look young.' The reason is that competing with young lords and trying to be the first to charge would be unseemly. Also, it would be regrettable if people were to despise him as an old warrior. He said, '...' and indeed it has dyed [him]. Wash it and look at it. When he said that, thinking it was so, he washed it and looked, and it had become white hair.

[7.8.2] The matter of wearing a brocade hitatare: when Saitō Bettō took his final leave, he went to the Minister and said, "It is not a matter of my own person alone, but when I went to the East the year before last, startled by the sound of waterfowl wings, I fled from Kambara in Suruga Province without shooting even a single arrow. That is the shame of my old age, and only this matter." This time, heading to the northern provinces, I shall die in battle. As for that, Sanemori was originally a man of Echizen Province, but in recent years, having received a domain, he was made to reside in Nagai in Musashi. It is a metaphor for that. There is a saying: 'Return to your hometown wearing brocade.' Please grant me a brocade hitatare. When he said this, the Minister said, "How well you have spoken!" And so saying, he granted him a brocade hitatare, it is said. The Zhu Maichen of old waved his brocade sleeves on Mount Kuaiji, and the Saitō Bettō of today, they say, raised his name in the streets of the province he came to. Leaving behind only a name that will not decay, his corpse becomes dust at the end of the Koshi road—how sad it is!

[7.8.3] On the seventeenth day of the fourth month, when he departed the capital with over a hundred thousand horsemen, it did not seem that he could show his face anywhere; but now, returning in the latter part of the fifth month, his force is barely over twenty thousand horsemen. "When you drain the stream to fish, they say you get many fish, but next year there are no fish." When one burns the forest to hunt, though it is said that one obtains many beasts, the next year there are no beasts. Thinking of the future, one should have left a little behind. And there were, it is said, people who said so.

[7.9.1] Kazusa no kami Tadayoshi and Hida no kami Kageie had both become monks when the lay priest chancellor died the year before last, but this time, hearing that all their children had perished in the northern provinces, perhaps because of the accumulation of that grief, they finally died of lamentation. Beginning with these, parents were left behind by their children, wives were separated from their husbands, and surely it was so in distant and nearby provinces alike. Throughout the capital, in every house they shut their gates and doors, and with voices raised in prayer they chanted the Buddha's name; the clamor was tremendous.

[7.9.2] On the first day of the sixth month, the Chamberlain and Right Gate Guard Lieutenant Sadanaga summoned the Junior Assistant of the Office of Deities, Ōnakatomi no Chikatoshi, to the lower entrance of the Courtiers' Hall and conveyed the imperial command: "If the warfare is quelled, an imperial visit to the Grand Shrine shall be made." The Grand Shrine of Ise, which descended from Takamagahara, was first established in the 25th year, 3rd month of the reign of Emperor Suinin, when the great pillar was firmly planted at the lower rock base on the upper reaches of the Isuzu River in Watarai District, Ise Province, from the village of Kasanui in Yamato Province. Since the first offering of prayers, among the great and small deities and the unseen realms of the more than 3,750 shrines in the sixty-odd provinces of Japan, it is without peer. However, although there had been no imperial visits in successive reigns, in the time of Emperor Nara there was a man called Fujiwara no Hirotsugu, who was the grandson of the Minister of the Left Fuhito, the son of the Consultant and Minister of Ceremonial Utsugu, and held the offices of Junior Captain of the Right Inner Palace Guards and Assistant Governor-General of Dazaifu. In the tenth month of the fifteenth year of Tenpyō, in Matsura District of Hizen Province, he gathered tens of thousands of rebels and was about to endanger the state. It is said that when Ōno no Azumahito was made Great General and Fujiwara no Hirotsugu was pursued and punished, the Emperor first made an imperial visit to the Grand Shrine of Ise, and this became the precedent. That Hirotsugu had a horse that could go up to the capital and back from Matsura in Hizen in a single day. Even when he was pursued and attacked, after the rebels of his side had fled and all had perished, he mounted that horse and galloped into the sea, so it is said. Among the many terrifying events that occurred after his death, on the eighteenth day of the sixth month of Tenpyō 16, at the Kanzeon-ji temple of the Dazaifu in Mikasa District, Chikuzen Province, the officiating priest at the dedication ceremony was, it is said, the Sōjō Genbō. When he ascended the high seat and struck the bell of homage, suddenly the sky clouded over, thunder roared terribly, and it fell upon Genbō, taking his head and entering into the clouds. This was heard to be because he had performed a curse to subdue Hirotsugu.

[7.9.3] This archbishop was a person who, when Kibi no Daijin went to Tang China, accompanied him and brought back the Hosso sect. The Tang people laughed at the name Genbo, saying, "Genbo has the sound of 'returning to ruin.' In any case, he is a person who will meet with trouble after returning to Japan. So they divined, it is said. On the eighteenth day of the sixth month of the same Tenpyō nineteenth year, he wrote on the skull the inscription 'Genbō' and dropped it in the garden of Kōfukuji; in the air, with a voice as if of a thousand people, there was a loud laugh. This is because Kōfukuji is a temple of the Hossō sect. The disciples of that bishop took it, built a mound, placed the skull inside, named it 'Head Mound', and it remains to this day. This is exactly what the spirit of Hirotsugu caused. Because of this, the departed spirit is worshipped, and now it is called the Mirror Shrine of Matsura.

[7.9.4] In the reign of Emperor Saga, when Emperor Heizei, the retired emperor, disturbed the realm at the persuasion of Naishi-no-kami, for the sake of prayers on that occasion, the third imperial princess, Princess Yushi, was sent to the Kamo Saiin. This was the beginning of the Saiin. In the reign of Emperor Suzaku, because of the military disturbances of Masakado and Sumitomo, the special festival of Hachiman was begun. This time too, following such precedents, various prayers were begun.

[7.10.1] Kiso, arriving at the provincial capital of Echizen, summoned his family and retainers and held a council. Indeed, Yoshinaka will pass through Omi Province to enter the capital, and the usual mountain monks may well try to block him. Breaking through would be easy, but the Heike, at this time, do not speak of the Buddha's law; they destroy temples, kill monks, and commit evil deeds. If those who go to the capital to protect them join with the Heike, then fighting against the monks of Mount Hiei would be a second act no different from the first. This is indeed a serious matter. What should we do? When he said this, Daibu-bō Kakumyō, who was included among the scribes, stepped forward and said, "The monks of the mountain gate number three thousand; they are by no means of one mind, but each has his own thoughts and intentions." There may be monks who say they will side with the Genji, and there may also be many who say they will join the Heike; send a letter and see. The matter will probably appear in the reply letter. When he said this, [the other] replied, "This proposal is indeed reasonable; then write it." So he had Kakumyō write the letter and sent it to the mountain gate. In that letter it said:When Yoshinaka carefully observes the Heike's evil deeds, since the Hogen and Heiji eras they have long lost the propriety of a subject.Nevertheless, high and low alike wring their hands, and clergy and laity alike bow their heads in submission.They arbitrarily install and depose emperors, and greedily seize provinces and districts.Without discussing right or wrong, they arrest powerful families; without distinguishing guilt or innocence, they destroy high officials and courtiers.They seize their assets and give them all to their retainers; they confiscate their estates and shamelessly bequeath them to their descendants.Above all, in the third year of Jishō, in the eleventh month, he removed the Cloistered Emperor to the detached palace at Jōnan, and exiled the Chancellor to the remote region west of the sea.The people did not speak out, but on the roads they expressed their feelings with their eyes.Moreover, in the fourth year of the same era, in the fifth month, he surrounded the vermilion pavilion of the Second Prince, and caused the dust of the ninefold palace to be startled.At that time, when the Imperial Prince, in order to escape an unjust harm, secretly entered Onjō-ji, Yoshinaka, having received the imperial command beforehand, was about to raise his whip, but the resentful enemies filled the streets, and the advance guard lost the way.Even the Minamoto clan in the nearby provinces did not come to serve; how much less those in distant provinces?However, because Onjōji was beyond his means, while he was making them go to the Southern Capital, they fought at Uji Bridge.The general, the Third Rank novice Yorimasa, father and son, made light of their lives and esteemed righteousness, and though they strove for the merit of a single battle, they could not escape the attack of the many, and exposed their bodies to the moss of the old bank, and let their lives flow in the waves of the long river.He engraved the purport of the imperial command on his heart and dispelled the vengeful spirits of his comrades.Because of this, the Genji of the eastern and northern provinces each planned to go to the capital, desiring to destroy the Heike.In the autumn of the previous year, Yoshinaka, in order to fulfill his long-cherished desire, raised his banner and took up his sword, and on the day he departed from Shinano Province, Jō no Shirō Nagamochi, a resident of Echigo Province, led tens of thousands of soldiers to attack him, and they fought at Yokota Riverbank in that province.Yoshinaka, with barely three thousand horsemen, defeated those tens of thousands of soldiers.When the rumor spread widely, the Taira commander, leading a hundred thousand soldiers, set out for the Hokuriku region.At the fortresses of Koshi Province, Kaga Province, Tonami, Kurozaka, Shiozaka, Shinohara, and others, they fought several battles.He devised strategies within the command tent and gained victory right before his eyes.If you attack them, they will surely lie down; if you assault them, they will surely surrender.It is no different from the autumn wind tearing the banana leaves.It is the same as the winter frost withering the clustered leaves.This is entirely the aid of the gods and Buddhas, and not at all Yoshinaka's military strategy.After the Heike's defeat, he is a person who plans to enter the capital.Now, passing the foot of Mount Hiei, he should enter the streets of the capital.At this time, there was secretly a doubt.Now, are the monks of Mount Hiei siding with the Heike, or are they siding with the Genji?If they should aid those rebels, we must fight against the monks.If we engage in battle, the destruction of Mount Hiei will be imminent.Alas! While the Heike disturb the imperial mind and destroy the Buddhist Law, in order to quell their evil deeds, we raise a righteous army; but suddenly, against three thousand monks, we would bring about an unexpected battle.Alas! If, out of deference to the Medicine King and the Mountain King, I delay my journey, then as a negligent minister of the court, I will forever leave behind the reproach of having blemished my military strategy.I am at a loss as to whether to advance or retreat, and so I report the situation.I earnestly hope that the three thousand monks, for the sake of the gods, for the sake of the Buddha, for the sake of the country, and for the sake of the sovereign, will join forces with the Genji, punish the rebels, and bask in the great benevolence.I cannot bear the depth of my sincerity.Yoshinaka, with awe and trembling, respectfully states.
[7.10.2] In the second year of Juei, on the tenth day of the sixth month, Minamoto no Yoshinaka
[7.10.3] presented to the Reverend Master Eikōbō
[7.10.4] so it was written.

[7.11.1] As expected, the monks of the mountain gate opened and read this letter, and their opinions were divided. Some monks said they would side with the Genji, while others said they would side with the Heike. Opinions differed, and there were various views. The old monks deliberated and concluded: 'We should pray for the eternal reign of the Emperor, the golden-wheel-turning holy ruler.' The Heike are the maternal relatives of the current emperor, and they show reverence to the mountain temple. Therefore, up to now, we have prayed for their prosperity. However, their evil deeds exceed the law, and all people turn against them. Although they sent punitive forces to the provinces, they were instead destroyed by the foreign enemies. The Genji, since recent years, have won victory in battle after battle, and their fortunes are about to open. Why should we, alone on this mountain, side with the Heike whose fortunes are exhausted, and turn against the Genji whose fortunes are opening? They all agreed that they should abandon their obligation to the Heike and follow the Genji's request for alliance, and sent a reply. Lord Kiso again summoned his retainers and had Kakumyo open this reply. The official letter of the tenth day of the sixth month arrived on the sixteenth of the same month; upon opening and reading it, the gloom of many days was dispelled at once.In general, the evil deeds of the Heike have continued for many years, and the disturbances in the imperial court have never ceased.The matter is on people's lips; it cannot be forgotten.As for Mount Hiei, it is a sacred temple in the northeast of the imperial capital, where prayers for the peace of the nation are offered.However, the whole realm has long been invaded by that wicked rebellion, and the four seas have not obtained their peace.It is as if the wheel of the Dharma of the exoteric and esoteric teachings has ceased, and the protective power of the guardian deities has repeatedly declined.Here, you were fortunately born into a noble family that has been a military house for generations, and happily you are a person of the current select rank.He devises a clever stratagem beforehand and suddenly raises righteous troops.Forgetting the life that may die ten thousand deaths, he establishes the merit of a single battle.His labors have not yet passed two years, but his name has already spread throughout the four seas.The monks of our mountain all rejoiced.For the sake of the nation and for the sake of successive generations, they felt gratitude for military achievements and military strategies.If it is like this, then they rejoice that the earnest prayers on the mountain are not in vain, and they know that the protection of the realm is without negligence.From this temple and other temples, the eternal Buddhist teachings, and from the main shrines and branch shrines, the enshrined deities, surely rejoice that the teachings will flourish again, and rejoice that reverence will return to its former state.Please bestow your wise discernment upon the hearts of the monks.Thus, in the unseen realm, the Twelve Divine Generals, as messengers of the Healing King and Good Sage, will join the brave warriors in pursuing and destroying the rebels; in the visible realm, the three thousand monks will temporarily cease their diligent practice of study and contemplation, and will support the imperial army in punishing the evil monks.The Brahmanic wind of the Ten Vehicles of Calm and Insight will sweep the wicked monks out of Japan, and the Dharma rain of the Three Mysteries of Yoga will turn the present age back to the ancient days of Emperor Yao.The general opinion was thus.Consider this carefully.
[7.11.2] On the second day of the seventh month of the second year of Juei, the great assembly of monks...
[7.11.3] Thus it was written.

[7.12.1] The Heike, not knowing this even in a dream, since it was a time when Kōfuku-ji and Onjō-ji were harboring resentment, would not comply even if persuaded. Our family has not yet incurred the enmity of the mountain temple, and the mountain temple also does not harbor disloyalty toward our family. Thinking to swear an oath to Sannō Daishi and win over the three thousand monks, ten court nobles of the clan wrote a joint petition and sent it to the mountain temple. In that letter it said:Respectfully, we vow to regard Enryakuji as our family temple and Hiyoshi Shrine as our family shrine, and to revere solely the Tendai Buddhist teachings. The members of our clan have especially made vows to this effect.As for the reason, Mount Hiei is the place where, during the reign of Emperor Kanmu, after the Great Teacher Dengyo returned from China, he spread the teaching of perfect and sudden enlightenment and transmitted the great precepts of Vairocana; since then, it has been a sacred peak where Buddhism flourishes, and it serves as a temple for the protection of the nation.Now, the exile in Izu Province, Minamoto no Yoritomo, does not repent of his own crime, but rather mocks the imperial law.Moreover, the Minamoto clan members who participate in the treacherous plot and join in the conspiracy, such as Yoshinaka and Yukiie, form factions and are numerous.They plunder and occupy several provinces, both neighboring and distant, and seize all local products and tributes.Accordingly, some pursued the achievements of successive generations of meritorious service, while others relied on their skill in the arts of bow and horse, and they were to swiftly attack and subdue the rebels, and to suppress the wicked faction; even if only slightly, having received the imperial command, they plotted the subjugation of the enemy.Here, in the battle formations of fish scales and crane wings, the imperial forces gained no advantage, and the might of star banners and lightning halberds seemed to favor the rebels.If it were not for the divine protection of the gods and Buddhas, how could the rebellion and chaos be quelled?Therefore, we solely devote ourselves to the Buddhist teachings of the Tendai sect and rely on the divine favor of Hiyoshi.How much more so, when we humbly consider our ancestors, we should be called the descendants of the original vow.You should revere them all the more, you should respect them all the more.From now on, if there is joy in the mountain gate, we shall make it the joy of our whole clan; if there is anger in the shrine family, we shall make it the anger of our whole family, and each of us will pass this down to our descendants and never let it be lost.The Fujiwara clan has long taken Kasuga Shrine and Kofukuji Temple as their clan shrine and clan temple, and has devoted themselves to the Hosso sect of Mahayana Buddhism.The Taira clan has taken Hiyoshi Shrine and Enryakuji Temple as their clan shrine and clan temple, and has now encountered the teaching of perfect and immediate enlightenment.That is a relic of the past; think of the honor and glory for the family.This is the present vow and prayer: on behalf of my lord I entreat punishment upon his enemies.I humbly pray: may the Seven Shrines of Sannō, the prince and his retinue, the holy host protecting the entire mountain east and west, the Medicine Master of the Twelve Great Vows, the Sunlight and Moonlight Bodhisattvas and the Twelve Divine Generals, illuminate my undivided sincerity and grant their unique divine response.Meanwhile, the rebels with their wicked plots and treacherous hearts will have their hands bound at the camp gate, and the violent and cruel will have their heads sent to the capital.Therefore the court nobles of the family, with one voice, made obeisance and swore as above.
[7.12.2] Junior Third Rank, Acting Governor of Echizen, Taira no Ason Michimori
[7.12.3] Junior Third Rank, acting concurrently as Middle Captain of the Right Palace Guards, Taira no Ason Sukemori.
[7.12.4] Senior Third Rank, acting as Provisional Middle Captain of the Right Palace Guards and concurrently Governor of Iyo, Taira no Ason Koremori.
[7.12.5] Senior Third Rank, acting as Middle Captain of the Left Palace Guards and concurrently Governor of Harima, Taira no Ason Shigehira.
[7.12.6] Senior Third Rank, acting as Captain of the Right Gate Guards and concurrently Governor of Ōmi and Tōtōmi, Taira no Ason Kiyomori.
[7.12.7] Councillor, Senior Third Rank, Superintendent of the Empress Dowager's Palace, concurrently Director of the Office of Palace Repairs and Governor of Kaga and Etchū, Taira no Ason Tsunemori.
[7.12.8] Junior Second Rank, Acting Middle Counselor, concurrently Commander of the Left Palace Guards and Great General for Subduing the Barbarians, Taira no Ason Tomomori.
[7.12.9] Junior Second Rank, Acting Middle Counselor, concurrently Governor of Hizen, Taira no Ason Norimori.
[7.12.10] Senior Second Rank, Acting Major Counselor, concurrently Inspector of Dewa and Mutsu, Taira no Ason Yorimori.
[7.12.11] Junior First Rank, Taira no Ason Munemori.
[7.12.12] Respectfully submitted on the fifth day of the seventh month of the second year of Juei.
[7.12.13] Thus it was written.

[7.12.14] The head priest took pity on this and did not immediately present it. He confined himself in the shrine of Jūzenji Gongen, performed incantations for three days, and after that presented it to the monks. The one poem that at first did not seem to exist appeared in the first volume of the written petition.

lg.l: 平かに花咲く宿も年ふれば、西へ傾く月とこそなれ。

div.p: [7.12.15] Sannō Daishi took pity on this and said, "Let the three thousand monks join forces." However, because his conduct over the years and days had gone against the divine will and betrayed people's expectations, though he prayed, his prayers were not answered, and though he spoke, they would not yield. The monks truly pitied the situation, but they said, "We have already sent a reply agreeing to the Genji. Now we cannot lightly change that decision. Saying thus, there was no monk who would permit this.

[7.13.1] On the fourteenth day of the same seventh month, Higo no kami Sadayoshi, having subdued the rebellion in Chinzei, went up to the capital leading more than three thousand horsemen, including the Kikuchi, Harada, and Matsuura bands. Although the western provinces were barely pacified, the warfare in the eastern and northern provinces would not quiet down at all.

[7.13.2] Around midnight on the twenty-second of the same month, the area around Rokuhara was in a great uproar. They put saddles on horses, tightened the girths, and carried various things away to the east, west, south, and north to hide them. It was as if the enemy had just now burst in. What was heard after dawn was that there was a man called Mino Genji, Sado no Jō Shigetada. At the time of the Hōgen battle in the first year of Hōgen, when Chinzei Hachirō Tametomo was defeated by the enemy forces and became a fugitive, he was captured and brought forth; as a reward for that, although he had originally been a lieutenant of the Palace Guards, at that time he became a lieutenant of the Right Gate Guards. Because of this, he was hated by his own clan and flattered the Heike; but that night, around midnight, he rushed to Rokuhara and reported: "Kiso has already attacked from the northern provinces with more than fifty thousand horsemen, and they are filling up Hieizan East Sakamoto." It was because they had reported that Tate Rokurō Chikatada, the retainer, and Daibu Bō Kakumyō, the scribe, with more than six thousand horsemen, vied to climb Mount Hiei, and all three thousand monks, united in purpose, were about to attack the capital. The Heike people were greatly alarmed and dispatched punitive forces in all directions. As commander-in-chief, the new Middle Counselor Tomomori and the former Third Rank Middle Captain Shigehira, with a total force of over three thousand horsemen, left the capital and first encamped at Yamashina. Echizen no Sanmi Michimori and Noto no Kami Noritsune defended Uji Bridge with more than two thousand horsemen. Sama no Kami Yukimori and Satsuma no Kami Tadanori guarded the Yodo road with more than a thousand horsemen.

[7.13.3] On the Genji side, it was heard that Jūrō Kurōdo Yukiie entered from Uji Bridge with several thousand horsemen. It was also said that Mutsu no Shinhanji Yoshimasa's son, Yada no Hanji-dai Yoshikiyo, went up to the capital via Mount Ōe. When it was heard that the Genji of Settsu and Kawachi were entering the capital together like clouds and mist, the Heike people, thinking that from now on they could only meet their fate in one place, called back to the capital all the punitive forces that had been sent in various directions. In the capital, the place of fame and profit, the cock crows and there is no peace. Even in a well-governed age it is like this. How much more so in a disordered age! He thought he would like to go deep into the depths of Mount Yoshino, but all the provinces and the seven circuits had turned against him. Which bay would be safe? Since it is the golden words of the Tathagata and the wondrous text of the One Vehicle that say, "The three realms are without peace, like a burning house," how could one deviate from it even slightly?

[7.13.4] On the night of the twenty-fourth day of the same seventh month, when the night was deep, the former Inner Minister Lord Munemori went to the Rokuhara mansion where Kenreimon-in was staying and said, "I had thought that the state of this world, even if it came to this, would somehow be otherwise, but now it has come to this." Although everyone was saying, "Let us do something within the capital," since it would be regrettable to show them a shameful sight before their very eyes, I think I would like to take both the Retired Emperor and the Empress, and make a royal progress to the western provinces, and see what happens. When he said this, the Empress replied, "Now, whatever happens, it will be as you decide." Saying this, she could not hold back the tears that overflowed onto the sleeves of her robe. The minister, too, appeared to be wringing the sleeves of his court robe.

[7.13.5] That night, the Cloistered Emperor, having secretly heard that the Heike would seize him and flee outside the capital, left the palace stealthily with only the Middle Captain of the Right Umanosuke, the son of the Consultant Azechi Dainagon Sukekata, as his attendant, and went to Kurama. People did not know this. Among the Heike warriors there was a man called Tachibana no Uchisae Mon no Jō Sueyasu. He was a brave warrior, and was also employed by the Cloistered Emperor. That very night, while I was on night duty at Hōjūji-dono, the usual palace direction became noisy and the ladies-in-waiting were weeping secretly, so as I wondered what it could be, I heard a voice saying, "The Cloistered Emperor has suddenly appeared—where is he going?" I heard a voice saying that. "How shocking!" Saying that, he immediately rushed to Rokuhara and reported this to the Minister, who said, "No, it must be a mistake." While saying that, without waiting to hear more, he hurried to Hōjūji-dono and went to see him, but indeed he was not there. The court ladies in attendance, beginning with Nii-dono and Tango-dono, did not move at all. "What is it? What is it?" But even though they said that, there was not a single person who said, "I know where he has gone." There was not a single person who said, "I know where he has gone," and everyone was in a state of astonishment.

[7.13.6] Meanwhile, when it was said that the Cloistered Emperor had not returned to the capital, the uproar in the capital was extraordinary. Moreover, the sight of the Heike people suddenly panicking—even if enemies had broken into each house, there is a limit, and it seemed they could not have been more flustered than this. For days they had been preparing to take the Heike emperor and the court and to make an imperial journey to the western provinces, but now that they had been abandoned, they felt like rain not staying at the base of a tree they relied on.

[7.13.7] Nevertheless, saying, "At least let the imperial procession take place," when the imperial palanquin had already arrived around six in the morning, the emperor, being only six years old this year and still very young, was taken aboard without any concern. His mother, Kenreimon'in, rode in the same palanquin. "Hand over the Naishidokoro, the sacred jewel, and the sacred sword." Take along the seal, the time-tablet, the sword Genjō, and the bell Suzuka, and the like. Thus commanded the Taira Grand Counselor Tokitada, but in the excessive haste, many were the things that were dropped and lost. He also forgot to take the sword of the daytime chamber. At that time, only three men—Tokitada, the Kura no Kami Nobumoto, and the Sanuki Middle Captain Tokizane—attended in formal court dress. The guards of the palace gates, wearing armor and carrying bows and arrows, attended. The imperial procession went west along Shichijo and south along Suzaku.

[7.13.8] When it dawned, it was the twenty-fifth day of the seventh month. The Milky Way had already opened, clouds trailed over the eastern ridge, the dawn moon shone white and clear, and the crowing of cocks was again urgent. Even in a dream, I never saw such a thing. The sudden bustle of the capital's relocation last year—now I realize it was an omen of this.

[7.13.9] The Regent, too, was accompanying the imperial procession, and when he looked out from his carriage at the intersection of Shichijo and Omiya, a boy with his hair tied up in a topknot darted across in front of the carriage, and on the boy's left sleeve the characters "Spring Day" appeared. When he wrote "Spring Day" and read it as "Kasuga," he thought with confidence that the Kasuga Great Deity, protector of the Dharma, was guarding the descendants of the Great Minister of the Fujiwara, and it seemed to be the voice of that boy.

lg.l: いかにせん藤の末葉のかれゆくを、唯春の日に任せてや見ん。

div.p: [7.13.10] Calling his attendant Shindō Saemon-no-jō Takanori close, he said, "When I consider the situation carefully, although it is a royal progress, the imperial outing cannot be accomplished; why do you think the future is so unreliable?" When he said this, the ox driver exchanged glances with him. Immediately understanding, he turned the carriage around and drove up Ōmiya as if flying, and entered Chisoku-in in the Kitayama area.
[7.14.1] Heike retainer Etchū no Jirō Hyōe Moritsugu, hearing this, pressed forward eagerly to pursue and stop them, but was restrained by the others and stayed.

[7.14.2] Lord Komatsu no Sanmi Chūjō Koremori, though he had been preparing himself for this day by day, when it actually came, he was grief-stricken. The one called Kitagata was the daughter of the late Nakamikado no Shin Dainagon Narichika. Her peach-blossom face was flushed with tears, her rouged eyes were alluring, her willow hair was disheveled by the wind; she did not seem like a person of this world. There was a young lord called Rokudai Gozen, who had turned ten, and his younger sister, a princess of eight. As all these people followed after him, the Third Rank Middle Captain said, "As I have been saying these days, I am going to flee to the western provinces together with the clan." Though I should accompany you to the very end, since enemies lie in wait even on the road, it would be difficult to pass safely. Even if you hear that I have been killed, you must by no means change your appearance. The reason is that you should show yourself to anyone, save yourself, and raise your little ones. How could there be no one who feels affection for you? Though he tried to console her, the lady of the north gave no reply and lay down pulling the covers over herself. When he was about to set out, she clung to his sleeve and said, "In the capital there is no father and no mother; after I am abandoned, who will there be for me to rely on?" It is hateful to hear that I should show myself to just anyone. If there is a bond from a previous life, even if you take pity on me, should I expect affection from every person? We vowed to accompany each other to the end, to vanish like dew on the same field, to become water-weeds at the bottom of the same river; but now, the intimate words of a sleepless night have all turned to lies. 責ては身一つならば如何がせん。 捨られ奉る身の憂さ、思知ても留まりなん。 少き者共をば、誰に見讓り、如何にせよとか思召す。 恨しうも留め給ふ者哉。 」と、且は恨み且は慕ひ給へば、三位中將宣ひけるは、「誠に人は十三、我は十五より見初奉り、火の中水の底へも、倶に入り倶に沈み、限ある別路迄も後れ先立じとこそ申しかども、かく心憂き有樣にて、軍の陣へ趣けば、具足し奉て、行方も知ぬ旅の空にて、憂目を見せ奉らんも、うたてかるべし。 其上今度は用意も候はず。 何くの浦にも心安う落著いたらば、其よりこそ迎へに人をも奉らめ。 」とて、思ひ切てぞ立れける。 中門の廊に出て、鎧取て著、馬引寄させ、既に乘らんとし給へば、若君姫君走出でて、父の鎧の袖、草摺に取附き、「是はされば何地へとて、渡せ給ぞ。 我も參ん、我も行ん。 」と面々に慕ひ泣給ふにぞ、浮世のきづなと覺えて、三位中將、いとゞ爲方なげには見えられける。

[7.14.3] さる程に御弟新三位中將資盛卿、左中將清經、同少將有盛、丹後侍從忠房、備中守師盛、兄弟五騎馬に乘ながら、門の中へ打入り、庭にひかへて、「行幸は遙に延させ給ひぬらん、如何にや今迄。 」と、聲々に申されければ、三位中將馬に打乘て出給ふが、猶引返し、縁の際へうち寄せて、弓の弭で御簾をさと掻揚げ、「是御覽ぜよ各、少き者共が餘りに慕ひ候を、とかうこしらへ置んと仕る程に、存の外の遲參。 」と宣ひもあへず、泣かれければ、庭にひかへ給へる人々、皆鎧の袖をぞ濡されける。

[7.14.4] こゝに齋藤五、齋藤六とて、兄は十九、弟は十七に成る侍あり。 三位中將の御馬の左右のみづつきに取著き、何く迄も御とも仕るべき由申せば、三位中將宣ひけるは、 「己等が父齋藤別當北國へ下し時、汝等が頻に伴せうと云しかども、存ずる旨が有ぞ とて、汝等を留置き、北國へ下て遂に討死したりけるは、かゝるべかりける事を、故い者で、兼て知たりけるにこそ。 あの六代を留て行に、心安う扶持すべき者のなきぞ。 誰理を枉て留まれ。 」と宣へば、力及ばず、涙を押へて留りぬ。 北方は、「年比日比、是程情なかりける人とこそ、兼ても思はざりしか。 」とて臥まろびてぞ泣かれける。 若君姫君女房達は、御簾の外迄まろびいで、人の聞をも憚らず聲をはかりにぞ喚叫び給ひける。 此聲々耳の底に留て、西海の立つ浪の上、吹風の音迄も聞く樣にこそ思はれけめ。
[7.14.5] 平家都を落行に、六波羅、池殿、小松殿、八條、西八條以下、一門の卿相雲客の家々、二十餘箇所、次々の輩の宿所々々、京白川に四五萬の在家一度に火をかけて、皆燒拂ふ。

[7.15.1] 或は聖主臨幸の地也。 鳳闕空しく礎を殘し、鸞輿只跡を留む。 或は后妃遊宴の砌也。 椒房の嵐聲悲み、掖庭の露色愁ふ。 粧鏡翠帳の基戈林釣渚の館、槐棘の座えん鸞の栖、多日の經營を空うして、片時の灰燼と成果ぬ。 況や郎從の蓬篳に於てをや。 況や雜人の屋舎に於てをや。 餘炎の及ぶ所、在々所々數十町也。 強呉忽に亡て、姑蘇臺の露荊棘に移り、暴秦既に衰て、咸陽宮の烟へいけいを隱しけんも、かくやと覺て哀也。
日來は函谷二かうの嶮しきを固うせしか共、北狄の爲に是を破られ、今は江河けい渭の深きを憑みしか共、東夷の爲に是を取られたり。 豈圖きや、忽に禮儀の郷を攻出されて、泣々無智の境に身を寄んとは。 昨日は雲の上にて雨を降す神龍たりき。 今日は肆の邊に水を失ふ枯魚の如し。 禍福道を同うし、盛衰掌を反す。 今目前にあり、誰か是を悲ざらん。 保元の昔は春の花と榮しかども、壽永の今は秋の紅葉と落果ぬ。

[7.15.2] 去治承四年七月大番の爲に上洛したりける畠山庄司重能、小山田別當有重、宇都宮左衞門尉朝綱、壽永迄、召籠られたりしが、其時既に斬るべかりしを、新中納言知盛卿申されけるは「御運だに盡させ給ひなば、是等百人千人が頸を斬せ給ひたりとも、世を取らせ給はん事難かるべし。 故郷には妻子所從等如何に歎き悲み候らん。 若し不思議に運命開けて、又都へ立歸らせ給はん時は、有難き御情でこそ候はんずれ。 只理を枉げて、本國へ返し遣さるべうや候らむ。 」と申されければ、大臣殿、「此義尤然るべし。 」とて暇を給ぶ。 是等首を地に著け、涙を流いて申けるは、「去治承より今までかひなき命を扶けられ參せて候へば、何くまでも御供仕て行幸の御ゆくへを見參 せん。」と頻に申けれ共、大臣殿、「汝等が魂は皆東國にこそあるらんに、ぬけがら ばかり西國へ召具すべき樣なし。急ぎ下れ。」と仰られければ、涙を押へて下けり。 是等も二十餘年の主なれば、別れの涙押へ難し。

[7.16.1] 薩摩守忠度は、いづくよりか歸られたりけん、侍五騎、童一人、我身共に七騎取て返し、五條の三位俊成卿の宿所におはして見給へば門戸をとぢて開かず。 忠度と名乘給へば、落人歸り來たりとて、其内噪ぎあへり。 薩摩守馬より下り、自高らかに宣ひけるは、「別の子細候はず、三位殿に申べき事有て、忠度が歸り參て候。 門を開れず共、此際迄立寄らせ給へ。 」と宣へば、俊成卿「さる事あるらん。 其人ならば苦かるまじ。 入れ申せ。 」とて、門をあけて對面有り。 事の體何となうあはれなり。 薩摩守宣ひけるは、「年來申承はて後、愚ならぬ御事に思ひ參らせ候へ共、この二三年は京都の噪、國々の亂併當家の身の上の事に候間疎略を存せずといへども、常に參り寄る事も候はず。 君既に都を出させ給ひぬ。 一門の運命はや盡候ぬ。 撰集の有るべき由承りしかば、生涯の面目に、一首なり共御恩を蒙らうと存じて候しに、やがて世の亂出で來て、其沙汰なく候條、唯一身の歎きと存ずる候。 世靜まり候なば勅撰の御沙汰候はんずらん。 是に候ふ卷物の中に、さりぬべきもの候はゞ、一首なりとも御恩を蒙て、草の蔭にても嬉しと存候はば、遠き御守りとこそ成參せ候んずれ。 」とて、日來詠置れたる歌共の中に、秀歌と覺きを百餘首書集られたる卷物を、今はとて打立れける時、是を取て持れたりしが、鎧の引合せより取出でて、俊成卿に奉る。 三位是をあけて見て、「かゝる忘れ形見を給り置候ぬる上は、努々疎略を存ずまじう候。 御疑あるべからず。 さても只今の御渡りこそ情も勝れて深う、哀れも殊に思ひしられて感涙抑へ難う候へ。 」と宣へば、薩摩守悦で「今は西海の浪の底に沈まば沈め、山野に尸をさらさばさらせ、浮世に思置く事候はず。 さらば暇申て。 」とて、馬に打乘り、甲の緒をしめ、西を指いてぞ歩せ給ふ。 三位後を遙に見送て立たれたれば、忠度の聲と覺しくて、「前途程遠し、思を雁山の夕の雲に馳。 」と、高らかに口ずさみ給へば、俊成卿、いとゞ名殘惜しう覺えて、涙を抑てぞ入給ふ。 其後世靜て、千載集を撰ぜられけるに、忠度のありし有樣、言置し言の葉、今更思出て哀なりければ、彼の卷物の中に、さりぬべき歌幾らもありけれど、勅勘の人なれば、名字をば顯されず、「故郷花」といふ題にて詠まれたりける歌一首ぞ、讀人しらずと入られける。

lg.l: さゝ浪や志賀の都はあれにしを、昔ながらの山櫻かな。

div.p: [7.16.2] 其身朝敵と成にし上は、仔細に及ばずと云ながら、恨めしかりし事共なり。

[7.17.1] 修理大夫經盛の子息、皇后宮亮經正、幼少にては、仁和寺の御室の御所に、童形にて、候はれしかば、かゝる怱劇の中にも、其御名殘きと思出て、侍五六騎具して、仁和寺殿へ馳參り、門前にて馬より下り、申入られけるは、「一門運盡て今日既に帝都を罷出候。 浮世に思ひ殘す事とては、唯君の御名殘計也。 八歳の時參り始め候て、十三で元服仕り候し迄は、相勞る事の候はぬ外は、白地にも御前を立去事も候はざりしに、今日より後西海千里の浪路に趣いて、又何の日、何の時、歸り參るべしとも覺えぬこそ口惜う候へ。 今一度御前へ參て、君をも見參せたう候へども、既に甲冑を鎧ひ弓箭を帶し、あらぬ樣なる粧に罷成て候へば、憚存候。 」とぞ申されける。 御室哀に思召し、「唯其姿を改めずして參れ。 」とこそ仰せけれ。 經正其日は、紫地の錦の直垂に、萠黄匂の鎧著て、長覆輪の太刀を帶き、切斑の矢負ひ、滋籘の弓脇に挾み、甲をば脱高紐にかけ、御前の御坪に畏る。 御室やがて御出有て、御簾高く揚させ「是へ／＼」と召されければ、大床へこそ參られけれ。 供に具せられたる藤兵衞有教を召す。 赤地の錦の袋に入たる御琵琶持て參たり。 經正是を取次で、御前にさし置き申されけるは、「先年下し預て候し青山持せて參て候。 餘りに名殘は惜しう候へども、さしもの名物を、田舎の塵に成ん事口惜う候。 若不思議に運命開けて、又都へ立歸る事候はゞ、其時こそ猶下し預り候はめ。 」と泣々申されければ、御室哀におぼしめし一首の御詠をあそばいて下されけり。

lg.l: あかずして別るゝ君が名殘をば、後の形見につゝみてぞおく。

div.p: [7.17.2] 經正御硯下されて、

lg.l: 呉竹のかけひの水はかはれども、猶すみあかぬ宮の中かな。

div.p: [7.17.3] さては暇申て出られけるに、數輩の童形、出世者、坊官、侍僧に至迄、經正の袂にすがり、袖を引へて、名殘を惜み、涙を流さぬは無りけり。 其中にも經正幼少の時、小師でおはせし大納言法印行慶と申は、葉室大納言光頼卿の御子也。 餘に名殘を惜みて、桂河の端迄打送り、さてもあるべきならねば其より暇請うて泣々別れ給ふに、法印かうぞ思續け給ふ。

lg.l: あはれなり老木若木も山櫻、おくれ先だち花は殘らじ。

div.p: [7.17.4] 經正の返事には、

lg.l: 旅衣よな／＼袖をかたしきて、思へば我は遠くゆきなん。

div.p: [7.17.5] さて、卷て持せられたる赤旗、さと指上げたり。 あそこ爰にひかへて待奉る侍共、「あはや」とて馳集まり、其勢百騎許鞭をあげ、駒を早めて、程なく行幸に逐つき奉る。
[7.18.1] 此經正十七の年、宇佐の勅使を承てくだられけるに、其時青山を給て、宇佐へ參り、御殿に向ひ參り、祕曲を彈給ひしかば、いつ聞馴たる事は無れ共、供の宮人推竝て、緑衣の袖をぞ絞ける。 聞知らぬ奴子迄も村雨とは紛はじな。 目出かりし事ども也。
[7.18.2] 彼青山と申す御琵琶は、昔仁明天皇御宇、嘉祥三年の春、掃部頭貞敏渡唐の時、大唐の琵琶博士廉妾夫に逢ひ、三曲を傳へて歸朝せしに、玄象、獅子丸、青山、三面の琵琶を相傳して渡りけるが、龍神や惜み給ひけん、浪風荒く立ければ、獅子丸をば海底に沈めぬ。 今二面の琵琶を渡して、吾朝の御門の御寶とす。

[7.18.3] 村上聖代應和の比ほひ、三五夜中の新月白く冴え、凉風颯々たりし夜半に、御門清凉殿にして、玄象をぞ遊されける。 時に影の如くなる者、御前に參じて、優にけだかき聲にて、唱歌を目出たう仕る。 御門御琵琶を差置かせ給て、「抑汝は如何なる者ぞ。 何くより來れるぞ。 」と御尋あれば、「是は昔貞敏に三曲を傳へし大唐の琵琶博士、廉妾夫と申す者で候が、三曲の中、祕曲を一曲殘せるに依て、魔道に沈淪仕て候。 今御琵琶の御撥音妙に聞えて侍る間、參入仕る處也。 願くは此曲を君に授け奉り、佛果菩提を證すべき」由申て、御前に立られたる青山を取り、轉手をねぢて、祕曲を君に授け奉る。 三曲の中に上玄、石上是也。 其後は、君も臣も恐させ給て、此御琵琶を遊し彈く事もせさせ給はず、御室へ參せられたりけるを、經正の幼少の時御最愛の童形たるに依て、下し預りたりけるとかや。 甲は紫藤の甲、夏山の嶺の緑の木間より、有明の月の出るを、撥面に書かれたりける故にこそ、青山とは附られたれ。 玄象にも相劣らぬ希代の名物なりけり。

[7.19.1] 池の大納言頼盛卿も、池殿に火を懸て出られけるが、鳥羽の南の門に引へつゝ、「忘たる事あり。 」とて、赤印切捨て、其勢三百餘騎都へ取て歸られけり。 平家の侍越中次郎兵衞盛嗣、大臣殿の御前に馳參て「あれ、御覽候へ、池殿の御留まり候に、多の侍共の付參らせて、罷留まるが、奇怪に覺え候。 大納言殿迄は恐れも候、侍共に矢一つ射懸候はん。 」と申ければ。 「年比の重恩を忘て、今此有樣を見果ぬ不當人をば、さなくとも有なん。 」と宣へば、力及ばで留まりけり。 「さて小松殿の君達は如何に。 」と宣へば「未御一所も見えさせ給はず。 」と申す。 其時、新中納言殿、涙をはらはらと流いて「都を出て未だ一日だにも過ざるに、何しか人の心共の變行くうたてさよ。 まして行末とてもさこそはあらんずらめと思しかば都の内で如何にも成らんと、申つる者を。 」とて、大臣殿の御方を、世にも恨げにこそ見給ひけれ。

[7.19.2] 抑池殿の留まり給ふ事を如何にと云に兵衞佐頼朝、常は頼盛に情をかけて、「御方をば全く愚に思ひ參らせ候はず。 只故池殿の渡らせ給ふとこそ存候へ。 八幡大菩薩も御照覽候へ。 」など、度々誓状を以て申されける上、平家追討の爲に討手の使の上る度ごとに、「相構て池殿の侍共に向て弓引な。 」と情を懸れば「一門の平家は運盡き既に都を落ぬ。 今は兵衞佐に助られんずるにこそ。 」と宣ひて、都へ歸られけるとぞ聞えし。 八條女院の仁和寺の常磐殿に渡らせ給ふに參り籠られけり。 女院の御乳母子宰相殿と申す女房に、相具し給へるに依てなり。 「自然の事候はゞ、頼盛構へて助させ給へ。 」と申されけれども、女院、「今は世の世にても有らばこそ。 」とて、憑氣もなうぞ仰ける。 凡は兵衞佐許こそ、芳心は存ぜらるゝとも、自餘の源氏共は如何あらんずらん。 憖に一門には離れ給ひぬ。 浪にも磯にも附ぬ心地ぞせられける。 さる程に、小松殿の君達は三位中將維盛卿を始め奉て、兄弟六人其勢千騎許にて淀の六田河原にて、行幸に追附奉る。 大臣殿待うけ奉り嬉げにて、「いかにや今迄。 」と宣へば、三位中將、「少き者共が餘に慕ひ候を、とかうこしらへ置んと遲參仕候ぬ。 」と申されければ、大臣殿、「などや心つよう六代殿をば具し奉給候はぬぞ。 」と宣へば、維盛卿、「行末とても憑しうも候はず。 」とて、問ふにつらさの涙を流されけるこそ悲しけれ。

[7.19.3] 落行く平家は誰々ぞ。 前内大臣宗盛公、平大納言時忠、平中納言教盛、新中納言知盛、修理大夫經盛、右衞門督清宗、本三位中將重衡、小松三位中將維盛、新三位中將資盛、越前三位通盛、殿上人には、内藏頭信基、讃岐中將時實、左中將清經、小松少將有盛、丹後侍從忠房、皇后宮亮經正、左馬頭行盛、薩摩守忠度、能登守教經、武藏守知明、備中守師盛、淡路守清房、尾張守清定、若狹守經俊、兵部少輔正明、藏人大夫成盛、大夫敦盛、僧には二位僧都專親、法勝寺執行能圓、中納言律師仲快、經誦坊阿闍梨祐圓、侍には受領、檢非違使、衞府、諸司百六十人、都合其勢七千餘騎、是は東國北國度々の軍に此二三箇年が間、討泄れて、僅に殘る所也。 山崎關戸院に玉の御輿を舁居て、男山を伏拜み、平大納言時忠卿「南無歸命頂禮八幡大菩薩、君を始參せて、我等都へ歸し入させ給へ。 」と祈れけるこそ悲しけれ。 各後を顧給へば、霞める空の心地して、烟のみ心細く立のぼる。 平中納言教盛卿

lg.l: はかなしな主は雲井に別るれば、跡は煙とたちのぼるかな。

div.p: [7.19.4] 修理大夫經盛、

lg.l: 故郷をやけのの原にかへり見て、末もけぶりのなみぢをぞ行く。

div.p: [7.19.5] 誠に故郷をば、一片の烟塵に隔つゝ、前途萬里の雲路に赴れけん人々の心の中、推量られて哀也。

[7.19.6] 肥後守[_][6]貞能ほ、川尻に源氏待と聞て、蹴散さんとて、五百餘騎で發向したりけるが、僻事なれば歸り上る程に、宇度野の邊にて行幸に參り合ふ。 貞能馬より飛下り、弓脇挾み大臣殿の御前に、畏て申けるは、「是は、抑何地へとて落させ給候やらん。 西國へ下せ給たらば、落人とて、あそこ爰にて討散らされ浮名を流させ給はん事こそ口惜う候へ。 只都のうちでこそ、如何にも成せ給はめ。 」と申ければ、大臣殿、「貞能は知ぬか。 木曾すでに北國より五萬餘騎で攻上り、比叡山東坂本に滿々たんなり。 此夜半ばかり法皇も渡らせ給はず。 各が身ばかりならば如何がせん、女院二位殿に目の當り憂目を見せ參せんも、心苦しければ、行幸をも成し參らせ、人々をも引具し奉て、一まともやと思ふぞかし。 」と仰られければ、「左候はゞ、貞能は暇賜はて、都で如何にも成り候はん。 」とて、召具したる五百餘騎の勢をば、小松殿の君達に附奉り、手勢三十騎許で都へ引かへす。

[7.19.7] 京中に殘り留まる平家の餘黨を伐んとて、貞能が歸り入由聞えしかば、池大納言「頼盛が身の上でぞ有らん。 」とて、大に怖れ噪がれけり。 貞能は、西八條の燒跡に、大幕ひかせ一夜宿したりけれども、歸り入給ふ平家の君達一所も坐ねば、さすが心細うや思ひけん、源氏の馬の蹄に懸じとて、小松殿の御墓掘せ、御骨に向ひ奉て、泣々申けるは、「あな淺まし、御一門の御果御覽候へ。 『生ある者は必滅す。 樂み盡て悲み來る。 』と古より書置たる事にて候へ共、まのあたりかかる憂事候はず。 君は斯樣の事を先づ悟せ給ひて、兼て佛神三寶に御祈誓有て、御世を早うせさせまし／＼けるにこそ。 有難うこそ覺え候へ。 其時貞能も最後の御供仕るべう候ける物を、かひなき命を生て、今はかゝる憂目に逢候事こそ口惜う候へ。 死期の時は、必一佛土へ迎へさせ給へ。 」と泣々遙に掻口説き、骨をば高野へ送り、あたりの土をば賀茂川に流させ、 世の在樣たのもしからずや思けん、主と後合に、東國へこそ落行けれ。宇都宮をば貞 能が申預て、情有ければ、其好にや貞能又宇都宮を頼うで下られければ芳心しけると ぞ聞えし。

div.head: 7.20. 福原落

div.p: [7.20.1] 平家は小松三位中將維盛卿の外は、大臣殿以下妻子を具せられけれ共、次樣の人共はさのみ引しろふに及ばねば、後會其期を知らず、皆打捨てぞ落行ける。 人は何れの日、何れの時、必ず立歸べしと其期を定置だにも、久しきぞかし。 況や是は今日を最後、唯今限の事なれば、行くも止まるも、互に袖をぞ濕しける。 相傳譜代の好年比日比の重恩、爭か忘べきなれば、老たるも若きも、後のみ歸り見て、前へは進みもやらざりけり。 或は磯邊の波枕、八重の潮路に日を暮し、或は遠きを分け、嶮しきを凌ぎつゝ、駒に鞭打人もあり舟にさをさす者もあり、思々心々に落行けり。

[7.20.2] 平家は福原の舊都に著て、大臣殿然るべき侍共老少數百人召て仰られけるは、「積善の餘慶家に盡き、積惡の餘殃身に及ぶ故に、神明にも放たれ奉り、君にも捨られ參らせて、帝都を出て旅泊に漂ふ上は、何の憑みか有るべきなれ共、一樹の蔭に宿るも、前世の契淺からず、同じ流を掬ぶも、他生の縁尚深し。 如何に況や、汝等は一旦隨ひ付く門客にあらず、累祖相傳の家人也。 或は近親の好他に異なるも有り、或は重代芳恩是深きも有り。 家門繁昌の古へは、恩波に依て、私を顧みき。 今何ぞ芳恩を酬ひざらんや。 且は十善帝王、三種神器を帶して渡らせ給へば、如何ならん野の末山の奧迄も、行幸の御供仕らんとは思はずや。 」と仰られければ老少皆涙を流いて申けるは、「怪しの鳥獸も、恩を報じ徳を酬ふ心は候なり。 況や、人倫の身として、いかが其理を存知仕らでは候べき。 廿餘年の間、妻子を育み、所從を顧み候事、併ら君の御恩ならずといふ事なし。 就中に弓箭馬上に携る習ひ、二心あるを以て恥とす。 然ば則ち日本の外、新羅、百濟、高麗、契丹、雲の果海の果迄も、行幸の御供仕て、如何にも成候はん。 」と、異口同音に申ければ、人々皆憑氣にぞ見えられける。

[7.20.3] 福原の舊里に、一夜をこそ明されけれ。 折節秋の初の月は下の弦なり。 深更空夜閑にして、旅寢の床の草枕、露も涙も爭ひて、唯物のみぞ悲き。 何歸るべし共覺えねば、故入道相國の造り置き給ひし所々を見給ふに、春は花見の岡の御所、秋は月見の濱の御所、泉殿、松蔭殿、馬場殿、二階の棧敷殿、雪見の御所、萱の御所、人々の館ども五條大納言國綱卿の承て造進せられし里内裏、鴦の瓦、玉の甃、何れも／＼三年が程に荒果てゝ、舊苔徑を塞ぎ、秋の草門を閉づ。 瓦に松生ひ垣に蔦茂れり。 臺傾て苔むせり、松風ばかりや通ふらん。 簾絶え閨露は也、月影のみぞ差入ける。
明ぬれば福原の内裏に火を懸て、主上を始奉て人々皆御船に召す。都を立し程こそ無 れども是も名殘は惜かりけり。海士の燒藻の夕煙、尾上の鹿の曉の聲、渚々に寄する 浪の音、袖に宿かる月の影、千草にすだく蟋蟀のきり／＼す、惣て目に見耳に觸る事、 一として哀れを催し、心を痛しめずといふ事なし。昨日は東關の麓に轡を竝べて十萬 餘騎、今日は西海の浪に纜を解て七千餘人、雲海沈々として、青天既に暮なんとす。 孤島に夕霧隔て、月海上に浮べり。極浦の浪を分け、鹽に引かれて行船は、半天の雲 に泝る。 日數歴れば、都は既に山川程を隔て、雲井の餘所にぞ成にける。 遙々來ぬと思ふにも、唯盡ぬ者は涙なり。 浪の上に白き鳥のむれゐるを見給ひては、彼ならん、在原のなにがしの隅田川にて言問ひけん、名も睦敷き都鳥にやと哀也。 壽永二年七月二十五日に、平家都を落果ぬ。

div.p: [8.1.1] 壽永二年七月廿四日夜半許、法皇は按察使大納言資方卿の子息右馬頭資時ばかり御伴にて、竊かに御所を出させ給ひ、鞍馬へ御幸なる。 鞍馬寺僧ども、「是は猶都近くて惡う候なん」と申間篠の峯藥王坂など云ふ嶮き嶮難を凌がせ給て、横川の解脱谷寂場坊御所になる。 大衆起て、「東塔へこそ御幸在べけれ。 」と申ければ、東塔の南谷圓融房御所になる。 かゝりしかば、衆徒も武士も、圓融房を守護し奉る。 法皇は仙洞を出でて天台山に、主上は鳳闕を去て西海へ、攝政殿は芳野の奧とかや。 女院宮々は、八幡、賀茂、嵯峨、太秦、西山、東山の片邊りに附て、迯隱させ給へり。 平家は落ぬれど、源氏は未だ入替らず。 既に此京は主なき里にぞ成にける。 開闢より以來、かゝる事あるべしともおぼえず。 聖徳太子の未來記にも、今日の事こそ床しけれ。

[8.1.2] 法皇天台山に渡せ給と聞えさせ給しかば、馳參らせ給ふ人々、其比の入道殿と申は、前關白松殿、當殿とは近衞殿、太政大臣、左右大臣、内大臣、大納言、中納言、宰相、三位、四位、五位の殿上人、すべて世に人とかぞへられ、官加階に望をかけ、所帶所職を帶する程の人の、一人も漏るは無りけり。 圓融房には、餘りに參りつどひて、堂上堂下門外門内、隙はさまなく充々たる。 山門繁昌門跡の面目とこそ見えたりけれ。
[8.1.3] 同廿八日に法皇都へ還御なる。 木曾五萬餘騎にて守護し奉る。 近江源氏山本の冠者義高、白旗差て先陣に供奉す。 此二十餘年見えざりつる白旗の、今日始めて都へ入る、珍しかりし事共なり。

[8.1.4] 去程に十郎藏人行家、宇治橋を渡て都へ入る。 陸奧新判官義康が子、矢田判官代義清、大江山を經て上洛す。 攝津國河内の源氏共雲霞の如くに同く都へ亂入る。 凡京中には源氏の勢充々たり。 勘解由小路中納言經房卿、檢非違使別當左衞門督實家院の殿上の簀子に候て、義仲行家を召す。 木曾は赤地の錦の直垂に、唐綾威の鎧著て、いか物作の太刀を帶き、切斑の矢負ひ、滋籐の弓脇に挾み、甲をば脱ぎ高紐にかけて候。 十郎藏人は、紺地の錦の直垂に、緋威の鎧著て、金造りの太刀を帶き、大中黒の矢負ひ、塗籠籐の弓脇に挾み、是も甲をば脱ぎ高紐にかけ、ひざまついて候ひけり。 前内大臣宗盛公以下、平家の一族追討すべき由仰下さる。 兩人庭上に畏て承る。 各宿所のなき由を申す。 木曾は大膳太夫成忠が宿所、六條西洞院を給はる。 十郎藏人は、法住寺殿の南殿と申す萱の御所をぞ給はりける。 法皇は主上外戚の平家に取らはれさせ給て、西海の浪の上に漂はせ給ふ事を、御歎き有て、主上竝に三種の神器、都へ返入れ奉るべき由、西國へ院宣を下されたりけれども、平家用ゐ奉らず。

[8.1.5] 高倉院の皇子は、主上の外三所おはしき。 二宮をば、儲の君にし奉らんとて、平家いざなひ參らせて、西國へ落給ぬ。 三四は都にまし／＼けり。 同八月五日、法皇此宮達を迎へ寄せ參らせ給て、先三の宮の五歳に成せ給ふを、「是へ／＼」と仰ければ、法皇を見參させ給ひて大にむつがらせ給ふ間、「とう／＼」とて出し參させ給ひぬ。 其後四の宮の四歳に成せ給ふを、「是へ」と仰せければ少も憚らせ給はず、やがて法皇の御膝の上に參せ給ひて、世にも懷氣にぞ坐しける。 法皇御涙をはら／＼と流させ給ひて、「げにもすぞろならむ者は、か樣の老法師を見て何とてか懷氣には思ふべき。 是ぞ我實の御孫にてぞまし／＼ける。 故院の少生に少も違せ給はぬ者哉。 かゝる忘れ形見を、今迄見ざりける事よ。 」とて、御涙塞あへさせ給はず。 淨土寺の二位殿、其時は未丹後殿とて御前に候はせ給ふが、「さて御讓は此宮にてこそ渡らせおはしまし候はめ。 」と申させ給へば、法皇「仔細にや。 」とぞ仰ける。 内々御占のありしにも、「四宮位に即せ給ひてば、百王迄も日本國の御主たるべし。 」とぞ勘へ申ける。

[8.1.6] 御母儀は七條修理大夫信隆卿の御娘なり。 建禮門院の未だ中宮にてまし／＼ける時其御方に宮仕給ひしを、主上常は召れける程に、うち續き宮あまた出來させ給へり。 信隆卿、御娘餘たおはしければ、如何にもして女御后にもなしたてまつらばやとねがはれけるに、人の家に白い鷄を千飼つれば、其家に必ず后出來たると云ふ事有りとて、鷄の白いを千そろへて飼はれたりける故にや、此御娘皇子數多生參せ給へり。 信隆卿内々うれしうは思はれけれども、平家にも憚り、中宮にも恐れ參せて、もてなし奉る事もおはせざりしを、入道相國の北方八條の二位殿、「苦しかるまじ、我育て參せて、儲の君にして奉らむ。 」とて、御乳母共あまた附て、そだて參せ給ひけり。

[8.1.7] 中にも四宮は、二位殿の兄法勝寺執行能圓法師の養君にてぞ坐ける。 法印平家に具せられて、西國へ落し時、餘りに遽噪いで、北方をも宮をも京都に棄置參せて下られたりしが、西國より急ぎ人を上せて、「女房宮具し參せて、よく／＼くだり給べし。 」と申されたりければ、北方斜ならず悦び、宮いざなひ參せて、西の七條なる處まで出られたりしを、女房の兄紀伊守教光、「是は物の附て狂給ふか。 此宮の御運は唯今開かせ給はんずる者を。 」とて、取留參せたりける次の日ぞ、法皇より御迎の車參りたりける。 何事も然べき事と申ながら四宮の御爲には、紀伊守教光は奉公の人とぞ見えたりける。 されども四宮位に即せ給ひて後、其情をも思召し出でさせ給はず、朝恩もなくして年月を送けるが、せめて思ひの餘りにや二首の歌を詠うで、禁中に落書をぞしたりける。

lg.l: 一聲は思ひ出てなけほとゝぎす、老蘇の森の夜半の昔を。
籠の内も猶羨まし山がらの、身のほどかくす夕顏の宿。

div.p: [8.1.8] 主上是を叡覽あて「あな無慚や、されば未だ世に長らへてありけるな。 今日まで是を思召寄らざりけるこそ愚なれ。 」とて、朝恩蒙り、正三位に敍せられけるとぞ聞えし。
